James  River. 

U.  S.  Flagship  Minnesota, 

Hampton  Roads,  November  15,  1861. 

Sir-  Two  pungies,  or  boats,  descended  the  James  River  m  company 
a  few  days  since!  One  had  a  white  flag  flying.  On  being  boarded  by 
a  boat  from  the  Cumberland  four  white  men  were  found  as  their  crews, 
and  all,  I  suppose,  were  fishermen.  Two  of  them  were  provided  with 
passes  from  the  insurgent  authorities  permitting  them  to  supply  Rich¬ 
mond,  etc.,  with  fish  out  of  the  James  River,  and  m  this  business,  it 
seems,  they  had  been  engaged  for  some  time  past.  They  wanted,  they 
said  to  get  back  to  their  homes  in  Maryland,  and  seemed  to  think, 
from  what  I  gather,  that  they  had  been  engaged  m  an  innocent  business. 

One  had  quite  a  large  sum  of  money  about  him— some  500  and  odd 
dollars — and  another  had  a  smaller  sum,  all  of  which  is  in  charge  of  the 
pavmaster  of  the  Cumberland.  The  men  are  retained  on  board  that 
ship  by  my  orders  as  prisoners,  and  I  beg  to  ask  if  I  may  send  them  to 

Boston  in  the  Release. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

L.  M.  Goldsborougii, 

Flag-Officer.

H.  S.  Flagship  Minnesota, 

Hampton  Roads,  November  15,  1861. 

Sir  :  In  answer  to  your  communication  of  yesterday,  I  send  you  here¬ 
with  a  copy  of  a  report*  just  received  from  an  officer  whom  I  dispatched 
immediately  on  getting  your  communication  to  make  a  reconnoissance 
in  and  about  York  Biver. 


In  ieply  to  your  note  of  to-day,  I  have  to  say  that  I  have  ordered  a 
vessel  to  go  off  York  Biver  and  guard  it  carefully  until  further  orders 
and  another  to  do  the  same  thing  off  Cherrystone  Inlet. 

TVitli  two  vessels  off  the  Bappaliannock,  one  off  York  Biver  the 
lower  Potomac  well  supplied,  and  Cherrystone  Inlet  guarded,  it  is 
hardly  probable  that  the  enemy  can  get  either  men  or  arms  over  from 
the  western  to  the  eastern  shore  of  Virginia.  Besides  the  above  ves¬ 
sels,  I  have  a  steamer  guarding  the  Chesapeake,  lying  generally  between 
Lynn  Haven  Bay  and  the  eastern  shore  of  Virginia,  but  keeping  a  good 
lookout  in  all  directions.  I  can  make  no  better  disposition  of  the  force 
available  under  my  control.  I  have  a  letter  from  General  Dix,  inform¬ 
ing  me  that  a  sloop  had  left  the  eastern  for  the  western  shore  of  Virginia 
to  procure  rifled  guns.  Every  necessary  order  has  been  given  with 
regard  to  her.

General:  I  have  two  vessels  off  the  moutb  of  the  Rappahannock

York  River.  The  lower  Potomac  is  abundantly  supplied  with  them.

insurgents  in  boats  or  vessels  will  be  likely  to  get  safely  over  from  the 
western  to  the  eastern  shore  of  Virginia.  May  I  add  that  if  1  could 
have  received  earlier  intelligence  of  the  contemplated  movement  of 
your  troops,  I  should  perhaps  have  been  better  prepared  at  this  moment 
to  second  them.  As  it  is,  I  shall  do  my  best,  and  upon  this  you  may 
depend. 

With  great  respect,  yours,  most  truly,

Instructions  from  Flag-Officer  Goldsborough ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding 

A  orth  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  to  Commander  Smith,  U.  S.  Navy, 

commanding  U.  S.  ship  Congress ,  regarding  use  of  night  signals. 

IT.  S.  Flagship  Minnesota, 

Hampton  Roads ,  November  18,  1861. 

Sir:  You  are  aware  that  the  regular  signals  of  our  Navy  are  not 
allowed  on  board  any  of  the  vessels  of  the  squadron  except  the  regular 
men-of-war. 

The  threatened  attack,  if  made  at  all,  will,  in  all  probability,  be 
made  upon  you  at  night,  and  a  few  night  signals  may  be  necessary. 
I  therefore  wish  to  suggest  to  you  that  it  would  be  well  to  give  in 
manuscript  a  few  of  the  numbers,  with  their  meaning,  out  of  the  book 
(such  only  as  will  be  likely  to  be  wanted  at  night)  to  the  Lockivood  aud 
Shawsheen ;  to  furnish  both  vessels  with  Coston’s  signals,  and  then  to 
exercise  all  the  vessels  once  or  twice,  to  be  sure  that  everything  will  be 
understood,  giving  to  the  general  on  shore  notice  of  your  intention,  so 
as  not  to  create  unnecessary  disturbance  in  his  camp. 

There  are  several  sets  of  Costou’s  signals  on  board  the  Congress ; 
some  of  long  duration  and  some  of  short.  The  latter  will  answer  well 
for  a  distance  not  exceeding  4  or  5  miles;  the  former  can  be  distinctly 
made  out  at  a  distance  of  even  10  miles. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Flag-  Officer. 

Commander  Wm.  Smith, 

Commanding  U.  S.  S\  hip)  Congress.

Instructions  of  Flag-Officer  Goldsborough,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  North 
Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  to  Commander  Smith,  U.  S.  Navy,  com¬ 
manding  U.  S.  ship  Congress,  regarding  the  preparation  of  the  vessels 
under  his  command  for  the  threatened  attack  of  the  enemy. 

U.  S.  Flagship  Minnesota, 

Hampton  Roads ,  November  18,  1861. 
Sir  :  I  send  you  the  Hetzel  to-day  to  assist  against  the  enemy  when¬ 
ever  he  may  venture  to  carry  into  effect  his  threatened  attack.  Like 
almost  every  other  small  steamer  that  comes  to  my  orders,  she  needs 
some  slight  repairs,  such  as  calking  of  sponsons,  adjustment  of  parts 


440 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


of  engine,  etc.  Have  these  things  done,  if  you  please,  without  delay, 
and  let  your  carpenters  and  other  mechanics  assist  in  doing  the  work. 
They  are  not,  however,  of  a  character  to  prevent  the  vessel  from  per¬ 
forming  fighting  service  at  Newport  News  at  any  moment,  and  the 
repairs  must  be  carried  on  in  such  a  way  as  not  to  disqualify  her  foi 
prompt  service  of  the  sort.  I  will  thank  you  to  inform  me  when  they 
are  all  as  well  completed  as  they  can  be.  As  a  matter  of  course,  all  the 
vessels  now  at,  or  that  may  be  sent  to  Newport  News  are  to  act  under 
your  orders,  and  you  will  make  all  your  arrangements  accordingly, 
in  your  judgment  necessary,  have  mechanics  detailed  from  the  Cumber¬ 
land ,  or  any  other  vessel  composing  your  force,  to  assist  in  doing  the 
repairs  of  the  Iletzel,  for  I  wish  them,  I  repeat,  to  be  finished  as  early 
as  practicable.  Let  me  know  in  time  when  coal  will  be  wanted,  and  I 
will  send  a  schooner  load  of  it  up  to  you.  If  you  think  it  best,  1  will 
do  so  at  once.  As  for  provisions,  you  can  supply  the  steamers  with 
them  from  either  your  ship  or  the  Cumberland,  or  from  both ;  and  a,s  loi 
water,  each  vessel  surely  can  get  it  for  herself  at  or  about  the  landing. 
Should'  there  be  a  deficiency  of  men  on  board  any  of  the  steamers,  make 
it  good,  temporarily,  with  the  supernumeraries  you  have  at  hand  on 
board  the  Congress  and  Cumberland ,  or  rather  by  using  them  in  such 
numbers  as  you  may  judge  expedient.  In  short,  make  the  best  arrange¬ 
ment  you  can  in  any  way  to  secure  the  most  successful  results,  to  cap¬ 
ture  every  vessel  of  the  enemy  that  may  present  herself,  if  possible. 
I  beg  that  every  precaution  may  be  taken  to  guard  against  effects  of 
incendiary  vessels,  for  these,  I  am  assured,  the  enemy  intend  to  use. 
Your  idea  of  a  length  made  up  of  chain  and  rope,  with  a  grapnel  at 
the  chain  end  and  a  kedge  at  the  rope  one,  strikes  me  very  favorably, 
and  each  vessel  should  be  provided  with  the  apparatus  and  prepared 
to  use  it  promptly.  Grapnels,  if  needed,  can  readily  be  made  by  your 
armorers  in  a  very  simple  way.  We  have  none  to  spare  hereabouts. 
I  will  endeavor  to  visit  you  before  long,  but  at  present  I  am  hourly 
expecting  to  be  called  to  Washington  on  important  public  business. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Flag-  Officer. 

Commander  Wi.  Smith,

Report  of  Lieutenant  Braine ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  8.  8.  Monti- 
cello,  of  a  slight  engagement  with  a  mashed  battery  near  New  Inlet, 
North  Carolina,  November  18,  1861. 

U.  S.  S.  Monticello, 
Hampton  Roads,  December  8 ,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  that  on  the  morning  of  the  18th 
November,  while  reconnoitering  near  New  Inlet,  North  Carolina,  a 
masked  battery  opened  fire  upon  us,  which  we  promptly  returned. 
After  firing  three  shots  the  battery  ceased  firing.  Knowing  it  was  not 
the  object  of  the  blockading  vessels  to  engage  land  batteries,  I  also 
ceased  firing  and  drew  off.  A  few  days  after  some  contrabands  came 
off  to  the  ship.  From  them  I  learned  that  we  dismounted  one  of 
their  guns. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

D.  L.  Braine, 
Lieutenant,  Commanding. 

Flag-Officer  L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Commanding  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Flag-Officer  Goldsborough,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  North 

Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  of  the  arrival  at  Hampton  Roads  of 

the  TJ.  S.  steamers  Hetzel  and  Rhode  Island  and  the  Spanish  bark 

Providencia. 

U.  S.  Flagship  Minnesota, 

Hampton  Roads,  November  18,  1861. 

Sir:  The  Hetzel  arrived  here  yesterday  afternoon  and,  as  usual  with 
all  the  small  steamers  that  come  here,  with  a  long  list  of  complaints 
about  condition.  I  have  ordered  her  to  be  fixed  up  immediately  by  our 
own  mechanics. 

The  Rhode  Island  arrived  here  last  night  from  the  south,  and  left 
again  this  morning  for  New  York. 

The  Spanish  bark  Providencia  reached  here  a  few  days  ago,  and  sailed 
this  morning  for  New  York,  to  be  given  up  to  the  Spanish  consul  there. 
This  is  the  vessel  about  which  I  have  already  written  to  the  Depart¬ 
ment — the  one  whose  mate  and  papers  were  brought  here  by  the  Monti- 
cello  and  which  was  subsequently  seized  by  the  Alabama  because  she 
had  not  those  papers  on  board.! 

Commander  Sartori,  unfortunately,  ordered  her  to  be  brought  in  here, 
instead  of  sending  her  at  once  to  New  York,  where  she  professed  to  be 
bound. 

I  have  already  called  the  attention  of  the  commander  of  the  Cam¬ 
bridge  to  the  manner  he  is  said  to  have  treated  English  subjects  taken 
out  of  vessels  seized  for  violating  our  blockade,  and  so  soon  as  I  get  his 
written  statement  upon  the  subject  I  will  forward  it  to  the  Department. 

Bespectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Flag-  Officer. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

at  anchor  the  leak  is  very  little,  and  when  the  water  shall  be  smooth

A  few  days  since  a  shot  was  thrown  from  Pig  Point  which  tell  within

gun  and  bill  ports,  which  I  do  not  think  will  be  any  injury  to  the  ship. 
I  have  no  doubt  that  before  she  makes  another  cruise  she  will  be  altered 
to  carry  pivot  guns.  With  our  present  armament,  should  the  enemy’s 
steamers  stand  off  at  long  shot,  we  should  only  be  a  good  target  for 
them,  as  none  of  our  guns  could  throw  a  shot  to  them. 

We  can  muster  six  rifled  cannon  among  the  shipping,  and  there  are 
two  at  camp.  The  enemy’s  steamers  I  think  will  muster  twelve. 

Will  you  please  inform  me  what  disposition  is  to  be  made  of  the  three

Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  to  Lieutenant  Murray,  U.  S.  Navy,

island  of  Chincoteague. 

U.  S.  Flagship  Minnesota, 

Hampton  Roads,  November  18,  1861. 
Sik  :  I  send  you  by  the  sloop  Granite  the  provisions  you  required, 
and  as  soon  as  you  have  taken  them  on  board  I  wish  you  to  send  her 
back  to  me,  as  I  need  her  services  here  particularly. 

I  will  send  you  at  an  early  day  authority  to  allow  some  of  the  inhab¬ 
itants  of  the  island  of  Chincoteague,  under  prescribed  conditions,  to 
carry  their  oysters  to  Philadelphia  and  New  York  and  to  bring  back 
in  return  articles  necessary  for  support  and  comfort.  Printed  forms  will 
be  given  to  you  concerning  the  matter,  and  these  you  will  be  directed 
to  use  at  your  discretion. 

It  is  my  intention  to  send  a  steamer  to  your  relief  in  the  course  of  a 
short  time,  or  rather  as  soon  as  I  can  avail  of  one  suitable  for  the  pur¬ 
pose.  Can  one  drawing  11  or  12  feet  answer?  Inform  me  what  draft 
of  water  there  is  around  and  about  the  inlet. 

There  is  a  man  by  the  name  of  Francis  Johnson  living  at  a  place 
called  Nashville,  Accomac  County,  mouth  of  Swan’s  Gut  Creek,  with 
whom  you  can,  perhaps,  put  yourself  in  communication  to  advantage. 
He  can  and  will  afford  valuable  in  formation*  about  everything  in  Acco¬ 
mac.  Although  he  talks  secession  sentiments,  yet  he  is  in  reality  a 
thorough  Fniou  man.  He  is  a  German  by  birth,  is  very  intelligent, 
speaks  several  languages  (but  English  only  indifferently)  well.  He  has 
been  already  directed  to  present  himself  on  board  of  you  whenever  you 
may  require  him  to  do  so.

He  is  about  5  feet  10  inches  high,  slim,  grayish  eyes,  brown  hair,  and 
perhaps  30  years  of  age. 

I  a  in  satisfied  that  you  can  trust  him.  Accomac  is  to  be  invaded 
to-day  by  several  thousand  of  our  troops— some  4,000  or  5,000. 

Let  me  know  if  you  are  again  in  want  of  coal. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,

Consulate  of  the  United  States  of  America, 

London,  November  1,  1861. 

Sir:  The  iron  screw  steamer  Gladiator  has  been  purchased  by  the 
Confederates  and  is  now  in  the  Thames  loading  with  arms  and  ammu¬ 
nition,  and  those  who  control  her  here  say  she  can  and  will  run  the 


444  NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

blockade.  She  is  about  700  tons,  a  good,  fast  vessel,  and  will  take  out 
a  very  valuable  cargo,  mostly  real  Enfield  rifles,  powder,  cartndges^ 
caps,  shells,  etc.  Sbe  will  be  full,  and  yet  not  be  able  to  take  out  one- 
half  the  cargo  they  have  prepared  for  her.  Sbe  will  be  followed  by  a 
clipper  bark  with  the  balance. 

The  Gladiator  will  sail  by  the  middle  of  next  week,  perhaps  earlier. 
Sbe  is  entered  outward  for  Nassau,  and  will  sail  under  British  papers 
and  colors.  But  this  is  for  her  protection  only,  as  she  has  been  sold 
to  the  Confederates,  and  their  purpose  is  to  get  her  into  one  of  the 
Southern  ports.  On  this  you  may  rely.  As  she  will  be  on  the  Ameri¬ 
can  coast  by  the  time  the  several  blockading  forces  can  be  warned  of 
her  approach,  not  a  moment  is  to  be  lost  in  preparing  to  receive  her. 

I  can  have  all  the  particulars  of  her  cargo,  but  not  in  time  for  this 
week’s  steamer.  But  it  will  be  larger  and  more  valiiable  than  that  of 
the  Fingal.  I  will  try  to  see  her  and  send  a  description  by  mail,  via 
Queenstown,  to-morrow  evening. 

She  is  iron,  like  the  Bermuda  and  Fingal ,  but  neither  is  iron  plated. 

The  ship  Alexander ,  Captain  Brown,  of  Portsmouth,  Va.,  of  about 
GOO  tons,  is  loading  at  Bristol  with  salt,  etc.,  and  she  will  be  got  into  a 
Southern  port  if  possible. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  your  obedient  servant, 

F.  H.  Morse, 

Consul, 

Hon.  Wm,  H.  Seward, 

Secretary  of  State. 


Consulate  of  the  United  States  of  America, 

London ,  November  2 ,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  just  returned  from  a  short  trip  down  the  river  to  see  the 
Confederate  steamer  Gladiator.  She  is  an  iron  screw  boat,  with  a 
round  stern,  flush  deck,  upright  stem,  no  figure  or  billet  head,  bottom 
painted  copper  colored,  black  from  water  to  rail.  She  has  three  masts, 
with  three  yards  on  the  foremast;  smoke  pipe  between  the  fore  and 
main  masts.  She  is  a  fine  looking  vessel  and  is  taking  in  cargo  rapidly, 
and  will  sail  about  next  Tuesday.  She  will  take  out  a  large  quantity 
of  Enfield  rifles,  besides  ammunition,  clothing,  etc. 

As  she  has  been  purchased  and  is  without  any  question,  notwith¬ 
standing  her  British  papers,  a  rebel  ship,  1  wish  we  had  a  vessel  here 
to  send  out  for  her. 

I  send  a  description  more  in  detail.  I  judge  she  will  draw  about  12 
feet  of  water  when  loaded. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  your  obedient  servant, 

F.  H.  Morse, 

Consul. 

Hon.  Wm.  H.  Seward, 

Secretary  of  State.

Report  of  Flag-Officer  Goldsborough ,  U.  8.  Navy ,  commanding  North 

Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  of  the  arrival  at  Hampton  Roads  from 

New  1  ork,  of  the  TJ.  8.  vessels  Whitehead ,  Isaac  N.  Seymour ,  and  Morse. 

U.  S.  Flagship  Minnesota, 
Hampton  Roads ,  Virginia ,  November  20 ,  1861. 

Sir  :  The  propeller  Whitehead ,  tug  Isaac  N.  Seymour ,  and  ferryboat 
Morse  have  all  reached  here  in  safety  from  New  York.  No  appoint¬ 
ments  were  given  to  their  engineers  there,  nor,  indeed,  were  any  per¬ 
manent  arrangements  made  with  them.  They  were  told,  it  seems,  that 
everything  of  this  sort  would  be  fixed  here.  As  they  are  all  repre¬ 
sented  to  me  as  good,  sober,  and  capable  men,  I  shall  take  the  liberty 
of  conferring  upon  them  acting  appointments  as  second  and  third 
assistants,  subject  to  the  approval  of  the  Department. 

The  captain  of  the  ferryboat  is  very  strongly  recommended  to  me  as 
a  first-rate  man  for  the  situation,  an  excellent  coast  pilot,  and  long 
accustomed  to  the  management  of  vessels  of  this  kind.  His  looks 
certainly  confirm  in  a  striking  degree  the  praises  lavished  upon  him. 
I  propose  to  appoint  him  an  acting  master,  subject  to  the  approval  of 
the  Department.  He  has  a  young  man  with  him  also  well  recommended 
for  his  sobriety,  intelligence,  and  skill  in  running  ferryboats,  and  his 
services  on  board  of  her  I  propose  to  secure  by  appointing  him  a  mas¬ 
ter’s  mate,  subject,  likewise,  to  the  approval  of  the  Department. 

Neither  of  these  vessels  is  armed.  I  intend,  however,  to  put  two 
9  inch  guns  on  board  the  ferryboat,  and  for  the  present,  one  32-pounder 
on  board  each  of  the  others,  as  soon  as  I  can  have  them  suitably  pre¬ 
pared  for  the  purpose. 

I  have  detailed  Masters  Wells  and  French,  of  this  ship,  to  command 
the  Isaac  N.  Seymour  and  Whitehead ,  respectively. 

The  firemen  and  coal  heavers  who  came  around  in  these  vessels,  and 
who  are  disposed  to  remain  by  them,  I  intend  to  enlist  regularly. 

In  all  our  public  vessels,  however  small  or  transiently  employed,  it 
is,  I  find,  absolutely  indispensable  to  good  order  and  discipline  to  have 
a  suitable  naval  organization.  Otherwise  confusion  and  trouble  are 
constantly  occurring. 

As  early  as  possible  I  will  advise  the  Department  of  the  appoint¬ 
ments  mentioned. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Flag-  Officer. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  I).  C.

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Humphrey,  U.  S.  Navy,  command¬ 
ing  U.  S.  S.  Young  Rover,  of  affairs  in  York  River ,  Virginia. 

U.  S.  Steam  Bark  Young  Rover, 
Chesapeake  Bay,  off  York  River,  November  20,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  hi  accordance  with  your  order 
the  Young  Rover  left  Hampton  Roads  on  Friday,  the  15th  instant,  at 
11:30  a.  m.,  for  the  mouth  of  York  River.  During  the  afternoon  of 
that  day,  the  wind  being  strong  from  the  north  and  the  tide  running 
ebb,  made  but  little  headway,  and  at  11  p.  m.  came  to  anchor,  Old 
Point  bearing  S.  W.  by  S. 

On  Saturday,  16th,  blew  with  violence  from  N.  N.  W.,  so  much  so, 
did  not  get  underway. 

On  Sunday,  the  17th,  at  7  a.  m.,  commenced  getting  underway,  wind 
fresh  from  N.  W.  At  11  a.  m.  stood  in  to  the  northward  of  York  Spit, 
intending  to  anchor  so  as  to  command  the  mouth  of  York  River  and 
Mobjack  Bay,  but  afterwards  decided  to  stand  off  up  the  bay  and 
return  and  anchor  after  dark.  At  2:30  p.  m.,  while  standing  inshore, 
heading  W.  S.  W.  by  the  wind  toward  a  schooner  at  anchor  close  under 
the  land,  struck  the  bottom.  Laid  the  topsails  to  the  mast,  reversed 
engine,  and  came  off  without  damage.  The  pilot  at  the  time  was  stand¬ 
ing  by  the  leadsman,  who  had  just  called  5  fathoms.  Soon  after  get¬ 
ting  off,  the  schooner  got  underway  and  stood  on  up  the  bay.  Bore  up 
and  ran  down  and  at  6:30  came  to  anchor,  New  Point  Comfort  light¬ 
house  beariug  N.  N.  W.,  distant  21  miles. 

Monday,  the  18th.— Wind  fresh  from  N.  W. ;  continued  at  anchor. 
The  boiler  having  sprung  a  leak  over  the  furnace,  was  compelled  to 
draw  the  fire  to  stop  the  leak.  At  11:30  p.  m.  a  boat  came  alongside 
containing  a  white  man  calling  himself  William  Hudgins,  and  having 
a  pass  to  that  effect  purporting  to  be  signed  by  William  W.  Lamb, 
mayor  of  Norfolk,  dated  November  15.  He  states  that  he  was  born 
near  New  Point  Comfort  light- house;  has  a  family;  has  been  employed 
in  the  Gosport  [Norfolk]  navy  yard  nine  years  as  a  carpenter;  that  he 
was  suspected  of  being  a  Union  man ;  that  he  had  been  trying  to  get 
away  some  time;  that  yesterday,  when  crossing  Mobjack  Bay  from 
Severn  River,  he  saw  the  ship  lying  at  anchor,  and  after  dark  he  stole 
a  boat  and  came  off.  He  says  his  wife  has  a  son  on  board  the  Cumber¬ 
land,  William.  Oakley.  I  questioned  him  in  regard  to  the  Merrimack. 
He  thinks  she  will  not  be  ready  this  winter;  that  they  are  just  putting- 
iron  gratings  over  the  roof.  At  Gloucester  Point,  he  says,  there  are  a 
great  many  troops,  but  he  did  not  hear  of  any  movement  to  be  made 
across  the  bay.  He  saw  eight  or  ten  boats  there  of  35  or  40  tons  burden. 
The  York  Spit  light  boat  and  a  sloop  are  fitting  out  as  privateers.  He 
also  heard  some  talk  of  a  mail  boat  running  twice  a  week  across  the 
bay. 

Tuesday,  the  19th. — Wind  fresh  from  N.  W.  to  N. ;  continued  at  anchor. 
Saw  several  small  sloops  and  schooners  in  Mobjack  Bay  and  York  River. 

Wednesday,  20th. — 9  a.  m.  got  underway  and  steamed  up  Mobjack 
Bay  to  the  mouth  of  Severn  River.  Saw  one  schooner  and  one  sloop 
run  across  from  Severn  River  to  East  River.  Fired  one  shot  at  the 
schooner,  but  the  water  being  so  shoal  could  not  get  near  enough  to 
reach  her.  At  4 : 30  anchored,  New  Point  light-house  bearing  N.  by  W., 
distant  3£  miles. 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  447 

Thursday ,  the  21st. — The  steam  tug  Young  America ,  has  just  come 
alongside,  bound  to  Hampton  Roads,  and  I  avail  myself  of  the  oppor¬ 
tunity  to  send  the  deserter  from  Norfolk. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  Humphrey, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Commanding.

[Enclosure.] 

Consulate  of  the  United  States  of  America, 

London,  October  26,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  regard  it  my  duty  to  report  to  you  that  the  Confederates  con¬ 
tinue  very  active  in  this  country  and  are  collecting  material  of  war  at 
various  points  for  shipment.  Of  Enfield  rifles  they  have  thousands 
now  ready  for  shipment,  and  have  all  the  armories  here  at  work  for 
them.  With  these  and  what  they  are  getting  at  Birmingham  they 
must  be  receiving  not  far  from  1,500  per  week.  We  can  not,  with 
the  means  at  our  disposal,  get  on  the  track  and  follow  to  vessels  all 
their  shipments,  for  they  adopt  every  possible  expedient  to  deceive  us. 
A  direct  shipment  is  rarely  made.  All  their  goods  move  about  the 
country  from  point  to  point,  and  are  generally  transshipped  even 
before  they  leave  the  country  But  you  may  rely  on  the  fact  that  large 
quantities  of  all  kinds  frequently  leave  this  country  for  the  rebel 
States,  and  every  measure  that  promises  the  least  hope  of  success  will 
be  resorted  to  to  get  them  in. 

I  learned  last  evening  that  the  same  house  that  negotiated  the  condi¬ 
tional  sale  of  the  Victoria  and  Adelaide  are  in  treaty  for  war  steamers 
belonging  to  the  East  India  Company.  It  is  said  they  are  intended 
for  the  Confederates.  The  steamers  Victoria  and  Adelaide  are  still 
undergoing  repairs  here. 

I  had  the  honor  of  receiving  your  dispatch  informing  me  that  orders 
sufficiently  extensive  had  been  sent  to  this  country  to  absorb  all  the 
Enfield  rifles  that  can  be  made  in  this  country  for  the  coming  two  years, 
except  such  as  are  made  for  the  English  Government.  Permit  me  to 
say,  with  all  becoming  respect  and  deference,  that  this  liberality  will 
not  secure  what  we  desire  unless  conducted  differently.  When  I  came 
to  this  country,  realizing  what  our  wants  must  soon  be  for  arms,  I  lost 
no  time  in  making  myself  pretty  thoroughly  acquainted  with  the  gun 
trade  of  this  country — the  capacity  of  the  several  armories,  the  quality 
of  the  arms  turned  out  by  each,  their  prices,  mode  of  inspection  when 
sold  to  others  besides  the  British  Government,  etc.  I  had  unusual 
facilities  for  acquainting  myself  with  [the]  question  and  thought  it  my 
duty  to  improve  it. 

After  the  battle  of  Bull  Run  I  felt  so  thoroughly  impressed  with  the 
idea  that  the  Enfield  rifle  would  be  largely  called  for  that  I  very 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  449 


quietly,  through  Mr.  McFarland,  the  Massachusetts  agent  for  the  pur¬ 
chase  of  arms  here,  an  engineer  and  practical  gnnmaker,  and  without 
being  known  in  the  transaction  myself,  obtained  the  best  offer  I  could 
from  all  the  armories  here,  and  from  the  directors  of  the  gun  trade  at 
Birmingham,  for  all  the  thoroughly  inspected  guns  they  could  dispose 
of  for  the  then  coming  four  or  six  months. 

When  Mr.  Shyler  first  came  here  we  had  everything  ready  and  held 
the  written  offers  from  all  the  responsible  and  best  makers  in  this 
country  at  65s.  (sterling)  each.  Mr.  S.  did  [not]  feel  authorized  to  take 
charge  of  the  matter  and  close  the  contracts,  and  consequently 
the  supply  from  this  city  has  gone  into  Southern  hands,  the  agents  of 
the  Confederates  then  standing  ready  to  take  them  at  66s. 

At  Birmingham  several  persons,  all  pretending  to  be  purchasing  for 
theU.  S.  Government,  are  bidding  against  each  other,  and  have  run 
up  the  price  of  rifles,  which  receive  only  a  nominal  inspection  and  some 
none  at  all,  from  60  up  to  75  and  80s.  (sterling)  each,  and  not  as  many 
guns  are  made  there  now  as  when  they  were  sold  at  60s.  each,  and  of  far 
better  quality  then  than  now,  owing  to  more  frequent  strikes  of  work¬ 
men,  and  there  being  much  inferior  quality  of  materials  now  used  there. 
The  Confederates  are  getting  the  same  guns  at  Birmingham,  but  not 
enough  to  disturb  the  market.  The  price  has  been  run  up  entirely  by 
those  claiming  to  be  the  agents  of  Government  and  by  parties  from  New 
York,  buying  on  speculation.  The  only  remedy  for  this  bad  state  of 
things  is  for  the  Government  to  refuse  to  have  anything  to  do  with 
speculators  and  put  its  own  business  all  into  the  hands  of  one  com¬ 
petent  man,  and  then  we  should  get  more  guns  than  now,  of  far  better 
quality,  and  for  at  least  10s.  less  on  each  gun.  Could  our  Government 
do  this,  and  have  each  gun  thoroughly  inspected  here,  guns  would 
fall  in  one  week  to  60s.  and  be  of  better  quality  and  more  of  them  made. 

In  making  this  statement  I  trust  I  have  not  gone  beyond  the  nature 
of  my  duties.  I  see  the  evil  so  plainly,  and  it  is  working  so  disas¬ 
trously  for  us,  that  I  considered  it  my  duty  to  direct  your  attention  to 
the  question. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  sincerely,  your  obedient  servant, 

F.  H.  Morse, 

Consul. 


Hon.  Wm.  H.  Seward, 

Secretary  of  State.

Report  of  Commander  Smith,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  If.  S.  ship  Congress, _ 
of  the  shelling  by  the  U.  S.  steamers  Shaw  sheen  and  J.  L.  Lockwood  of 
a  Confederate  encampment  above  Newport  News,  Va. 


U.  S.  Frigate  Congress, 

Newport  News,  November  23,  1861. 

Sir:  Yesterday  afternoon  General  Phelps  sent  Captain  [Francis  A.] 
Silva  to  inform  me  that  a  regiment  of  Virginia  infantry  had,  within  a 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  451 

few  days  past  encamped  on  the  Yorktown  road,  a  few  miles  above  Camp 
Du  tier,  and  about  three-quarters  of  a  mile  from  the  river  bank:  that 

ley  had  no  artillery,  and  that  there  were  no  batteries  alongshore 
between  the  encampment  and  our  anchorage,  and  requested  me  to  send 
some  ot  the  small  steamers  up  the  river  as  near  as  possible  to  them 
and  shell  them  for  the  purpose  of  driving  them  from  their  present 
encampment. 

I  put  Captain  Silva  aud  the  pilot  of  the  Cumberland  on  board  the 
bhaw sheen  (as  guide  and  pilot)  and  ordered  her  and  the  Lockwood  to 
proceed  up  the  river  and  shell  the  enemy.  They  left  here  about  dusk, 
but  before  reaching  their  destination  got  aground  and  were  detained 
some  time.  Between  12  and  1  o’clock  they  reached  the  place,  which 
was  recognized  by  Captain  Silva,  who  knew  it  from  having  been  there 
occasionally  in  performing  his  duties  of  patrol,  and  they  saw  two  of  the 
enemy’s  fires,  one  a  signal  and  the  other  a  picket  fire.  They  opened 
on  the  fires  and  the  space  between  them  where  the  camp  was  supposed 
to  be,  and  gave  them  a  dozen  rounds  from  each  steamer. 

As  I  knew  from  Captain  Silva  before  they  left  that  they  would  not 
be  able  to  see  the  enemy,  and  would  have  to  fire  pretty  much  at  ran¬ 
dom,  I  had  ordered  them  not  to  expend  many  shells  on  the  enemy, 
supposing  that  a  few  would  have  the  effect  desired  by  the  general, 
to  let  them  know  that  they  were  in  a  dangerous  locality  and  that  it 
would  be  advisable  for  them  to  shift  their  quarters. 

The  boats  were  back  at  their  anchorage  at  half  past  2  o’clock  this 
morning. 

The  navigation  above  this  point  is  so  intricate  and  our  pilots  are  so 
little  acquainted  with  the  channel  that  if  the  general  again  desires  a 
similar  expedition  I  shall  have  to  decline  it,  though  anxious  to  help 
him  whenever  it  can  be  prudently  done. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  Smith, 

Commanding  TJ.  S.  Frigate  Congress. 

Flag-Officer  L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  Hampton  Roads.

Instructions  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Flag-Officer  Goldsborough, 
JJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  regard¬ 
ing  commanding  officers. 

Confidential.]  Navy  Department, 

Washington ,  November  25,  1861. 

Sir:  Since  the  efficiency  of  the  blockade  depends  in  a  great  measure 
upon  the  professional  skiil  of  each  individual  commander,  the  Depart¬ 
ment  enjoins  upon  the  flag-officers  a  vigilant  supervision  of  the  move¬ 
ments  of  each  vessel  under  their  command.  A  large  number  of  most 
efficient  steamers  are  being  pressed  to  completion,  and  the  Department 
desires  to  assign  these,  as  far  as  the  public  service  will  admit,  to  those 
officers  who  have  performed  at  sea  most  faithfully  the  duties  of  the 
blockade.  You  will  therefore  keep  the  Department  advised  of  the  rela¬ 
tive  merit  of  each  and  every  commander  attached  to  your  squadron, 
and  take  care  that  no  case  of  individual  merit,  or  the  reverse,  occurs 
without  a  full  investigation  and  report  to  the  Department. 

The  Department  also  desires  a  particular  report  relative  to  the 
officers  formerly  in  the  Navy,  and  now  serving  under  acting  appoint¬ 
ments,  and  those  now  attached  to  seagoing  vessels  who  are  on  the 
retired  list.  As  full  authority  is  given  to  the  flag-officers  to  send  home 
the  inefficient  and  apathetic,  and  make  any  changes  in  the  command¬ 
ing  officers  that  the  public  service  demands,  the  Government  will  hold 
them  responsible  for  the  efficiency  of  each  single  ship.  Rank  has  its 
merits,  but  no  consideration  will  be  given  to  it  unless  accompanied 
with  enthusiastic  devotion  to  the  suppression  of  this  rebellion  and 
professional  fidelity  to  the  duties  imposed. 

Very  respectfully,  etc., 

Gideon  Welles. 

Flag-Officer  L.  M.  Goldsboroiigh, 

Oomdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  Hampton  Roads.

IT.  S.  Frigate  Congress, 
Newport  News,  December  2,  1861. 

Sir:  This  morning  about  6  o’clock  a  rebel  steamer  (supposed  to  be 
the  Yorktown )  came  down  James  River  and  opened  fire  on  onr  steam¬ 
ers,  which  were  anchored  (as  they  have  been  at  night  for  some  time

past)  across  tlie  channel  about  a  mile  and  a  half  above  this  anchorage. 
The  fire  was  returned  by  all  of  our  steamers,  which  got  ^'derwaj ,  and 
was  kept  up  for  about  an  hour,  all  the  vessels  drifting  up  with  the  flood 
tide,  when  the  rebel  retired  and  our  steamers  returned  to  this  anchorage. 

Three  or  four  of  the  rebel  shells  fell  near  our  vessels  without  doing 
any  damage.  It  is  not  certain  that  any  of  our  shells  reached  the  enemy. 
Lieutenant  Commanding  Colhoun,  of  the  Shawsheen,  thinks  that  two  of 
his  shells  struck,  or  went  beyond  the  rebel,  as  he  did  not  see  them 
explode  or  fall  into  the  water,  and  he  had  seen  all  of  the  others  fall  or 

eXf  think  the  object  of  the  rebel  commander  was  to  ascertain  the  range 
of  our  guns;  oniy  two  of  them  could  have  reached  him. 

I  do  not  think  the  rebel  was  any  time  nearer  than  4  miles  to  either 

of  our  ships.

Letter  from  Commander  Smith,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  ship  Congress,  to  Flag-Officer 
Goldsborough,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 


U.  S.  Frigate  Congress, 

Newport  News ,  December  7 ,  1861. 

Sir:  I  return  you  the  slip  from  the  Richmond  Dispatch  which  you 
kindly  sent  me  to-day,  with  my  thanks  for  the  same.  I  don’t  think 
Commander  Tucker’s  report  does  him  any  great  credit.  Lf  took  him 
two  weeks  to  make  up  his  mind  to  come  down  to  “  surprise  and  attack 
our  steamers,  and  when  he  did  come,  the  first  shell  that  struck  his  vessel 
took  all  the  starch  out  of  him,  and  he  returned  to  his  anchorage,  u  the 
enemy  evincing  no  disposition  to  follow  him.”  He  forgot  to  tell  his 
Secretary  that  the  fioodtide  was  drifting  all  of  the  steamers  up  the 
river,  and  that  when  he  retired  from  the  contest,  they  were  2  miles 
farther  up  than  when  it  began.  If  they  did  not  get  near  enough  to 
him,  he  should  have  held  on  till  they  drifted  up. 

I  had  a  Boston  paper  which  I  wished  to  send  you,  but  it  has  been 
mislaid,  containing  a  paragraph  from  the  Richmond  Dispatch,  stating 
that  in  the  attack  made  by  the  steamers  Hetzel  and  Lockwood  on  the 
rebel  camp  above  this  place  some  nights  since,  the  rebel  loss  was  fif¬ 
teen  killed,  wounded,  and  missing.  This  was  not  so  bad,  considering 
that  the  place  was  hunted  up  in  the  night  and  fired  on,  at  a  guessed 
distance  of  about  a  mile  and  a  half.  Captain  Silva,  who  was  the  guide 
on  the  occasion,  informed  me  to-day  that  the  rebels  had  broken  up 
their  camp,  where  they  were  preparing  for  winter  quarters,  and  had 
moved  off. 

Very  respectfully  and  truly, 

W.  Smith. 


Flag-Officer  L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  Hampton  Hoads.

Report*  °f  Commander  Tucker,  C.  S.  Navy,  commanding  C.  S.  S.  Patrick  Henry. 


0.  S.  S.  Patrick  Henry, 

Off  Mulberry  Island ,  James  River ,  Va.,  December  2,  1861. 

Sir  :  Since  the  18th  of  November  the  enemy  have  accumulated  at 
Newport  News  several  small  gunboats  and  armed  tugs.  Learning  that 
they  were  in  the  habit  of  sending  several  of  these  gunboats  up  the 
river  at  night  and  withdrawing  them  in  the  morning,  induced  me  to 
take  the  first  favorable  opportunity  to  surprise  and  attack  them. 

This  morning  being  dark  and  suitable  for  the  enterprise,  I  left  our 
anchorage  off  Mulberry  Island  at  4  o’clock  a.  m.  and  proceeded  cau¬ 
tiously  down  the  river,  all  lights  carefully  concealed. 

I  regret,  however,  to  say  that  I  was  disappointed  in  not  finding  the 
steamers  as  high  up  the  river  as  I  expected. 

At  early  daylight  we  discovered  four  steamers  anchored  in  line,  this 
side  of  the  frigates,  but  in  supporting  distance  of  them  and  the  battery 
at  Newport  News. 

We  rounded  to  at  a  supposed  distance  of  a  mile  and  commenced  the 
attack  with  our  port  battery  and  pivot  guns,  which  was  returned  by 
the  steamers  and  the  battery  on  shore  from  rilled  and  other  guns.  Many 
ot  the  rifled  shells  came  near  and  over  us,  and  one  struck  us,  going- 
through  the  pilot  house  and  exploding  in  the  starboard  hammock  net¬ 
tings,  producing  slight  injury  and  wounding  one  of  the  pilots  and  a 
seaman  very  slightly  by  the  splinters. 

The  engagement  lasted  two  hours,  when  we  returned  to  our  anchor¬ 
age,  the  enemy  evincing  no  disposition  to  advance,  either  during  the 
engagement  or  afterwards.  We  expended  28  shells  and  13  solid  shot, 
some  of  which  must  have  struck,  but  with  what  injury  to  the  enemy 
we  are  unable  to  say. 


**####* 
Very  respectfully,  your  obedient. servant, 

John  R.  Tucker, 

Commander.  C.  S.  Navy. 

Hon.  S.  R.  Mallory, 

Secretary  Navy,  Richmond.

Description  of  schooner  Stephen  Hart,  of - . 

London,  November  15 ,  1861. 

It  is  a  fore-and-aft  schooner,  with  a  square  fore-topsail.  She  is  [has  a] 
full  poop,  which  runs  forward  nearly  to  the  foremast,  and  on  the  rail 
are  stanchions  and  rail,  but  no  bulwarks  on  the  poop.  She  has  much 
shear,  and  the  masts  rake  considerably.  I  should  judge  her  Baltimore 
build. 


1.  A  forward  house  for  men.  2.  Along  billet-head,  gilt.  3.  A  rail 
along  the  poop.  4.  A  boom  on  the  foot  of  fore- staysail.  5.  Are  three 
iron  bands  around  the  mast,  which  look  as  if  it  had  been  fished.  6.  The 
foresail  hauls  out  and  in  on  the  yard,  and  fails  from  deck  up  and  does 
not  furl  on  the  yard.  7.  Is  maintop-staysail.  8.  A  square  stern.  9. 
Brass  balls  on  the  mastheads.  10.  Forestay  sets  up  at  the  knight- 
heads.  11.  Main  gaff-topsail. 


Edwin  G.  Eastman.

mer  dispatch,  has  nearly  completed  her  lading  of  salt  and  blankets 
and  will  sail  in  a  few  days.  She  will  clear  for  Halifax,  but  is  certainly 
going  south.  She  is  a  ship,  1,030  tons,  and  has  a  black  hull. 

I  understand  that  two  steamers  have  left  London  within  the  last 
fortnight  with  arms  and  munitions  of  war  for  the  South,  and  that 
another  has  been  bought,  the  Antelope ,  now  in  London. 

I  understand  also  that  Mr.  Sobel  is  in  London  trying  to  sell,  it  he 
has  not  already  sold,  the  Malacca  and  Rangoon  to  the  Southern  com¬ 
missioners.  Some  time  since  Mr.  S.  told  me  these  steameis  weie  on 
their  way  to  Liverpool,  but  must  have  been  deceiving  me,  as  I  iind 
they  arrived  at  London  soon  after. 

#  #  *  *  *  *  * 

Great  anxiety  is  felt  here  for  the  results  of  the  naval  expedition,  of 
the  sailing  of  which  we  were  advised  by  last  steamer. 

*  #  #  *  *  *  * 

With  high  respect,  I  have  the  honor  to  be,  your  obedient  servant, 

H.  Wilding. 

Hon.  Wm.  H.  Seward, 

Secretary  of  State,  Washington.

used  and  can  not  be  obtained.  1  have  written  to  New  York  to  see  if 
there  is  anything  with  6 -feet  draft  not  already  purchased.  The  arrival 
of  the  Nashville  at  Southampton  has  set  everybody  upon  us  again  to 
know  who  blockaded  Charleston  on  the  12th  of  October.  W e  are  going 
to  send  the  Vermont  to  Port  Royal  as  receiving  ship.  I  am  very  much 
obliged  to  Case  for  late  Southern  papers. 

We  can  get  plenty  of  light  draft  steamers,  such  as  run  from  Balti¬ 
more  to  eastern  shore.  Will  they  be  of  any  use?  I  trust  very  soon  to 
hear  that  you  have  dealt  a  blow  second  to  none  yet  delivered.

Report  of  Commander  Glisson,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TT.  S.  S.  Mount 
Vernon,  of  assistance  rendered  to  the  American  schooner  Allen  Mid 
dleton. 

U.  S.  S.  Mount  Yernon, 

Off  Cape  Lookout,  North  Carolina,  December  7,  1861. 
Sir:  I  have  to  inform  you  that  this  morning  at  10  o’clock  I  discov¬ 
ered  a  schooner  close  in  to  the  shore  to  the  northward  of  Cape  Lookout. 
I  immediately  weighed  and  proceeded  in  chase  of  her,  and,  on  over¬ 
hauling  her,  discovered  her  to  be  the  American  schooner  Allen 
Middleton,  of  East  Greenwich,  R.  I.,  from  Providence,  R.  I.,  for  Matan- 
zas,  Cuba,  with  a  cargo  of  hoops. 

The  schooner  was  leaking  badly,  she  having  sprung  a  leak  in  the 
N.  E.  gale  of  the  2d  instant.  Her  crew  was  completely  exhausted  and 
the  captain  applied  to  me  for  assistance  to  take  his  vessel  to  Hampton 
Roads,  Virginia.  This  request  I  considered  it  to  be  my  duty  to  accede 
to.  1  therefore  ordered  James  Daley,  ordinary  seaman,  and  Charles 
Johnson,  ordinary  seaman,  of  this  vessel,  to  proceed  in  her  to  that  port 
and  to  render  such  assistance  as  might  be  required.  On  the  arrival  of 
the  schooner  at  Hampton  Roads  1  have  instructed  the  captain  to  take 
the  two  men  on  board  of  your  vessel.

The  vessels  at  this  point  are  all  well,  and  we  are  maintaining  a  rigid 
blockade  of  this  port. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

O.  S.  Glisson, 
Commander ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Flag-Officer  L.  M.  Goldsborough,

Report  of  Lieutenant  Trenchard,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Rhode 
Island,  regarding  the  detention  of  the  British  schooner  Phantom. 

G.  S.  S.  Rhode  Island, 

Off  Cape  Fear,  December  9, 1861 ■ 

Sir:  I  have  to  report  that  last  night,  when  15  miles  southeast  of 
Cape  Lookout,  falling  in  with  the  British  schooner  Phantom,  thirteen 
days  from  St.  John’s,  island  of  Antigua,  West  Indies,  upon  the  exami¬ 
nation  of  her  papers  found  that  she  had  been  boarded  the  day  before 
by  the  U.  S.  S.  Mount  Vernon,  informed  of  the  blockade,  and  warned 
off,  the  vessel’s  cargo  consisting  of  sugar  and  molasses,  and  she  had 
cleared  for  New  York.  As  the  schooner  was  some  3  miles  nearer  shore 
than  when  boarded  the  day  before  by  the  Mount  Vernon,  is  clipper  built, 
Bnd  is  evidently  a  fast  sailing  vessel,  I  deemed  it  to  be  my  duty  to  take 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


467 


her  in  tow,  proceed  with  her  off  Beaufort  (which  was  near  by)  and  con¬ 
fer  with  Captain  Glisson,  the  senior  blockading  officer  there,  as  to  her 
disposition.  After  our  arrival  at  Beaufort  this  morning,  Captain  Glis¬ 
son  and  myself  proceeded  on  board  the  Phantom ,  and  upon  arriving 
there  were  met  by  her  captain,  who  protested  against  the  seizure  of  the 
vessel  upon  the  ground  of  its  having  been  calm  from  the  time  he  had 
been  warned  off  by  the  Mount  Vernon  up  to  the  moment  that  the  schooner 
had  been  boarded  by  the  Rhode  Island,  and  upon  a  critical  examination 
of  her  log  book  it  confirmed  the  captain’s  statement.  Commander 
Glisson  then  decided  in  consequence  of  its  being  calm,  the  vessel  had 
only  changed  her  position  by  drifting  during  the  interval  that  she  had 
been  boarded  by  the  two  vessels.  He  directed  me  then  to  permit  her 
to  continue  her  voyage  to  New  York.  After  supplying  the  vessels  off 
Beaufort,  the  Rhode  Island  towed  the  Phantom  out  to  nearly  the  posi¬ 
tion  where  boarded  and  permitted  her  to  continue  her  voyage,  the 
steamer  proceeding  on  her  course  southward. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Stephen  D.  Trenchard, 

Lieutenant ,  Commanding. 

Flag-Officer  L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

[Enclosure.] 

Headquarters, 
Baltimore,  December  7, 1861.  I 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  enclose  a  letter  and  a  draft  taken  from  a 
female  passenger  in  the  steamer  from  Fort  Monroe.  They  were  quilted 
in  her  petticoat,  but  she  protested  that  she  knew  nothing  about  the 
matter.  The  draft  is  for  $564.41,  drawn  by  Joseph  Creighton  on  Messrs. 
Maclean,  Maris  &  Co.,  in  favor  of  Messrs.  J.  and  D.MacKae  &  Co.,  and 
sent  by  the  latter  for  collection. 

The  letter  discloses  some  important  facts  in  regard  to  the  blockade 
at  Wilmington,  N.  C.,  where  the  draft  was  drawn. 

I  also  enclose  a  newspaper  (the  Richmond  [sic]  of  November  29),  con¬ 
taining  a  list  of  armed  vessels  in  the  service  of  the  insurgents,  with  the 
names  of  the  officers  and  a  list  of  the  house  of  delegates  of  Virginia. 

An  intercepted  letter  of  the  11th  November  shows  that  a  mail  com¬ 
munication  has  been  established  from  Tampico  to  Matamoras,  thence 
to  Cuba  and  to  the  United  States.  This  letter  was  sent  from  Virginia 
by  that  route. 

1  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  A.  Dix, 
Major-General,

[Subenclosure.] 

Wilmington,  N.  0.,  November  21,  1861. 

Dear  Sir:  The  Bruce  arrived  September  21,  and,  after  much  oppo¬ 
sition  and  delay,  as  detailed  in  our  letters,  by  the  vessel  and  via  Tampico, 
we  have  at  last  got  her  loaded,  as  per  bill  of  lading  and  invoice  enclosed. 
The  manufacturing  and  making  of  naval  stores  having  been  entire  } 
stopped  by  the  war,  we  were  obliged,  being  unable  to  get  anything  but 
comfmerciall  rosin  at  any  reasonable  rates,  to  put  on  board  a  cargo  of  our 
own,  bought  for  a  vessel  to  arrive,  which  we  place  at  cost  to  us  and  pro¬ 
pose  to  have  you  sell  for  our  joint  account  and  risk,  placing  tliefi  eight  at 
$4,000  for  the  voyage,  which  is  [the]  rate  at  which  we  were  oneied,  and 
others  chartered  a  vessel  of  same  capacity  at  the  same  time.  The  cargo 
was  all  repacked  and  delivered  in  first-rate  order.  The  pale  rosin  was 
the  only  lot  here  and  is  equal  to  any  ever  shipped  hence.  We  regard 
this  as  better  than  taking  a  freight,  and  the  best  arrangement  possible 
under  the  circumstances,  and  trust,  as  we  doubt  not,  you  will  also  view 
it.  We  leave  you  to  effect  insurance,  and  have  filled  up  our  invoice  and 
bill  of  lading  as  your  property,  so  that  in  case  of  capture  you  can  treat 
it  as  such.  We  have  drawn  against  this  on  you  at  three  days,  favor  of 
Alex.  McRae,  payable  in  London,  for  £1,250  sterling,  being  about  one- 
half  the  cost,  and  bill  disbursements,  which  latter  goes  by  vessel,  with 
samples  rosin,  etc.  Captain  Muir  thinks  he  will  have  a  chance  to  get 
safely  to  sea  in  a  few  days,  as  the  blockade  is  very  irregular  and  inef¬ 
fectual.  A  vessel  came  in  safely  this  week.  Captain  M.has  protested, 
and  we  think  can  recover  damages  for  detention.  W e  are  so  advised  by 
the  British  consul. 

Yours,  very  respectfully, 

’  J.  AND  D.  MAORAE  &  Co. 

I  Mr.  William  Gough, 

Bristol ,  England. 

Salt,  $5  per  bushel,  $15  per  sack;  blankets,  shoes,  gray  cloths  and 
cassimeres,  pig  and  hoop  iron,  kerseys  and  military  stores,  block  tin, 
etc.,  all  very  scarce  and  command  extreme  prices.  We  would  like  a 
joint  interest  in  a  shipment  including  any  of  the  above  articles. 

Please  forward  enclosed  letter.  If  you  should  not  hear  from  us  mean¬ 
time,  when  sales  are  closed,  please  place  any  balance  to  our  credit  with

Letter  from  Brigadier- General  Burnside ,  U.  S.  Army ,  to  Flag-Officer 
Goldsborough ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading 
Squadron ,  regarding  preparations  for  the  expedition  to  Roanoke  Island, 
North  Carolina. 

Yew  York,  December  9,  1861. 

Commodore  :  By  the  direction  of  General  Burnside  I  have  the  honor 
to  say  that  since  his  letter  to  you  was  given  to  Captain  D’Wolf,  that  while 
he  leaves  the  direction  of  the  Peabody  entirely  to  you,  he  has  become 
more  of  the  opinion  that  the  secrecy  of  the  expedition  will  be  better 
preserved  by  landing  her  stores  at  Old  Point,  instead  of  Hatteras  Inlet. 
You  will  remember  that  it  was  the  original  plan  of  General  McClellan 
to  have  the  depot  at  Old  Point.  Should  it  seem  to  you  also  to  be 
advisable,  and  you  do  not  want  the  ship  at  present,  she  can  return  here 
at  once  for  another  load. 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  469 

There  are  supplies  at  Annapolis,  and  the  general  will  send  down 
immediately  to  Hatteras  Inlet  several  transports  with  stores,  and  of 
light  draft,  which  will  anchor  inside  of  the  inlet  without  its  being  known 
that  they  are  attached  to  this  expedition. 

There  are  now  ten  regiments  at  Annapolis.  The  other  five  can  be 
concentrated  there  without  delay,  and  the  transports  are  all  expected 
to  leave  here  for  Annapolis  this  week,  so  that,  in  all  probability,  by  the 
middle  of  the  next  the  force  can  be  embarked. 

This  note  will  be  handed  you  by  Lieutenant  Fearing,  aid  to  the 
general.  He  will  communicate  with  you  and  you  may  place  in  him  the 
most  implicit  confidence.  Should  there  be  any  instructions  which  you 
would  prefer  to  give  him  verbally,  have  no  hesitation  in  trusting  iiim 
fully.  As  soon  as  convenient  he  will  return  to  New  York. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Lewis  Bichmond, 
Assistant  Adjutant- General. 

[Commodore  Goldsborough, 

Old  Point  Comfort .] 


Dear  Commodore  :  Since  writing  the  above  I  have  received  your 
note.  We  have  ten  propellers  of  light  draft,  each  carrying  one  30- 
pounder  Parrott  gun  and  two  12-pounder  Wiard  rifled  guns ;  also  there 
are  five  floating  batteries,  with  from  two  to  three  12-pounder  rifled  guns 
each,  and  two  small  howitzers  each  for  shells.  The  names  I  will  send  by 
mail  to-day.  I  will  make  arrangements  for  gunners  to  take  the  places 
of  those  I  expected  from  you. 

As  to  transports,  the  Peabody ,  of  course,  is  at  your  service,  and,  if 
you  will  send  word  by  my  aid  what  additional  means  you  will  want, 
I  will  furnish  it  at  once.  Your  message  about  signals  I  will  give  to 
Hazard. 

The  Department  has  made  the  arrangements  for  coal.  We  shall  find 
it  at  the  inlet. 

The  work  here  is  going  on  with  all  possible  dispatch,  but  should  you 
think  it  better  to  start  at  once  with,  say,  5,000  or  6,000  men  and  let  the 
others  follow  soon  after,  send  word  by  my  aid  and  we  can  go  this  week. 

I  omitted  to  say  that  I  have  seven  sailing  vessels  with  one  rifled  gun 
each,  but  I  should  hardly  be  able  to  use  them  in  action. 

The  propellers  will  draw  from  6  to  8  feet  each;  the  sailing  vessels,  7 
to  9;  the  floating  batteries,  2  feet. 

Yours,  truly, 


A.  E.  Burnside. 


Commodore  Goldsborough, 

Old  Point  Comfort.

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  I  let  go  my  anchor  on  the  even¬ 
ing  of  November  7,  Too’s  Point  bearing  S.  S.  E.,  distant  1  mile. 

Friday  morning  saw  eight  schooners  just  inside  of  us,  distant  about 
3  miles,  under  the  protection  of  the  guns  on  Gloucester  Point.

Yorktown  and  Gloucester  Point  strike  about  2  miles  from  us. 

We  have  as  yet  seen  no  indications  of  the  building  of  batteries  on 

shore  on  either  side  of  us.  ...  .

Letter  from  Brigadier- General  Burnside ,  U.  S.  Army ,  to  Flag-Officer 
Goldsborough ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading 
Squadron,  transmitting  a  list  of  the  vessels  of  his  fleet. 


New  York.  December  12,  1861. 

My  Dear  Commodore:  Enclosed  I  hand  you  list  of  my  armed  ves¬ 
sels,  with  a  statement  of  their  tonnage  and  armament.  Everything 
connected  [with]  the  expedition  here  is  moving  on  rapidly,  and  I  am 
satisfied  that  the  vessels  will  all  be  off  by  the  last  of  the  week,  so  that 
by  the  first  of  the  next  I  shall  have  transportation  at  Annapolis  suffi¬ 
cient  for  my  whole  command,  from  12,000  to  15,000  men.  You  can  judge 
better  than  myself  as  to  the  time  it  will  require  to  embark  them. 

The  information  you  ask  in  reference  to  signals,  etc.,  I  give  in  Cap¬ 


tain  Hazard’s  own  words. 

In  addition  to  Blunt’s  Maritime  Signals,  which  all  of  my  vessels 
have,  each  armed  vessel  of  my  expedition  (fourteen  in  number)  will  be 
furnished  here  by  Blunt  with  a  set  of  naval  signals  as  you  wished. 
Therefore,  will  you  have  the  kindness  to  arrange  signals  for  them  in  a 
little  book  as  you  proposed? 

I  shall  leave  here  on  Saturday  night  for  Washington  and  hope  to 
meet  you  soon  after. 

Yours,  very  truly, 

A.  E.  Burnside. 


Commodore  Goldsborough,  TJ.  S.  Navy.

Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Flag-Officer  Ooldsborough ,  TJ.  S. 
Navy ,  commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  giving  infor¬ 
mation  regarding  the  blockade  rtmner  Bruce. 

Navy  Department,  December  13, 1861. 
Sir  :  I  submit  for  your  information  the  following  extract  from  a  letter 
from  a  female  passenger  in  the  steamer  from  Fort  Monroe  to  Baltimore: 

The  Bruce  arrived  21st  September,  and  after  much  opposition  and  delay,  as  detailed 
in  our  letters,  by  the  vessel  and  via  Tampico,  we  have  at  last  got  her  loaded.  *  *  * 
Captain  Muir  thinks  he  will  have  a  chance  to  get  safely  to  sea  in  a  few  days, 
as  the  blockade  is  very  irregular  and  ineffectual.  A  vessel  came  in  safely  this 
week.  *  *  * 

The  letter  is  dated  at  Wilmington,  21st  November,  1861,  and  enclosed 
a  draft  for  parties  in  England. 

I  am,  respectfully,  etc.,  Gideon  Welles. 

Flag  Officer  L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  Hampton  Roads. 


Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Browne,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding 
U.  S.  bark  Fernandina,  transmitting  report  of  a  slight  affair  in  Little

TJ.  S.  Bark  Fernandina, 

Off  Wilmington ,  December  14,  1861. 
Sir  :  I  have  to  report  that  a  succession  of  calms  since  leaving  Hamp¬ 
ton  Roads  protracted  my  passage  to  this  place.  On  the  11th  instant  I 
took  a  heavy  gale  from  FI.  FT  .E.,  which  lasted  thirty-six  hours.  The 
side  lights  leak  much  worse  than  before  they  were  fixed. 

Enclosed  please  find  a  tabular  statement  of  vessels  spoken  and 
boarded  as  per  your  instructions,  and  also  an  official  report  of  an  affair 
which  took  place  on  the  13th  instant  off  Little  River  Inlet. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Geo.  W.  Browne, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant,  in  Command. 
Flag-Officer  L.  M.  Goldsborough,

NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


[Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  Bark  Fernandina, 

Off  Wilmington ,  December  14,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  to  report  that  on  the  evening  of  the  13th  instant,  off 
Little  River  Inlet,  North  Carolina,  I  observed  numerous  fires.  Some 
forty  were  counted  in  one  place,  and  several  others  in  scattered  posi¬ 
tions  of  from  1  to  2  miles  apart  along  the  coast. 

At  7  p.  m.  I  tacked  and  stood  in  to  reconnoiter.  On  nearing  the 
shore  I  observed  several  bodies  of  men,  which  caused  me  to  believe 
there  was  an  encampment  of  Confederate  troops  and  the  distant  fires 
were  their  picket  guard. 

After  having  burned  a  preparatory  signal  and  receiving  no  answer, 
I  opened  fire  with  my  starboard  battery  on  the  men  and  fired,  several 
of  the  shots  being  heard  to  strike  some  hard  substance  very  distinctly. 

At  this  time  the  vessel  was  within  700  yards  of  the  beach  in  4 
fathoms  of  water;  could  see  the  men  on  shore  running  plainly.  After 
firing  three  rounds  with  the  starboard  battery,  tacked  ship  and  fired 
one  round  of  shot  and  one  shell  from  port  battery.  By  this  time  the 
fires  were  mostly  extinguished.  Secured  the  batteries  and  proceeded 
on  our  course. 

From  the  aiipearance  of  things  I  am  now  led  to  believe  the  fires  were 
signals  for  some  vessel  endeavoring  to  run  a  cargo. 

Having  stood  close  in  during  the  morning,  and  seen  several  men  on 
the  beach,  they  perhaps  supposed  I  was  the  vessel  expected,  or  one 
wishing  to  run  the  blockade. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Geo.  W.  Browne, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  in  Command. 

Flag-Officer  L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Commander  Smith,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  ship  Congress, 
regarding  a  request  for  cooperation  with  the  Army  against  an  antici¬ 
pated  attack  from  the  enemy. 

U.  S.  Frigate  Congress, 

Newport  News,  December  14,  1861. 

Sir:  General  Mansfield  paid  me  a  visit  to-day  and  informed  me 
that  he  anticipated  an  attack  on  his  camp  from  ten  or  more  thousand 
of  the  enemy.  His  plan  is  to  meet  them  at  the  outermost  picket  and  take 
with  him  from  the  camp  all  of  his  disposable  troops.  To  enable  him 
to  muster  as  large  a  force  as  possible,  he  wishes  assistance  from  the 
ships  of  sailors  to  man  seven  guns  on  the  upper  and  rear  sides  of  his 
barricades,  our  field  howitzers  to  operate  with  his  field  artillery,  and 
our  marines  as  regular  troops,  to  show  an  example  of  military  discipline 
to  the  militia  infantry. 

He  thinks  the  attack  will  be  made  on  the  camp  alone.  I  think  if  an 
attack  is  made  it  will  be  a  combined  one  of  the  enemy’s  steamers  and 
land  forces  on  our  shipping  and  camp.  I  told  the  general  so,  and  also 
that  in  such  case  we  should  have  to  take  care  of  ourselves  and  could 
render  him  no  assistance.  He  has  no  idea  of  when  the  attack,  if  any, 
will  be  made;  it  is  all  surmise  with  him. 

Very  respectlully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  Smith, 

Commanding  TJ.  S.  Frigate  Congress. 

Flag-Officer  L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  Hampton  Roads. 


Order  of  Flag- Officer  Goldsborough ,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  North

Report  of  Commander  Green,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  ship  James¬ 
town,  of  the  capture  by  that  vessel  of  the  sloop  Havelock. 

U.  S.  Sloop  of  War  Jamestown, 

Lat.  — ,  Long.  — ,  December  15,  1861. 

Sir:  On  the  12th  instant  Commander  Glisson,  in  the  Mount  Vernon, 
arrived  off  Cape  Fear,  and  communicated  with  me  and  at  the  same  time 
with  the  bark  Amanda. 

After  directing  the  Amanda  to  proceed  to  New  Inlet,  to  ascertain 
what  vessel  was  blockading  that  entrance,  he  ran  in  to  anchor  near  the 
bar  on  the  west  side  of  the  shoals. 

I  stood  out  with  this  ship  toward  the  end  of  the  shoal.  A  heavy 
gale  came  on,  compelling  me  to  heave  the  ship  to.  She  drifted  during 
the  gale,  which  lasted  two  days  and  a  half,  to  the  southward  and  west¬ 
ward  off  Cape  Romain.  This  morning,  while  standing  on  our  course 
toward  Cape  Fear,  overhauled  and  captured  the  sloop  Havelock,  with  a 
British  register.  The  vessel  was  formerly  the  Noank,  built  in  Connec¬ 
ticut.  She  shipped  her  crew  on  the  6th  of  October  in  Charleston,  S.  C., 
and  ran  the  blockade  without  any  clearance.  She  is  now  cleared  from 
Matanzas  for  Philadelphia.  The  master  remarked  that  he  was  starving, 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  477 

and  had  to  do  something  for  a  living.  She  has  a  cargo  of  cigars  and 
coffee,  but  had  no  manifest  filled.  When  asked  for  it,  he  replied  that 
it  was  not  necessary  to  fill  it  until  within  3  leagues  of  the  land. 

The  Amanda  is  almost  out  ot  water  and  must  be  supplied  to  enable 
her  to  go  north.  This  ship’s  allowance  will  be  reduced  so  far  as  to  com¬ 
pel  me  to  start  on  my  return  to  Hampton  Roads  by  the  25th,  unless  the 
Mount  Vernon  can  give  the  supply,  in  which  case  I  can  remain  a  few 
days  longer. 

1  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Charles  Green, 

__  ^  Commander. 

h  lag-Omcer  L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  /Squadron ,  Hampton  Roads. 

A  clearance  was  afterwards  found  stowed  away,  signed  by  the  col¬ 
lector  and  naval  officer.  It  is  a  regular  Confederate  States  paper. 

C.  Green. 


Report  of  Commander  Glisson ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  TJ.  8.  S.  Mount 
Vernon ,  regarding  the  blockade  of  Wilmington ,  N.  C. 

TJ.  S.  S.  Mount  Yernon, 

Off  Wilmington ,  N.  C.,  December  15,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  to  report  to  you  that  I  arrived  off’  this  port  on  the  11th 
instant  and  have  been  since  that  time  actively  engaged  in  blockading 
this  place. 

The  water  on  board  of  the  bark  Amanda  being  nearly  exhausted,  I  have 
ordered  her  to  proceed  to  Hampton  Roads  to  fill  up  with  everything 
that  she  may  require.  The  Jamestown  has  but  twenty-five  days’  water 
on  board,  and  the  coal  on  board  of  this  vessel  will  be  out  about  the  1st 
of  January,  1862. 

I  have  ordered  the  commander  of  the  Amanda  to  use  every  exertion 
to  return  as  soon  as  possible.  The  bark  Fernandina  arrived  here  yes¬ 
terday,  and  I  have  directed  her  to  cruise  off  New  Inlet,  to  the  north¬ 
ward  of  the  Frying  Pan  Shoals. 

There  are  two  armed  steamers  in  the  river,  viz,  the  North  Carolina 
and  the  Cncle  Ben.  They  show  themselves  near  the  fort  occasionally. 
I  shall  keep  a  good  lookout  for  them. 

We  are  all  well  on  board,  and  everything  is  quiet  off  Wilmington. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

O.  S.  Glisson, 
Commander ,  U.  8.  Navy. 

Flag  Officer  L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Commanding  the  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 


Report  of  Acting  Lieutenant  Cavendy ,  U .  8.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  8. 
bark  Gemsbok ,  of  the  cruise  of  that  vessel  from  Boston ,  and  the  capture 
of  the  schooner  Mary  F.  Pindar. 

U.  S.  Bark  Gemsbok, 

Off  Beaufort ,  N.  C.,  December  15,  1861. 
Sir:  In  compliance  with  instructions,  I  herewith  send  you  at  the 
earliest  opportunity  a  list  of  the  officers  and  crew  of  this  vessel  from 
the  date  of  leaving  Boston,  the  time  of  her  going  in  commission,  August 


478  NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

30,  1861,  to  December  15, 1861,  inclusive.  Also  1  would  make  mention 
that  on  September  22  I  captured  the  schooner  Mary  F.  Pindar ,  of 
Edenton,  N.  C.,  and  placed  a  prize  master  (Burke)  and  crew  on  board 
of  her  and  dispatched  her  to  Hampton  ltoads,  where  I  learned,  on  my 
arrival  there,  through  the  pilot,  she  had  arrived.  Since  then  I  have 
heard  nothing  from  her. 

On  the  12th  November,  when  running  down  the  shore  toward  Bogue 
Inlet,  fell  in  with  the  wreck  of  the  steamer  Union ,  one  of  the  Port  Royal 
expedition.  A  great  number  of  people  were  collected  on  and  around 
her,  engaged  in  removing  what  remained  valuable  in  her.  I  opened  a 
brisk  fire  on  them,  which  effected  their  immediate  dispersal.  No  doubt 
several  of  them  were  killed,  as  the  shells  fell  amidst  them. 

On  the  18th  of  November  the  U.  S.  propeller  Mount  Vernon ,  Com¬ 
mander  Glisson,  arrived  here.  I  reported  to  him,  after  which  I  ran 
down  to  Bogue  Inlet,  where  I  saw  several  schooners,  large  and  small, 
inside  of  the  inlet,  which  I  communicated  to  the  commander,  who  directed 
me  to  proceed  there.  Being  8  feet  of  water  on  the  bar,  no  doubt  it  has 
been  heretofore  a  thoroughfare  for  vessels  transporting  their  cargoes 
through  Bogue  Sound  to  Beaufort. 

Two  large  ships  are  lying  in  Beaufort  harbor;  to  all  appearances 
from  this  vessel,  [they]  are  discharging  their  cargoes  and  fitting  them¬ 
selves  out  for  war  purposes. 

I  have  the  honor  to  remain,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Edw.  Cavendy, 

Acting  Lieutenant ,  Commanding . 

L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Flag -Officer,  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  Hampton  Boads.

Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  the  flag-officers  commanding 

blockading  squadrons,  forwarding  information  regarding  the  British 

bark  Neptune. 

Navy  Department,  December  16, 1861. 

Sir:  The  following  information  has  been  communicated  to  the  Secre¬ 
tary  of  State  by  the  United  States  consul  at  Bermuda  under  date 
November  23, 1S61: 

The  brig  ,4.  B.  Cook  arrived  there  the  previous  day,  the  master  of 
which  vessel  says  he  fell  in,  on  the  19th  of  November,  with  the  British 
bark  Neptuu^^  of  Falmouth,  England,  in  latitude  30°  40;,  longitude 
73°  50'. 

The  master  of  the  Neptune  enquired  about  the  blockade,  stated  that 
he  had  a  cargo  of  300  tons  of  coal,  200  tons  of  hardware  in  case,  and 
40  rifled  cannon;  that  they  had  been  in  that  vicinity  about  a  week, 
and  were  expecting  a  vessel  from  Charleston  to  take  this  hardware 
and  cannon,  and  then  they  were  going  to  a  Northern  port  to  sell  their 
coal. 

The  master  of  the  A.  B.  Cook  was  disposed,  from  the  appearance  of 
things,  to  place  more  confidence  in  the  statement  of  the  seamen  than  in 
that  of  the  master  of  the  Neptune. 

I  am,  respectfully,  etc., 

Gideon  Welles. 

Flag-Officer  W.  W.  McKean, 

Commanding  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron. 

Flag-Officer  Saml.  F.  Du  Pont, 

Commanding  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Flag-Officer  L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

I  am  highly  pleased  that  the  U.  S.  S.  Santiago  de  Cuba Commamler 
Ridgely,  has  been  ordered  to  these  waters.  She  arrived  on  the  lot 
and  again  left  the  harbor  on  the  morning  of  the  19tli.  She  came  at  the 
right  time,  as  many  vessels  were  here  loading  for  Southern  ports,  a 
others  arriving  daily  for  the  same  purpose.  Commander  Lnlgely  wi 
therefore  have  opportunities  for  carrying  out  his  instructions. 

1  learned  vesterday  from  a  reliable  source  from  Key  YVest,  that 
fourteen  small  vessels  went  into  Nassau  last  week  with  produce  D  oiii 
Charleston,  Savannah,  etc.,  and  changed  their  Hags  to  Englis  . 
The  arrivals  of  such  vessels  to  take  cargoes  for  the  blockaded  ports 
have  been  so  numerous  of  late  that  it  is  becoming  difficult  to  keep  the 
run  of  them.  It  is  expected,  however,  that  the  presence  of  an  efficient 
armed  steamer  will  check  the  business  very  effectually. 

With  great  respect,  your  obedient  servant,

Hatteras  Inlet,  December  17,  1861. 

Sir:  On  Sunday,  the  15tli  instant,  the  schooner  Charity ,  of  Provi¬ 
dence,  R.  I.,  Captain  A.  F.  White,  arrived  here  with  a  general  cargo  on 
board,  a  list  of  which  is  herewith  enclosed,  marked  A.  By  the  papers 
on  board  it  appears  that  she  cleared  from  Providence  on  November  13, 
for  Alexandria,  Ya.,  but  instead  of  proceeding  to  that  port  went  to 
Baltimore.  From  Baltimore  she  again  sailed  under  a  license  (a  copy 
of  which  is  enclosed  marked  B)  which  expressly  forbids  her  proceeding 
to  any  port  south  of  Maryland,  under  penalty  of  confiscation.  For 
these  reasons,  the  nature  of  the  cargo,  the  deliberate  violation  of  the 
license,  and  the  evident  intention  of  trading  with  the  enemy,  I  have 
seized  her  and  sent  her  to  New  York  in  charge  of  a  prize  crew  for 
adjudication. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

R.  Werden, 
Lieutenant ,  Commanding.

vessel  for  such  purpose;  nor  shall  said  vessel  be  allowed  to  touch  any 
coast  south  of  Maryland,  and  in  no  instance  to  board,  or  allow  anyone 
else  to  board,  any  foreign  vessel  for  any  purpose  whatever,  either  going 
or  returning,  nor  to  take  on  board  any  passenger,  baggage,  or  goods  of 
any  kind  from  said  vessel  without  a  special  permit  from  the  custom¬ 
house,  under  the  penalty  of  the  confiscation  of  said  vessel,  per  act  of 
Congress  approved  July  13,  1861. 

This  permit  to  be  good  until  the  31st  day  of  December.

Letter  from  W.  H.  Lyons,  esq.,  to  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy,  regarding  the 
preparations  of  the  Confederates  at  the  Norfolk  navy  yard  and  vicinity. 

Portsmouth,  Va.,  December  18,  1861. 

Dear  Sir  :  Permit  me  to  lay  before  you  a  few  facts  connected  with 
the  Gosport  [Norfolk]  navy  yard  and  the  neighboring  vicinity. 

First.  The  steamer  Merrimack  is  now  in  the  dry  dock.  She  has  been 
cut  down  2  feet  below  the  water  line  and  a  roof  or  covering  of  wood  28 
inches  thick  at  an  angle  of  30  degrees.  There  is  10  feet  of  the  top  flat, 
with  a  heavy  grating  of  wrought  iron,  and  the  balance  is  covered  with 
plates  of  iron  3  inches  thick.  The  bow  has  a  casting  made  in  the  shape 
of  wedge  and  weighing  2  tons  for  the  purpose  [of  |  sinking  ships.  She 
is  to  carry  eight  guns  of  large  caliber,  three  on  a  side  and  one  on  the 
bow  to  command  three  portholes.  The  one  on  the  stern  commands 
only  one.  These  guns  were  made  in  Richmond  and  rifled  in  this  yard, 
and  they  calculate  to  have  her  finished  by  the  1st  of  February. 

Second.  There  are  three  Englishmen  now  in  the  yard  who  have  been 
imported  to  manufacture  Armstrong  guns.  They  have  got  the  furnaces 
up  and  are  putting  up  a  heavy  trip  hammer  and  I  think  they  will  be 
ready  to  commence  work  by  the  1st  of  January. 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  483 

Thiid.  They  ai'e  now  raising  the  two  old  74s  which  were  sunk  and 
are  going  to  sink  them  in  the  channel  at  Craney  Island,  where  they 
na\e  driven  spiles  and  fastened  anchor  chains  from  one  to  the  other 
to  keep  the  ships  from  coming  up.  They  are  very  badly  frightened 
since  the  taking  of  Port  Royal  and  threaten  to  burn  the  yard  and  the 
two  cities,  provided  the  Yankees  come  to  take  the  place,  but  it  is  all 
balderdash.  They  are  frightened  almost  to  death  and  will  make  a  good 

Fourth.  They  have  thrown  up  an  entrenchment  around  Portsmouth, 
commencing  a  little  below  the  naval  hospital  and  running  in  a  south¬ 
westerly  direction  and  terminating  about  1  mile  above  the  navy  yard, 
n  here  it  crosses  the  railroad  they  have  a  North  Carolina  regiment 
stationed  and  three  32-pound  guns  mounted  and  some  seven  or  eight 
others  at  different  points  along  the  line. 

Fifth.  The  whole  available  lorce  in  and  around  Portsmouth  and  Nor¬ 
folk  and  up  as  far  as  Suffolk  does  not  exceed  15,000  troops  and  there  is 
one-third  of  them  that  will  not  lire  a  gun  at  the  glorious  Star-Spangled 
Banner  and  there  is  over  one  half  of  the  citizens  of  Portsmouth  and 
Norfolk  that  are  waiting  patiently  for  the  time  to  come  when  the  stars 
and  stripes  will  wave  again  triumphantly  from  the  same  flagstaff  where 
it  floated  for  many  years. 

Sixth.  Although  I  do  not  wish  or  intend  to  dictate  to  the  Govern¬ 
ment,  I  think  that  this  yard  ought  to  be  taken  as  soon  as  possible  before 
they  get  to  manufacturing  those  Armstrong  guns;  and  not  only  that, 
this  yard  is  the  mainstay  of  the  bogus  Confederacy.  They  are  manu¬ 
facturing  at  the  rate  of  150  shot  and  shell  per  day  and  are  now  build¬ 
ing  three  gunboats  to  be  propelled  by  steam  and  the  machinery  to  be 
built  in  the  yard,  also  all  the  boats  in  North  Carolina  have  their  repairs 
done  here  and  they  are  rifling  all  the  guns  that  were  left  in  the  yard. 

There  is  a  great  deal  of  dissatisfaction  existing  amongst  the  people, 
and  the  Union  men  are  beginning  to  breathe  more  free. 

The  bearer  of  this  letter  you  will  please  to  allow  to  return  and  bring 
such  little  trinkets  she  may  want  for  her  own  family,  for  I  can  vouch 
for  her  that  no  secessionist  will  ever  be  benefited  by  her. 

It  is  now  midnight,  and  I  hope  you  will  excuse  any  mistakes,  and 
may  the  Almighty  God,  the  Ruler  of  the  Universe,  give  you  health  and 
strength  to  see  our  country  happy  and  prosperous. 

With  respect,  I  remain,  your  most  obedient, 

W.  H.  Lyons. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

P.  S. — If  you  will  refer  to  your  files  in  the  clerk’s  office  you  will  know 
who  I  am.  I  was  an  applicant  for  the  post  of  master  machinist  in  the 
Gosport  [Norfolk]  navy  yard  in  April  last,  and  you  will  find  my  name 
also  in  the  list  of  those  who  voted  against  the  ordinance  of  secession.

U.  S.  S.  Young  Bover, 

York  River,  December  22,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  on  the  morning  of  the  18th, 
saw  a  body  of  men  at  work  on  the  shore  about  2  miles  to  the  westward

ot  us,  and  on  the  north  side  of  the  river;  also  saw  a  gun  mounted  so 
as  to  command  the  entrance  to  the  river.  Have  seen  these  small 
bodies  of  men  several  times  since.  At  one  time  saw  four  horsemen, 
t hren  dressed  in  gray  and  one  in  dark  blue  uniform.  They  rode  along 
the  beach  about  2  miles,  and  disappeared  in  the  woods  which  skirt  the

A  camp  is  visible  about  halfway  from  the  mouth  of  the  river  to  York- 
town,  the  drums  of  which  we  can  distinctly  hear  morning  and  evening, 
lliere  is  also  a  battery  of  at  least  two  guns  at  the  mouth  of  the 
I  oquosin  River.  A  e  have  seen  the  smoke  of  its  guns  several  times, 
also  a  volume  of  smoke  arising  constantly  for  two  days,  evidently  the 
burning  of  undergrowth  to  make  more  room.  At  1  o’clock  p.  m.  on  the 
l(>th  saw  a  large  volume  of  smoke  at  Yorktown,  which  continued  to 
arise  until  after  nightfall. 

Small  boats  are  constantly  crossing  the  river  above  us,  and  a  sloop 
visits  the  battery  first  spoken  of  every  morning. 

I  would  also  report  that  we  have  but  eight  days’  wood,  and  twenty 
days’  water,  and  twenty-five  days’  coal.  Being  obliged  to  haul  out 
into  the  bay  to  draw  the  fires  and  repair  the  boiler  slightly,  I  deem  it 
advisable  to  send  the  paymaster  with  this  and  to  ask  for  instructions 
with  regard  to  the  batteries  and  the  permitting  of  communications  by 
the  sloop  and  small  boats  above  mentioned. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Ira  B.  Studley, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding.
