Report  of  Captain  Marston ,  U.  S.  Navy,  senior  officer  in  Hampton  Roads, 
regarding  coal  supplied  to  tugs  chartered  by  the  War  Department. 

U.  S.  S.  Roanoke, 
Hampton  Roads,  January  25,  1862. 

Sir  :  I  beg  leave  to  report  to  you  that  I  this  day  had  an  application 
from  S.  Flanagan,  esq.,  of  Philadelphia,  for  35  tons  of  coal  for  four 
tugs  chartered  from  him  by  the  War  Department  for  General  Burn¬ 
side’s  expedition.  Mr.  Flanagan  informed  me  he  had  applied  to  Gen¬ 
eral  Wool  for  coal,  and  that  General  Wool  had  told  him  that  he  had 
nothing  to  do  with  it,  as  it  belonged  to  the  Navy.  These  tugs  have 
now  been  here  ten  days,  at  an  expense  of  $300  per  day  to  the  Govern¬ 
ment.  Under  these  circumstances  I  have  thought  it  advisable  to  give 
them  the  coal,  and  trust  my  so  doing  will  meet  your  approbation.  I 
can  not,  however,  see  why  the  coal  should  not  have  been  supplied  by 
the  military  department  at  this  place,  but  I  would  have  preferred  pay¬ 
ing  for  the  coal  myself  rather  than  there  should  have  been  any  draw¬ 
back  to  an  expedition  so  important  in  its  character,  and  in  which  the 
Navy  is  so  closely  connected. 

Verv  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  Marston, 
Captain  and  Senior  Officer. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington.

Report  of  Lieutenant  Worden ,  U.  8.  Wavy,  regarding  the  complement  of 
officers  and  crew  for  the  77.  S.  S.  Monitor. 

Navy  Yard,  Few  York,  January  27,  1862.  . 

Sir:  I  liave  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  your  communi¬ 
cation  of  the  24th  instant,  in  relation  to  the  complement  ot  officers  and 

crew  for  Ericsson’s  ironclad  battery. 

In  estimating  the  number  of  her  crew,  I  allowed  15  men  and  a  quar¬ 
ter  gunner  for  the  two  guns,  11  men  for  the  powder  division,  and 
for  the  wheel,  which  I  deem  ample  for  the  efficient  working  of  her  guns 
in  action.  That  would  leave  12  men  (including  those  available  in  the 
engineer’s  department)  to  supply  deficiencies  at  the  guns,  caused  by 
sickness  or  casualties.  I  propose  to  use  a  portion  of  the  petty  officers 
at  the  guns,  and  in  naming  the  number  of  that  class  I  thought  I  would 
be  enabled  to  obtain  a  better  class  of  men  for  that  purpose. 

It  is  believed  that  17  men  and  2  officers  in  the  turret  would  be  as 
many  as  could  work  there  with  advantage;  a  greater  number  would  be 
in  each  other’s  way  and  cause  embarrassment. 

The  limited  accommodations  of  the  battery  and  the  insufficiency  of 
ventilation  renders  it  important  that  as  few  as  is  consistent  with  her 
efficiency  in  action  should  be  put  in  her. 

In  relation  to  master's  mates,  one  might  be  ordered;  more  would 
overcrowd  her  accommodations  and  seems  to  be  unnecessary. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  L.  Worden, 
Lieutenant,  Commanding.

Report  of  Captain  Marston ,  V.  S.  Navy ,  senior  officer  in  Hampton  Roads, 
regarding  information  received  from  contrabands. 

IT.  S.  S.  Roanoke, 
Hampton  Roads,  January  28,  1862. 

Sir  :  I  beg  leave  to  report  that  15  contrabands  made  their  escape 
from  Sewell’s  Point  last  night  and  were  picked  up  by  one  of  our  tugs. 

These  contrabands  state  that  there  are  30  guns  at  Sewell’s  Point,  one 
of  which  is  11-inch;  that  there  are  5  guns  between  Sewell’s  Point  and 
the  Rip  Raps,  one  of  them  being  directly  opposite  that  place.  There 
are  about  2,500  troops  at  Sewell’s  Point,  most  of  them  from  North  Caro¬ 
lina,  Georgia,  and  Louisiana.  They  heard  that  the  Merrimaclc  was 
taken  out  of  clock  yesterday,  but  did  not  see  her.  There  are  from  4,000 
to  5,000  troops  at  Norfolk,  and  that  1,200  were  sent  from  thence  to 
Roanoke  Island  on  Saturday,  the  26th. 

Will  you  please  inform  me  what  I  shall  do  with  the  contrabands  who 
are  not  required  for  the  service. 

V ery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  Marston, 
Captain  and  Senior  Officer. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  Navy.

Report  of  Flag-Officer  Qoldsborough,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  North  At¬ 
lantic  Blockading  Squadron,  regarding  the  preparations  for  the  attack 
on  Roanoke  Island. 

U.  S.  Flag-Steamer  Philadelphia, 

Pamlico  Sound,  January  29,  1862. 

Sir  :  Since  my  last  communication  to  the  Department,  dated  J anuary 
23  and  26,  nothing  of  moment  has  occurred  in  this  quarter  beyond  the 
getting  of  a  number  more  of  the  vessels  belonging  to  General  Burn¬ 
side’s  branch  of  the  expedition  over  the  bulkhead  and  the  arrival  of 
the  Barney.  Both  this  vessel  and  the  Perry  got  over  the  bulkhead 
promptly,  and  they  make  the  number  of  our  naval  vessels  now  there, 
exclusive  of  the  Philadelphia,  19,  and  increase  the  number  of  their 
9-incli  guns  from  11  to  15.  Nothing  whatever  detains  us  from  making 
an  onward  movement  but  the  difficulties  attending  the  army  branch  of 
our  forces,  and,  indeed,  this  has  been  the  case  ever  since  the  19tli 
instant.  Were  it  not  for  the  number  of  troops  the  enemy  has  on 
Roanoke  Island  and  the  absolute  necessity  for  our  troops  to  assist  in 
subduing  them,  after  the  reduction  of  its  several  forts,  and  then  to 
occupy  it  immediately  in  force,  I  should  have  moved  off  alone  with  my 
own  branch  of  the  expedition  more  than  a  week  ago;  but  as  things 
stand  my  hands  are  emphatically  tied,  and  certainly  my  patience  is 
well-nigh  exhausted.  All  that  I  can  do  with  prudence,  so  far  as 
Roanoke  Island  is  concerned,  is  to  wait  until  General  Burnside  can  get 
himself  ready,  and  this  will  yet  require  several  days  more  of  good 
weather.  He  has  been  compelled  to  lighten  many  of  his  vessels  of 
everything  in  order  to  get  them  over  the  bulkhead,  which,  of  course, 
involves  the  necessity  of  reloading  and  of  reembarking  troops,  and  also 
of  consulting  suitable  opportunities  for  the  purpose. 

In  view  of  what  is  to  be  done  after  the  taking  of  Roanoke  Island, 
and  the  actual  state  of  things- in  regard  to  General  Burnside’s  vessels, 
I  beg  to  say  that  in  my  judgment  it  would  be  of  immense  benefit  to  our 
operations  if  all  the  smaller  class  of  new  gunboats,  drawing  not  over 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  537 

feet  of  water,  and  especially  those  having  a  rudder  at  each  end, 
could  be  sent  to  me  as  early  as  practicable. 

January  30.— The  steamer  that  was  to  have  been  dispatched  yester¬ 
day  by  the  army  for  Hampton  Roads,  and  to  have  conveyed  this  com¬ 
munication  among  others,  did  not  leave,  and  will  not,  I  am  now  informed, 
until  this  afternoon.  Since  yesterday  three  more  of  General  Burnside’s 
vessels  have  been  gotten  over  the  bulkhead,  and  all  of  them  of  an 
important  consequence  in  the  way  of  conveying  his  troops.  He  has 
now  enough  over,  I  think,  to  accomplish  our  ends  at  Roanoke  Island, 
and  I  dare  say,  from  our  conversation  yesterday,  that  he  himself  is  ot 
the  same  opinion.  If  so,  we  shall  certainly  soon  be  off  for  that  quarter, 
provided  the  weather  continues  to  allow  reloading  and  reembarking. 

I  am  happy  to  say  that  my  officers  and  men  enjoy  excellent  health, 
and  all  are  exceedingly  anxious  to  measure  arms  with  the  enemy.  None 
entertain  a  shadow  of  doubt  as  to  the  result,  unless,  forsooth,  he  has 
availed  of  our  unexpected  and  protracted  delay  here  to  strengthen 
himself  most  materially.  We  have  no  very  recent  intelligence  from 
Roanoke  Island,  nor  can  we,  despite  of  efforts,  procure  any.  As  to  the 
condition  of  things  there  three  weeks  ago  we  are  pretty  well  posted. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Flag-Officer ,  Commanding  Forth  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington ,  J).  C. 


Instructions  from  Flag-Officer  Goldsborough,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding 
North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  to  Commander  Rowan ,  U.  S. 
Navy,  commanding  second  division  in  Pamlico  Sound,  regarding  the 
shortening  of  fuzes  in  making  attack. 

U.  S.  Flag-Steamer  Philadelphia, 

Pamlico  Sound,  January  30,  1862. 

Sir:  In  passing  through  the  marshes,  where  it  is  quite  certain  we 
shall  encounter  the  enemy,  it  is  more  than  probable  that  we  shall  have 
to  go  considerably  nearer  to  his  guns  than  the  distance  due  to  a  5-second 
fuze  of  1,400  yards,  and  this  will  require  that  those  fuzes  should  be 
shortened  correspondingly  in  order  to  make  the  shells  tell  in  the  most 
effective  manner.  I  desire  therefore  that  you  will  put  the  commanding 
officers  of  your  division  on  their  guard  upon  this  point,  and  direct 
them,  if  necessary,  how  the  fuzes  may  be  properly  shortened.  By  con¬ 
sulting  the  pilots,  and  assuming  that  the  enemy  has  a  battery  just 
abreast  of  the  little  island  at  the  marshes,  which  island  we  shall  have 
to  leave  on  our  starboard  hand  in  going  through,  the  distance  in  view 
can  be  nearly  ascertained.  I  intend  no  delay  in  going  through  the 
marshes,  but  every  vessel  is  to  dash  ahead  as  fast  as  she  can  and 
at  the  vessels  of  the  enemy,  which,  probably,  will  be  drawn  up  to  give 
us  a  first  meeting  just  inside  the  marshes  and  within  supporting  dis¬ 
tance  of  the  small  battery  said  to  be  placed  thereat.  Our  first  hard 
fighting,  I  think,  will  be  at  Pork  Point,  on  Roanoke  Island,  and  about 
that  point  the  enemy’s  vessels  may  again  meet  us  after  being  driven  from 
the  marshes;  or,  indeed,  they  may  first  meet  us  there.  As  at  present 
advised  the  landing  of  our  army  will  take  place  at  Sandy  Point.  If 
there  be  a  battery  there,  about  which  doubts  are  entertained,  it  will 
have  to  be  silenced  at  once,  in  order  to  get  the  army  on  shore;  but  from 
the  best  information  I  can  gather  we  shall  find  it  vacant. 


538 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRQN. 


Use  your  own  discretion  entirely  about  having  any  5-second  fuzes 
shortened  in  anticipation  of  our  getting  up  to  the  marshes. 

The  generals  all  assure  me  that  they  will  certainly  be  ready  to  move 
in  a  day  or  two,  weather  permitting.  Our  first  move  will  be  from  this 
to  an  anchorage  a  few  miles  this  side  of  the  marshes.  There  we  sha  1 
remain  during  the  night,  being  careful  to  show  no  lights,  and  the  next 
morning  at  daylight  we  shall  move  onward  and  do  our  best.  1 

not  the  evening  before,  1  shall  hoist  my  flag  on  board  the  Southfield. 
I  wish  a  good  lookout  kept  for  signals  that  I  may  make  from  wherever 
my  flag  may  be  exhibited,  and  every  care  to  be  observed  m  their 
execution. 

Yerv  respectfully?  your  most  obedient  servant, 

L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Flag-  Officer.

Sir:  General  Burnside  has  now  over  the  bulkhead  all  the  vessels  of 
his  branch  of  the  expedition  that  he  needs,  and  he  assures  me  that  on 
Monday  next  at  the  furthest  he  will  be  ready  to  move.  If  so,  then  we

According  to  information  which  we  received  last  night  the  enemy  has 
2,300  men  on  the  island,  and  5,000  at  Nag’s  Head.  The  latter,  no  doubt, 
are  intended  for  the  twofold  purpose  of  securing  a  retreat  by  the  sea¬

Report  of  Captain  Marston,  U.  S.  Navy,  Senior  Officer  in  Hampton 

Roads,  regarding  firing  heard  in  the  direction  of  Beaufort  and  Roanoke 

Island,  North  Carolina. 

U.  S.  S.  Roanoke, 
Hampton  Roads,  February  1 ,  1862. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  the  arrival  during  the  past 
night  of  the  bark  Gemsbok ,  from  Beaufort,  N.  C.  Captain  Cavendy 
informs  me  that  on  Tuesday,  the  28tli  ultimo,  he  heard  heavy  firing  in 
the  rear  of  Beaufort,  but  has  no  conjecture  as  from  whom  it  proceeded. 
Captain  C.  also  reports  that  on  Thursday,  the  30th  ultimo,  at  9  o’clock 
a.  ra.,  while  off  Roanoke  Inlet,  he  heard  heavy  firing  in  the  direction  of 
Roanoke  Island,  leaving  on  my  own  mind  no  doubt  that  Flag-Officer 
Goldsborough  is  at  work. 

Captain  Cavendy  reports  verbally  the  Gemsbok’’ s  mainmast  as  rotten 
and  other  disabilities.  As  soon  as  I  receive  his  written  report  I  shall 
order  a  survey  and  report  to  you  the  result. 

The  weather  is  stormy,  with  rain,  which  detains  the  Jamestown  from 
sailing.  The  Jamestown  has  been  under  sailing  orders  for  two  days 
past. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  Marston, 
Captain  and  Senior  Officer. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.  Washington,  D.  C.

Order  of  Flag-Officer  Goldsborough,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  North 
Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  to  the  senior  officer  off  Wilmington , 
N.  C .,  to  send  the  U.  S.  S.  Chippewa  off  Nag’s  Head  to  dislodge  the 
enemy. 

U.  S.  Flag-Steamer  Philadelphia, 

Pamlico  Sound,  February  1,  1862. 

Sir  :  We  have  received  information  that  the  enemy  has  concentrated 
a  force  of  some  5,000  men  at  Nag’s  Head,  which,  as  you  are  doubtless 
aware,  lies  about  40  miles  to  the  northward  and  westward  of  Cape 
Hatteras.  Immediately  on  the  receipt  of  this,  I  wish  you  to  dispatch 
the  Chippewa  to  go  off  that  place,  approach  it  as  nearly  as  prudence 
and  safety  will  permit,  and  dislodge  the  enemy  if  he  be  there.  He  is 
said  to  be  stowed  away  in  the  woods  thereabouts.  Shelling  will  prob¬ 
ably  compel  him  to  stir  and  show  himself.  We  have  an  abundant  sup¬ 
ply  of  coal  at  Hatteras  Inlet,  and  any  vessel  of  ours  not  drawing  over 
11  feet  can  procure  it  there.  Should  it  be  that  the  Chippewa  can  not 
be  so  dispatched,  let  the  next  best  steamer  for  the  purpose  now  off' 
Wilmington  be  sent  to  the  point  indicated  without  delay.  Whether 
the  enemy  be  discovered  or  not,  1  wish  a  report  made  to  me  at  Hatteras 
Inlet  of  the  result  of  the  reconnoissance. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Flag-  Officer. 

Senior  II.  S.  Naval  Officer, 

Blockading  off  Wilmington ,  N.  C. 

P.  s._Lt  would  be  well  in  any  event  for  the  vessel  to  remain  off 
Nag’s  Head  for  several  days  after  she  gets  there,  as  we,  in  a  day  or  two 
from  this,  weather  permitting,  are  to  advance  upon  Roanoke  Island, 
and  the  enemy  may  be  compelled  to  retreat  by  the  way  of  Nag’s  Head. 
Then  her  guns  could  play  upon  him  with  great  advantage  to  our  purposes. 

Tj.  m.  g. 

p.  s.— Again :  The  shore  along  and  about  Nag’s  Head,  I  am  informed, 
is  comparatively  bold,  and  may  be  approached  by  a  vessel  of  moderate 
draft  quite  within  good  and  effective  cannon  range.  A  vessel  off'  there 
will  be  able  to  hear  very  distinctly  any  firing  going  on  at  Roanoke 
Island.  Indeed,  she  may  place  herself  at  a  distance  scarcely  exceeding

Report  of  Flag-Officer  Goldsborough,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  North 
Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  giving  information  received  from  Con¬ 
federate  deserters. 

U.  S.  Flag-Steamer  Philadelphia, 

Pamlico  Sound,  February  1, 1862. 

Sir  :  The  army  steamer  to  have  left  yesterday  for  Hampton  Roads 
did  not  depart,  in  consequence  of  bad  weather.  Five  of  the  enemy’s 
soldiers  came  to  us  yesterday  from  Middletown,  Hyde  County,  N.  O., 
in  a  small  schooner,  loaded  with  wood,  which  they  had  taken,  without 
authority,  to  effect  their  escape.  They  tell  us  that  at  least  two  thirds  of 
the  population  of  both  Hyde  and  Beaufort  counties  are  in  favor  of  the 
Union,  but  that  the  poor  are  held  in  entire  subjection  by  the  rich;  and 
also  that  the  greatest  consternation  exists  with  regard  to  this  expedi¬

February  2. — Supposing  the  report  to  be  true  that  the  enemy  had  con¬ 
centrated  5,000  men  at  Rag’s  Head,  I  yesterday  sent  an  order  to  the 
senior  naval  officer  off  Wilmington,  R.  C.,  to  dispatch  the  Chippeiva 
forthwith  to  that  place  to  dislodge  him  if  there,  and  to  ascertain  the 
tact  by  throwing  some  shells  among  the  woods  where  he  is  said  to  be 
sheltered.  In  case  of  any  difficulty  about  the  Chippeiva ,  the  next  best 
steamer  at  hand  off  Wilmington  is  to  be  sent  in  her  place.  Whichever 
steamer  be  sent,  she  is  to  remain  off*  Rag’s  Head  several  days  after 
reaching  there,  so  that,  in  case  of  a  retreat  of  the  enemy  from  Roanoke 
Island  by  that  way,  Ins  progress  may  be  interrupted.  The  officer  is 
informed  of  the  probable  time  that  our  attack  unon  the  island  will  take 
place,  and  he  can  place  himself  within  easy  hearing  distance  of  the 
scene.  An  army  steamer  conveyed  my  communication  to  Wilmington. 

General  Burnside  assures  me  that  he  will  be  ready  to  move  by  to-mor¬ 
row  morning.  Eothing  else  in  the  world  detains  me  from  moving  at  a 
moment’s  warning. 

L.  M.  G. 


Order  of  Captain  Marston,  U.  S.  Navy,  senior  officer  in  Hampton  Boads, 
to  Lieutenant  Braine ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  II.  S.  S.  Monticello,  to 
proceed  with  that  vessel  to  Baltimore  for  repairs. 

U.  S.  S.  Roanoke, 
Hampton  Boads,  February  2,  1862. 

Sir  :  You  will  proceed  to  Baltimore  with  the  Monticello,  under  your 
command,  for  the  purpose  of  having  your  engine  repaired  and  put 
in  order;  to  do  which  you  will  employ  either  of  the  three  following 
establishments,  viz:  Messrs.  John  Wells  &  Son,  Hazlehurst  &  Co.,  or 
Charles  Reeder.  You  will  please  make  the  best  terms  you  can  for  the 
Government  with  the  establishment  you  may  choose  to  employ,  and 
inform  me  what  the  probable  cost  will  be,  as  well  as  from  time  to  time 
how  you  proceed. 

You  will  use  every  possible  means  in  your  power  to  forward  the 
repair  of  your  engine  and  return  to  this  plaoe  at  the  earliest  day 
you  can. 

If  the  receiving  ship  at  Baltimore  can  accommodate  your  men  with¬ 
out  tresspassing  too  much  on  the  crew  of  that  vessel,  you  can  place 
your  men  on  board  of  her.  1  would  impress  on  you  the  necessity  of  your 
returning  to  Hampton  Roads  with  as  little  delay  as  possible. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  Marston, 
Captain  and  Senior  Officer. 

Lieutenant  Commanding  D.  L.  Braine, 

Commanding  Monticello.

Instructions  from  Flag-Officer  Coldsborough,  U.  8.  Navy,  commanding 

North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  to  Commander  Rowan,  U.  S. 

Navy,  commanding  second  division  in  Pamlico  Sound. 

U.  S.  Flag-Steamer  Philadelphia, 
Pamlico  Sound,  Sunday,  February  2,  1862. 

Sir  :  I  wish  you  to  have  two  steamers  detailed  to  take  in  tow  the 
Granite  and  Howard  when  we  come  to  move  Irom  this,  which,  as  at 
present  advised,  will  probably  be  early  to  morrow  morning. 

I  want  Lieutenant-Commanding  Jeffers,  on  our  approaching  Long 
Point  Shoal  [Long  Shoal  Point  ?],  to  place  a  buoy  on  its  outer  or  east¬ 
ern  extremity  in  case  of  finding  that  one  is  not  there  already ;  and, 
as  he  may  require  the  Granite's  services  for  the  purpose,  perhaps  his 
vessel  had  better  be  the  steamer  to  take  her  in  tow. 

When  the  time  arrives  for  getting  the  squadron  underway,  the  neces¬ 
sary  signal  will  be  made  by  me.  The  second  division,  under  your 
immediate  command,  is  to  be  the  leading  one,  observing  the  distribu¬ 
tion  of  columns,  with  as  many  vessels  of  each  arranged  abreast  in  the 
course  of  our  advance  toward  the  marshes,  as  circumstances,  con¬ 
venience,  and  safety  will  permit. 

In  order  to  distinguish  the  vessel  on  board  of  which  yon  may  at  any 
time  be,  and  for  the  security  of  regularity  and  system,  it  is  proper  that 
you  should  have  and  keep  hoisted  on  board  other  the  red  division  flag 
prescribed  by  the  signal  book,  and  this  course  I  desire  you  to  observe. 

On  reaching  the  neighborhood  of  the  place  where  I  now  intend 
anchoring  after  leaving  here,  I  shall  give  notice  by  first  making  the 
preparatory  signal,  and  I  shall  wish  the  vessels  of  your  division  to 
anchor  in  advance  of  all  the  rest. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Flag-  Officer. 

Commander  S.  C.  Rowan,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  Second  Division ,  U.  S.  Expedition,  Pamlico  Sound.

Order  of  Commander  Rowan ,  TJ.  8.  Navy,  commanding  naval  division  in 

Pamlico  Sound ,  to  the  commanding  officers  of  columns,  regarding  the 

advance  upon  Roanoke  Island. 

U.  S.  S.  Delaware, 
Pamlico  Sound,  February  2,  1862. 

Gentlemen  :  In  passing  this — the  marshes — where  it  is  thought  we 
shall  meet  opposition  from  a  battery  on  the  port  side  and  perhaps  the 
enemy’s  vessels  in  front  and  starboard  bow,  I  deem  it  advisable  to  move 
the  squadron  through  the  narrow  pass  in  the  river  laid  down  in  the 
accompanying  paper.  By  referring  to  this  paper  it  will  be  seen  that 
my  object  is  to  preserve  the  order  of  advance  in  three  columns  abreast 
till  we  approach  the  pass,  where  the  leaders  of  the  columns  will  so 
arrange  themselves  on  a  bow  and  quarter  bearing  on  the  Stars  and 
Stripes  which  will  enable  each  of  the  three  vessels  to  keep  up  a  tire  on 
the  fort  in  approaching  and  passing  it.  Having  passed  the  battery,  the 
order  abreast  will  be  restored,  after  which  we  must  be  governed  by 
circumstances. 

It  is  said  in  high  quarters  that  we  sail  to-morrow. 

I  send  shot  plugs  to  be  distributed  by  the  officers  to  their  columns. 

Let  it  be  understood  that  each  leader  keeps  his  column  intact,  with 
instructions  to  preserve  their  respective  stations,  and  not  break  the 
columns  unless  ordered  to  do  so  by  signal  to  the  commanders  of  col¬ 
umns  from  this  vessel,  or  the  commander  in  chief,  wherever  his  flag 
may  be. 

Wishing  all  success,  I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

[S.  C.  Rowan,] 

Commanding  Naval  Division  of  Forces  in  Pamlico  Sound. 

Captain  Weeden, 

Commanding  First  Column. 

Captain  Murray, 

Commanding  Second  Column. 

Captain  Davenport, 

Commanding  Third  Column. 

Should  there  not  be  room  to  pass  in  three  columns,  the  second  column 
will  give  way  and  fall  in  the  rear  of  the  third,  and  restore  order  as  soon 
[as]  the  narrows  are  passed. 


Letter  from  Captain  Van  Brunt,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Min¬

IT.  S.  S.  Minnesota,  February  2, 1862. 
My  Dear  Goldsborough:  I  have  just  learned  that  a  vessel  (trans¬ 
port)  would  leave  this  evening  for  Hatteras.  I  am  very  anxious  to  hear 
from  you.  The  Gemsbok  passed  Hatteras  on  the  29tli  and  heard  heavy 
firing  in  the  vicinity  of  Roanoke  Island,  which  put  us  all  upon  the  qtd 
vive.  I  send  you  a  number  of  letters  and  some  newspapers.  We  have 
very  little  news  here.  The  Merrimack  is,  without  doubt,  out  of  dock  and 
almost  ready  for  a  move.  I  am  anxiously  expecting  her  and  believe  I 
am  ready,  but  I  have  doubts  about  her  venturing  out  of  Elizabeth  River. 
I  understand  they  have  been  putting  down  moorings  for  her  about  a

mile  inside  of  Sewell’s  Point,  and  should  not  be  surprised  if  she  was 
only  used  for  harbor  defense,  as  I  am  told  she  floats  with  hei  looting  2, 
feet  underwater,  and  that,  in  consequence,  she  can  carry  no  battery. 
She  is  exceedingly  crank  and  would  be  unsate  if  she  happened  to  get 

across  the  tides  and  might  turn  turtle. 

I  hope  all  the  stores  sent  have  arrived  safely.  1  leas»e  tell  Gase  i  win

The  backgammon  does  not  flourish  since  you  left.  Doctor  Dillaicl

Report  of  Flag- Officer  Goldsborough ,  77.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  North 

Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  of  consultation  with  Brigadier- General 

Burnside ,  77.  S.  Army. 

U.  S.  Flag-Steamer  Philadelphia, 

'  Pamlico  Sound,  February  3,  1862. 

Sir  :  General  Burnside  was  not  quite  ready  to  move  his  force  this 
morning,  and  had  he  been  the  weather  would  have  detained  us.  He 
has  just  left  this  vessel,  after  holding  with  me  a  full  and  free  consul¬ 
tation  with  regard  to  the  details  of  our  operations.  Our  plans  are  as 
fully  matured  as  they  ivell  can  be,  and  everything  between  us  is,  I 
think,  sufficiently  understood.  He  will  certainly  be  ready  to  start 
very  soon. 

This  morning  19  contrabands,  as  they  are  popularly  called,  came  over 
to  us  from  Middletown,  Hyde  County,  N.  C.;  4  of  them  are  men,  5  are 
women,  and  the  rest  children.  At  my  request  General  Burnside  has 
ordered  all  of  them  to  be  received  and  cared  for  at  Fort  Hatteras. 
They  afford  us  no  information  of  value. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedieut  servant, 

L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Flag- Officer ,  Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington ,  I).  C. 


Report  of  Captain  Marston,  77.  S.  Navy,  senior  officer  in  Hampton  Roads, 
regarding  certain  vessels  of  the  blockading  force. 

U.  S.  S.  Roanoke, 
Hampton  Roads,  February  3,  1862. 

Sir:  I  had  this  pleasure  on  the  29th  ultimo,  informing  you  what  I 
had  done  relative  to  your  provisions,  which  I  have  no  doubt  will  be  with 
you  at  the  appointed  time. 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  545 

I  have  to  report  that  the  Albatross  and  Monticello  have  come  in,  both 
Tvitli  their  machinery  so  much  out  of  order  as  to  require  extensive 
repairs,  and  the  hull  ot  the  former,  especially  in  her  upper  works,  so 
very  defective  as  to  be  beyond  repairing  with  our  force  of  mechanics. 
1  have  been  directed  by  the  Department  to  send  them  to  Baltimore, 
whence  the  Monticello  sailed  yesterday,  and  the  Albatross  will  follow 
as  soon  as  some  things  are  done  for  her. 

The  commanders  of  these  vessels  have  strict  injunctions  to  effect 
their  repairs  with  all  possible  dispatch  and  return  to  this  place  instanter. 

Ihe  Gemsbok  arrived  yesterday  and  reported  all  well  off  Beaufort, 
none  ot  the  vessels  having  escaped  from  thence,  but  that  one  schooner 
attempted  to  do  so  and  got  on  shore  (inside),  where  she  now  lays  hiffh 
and  dry. 

The  Gemsbok  reports  her  fore  and  main  masts  rotten,  and  other 
detects,  and  I  have  ordered  a  survey  on  her,  which,  as  soon  as  the 
storm  subsides,  will  enter  on  its  duties.  I  am  in  hopes  that  the  Gemsbok 
will  not  be  detained  from  her  station;  if  she  is,  there  will  be  three  ves¬ 
sels  absent.  It  is  now  blowing  strong  from  E.  S.  E.,  with  snow.  I  have 
brought  to  the  attention  of  the  Department  the  absence  of  the  Albatross 
and  Monticello ,  and  shall  do  so  with  regard  to  the  Gemsbok  if  she  is 
deemed  unfit  to  return. 

V ery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  Marston, 

Captain. 

Flag-Officer  L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Commander  Glisson,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Mount 
Vernon,  regarding  the  blockade  of  Wilmington,  N.  C. 

U.  S.  S.  Mount  Yernon, 

Off  Wilmington,  N.  C.,  February  3,  1862. 

Sir  :  I  have  received  your  communication  of  the  2d  [1st]  instant  and 
regret  to  inform  you  that  I  am  the  only  vessel  now  off  this  port,  as  the 
U.  S.  steamers  Monticello  and  Chippewa,  being  both  out  of  coal,  had  to 
be  dispatched  to  Hampton  Boads  for  a  supply.  I  am  in  daily  anticipa¬ 
tion  of  the  return  of  the  Monticello,  as  she  left  here  on  the  25th  ultimo; 
directly  that  she  arrives  I  will  dispatch  her. 

As  there  is  so  much  at  stake  here  (the  North  Carolina  and  Gordon 
both  being  ready  to  run  the  blockade  at  any  moment)  it  would  be 
imprudent  to  leave  this  port  unguarded  at  this  juncture. 

Everything  is  quiet  off  this  place  and  we  are  all  well  on  board. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

O.  S.  Glisson, 
Commander,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Flag-Officer  L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Commanding  the  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

We  left  the  Philadelphia  navy  yard  on  the  morning  of  January  -9, 
but  owing  to  fog,  ice,  and  the  imperfect  working  of  our  machinery 
(that  now  for  the  first  time  was  tried  away  from  the  wharf)  the  pilot 
was  unwilling  to  proceed.  We  therefore  anchored  m  the  channel,  lhe 
next  morning  at  daybreak,  the  weather  being  a  little  more  favorable, 
we  got  underway  and  proceeded  down  the  Delaware.  , 

The  engine  worked  badly,  stopping  frequently  upon  its  center,  and 
the  rudder  seemed  to  have  little  influence  on  her  course— same  when 

Thatniglit  we  were  compelled  to  anchor  off  Bombay  Hook  light.  On 
Friday  morning  at  daybreak  we  were  again  underway,  and,  laboring 
under  the  same  difaculties  as  on  the  previous  day,  we  reached  the  Del¬ 
aware  Breakwater  at  3  in  the  afternoon.  The  chief  engineer  reported 
it  indispensably  necessary  that  certain  repairs  and  alterations  should 
be  made  in  the  engine.  It  was  patent  to  all  that  the  machinery  re¬ 
quired  overhauling,  and  I  directed  him  to  get  it  in  seaworthy  condi¬ 
tion.  On  Sunday  morning,  the  1st  instant,  the  necessary  changes 
having  been  made,  and  the  engine  being  reported  in  good  order,  we 
proceeded  to  sea,  and  shaped  our  course  toward  Hatteras  Inlet.  ui 
experience  on  Delaware  River  and  Bay  had  not  awakened  any  brilliant 
anticipations  in  regard  to  the  speed  or  seaworthy  qualities  of  the 
Miami:  but  I  felt  the  importance  of  making  all  haste,  and  determined 
to  strain  every  nerve  in  order  to  reach  our  destination,  lhe  wind  was 
moderate  from  the  north  and  westward,  the  water  smooth,  and,  under 
steam  and  the  head  sails,  we  got  along  passably  well  until  evening, 
when  the  wind  came  out  from  the  northward  and  eastward,  with  con- 
siderable  sea.  Then  the  radical  imperfections  of  the  vessel  began  to 
manifest  themselves  strikingly.  The  salt  water  and  heavy  rolling  of 
the  ship,  as  the  sea  increased,  rapidly  diminished  the  steam-producing 
capacity  of  the  boilers.  The  blower  was  put  on,  and  then  it  filled  the 
engine  room  with  strangulating  gas;  it  was  kept  on  for  most  of  the 
time,  yet  it  was  of  no  avail.  The  pressure  of  the  steam  continued  to 
sink  during  the  night  and  until  Monday  evening,  when  the  chief  engi¬ 
neer  reported  to  me  that  it  would  be  necessary  to  stop  the  engine,  in 
order  to  get  up  steam  enough  to  drive  ahead  at  all.  We  were  off  the 
Wimble  Shoals;  our  boilers  had  given  out;  our  sails,  simply  auxiliary, 
hardly  more  than  kept  steerageway  on  the  vessel,  which  seldom  an¬ 
swered  her  helm  until  it  was  put  hard  up  or  hard  down.  In  this  alto¬ 
gether  unseawortliy  condition,  with  the  Hatteras  coast  under  our  lee, 
our  only  resource  was  to  get  her  head  round  to  the  northward  and 
endeavor  to  reach  Hampton  Roads.  A  northeaster  of  any  violence 
must  have  inevitably  driven  us  on  shore.  A  heavy  northwester  would 
have  drifted  us  helplessly  into  the  Gulf  Stream.  Our  head  was  turned 
to  the  northward.  The  weather  was  thick,  rainy,  and  threatening,  but 
a  little  before  midnight  a  moderate  breeze  came  out  from  the  northward 
and  westward.  Favored  by  this,  and  stopping  the  engine  at  intervals 
until  a  good  head  of  steam  (soon  worked  off)  could  be  got  up  in  the 
boilers,  we  advanced  on  an  average  of  a  couple  knots  an  hour  through 
the  water.  Fortunately,  on  Tuesday,  about  sunset,  the  steamer  Con¬ 
stitution ,  Captain  Fletcher,  made  us,  and  at  6  p.  m.,  in  accordance 
with  my  request,  took  us  in  tow  and  brought  us  into  Hampton  Roads. 
I  can  only  make  a  hurried  report,  but  I  can  assure  the  Department  that 
the  Miami  is  altogether  unseaworthy  in  her  present  condition.  If 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  549 

greater  surface  be  given  to  lier  rudder,  and  if  her  boilers  can  be  in¬ 
creased  so  as  to  supply  sufficient  steam  to  propel  her  engines,  she  will 
make  a  very  good  sea  boat,  and  will  prove  herself  most  admirably 
adapted  to  lighting  service  in  the  shallow  bays  and  rivers  of  the 
Southern  coast. 

I  beg  leave  to  refer  to  the  report  of  Acting  Chief  Engineer  Victor 
for  details  as  to  the  behavior  of  the  engine  and  boilers. 

As  the  Miami  is  the  first  vessel  of  her  class  that  has  ever  been  to 
sea,  I  have  concluded  to  send  Lieutenant  Townsend  (with  the  com¬ 
manding  officer’s  permission),  to  whom  I  beg  to  refer  for  any  informa¬ 
tion  in  regard  to  the  vessel  the  Department  may  require. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  your  obedient  servant, 

A.  D.  Harrell,

Navy  Department,  February  6, 1862. 
Sir:  The  IT.  S.  consul  at  Halifax  [Nova  Scotia]  telegraphs  that  the 
British  schooner  Loanno  sailed  from  that  place  on  the  1st  instant,  with 
a  cargo  of  fish.  Her  reported  destination  is  Baltimore,  but  her  real 
destination  is  believed  to  be  some  Southern  blockaded  port. 

The  British  schooner  Success ,  81  tons,  is  reported  as  having  cleared 
from  St.  John,  New  Brunswick,  on  the  24th  ultimo,  for  Nassau,  with 
the  intention,  it  is  strongly  suspected,  of  attempting  to  run  the  block¬ 
ade.  She  has  a  cargo  of  oakum,  fish,  butter,  soap,  quinine,  pig  iron, 
etc.,  valued  at  $5,866.32  (actual  value  not  less  than  $10,000).  Her  des¬ 
tination  is  believed  to  be  some  port  in  South  Carolina  or  Florida.

General  Order.]  U.  S.  Flag-Steamer  Philadelphia, 

Off  Roanoke  Island,  February  9,  1862. 

To  the  officers  and  men  under  my  command  engaged  in  the  reduction  of 
Roanoke  Island : 

Your  efforts  of  yesterday  and  the  day  before  against  the  enemy  were 
alike  worthy  of  yourselves  and  the  sacred  cause  our  glorious  flag 

upholds,  ,  .  , 

I  thank  you  for  them,  and  congratulate  you  upon  the  results  achieved. 
No  commander  in  chief  could  have  been  more  gallantly  sustained,  or 
could  have  desired  a  more  gratifying  display  of  coolness,  skill,  and 
discipline. 

We  have  yet  more  work  of  the  kind  to  accomplish,  and  will  soon 
deliver  another  blow  to  crush  the  hydra  of  rebellion. 

From  what  I  have  already  witnessed,  I  am  sure  that  you  will  do  it 

well. 

L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Flag-Officer,  Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 


Detailed  report  of  Flag-Officer  Goldsborough,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  North  Atlantic  Block¬ 
ading  Squadron. 

IT.  S.  Flag-Steamer  Philadelphia, 

Off  Roanoke  Island,  February  18,  1862. 

Sir:  The  following  detailed  report  concerning  the  part  taken  by 
some  of  the  vessels  belonging  to  the  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squad¬ 
ron  in  the  engagement  of  the  7th  and  8th  instant,  I  have  now  the  honor 
to  submit: 

On  the  28th  ultimo  all  the  vessels  composing  the  naval  branch  of  our 
combined  expedition,  intended  by  my  arrangements  to  participate  in

the  reduction  of  Roanoke  Island  and  operate  elsewhere  in  its  vicinity, 
were  oyer  the  bulkhead  at  Hatteras  Inlet  and  in  readiness  for  service, 
but  owing  to  circumstances  already  communicated  to  the  Department, 
it  was  not  until  the  5th  instant  that  those  composing  the  army  branch 
of  it  were  similarly  situated. 

Ihe  naval  vessels  in  view,  all  of  which  were  placed  bv  me  under  the 
general  command  of  Commander  S.  C.  Rowan,  were ‘the  Stars  and 
Stripes,  Lieutenant  Commanding  Reed  Werden;  Louisiana ,  Lieutenant 
Commanding  A.  Murray;  Hetzel,  Lieutenant  Commanding  H.  K.  Daven¬ 
port;  Underwriter,  Lieutenant  Commanding  William  NT.  Jeffers;  Dela¬ 
ware,  Lieutenant  Commanding  S.  P.  Quackenbush;  Commodore  Perry, 
Lieutenant  Commanding  C.  W.  Flusser;  Valley  City ,  Lieuteuant  Com¬ 
manding  J.  C.  Chaplin;  Commodore  Barney,  Acting  Lieutenant  Com¬ 
manding  R.  T.  Renshaw;  Hunchback,  Acting  Lieutenant  Commanding 
E.  R.  Colhoun;  Southfield ,  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Commanding 
C.  F.  W.  Behm;  Morse,  Acting  Master  Commanding  Peter  Hays; 
Whitehead,  Acting  Master  Commanding  Charles  A.  French;  Lockwood, 
Acting  Master  Commanding  G.  W.  Graves;  Henry  Brinker,  Acting 
Master  Commanding  John  E.  Giddings;  J.  JV.  Seymour,  Acting  Master 
Commanding  F.  S.  Wells;  Ceres,  Acting  Master  Commanding  John 
MacDiarmid;  Putnam,  Acting  Master  Commanding  W.  J.  Hotchkiss; 
Shawsheen,  Acting  Master  Commanding  Thomas  J.  Woodward,  and 
Granite ,  Acting  Master’s  Mate  Commanding  E.  Boomer. 

During  our  detention  at  the  inlet  we  resorted  to  every  means  in  our 
power  to  get  accurate  information  of  the  enemy’s  position  and  prepara¬ 
tion,  and  we  obtained  enough  to  enable  us  to  arrange  our  programme 
of  attack,  which,  in  substance,  was  as  follows: 

The  naval  division  was  to  lead  from  the  time  of  starting  up  to  that 
of  encountering  the  enemy.  The  marshes,  in  case  of  being  defended 
by  a  battery  and  the  enemy’s  vessels,  were  to  be  passed  by,  noticing 
the  former  only  in  a  transitory  way,  and  by  dashing  without  delay 
directly  at  the  latter.  On  approaching  Roanoke  Island  sufficiently 
near,  the  batteries  at  Pork  and  Sandy  [Sand]  points  (if  any  at  the 
latter),  and  the  vessels  of  the  enemy,  if  drawn  up  to  meet  us,  were  to 
be  the  first  objects  assailed  by  the  naval  division,  aided  by  such  fight¬ 
ing  vessels  under  the  general  command  of  Commander  Samuel  F.  Hazard 
as  the  army  division  could  afford.  While  this  work  was  going  on,  the 
army,  under  cover  of  its  own  vessels  and  six  of  our  armed  launches, 
was  to  land  at  Ashby’s  Harbor,  or,  if  preferable,  a  portion  of  it  at 
Sandy  [Sand]  Point,  half  a  mile  above.  In  advancing  from  the  inlet, 
the  vessels  of  both  branches  of  the  expedition  were  to  observe  my 
signals. 

Early  on  the  morning  of  the  5th  the  necessary  general  signals  for  a 
move  were  thrown  out  from  the  Philadelphia,  and  as  soon  afterwards  as 
could  be  expected  for  so  large  a  number  of  vessels,  all  were  underway, 
with  the  naval  division  as  prescribed,  arranged  in  three  columns,  com¬ 
manded  respectively  by  Lieutenants  Commanding  Werden,  Murray, 
and  Davenport.  Although  the  weather  favored  us,  our  progress  was 
unavoidably  slow. 

Apprehending  that  the  buoy  on  the  eastern  extremity  of  Long  Shoal 
Point,  distant  some  20  miles  from  the  inlet,  might  have  been  removed, 
a  steamer  with  the  Granite  in  tow  was  sent  ahead  to  ascertain  the  fact, 
and  if  necessary  to  place  another,  already  prepared,  in  its  stead.  For¬ 
tunately  it  had  not  been  removed.  A  flag,  however,  was  placed  upon 
it,  a  signal  of  caution  was  made,  and  thus  the  shoal,  the  worst  obstruc¬ 
tion  in  the  way,  was  safely  avoided  by  each  and  all. 


552 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


At  sundown,  having  arrived  off  Stumpy  Point,  and  within  10  miles 
of  the  marshes,  the  whole  force  anchored  by  signal,  each  vessel  occu- 
pvinff  as  nearly  as  practicable  the  same  relative  position  toward  the 
rest  as  she  had  done  in  steaming.  Here  it  was  judged  expedient  to 
detail  a  small  party  to  visit  a  certain  house  on  the  mainland  tor  the 
purpose  of  securing,  even  forcibly,  the  services  of  a  certain  individual 
whose  name  had  been  given  to  us  at  the  inlet.  An  officer  took  it  m 
charge,  and  before  midnight  he  brought  the  man  to  me  on  board  the 

Philadelphia.  „  .  ™  , 

Early  the  next  morning,  accompanied  by  the  chief  of  my  Stan  ana 
fleet  captain,  Commander  Augustus  L.  Case,  Captain  s  Clerk  H.  Lr.  L. 
Fisher  as  signal  officer,  with  two  petty  officers  to  assist  him,  and  leu- 
tenants  Thos.  R.  Robeson  and  Nathaniel  S.  Barstow,  of  the  Army 
Signal  Corps,  with  their  party  of  four  men,  I  changed  my  quarters  tem¬ 
porarily  from  the  Philadelphia  to  the  Southfield ,  and  hoistea  my  flag  on 
board  of  her.  In  a  little  while  afterwards  our  whole  force,  by  signal, 
was  again  underway,  with  two  of  our  lighter  draft  steamers,  the  Ceres 
and  Putnam ,  a  mile  or  so  in  advance,  in  order  to  detect  either  the 
enemy  himself,  or  any  obstructions  he  might  have  concealed.  Ihe 
weather  was  now  thick  and  threatening,  and  of  course  bad  for  distant 
discoveries.  About  9  o’clock,  however,  it  cleared,  and  for  a  short  while 
in  the  direction  of  Roanoke  Island,  and  then  for  the  first  time  we  dis¬ 
tinctly  recognized  the  enemy’s  armed  and  other  vessels  lying  at  anchor 
apparently  close  in  with  the  shore,  between  Pork  and  Weir’s  points; 
but  in  an  hour  and  a  half  afterwards,  and  when  within  a  couple  of 
miles  of  the  marshes,  it  again  became  not  only  thick,  but  rainy  and 
windy,  and  this  induced  us  to  anchor  once  more,  still  observing  the  same 
general  order  of  relative  position  that  we  had  done  the  evening  before. 
In  the  course  of  the  afternoon  one  of  the  enemy’s  steamers  approached 
the  marshes  for  the  purpose,  no  doubt,  of  reconnoitering  our  force. 
She  met  with  no  opposition  from  us,  simply  because  we  were  not  unwill¬ 
ing  that  she  should  accomplish  her  wishes. 

The  following  morning,  Friday,  February  7,  at  daylight,  the  weather 
was  more  propitious,  and  the  sky  gave  evident  signs  of  a  clear  day. 
At  9  o’clock,  and  for  the  third  time  since  leaving  the  inlet,  the  whole 
force  was  put  underway  by  another  general  signal.  Besides  the  Ceres 
and  Putnam ,  the  Underwriter  also  was  placed  in  advance,  the  former 
two  to  keep  not  more  than  400  yards  ahead  of  the  flagship,  and  the 
latter  at  a  proper  time  to  go  as  much  beyond  that  distance  as  might 
be  necessary  to  discover  as  early  as  possible  if  a  battery  had  been 
erected  on  Sandy  [Sand]  Point.  The  marshes  were  soon  threaded  and 
astern  of  us.  Their  passageway  is  so  narrow  as  not  to  admit  more  than 
two  vessels  abreast,  and  in  this  order  they  kept  until  it  was  cleared, 
and  the  much  wider  waters  of  Croatan  Sound  were  reached.  Being 
anxious  to  make  a  decided  impression  upon  the  enemy  early  in  the  con¬ 
test,  all  the  vessels  with  9-inch  guns  were  ordered  to  close  up  around 
the  flagship.  At  10:30  a.  m.  the  enemy’s  vessels,  eight  in  number,  all 
being  drawn  up  behind  an  extensive  obstruction,  formed  by  a  double 
row  of  piles  and  sunken  vessels  stretching  well  across  the  sound,  and 
between  the  forts  on  Pork  and  Weir’s  points,  one  of  them  fired  a  heavy 
gun,  probably  intended  to  announce  generally  that  an  attack  was  just 
impending.  In  less  than  an  hour  afterwards,  the  Underwriter ,  failing 
to  draw  a  reply  to  a  shot  she  had  fired,  signaled  u  No  battery  on  Sandy 
[Sand]  Point.”  The  omission  to  guard  this  point  was  favorable  to  the 
arrangement  of  landing  the  troops  at  Ashby’s  Harbor.  Had  it  been 
protected,  our  difficulties  would  have  been  materially  increased.

Not  long  after  tliis  announcement  tlie  naval  division,  composed  and 
commanded  as  stated  above,  accompanied,  as  predetermined,  by  the 
Picket ,  Captain  Thomas  P.  Ives;  Hussar,  Captain  Frederick  Crocker; 
Pioneer ,  Captain  Charles  E.  Baker;  Vidette ,  Captain  John  L.  Foster; 
Ranger ,  Captain  Samuel  Emerson;  Lancer ,  Captain  M.  B.  Morley,  and 
Chasseur,  Captain  John  West,  of  the  army  division,  and,  keeping  in 
close  order,  had  approached  the  enemy  near  enough  to  begin  ' the 
attack  and  to  devote  the  most  of  its  firing  against  the  fort  on  Pork 
Point,  not  neglecting,  however,  the  enemy’s  vessels,  a  battery  between 
Pork  and  Weir’s  points,  and  another  on  Bedstone  Point,  all'  of  which 
opened  upon  us,  but  the  latter  only  occasionally  and  without  effect. 
By  noon,  our  vessels  having  approached  still  nearer,  the  action  became 
general  on  their  part  and  that  of  the  enemy.  At  1:30  p.  m.  the  effect 
of  our  firing  caused  the  barracks  behind  the  fort  at  Pork  Point  to 
burst  into  flames,  and  at  2 : 15  p.  m.  they  were  burning  furiously,  entirely 
beyond  redemption.  About  this  time,  our  vessels  being  placed  by  their 
respective  commanders  as  advantageously  as  circumstances  would  per¬ 
mit,  the  firing  was  the  hottest.  Throughout  the  sound  lying  between 
Boanoke  Island  and  the  mainland  the  depth  of  water  at  best  is  but 
little,  and  the  bottom  everywhere  is  essentially  lumpy  and  irregular. 
Even  at  the  distance  of  a  mile  and  more  from  the  shore  where  we  had 
to  approach,  scarcely  a  general  depth  at  low  water  of  more  than  7  feet 
is  to  be  found.  With  one  or  two  exceptions  none  of  our  vessels  drew 
less  than  7  feet,  and  some  of  them  drew  rather  more  than  8.  In  plac¬ 
ing  them,  therefore,  so  as  to  make  their  various  guns  tell  effectually, 
their  several  commanders  had  to  exercise  a  sound  discretion  and  to 
keep  in  view  the  consideration  due  to  the  use  of  shells  with  fuzes  fixed 
in  value  as  to  time.  To  have  used,  for  instance,  a  5-second  fuze  in 
shelling  uncovered  works  at  a  less  distance  than  about  1,400  yards 
would  not  have  secured  the  best  results. 

Toward  3  p.  m.  the  troops  embarked  on  board  of  light-draft  steamers 
and  boats  started  to  land  at  Ashby’s  Harbor.  The  place  was  guarded 
by  a  large  body  of  the  enemy  with  a  field  battery,  but  the  Delaware, 
with  Commander  Bowan  on  board  and  his  division  flag  at  her  mast¬ 
head,  having  very  judiciously  taken  up  a  flanking  position  to  the  south¬ 
ward  of  Pork  Point  battery,  and  thus  most  opportunely  being  near  at 
hand,  immediately  turned  her  guns  toward  the  harbor,  and  with  some 
9-inch  shrapnels  soon  cleared  the  way.  At  4:30  p.  m.  Pork  Point  bat¬ 
tery  and  the  one  next  to  the  northward  of  it  ceased  for  a  while  to  reply 
to  our  fire;  five  of  the  enemy’s  steamers,  apparently  injured,  went  back 
behind  Weir’s  Point,  and  the  first  landing  of  our  troops  took  place. 
At  5  p.  m.  those  batteries  again  opened  upon  our  vessels,  and  the 
enemy’s  steamers  once  more  put  forth  and  also  reopened  upon  us.  In 
about  forty  minutes,  however,  the  latter  were  compelled  a  second  time 
to  retire.  One  of  them,  the  Curlew ,  in  a  disabled  condition,  had  taken 
refuge  under  the  battery  on  Bedstone  Point.  At  0  p.  m.,  the  firing  of 
the  enemy  being  only  from  Pork  Point  and  at  long  intervals,  dark 
coming  on,  and  not  wishing  to  waste  ammunition,  I  ordered  the  signal 
“cease  firing”  to  be  made.  In  the  course  of  the  afternoon  our  six 
launches,  under  the  command  of  Midshipman  Benjamin  H.  Porter, 
landed  their  howitzers  and  joined  the  army,  for  the  purpose  of  com¬ 
manding  the  main  road  and  its  two  forks  during  the  night  and  assist¬ 
ing  in  more  active  operations  the  following  morning.  By  midnight 
some  10,000  of  our  troops  had  been  safely  landed  at  Ashby’s  Harbor, 
the  Delaware  having  taken  on  board  from  the  Cossack  some  800  and 
put  them  on  shore  at  10  p.  m.

February  8. — As  it  was  arranged  by  General  Burnside  that  his  forces 
should  move  at  a  very  early  hour  this  morning  from  where  they  had 
been  landed  and  begin  their  attack  upon  the  enemy,  and  as  the  direc¬ 
tion  they  were  required  to  take  would  in  all  probability  soon  bring  them 
in  the  line  of  tire  occupied  by  the  navy,  it  was  agreed  between  us  last 
night  that  to-day  the  vessels  should  not  renew  operations  until  I  could 
receive  word  from  him  that  their  missiles  would  not  be  destructive  to 
both  friends  and  foes.  At  daylight  none  of  the  enemy’s  vessels  except 
the  Curlew  could  be  discovered. 

At  9  a.  m.  a  continuous  firing  in  the  interior  of  the  island  told  us 
that  our  forces  were  hotly  engaged  about  midway  between  Ashby’s 
Harbor  and  Pork  Point  battery,  and  as  this  intelligence  also  assured 
«s  that  our  land  forces  were  not  then  in  the  range  of  our  line  of  fire, 
our  vessels,  without  waiting  to  hear  from  General  Burnside,  at  once 
moved  up  and  reengaged  the  forts.  At  this  work  they  continued  until 
the  firing  in  the  interior  evidently  slackened.  Then,  taking  it  for 
granted  that  our  troops  were  carrying  everything  before  them,  and 
thus  fast  approaching  the  rear  of  the  batteries,  I  again  ordered  the 
signal  u  cease  firing”  to  be  made.  At  the  time,  however,  the  work  on 
Pork  Point  was  so  reduced  that  it  did  not  use  but  one  gnu  against  us. 
Shortly  afterwards,  on  being  informed  by  one  of  General  Burnside’s 
aids  of  the  actual  state  of  things  on  shore,  I  was  induced  to  order 
another  demonstration  on  the  part  of  our  vessels,  but  before  firing  had 
generally  commenced  Commander  Rowan  came  on  board  the  Southfield , 
just  from  General  Burnside,  with  the  suggestion  that  it  would  be  better 
to  desist,  and  accordingly  they  were  recalled. 

At  1  p.  m.,  judging  that  the  time  had  arrived  for  clearing  a  passage¬ 
way  through  the  obstructions  alluded  to  above,  by  the  accomplishment 
of  which  both  the  battery  on  Redstone  Point  and  the  Curlew  might  be 
destroyed  and  our  advance  up  Albemarle  Sound  would  be  secured,  the 
Underwriter ,  Valley  City ,  Seymour ,  Lockwood ,  Ceres ,  Shaw  sheen ,  Put¬ 
nam,  Whitehead ,  and  Brinker  were  ordered  to  perform  the  service.  By 
4  p.  m.  one  of  them  had  overcome  the  difficulty  for  herself  and  reached 
the  other  side,  and  in  less  than  an  hour  more  a  sufficient  way  for  all 
the  rest  was  opened.  This  important  duty  could  not  have  been  under¬ 
taken  a  moment  earlier  than  it  was  without  exposing  our  vessels,  hud¬ 
dled  together,  to  the  converging  and  cross  fire  of  the  four  batteries  at 
Pork,  Weir’s,  and  Redstone  points,  and  another  one  situated  between  the 
former  two.  About  the  same  time  that  our  vessels  succeeded  in  burst¬ 
ing  through  the  barricades  the  American  flag  was  hoisted  over  the 
battery  at  Pork  Point,  and  in  a  few  minutes  afterward  the  enemy  him¬ 
self  fired  the  works  at  Redstone  Point,  and  also  the  steamer  Curlew . 
Both  blew  up  in  the  early  part  of  the  evening.  These  events  closed 
the  struggle,  which  had  now  lasted  throughout  two  days,  and  were 
essentially  the  last  scenes  enacted  in  securing  to  us  complete  posses¬ 
sion  of  the  island  of  Roanoke. 

A  statement  of  the  casualties  which  occurred  will  accompany  this 
communication.  They  amount,  in  all,  to  0  killed,  17  wounded,  and  2 
missing.  Considering  how  frequently  our  vessels  were  struck  it  is 
remarkable  that  more  did  not  take  place,  and  considering  the  character 
of  our  vessels  it  is  also  remarkable  that  none  of  them  were  even  put 
hors  de  combat  except  temporarily. 

It  now  remains  for  me  to  discharge  the  gratifying  duty  of  speakin°' 
of  the  officers  and  men  under  my  command  on  the  occasion  in  view. 
This,  ob\iously,  I  can  only  do,  as  it  were,  in  a  collective  way;  but  the 
reports  of  the  commanding  officers,  herewith  submitted,  upon  which 
necessarily  I  have  to  rely  and  in  which  I  place  every  confidence,  will 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  555 

be  found  more  circumstantial.  I  beg  to  commend  them  to  your  consid¬ 
eration.  The  commanding  officers  themselves  did  their  part  entirely 

o  my  satisfaction,  and  in  fact  in  a  most  admirable  manner.  The 
genei al  Older  I  issued  the  day  after  the  surrender,  a  copy  of  which 
accompanied  my  preliminary  report,  was  intended  to  convey  applause 
and  my  profound  gratitude  to  all  to  whom  it  relates,  and  i  therefore 
beg  that  it  may  be  so  regarded  by  the  Navy  Department.  I  pray,  too, 
that  to  the  bereaved  individuals,  whose  support  and  comfort  depended 
upon  those  who  are  now  among  the  honored  dead,  may  be  extended  the 
earliest  fostering  care  that  circumstances  will  permit. 

It  is  really  difficult  for  me  to  state  in  adequate  terms  how  largely  I 
feel  myself  indebted  to  Commanders  Rowan  and  Case  for  their  constant 
and  signal  services  throughout,  from  the  very  inception  of  the  expedi¬ 
tion  to  the  consummation  of  the  achievement  in  view.  They  hand  in 
hand,  with  their  marked  ability  and  sound  sense,  and  in  the  absence  of 
all  ordinary  facilities,  brought  about  at  Hampton  Roads  the  arming, 
manning,  and  equipment  of  the  many  vessels  sent  to  us  from  necessity 
m  an  unprepared  condition,  and  subsequently  they  both  labored  most 
conspicuously  and  faithfully  in  their  respective  spheres  of  action  to 
vanquish  difficulties  at  the  inlet  and  the  enemy  at  Roanoke.  In  short 
their  assistance  to  me  has  been  invaluable. 

I  am  promised  a  report  by  General  Burnside  with  regard  to  Midship¬ 
man  Porter’s  association  with  his  forces,  and  as  soon  as  it  comes  to 
hand  I  will,  with  pleasure,  forward  it  to  the  Department. 

Although  the  Philadelphia  did  not  participate  in  the  action,  because 
of  her  unfitness  for  the  purpose,  still  she  was  ever  near  at  hand  in 
readiness,  if  necessary,  to  tow  the  disabled,  receive  some  of  the 
wounded,  and  furnish  supplies.  Her  commander,  Acting  Master  Silas 
Reynolds,  is  every  way  worthy  of  his  trust. 

Mr.  Fisher  performed  the  important  duties  of  signal  officer  in  the 
most  commendable  manner.  Not  only  were  all  the  signals  ordered 
promptly  made,  but  no  mistake  whatever  occurred. 

Lieutenants  Robeson  and  Barstow,  of  the  Army,  were  ever  in  place, 
and  ready,  by  means  of  Myer’s  system  of  signals,  to  make  known  to 
those  not  accustomed  to  our  own  code  whatever  I  wished. 

It  will  afford  me  peculiar  pleasure,  sir,  to  communicate  to  you,  in 
due  season,  more  particular  information  with  regard  to  the  cases  of 
individuals  which  appear  to  me  to  merit  a  distinct  consideration  on  the 
part  of  the  Government. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Flag-Officer,  Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles,

Report  of  Lieutenant  Murray,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  second  column,  transmitting  an  account 
of  ammunition  expended  by  the  U.  S.  S.  Louisiana. 


U.  S.  S.  Louisiana, 

Fear  Roanoke  Island,  February  8,  1862. 

Sir  :  On  the  morning  of  the  7th,  in  obedience  to  signal,  I  got  under¬ 
way  with  the  column  under  my  command  and,  in  company  with  the 
main  body  of  the  naval  forces,  passed  through  the  marshes  without 
accident  to  any  vessel,  except  the  one  under  my  immediate  command, 
which  struck  au  obstruction  in  the  channel,  swung  entirely  round 
bearing  her  weight  upon  the  propeller. 

Whilst  in  this  position  I  hastened  to  the  advance,  to  sustain  the  flag- 
officer,  the  9-inch  gun  vessels. 

A\  hen  the  naval  division  of  the  fleet  had  passed,  our  vessel,  with  the 
aid  of  the  Seymour,  was  (with  the  loss  of  a  flange  from  her  propeller) 
clear,  and,  to  the  great  satisfaction  of  officers  and  crew,  we  overtook 
our  position  and  were  enabled  to  close  with  the  enemy’s  fortifications 
and  share  with  the  other  two  columns  in  a  bombardment  which  has 
ended  in  a  victory  creditable  to  our  arms  and,  what  is  better,  of  incal¬ 
culable  benefit  to  our  cause. 

The  Louisiana,  early  in  the  action,  was  set  on  fire  and  otherwise 
severely  injured  by  the  explosion  of  an  80-pound  rifled  projectile  fired 
from  the  enemy’s  works  into  her  forehold.  In  six  minutes  from  the 
time  she  was  struck  the  fire  was  out  and  the  ship  reengaged  the  enemy. 
The  promptitude  and  coolness  with  which  the  officers  and  men,  under 
the  enemy’s  fire  and  amid  so  much  that  was  combustible  around  them, 
went  to  the  duty  of  extinguishing  the  flames  was  extremely  gratifying 
to  me  as  an  exhibition  of  high  discipline.  It  is  my  greatest  pleasure 
as  well  as  duty  to  say  that  during  the  two  days’  action  I  had  occasion 
only  to  admire  the  untiring  patience  and  cheerful  courage  of  both 
officers  and  crew. 

The  Barney  took  a  position  which  Acting  Lieutenant  Eenshaw 
thought  most  suitable  for  the  efficiency  oi  his  IX-inch  guns,  and  main¬ 
tained  it  until  his  shell  were  expended.  The  fire  of  the  Barney  was 
excellent. 

The  Hunchback ,  Acting  Lieutenant  Colhoun,  took  a  position  very 
near  the  batteries  and  sustained  considerable  damage  from  the  fire  of 
the  enemy,  which  she  is  now  repairing.  During  the  whole  of  the 
engagement,  and  in  spite  of  her  injuries,  she  maintained  her  proximity 
to  the  enemy,  to  his  great  apparent  embarrassment  and  to  the  admira¬ 
tion  of  the  other  ships. 


558 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


The  Seymour  and  Lockwood ,  Acting  Masters  Commanding  [F.  S.] 
Wells  and  [G.  W.]  Graves,  were  conspicuously  in  the  foreground 
throughout  the  bombardment,  these  gentlemen  meriting  my  entire 
satisfaction. 

The  sloop  Granite ,  Master’s  Mate  Boomer,  commanding,  left  out  in

list  of  officers.

A.  Murray,

Report  of  Lieutenant  Davenport,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  third  column,  transmitting  report 

of  casualties  on  the  U.  S.  S.  Hetzel. 

G.  S.  S.  Hetzel, 

Croatan  Sound,  North  Carolina,  February  9,  1862. 
Sir:  I  beg  leave  to  make  the  following  report: 

Being  at  anchor  in  Pamlico  Sound  above  the  swash  at  8  a.  m.  of 
Thursday,  the  6th  instant,  in  pursuance  of  signal  got  underway  and 
steamed  slowly  up  the  sound  iu  order  of  three  columns,  as  directed. 


United  States  Steamer  Hetzel. 
Made  from  crude  water-color  drawing. 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


559 


At  5:30  p.  m.  a  strange  steamer  reported  in  sight. 

At  5:55  p.  in.,  in  obedience  to  order,  came  to  anchor  near  marshes 
at  lower  end  of  Eoanoke  Island. 

At  10  a.  m.  of  Friday,  the  7th,  got  underway  and  steamed  through 
the  marshes  in  two  columns,  as  directed. 

At  10:30  a.  in.  saw  eight  of  the  enemy’s  gunboats  lying  above  a  bat 
tery  at  Pork  Point,  on  Eoanoke  Island,  and  behind  a  line  of  obstruc¬ 
tions  consisting  of  spiles  driven  and  vessels  sunk  across  the  channel 
in  range  of  this  battery.  Obeyed  signal  “To  follow  and  engage  the 
enemy.” 

At  11 : 38  a.  m.  a  shot  was  fired  from  one  of  the  enemy’s  gunboats, 
answered  by  one  of  our  vessels.  The  battery  soon  opened"  and,  the 
order  being  given  “To  close  in  upon  the  enemy,”  the  firing  became 
general. 

At  1  p.  m.  a  shot  from  one  of  the  guns  carried  away  the  upper  part 
of  the  enemy’s  flagstaff,  bringing  his  flag  down  by  the  run;  it  was  soon 
replaced,  however,  on  a  smaller  staff'  on  the  breastwork. 

At  1:30  ii.  m.  enemy’s  quarters  near  the  battery  set  on  fire  by 
exploding  shell. 

At  2: 10  p.  in.  a  32-pounder  round  shot  struck  us  on  the  water  line, 
just  abaft  the  starboard  wheel,  lodging  in  the  coal  bunker  of  that  side. 
Signaled  the  fact  to  the  flagship  and  withdrew  from  action  to  repair 
damages. 

At  2:40  p.  m.,  having  temporarily  repaired  the  injury  sustained, 
went  again  into  action.* 

At  4: 05  p.  m.  a  rifle  shell  from  one  of  the  enemy’s  vessels  exploded 
over  us,  and  one  of  the  fragments  striking  Master’s  Mate  Charles 
Harris  on  the  head,  killed  him  instantly. 

At  5:15  p.  m.  our  80-pounder  rifled  gun  aft  burst  in  the  act  of  firing 
a  solid  shot,  prostrating  every  man  at  the  piece  and  wounding  six  of 
them,  three  severely,  but  fortunately  killing  none.  The  part  forward 
of  the  trunnions  fell  upon  the  deck ;  one-third  of  the  breech  went  over¬ 
board,  carrying  away  the  port  bulwarks;  another  flew  high  into  the 
air  and  fell  into  the  water  just  alongside;  and  the  remaining  portion, 
weighing  about  1,000  pounds,  was  driven  through  the  deck,  breaking 
in  one  of  the  beams,  passed  through  the  magazine  and  the  deck  below, 
and  lodged  upon  the  keelson.  The  magazine  was  set  on  fire  and  only 
extinguished  in  time  to  avoid  an  explosion  and  utter  destruction  of  the 
ship  aud  all  on  board  by  the  presence  of  mind,  promptitude,  and  intre¬ 
pidity  of  Lieutenant  Charles  L.  Franklin,  executive  officer,  whom  I 
beg  to  recommend  to  your  especial  consideration  and  that  of  the 
Department. 

Eeported  accident  to  flagship,  and  at  6  p.  m.  anchored  beyond  range 
of  the  enemy’s  guns. 

On  Saturday,  the  8th,  at  8:30  a.  m.,  went  in  and  reported  to  Com¬ 
mander  Eowan,  aud  at  9  a.  m.  went  alongside  steamer  Philadelphia  and 
received  on  board  carpenters  to  repair  damages  sustained  by  bursting 
of  gun. 

Proceeded  thence  to  sloop  Granite  and  took  from  her  a  long  32- 
pouuder  with  shot  and  shell;  left  her  side  at  3  p.  m.  and  anchored 
near  by. 

At  1  p.  m.  Master  Daniels  left  the  ship  for  the  purpose  of  taking 
command  of  party  with  launch  howitzers,  appointed  to  act  in  concert 
with  the  land  forces. 

At  3:30  p.  m.  the  body  of  Mr.  Harris  was  taken  on  shore  at  Eoanoke 
Island  and  solemnly  interred. 


560 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


At  4:30  p.m.  observed  the  American  flag  flying  over  the  battery, 
the  enemy  having  abandoned  it.  . 

Where  all  behaved  with  such  coolness  and  courage  and  devotion  m 
sustaining  the  honor  of  our  flag,  it  is  difficult  to  discriminate;  but  I 
can  not  refrain  from  expressing  my  high  appreciation  of  the  conduct, 
both  professional  and  otherwise,  of  Acting  Assistant  Surgeon  N.  L. 
Campbell,  who,  being  the  first  to  discover  the  ship  to  be  on  fire,  sent 
the  men  to  the  hose,  directed  the  engineer  to  turn  on  the  water,  and 
then  gave  his  attention  to  the  wounded,  inspiring  the  men  by  his 
coolness 

Acting  Assistant  Paymaster  E.  P.  Hebevton,  although  quite  unwell, 
volunteered  to  act  as  signal  officer  ana  to  take  the  notes  ot  the  action; 
and  I  must  acknowledge  the  faithful  manner  in  which  he  performed 
those  duties.  At  the  moment  of  our  gun  bursting  he  was  standing 
near  by,  and,  although  escaping  unwounded,  was  severely  shaken  by 
the  concussion. 

The  engineer  department  was  managed  in  a  manner  that  excited 
my  warmest  praises. 

In  conclusion,  I  beg  leave  to  express  my  thanks  to  all  my  officers  and 
men  for  their  conduct  in  the  action. 

I  enclose  herewith  the  surgeon’s  report  of  casualties,  and  have  the 
honor  to  remain,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

H.  K.  Davenport, 

Lieutenant,  Commanding. 

Commander  S.  C.  Rowan,  IT.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  Flotilla,  etc.,  Groatan  Sound,  North  Carolina.

U.  S.  S.  Hetzel, 

Croatan  Sound,  North  Carolina,  February  7,  1862. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  following  casualties  on  board 
this  ship  during  the  engagement  of  to-day: 

Killed. — 1.  Mr.  Charles  Harris,  acting  master’s  mate,  by  explosion  of 
shell. 

Wounded. — 1.  Charles  Clarke,  boatswain’s  mate,  severely.  2.  Joseph 
1ST.  Ingersoll,  ordinary  seaman,  severely.  3.  William  Smith,  ordinary 
seaman,  severely.  4.  Henry  Bryant,  ordinary  seaman,  slightly.  5. 
Tully  McIntyre,  seaman,  slight  contusion.  6.  Henry  P.  Thompson, 
coal  passer,  slightly. 

The  wounded  all  sustained  their  injuries  by  the  bursting  of  our  rifled 
80-pounder  Dahlgren  gun. 

Respectfully  submitted. 

N.  L.  Campbell, 

Acting  Assistant  Surgeon,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Lieutenant  H.  K.  Davenport, 

Commanding  U.  S.  S.  Hetzel,  Croatan  Sound,  North  Carolina.

Report  of  Lieutenant  Jeffers,  IT.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Underwriter. 

U.  S.  S.  Underwriter, 

Off  Roanoke  Island ,  February  9,  1862. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  submit  the  following  report  of  the  operations 
ol  this  vessel  curing  the  two  days  preceding  the  capture  of  Eoanoke 
Island  and  dependent  fortifications. 

At  10  a.  m.  on  the  7th  I  weighed  in  obedience  to  your  instructions 
and  led  m,  accompanied  by  the  Ceres  on  one  bow  and  the  Putnam  on 
the  other,  to  define  the  limits  of  the  channel  and  pilot  the  fleet  The 
latter  vessel  soon  grounded  on  the  west  side  of  the  channel,  but  mv 
pilot  proving  an  excellent  one  I  kept  in  the  best  water,  and  about  10:30 
on  passing  the  marshes,  discovered  the  enemy’s  vessels,  which  were 
subsequently  found  to  be  drawn  up  behind  a  barricade  of  sunken  ves¬ 
sels  and  piles  stretching  entirely  across  the  sound,  supported  at  each 
extremity  by  formidable  batteries.  On  discovering  the  advance  of  the 
flotilla  the  rebels  fired  an  alarm  gun. 

V  hen  distant  about  2£  miles,  I  fired  a  shell,  and  subsequently  a 
second  one  at  the  fort,  but  did  not  provoke  a  reply.  On  your  coming 
up  abeam  m  the  Southfield ,  the  rebel  vessels  opened  fire,  which  was 
deliberately  returned.  As  the  other  vessels  gradually  came  up  and  the 
N  w  R— VOL  6 - 3G

channel  widened  sufficiently  for  maneuvering,  the  action  became  gen¬ 
eral  with  vessels  and  forts,  the  former  retiring  before  us. 

As  your  instructions  required  me  to  direct  my  attention  to  the ^ves¬ 
sels,  I  moved  up  quite  near  the  barricade,  but  soon  found  that  then 
batteries  were  carefully  constructed,  and  as  I  approached  I  remarked 
gun  after  gun  firing  through  embrasures,  four  ot  which  I  ascertained 
enfiladed  the  barricade.  As  it  was  no  part  of  the  plan  of  attack  to 
force  the  barricade  before  the  reduction  of  the  forts  or  their  serious 
iniurv,  I  allowed  my  vessel  to  drop  back  with  the  current  to  a  position 
where  but  two  guns  bore  upon  her;  these  only  fired  at  me  occasionally. 

The  vessels,  however,  kept  up  a  continued  fire  on  the  most  advanced 
vessels  on  the  left  of  our  line.  In  return  I  made  the  most  deliberate 
firing,  averaging  a  shot  from  each  of  my  rifled  guns  about  once  m  eight 

A  fort  on  Bedstone  Point,  also  one  at  Weir’s  Point,  occasionally  fired 
a  rilled  gun  at  us,  but  at  a  range  too  distant  for  any  effect  except  by 

mere  chance.  ~.  T 

About  3  p.  m.,  the  rebel  steamers  being  a  long  distance  off,  I  edged 
over  toward  the  battery  and  fired  a  dozen  8-inch  shells,  most  of  which 
made  good  practice;  then  returned  to  my  station,  which  I  retained  until 
the  general  signal  to  cease  firing  was  made. 

The  next  morning  I  went  up  and  exchanged  a  few  shots  with  the  bat¬ 
teries,  but  ceased  upon  the  recall  being  made. 

In  the  afternoon,  with  the  steamers  placed  under  my  orders,  viz, 
Underwriter  Valley  City,  Seymour ,  Lockwood,  Ceres ,  Shaw  sheen,  Putnam, 
Whitehead ,  and  Brinker ,  I  proceeded  to  the  barricade  for  the  purpose 
of  removing  a  sufficient  number  of  piles  to  allow  the  passage  ot  the 

vessels  of  the  squadron.  .  T  ,  . 

The  principal  difficulty  consisted  in  finding  the  channel.  In  doing 
this  the  Putnam  grounded,  and  as  she  was  in  a  most  exposed  position, 
if  a  rebel  steamer  lying  at  Redstone  Point  had  advanced,  I  anchored 
and  sent  other  tugs  to  assist  in  getting  her  off.  In  the  meanwhile  I 
sent  boats  to  sound,  and  soon  discovered  several  points  of  passage  prac¬ 
ticable  after  removing  a  few  piles. 

The  Ceres,  however,  which  I  had  sent  on  that  duty,  found  a  passage 
of  sufficient  width  between  an  unfinished  row  of  piles  and  a  sunken 
schooner.  On  this  fact  being  reported  to  me,  I  sent  her  v  ith  se\  era!  of 
the  pilots  to  pass  through  it,  examine  beyond,  and  fix  the  position  of  the 
northeast  point  of  Fulker’s  Shoals.  She  had  passed  about  a  quarter  of 
a  mile  beyond  the  barricade  when  I  observed  some  200  men  in  squads 
running  down  to  a  battery  plainly  visible  near  Weir’s  Point.  I  imme¬ 
diately  recalled  her. 

While  deliberating  on  the  propriety  of  passing  through  the  opening 
thus  discovered,  and  exposing  the  vessels  to  the  converging  and  cross 
fire  of  the  batteries  at  Pork,  Weir’s,  and  Redstone  points,  our  flag  was 
seen  entering  the  battery  at  Pork  Point.  I  immediately  got  underway 
and  passed  the  barricade,  touching  for  a  short  time  on  a  wreck,  owing  to 
one  of  the  other  vessels  getting  athwart  my  bows.  As  soon  as  it  was  per¬ 
ceived  that  we  were  passing  the  barricade  the  rebels  fired  the  buildings 
and  subsequently  exploded  the  magazine  of  the  fort  on  Redstone  Point. 
The  steamer  lying  there  was  also  fired,  showing  that  she  must  have 
been  disabled  by  our  fire  of  yesterday.  While  I  was  fast  closing  the 
passage  the  Lockwood  cut  the  chain  fastening  two  vessels  together  and 
floated  one  of  them  out,  thus  clearing  a  passage  for  herself  and  other 
vessels,  and  the  Valley  City  made  a  dash  at  a  row  of  piles  and  forced  a 
passage  between  them.

Report  of  Lieutenant  Quackenbush,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Delaware. 

U.  S.  S.  Delaware, 

Off  Roanoke  Island ,  February  9 ,  1862. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  herewith  submit  to  you  the  following  report  • 

On  the  7th  day  of  February,  1862,  at  10  a.  m.,  the  II.  S.  S.  Delaware, j 
in  obedience  to  a  general  signal  from  the  IJ.  S.  flagship  Southfield ,  got 
underway  and  proceeded  through  the  marshes  toward  the  battery  on 
Roanoke  Island,  known  as  Fort  Sullivan  or  Pig  [Pork]  Point,  mounting 
nine  guns,  which  fort  we  attacked  at  11 : 30  a.  in.,  and  continued  the  fire, 
gradually  closing  in  until  about  3  p.  m.,  when  we  ran  within  a  ship’s 
length,  of  the  shore  for  the  purpose  of  flanking  the  fort,  from  which 
position  we  rendered  good  service  by  throwing  shell  of  5-second  fuze. 

About  this  time  I  left  the  vessel  accompanied  by  my  acting  aid  Act¬ 
ing  Assistant  Paymaster  F.  E.  Curtis,  landed  on  Eoanoke  Island,  dis¬ 
tant  some  1,000  yards  from  Fort  Sullivan,  and  took  possession  of  a  rebel 
tent,  bringing  the  same  on  board,  after  which,  observing  a  light-draft 
army  transport  containing  IT.  S.  troops  proceeding  toward  the  shore 
we  ran  down  for  tlie  purpose  of  covering  their  landing,  which  object  we 
fully  accomplished  by  driving  off  with  shell  a  large  number  of  Con¬ 
federate  troops,  secreted  in  the  woods  in  close  proximity  to  our  landing 

plclC0« 

At  5:15  p.  m.  reported  to  the  flagship  and  then  landed  the  Fifty-first 
Pennsylvania  Regiment,  successfully  accomplishing  it  by  8  p.  m.,  when 
we  hauled  off  and  anchored  some  100  yards  from  the  shore,  remaining 
there  during  the  night  for  the  purpose  of  protecting  the  troops  that  had 
already  landed. 

The  following  morning,  at  the  request  of  General  Burnside,  sent  Act¬ 
ing  Master  Chase  in  command  of  ten  soldiers  of  the  Ninth  New  Jersey 
Regiment  and  two  boats’  crews  on  shore  for  the  purpose  of  reconnoiter- 
iug.  They  were  accompanied  by  Captain  D’Wolf,  IT.  S.  Army,  and 
returned  at  11  a.  m. 

After  which,  and  during  the  afternoon,  rendered  assistance  to  the 
wounded  on  shore  by  sending  them  the  necessary  medical  attendance, 
warm  water,  etc. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  P.  Quackenbush, 

Lieutenant ,  Commanding. 

Stephen  C.  Rowan, 

Commanding  U.  S.  Flotilla  in  Pamlico  Sound.

Abstract  log  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Delaware. 

February  7,  1862.— At  9:30  a.  m.  got  underway  and  proceeded  on 
cautiously  toward  tlie  enemy's  batteries  on  the  western  end  of  the 
island.  Opened  Are  at  11:30  with  rifle  howitzer  with  shell.  IX-mcli 
gun  opened  lire  a  few  moments  later,  and  the  32-pounder  at  12:30  p.  in. 
Ceased  firing  at  4.  At  3  launched  the  gig,  in  command  of  Commander 
Quackenbush,  and  went  ashore  within  1  mile  of  the  enemy.  Took  pos¬ 
session  and  brought  off  to  the  ship  one  soldiers’  tent.  Retreated  back 
to - at  4:30,  and  landed  troops  of  Fifty-first  Pennsylvania  Regi¬ 

ment,  taken  off  transport  steamer. 

February  8.— At  12:30  p.  m.  ran  to  the  Southfield,  flagship;  proceeded 
to  shore  opposite  temporary  hospital;  sent  surgeon  and  men  to  assist 
the  wounded.  Backed  out  from  shore  and  ran  to  upper  fort,  which  had 
been  taken  possession  of  by  General  Burnside.  Took  the  general  off 
in  our  gig  to  the  flagship.  Returned  to  the  shore  at  8 : 30. 


Report  of  Lieutenant  Flusser,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  IT.  S.  S.  Commodore  Perry. 

U.  S.  S.  Commodore  Perry, 

Off  Elizabeth  City ,  February  16,  1862. 

Sir:  In  the  action  at  Roanoke  Island,  on  the  7th  instant,  we  fired 
two  shots  at  the  enemy’s  steamers  at  long  range  at  thirty  minutes  past 
noon,  and  then  closed  in  and  opened  fire  on  the  battery. 

At  4  p.  m.  ran  out  of  fire,  loaded  our  remaining  shells,  and  resumed 
our  position. 

Fired  during  the  day  172  IX-inch  shells  and  20  shrapnel,  at  distances 
from  2,000  to  800  yards. 

We  were  hit  by  round  shot  from  the  battery  seven  times,  five  times 
in  the  hull.  One  shot  passed  through  the  magazine  and  through  an 
empty  powder  tank,  another  went  between  the  engine  and  boiler  and 
through  one  of  the  water  tanks;  two  shots  struck  the  starboard  wheel. 
We  were  not  materially  injured. 

Andrew  Horton,  private,  Company  D,  Fourth  Rhode  Island  Volun¬ 
teers,  had  a  leg  broken  by  a  splinter.  Xo  other  casualties.  My  officers 
and  men  behaved  well. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  W.  Flusser, 
Lieutenant,  Command, toy. 

Commander  S.  C.  Rowan,  U.  S.  Navy.
