U.  S.  S.  Commodore  Perry, 

Cobbs  1  oint  Battery ,  Pasquotank  River ,  February  16,  1862. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  as  follows  concerning  this  vessel  in 
the  action  with  the  Pork  Point  battery  and  the  rebel  fleet,  on  the  7th 

At  thirty  minutes  past  noon  fired  two  shells  at  one  of  the  enemy’s 
steamers,  and  then  closed  in  and  opened  fire  on  the  battery.  At  4  p 
m.,  haying  fired  away  all  our  loaded  shell  and  shrapnel,  ran  out  of 
range,  loaded  the  remainder,  and  resumed  our  former  position.  Fired 
away  our  last  charge  of  powder  just  as  the  signal  was  made  to  cease 

ling.  A  e  threw  170  shells  and  20  shrapnel  at  the  battery,  at  dis¬ 
tances  varying  from  2,000  to  800  yards,  and  fuzes  from  fifteen  second 
to  three  second. 

I  fired  the  greater  number  of  the  shots  myself,  and  I  think  our  fire 
was  very  good.  Acting  Master’s  Mate  Henry  Smith,  at  the  after  gun, 
fired  excellently  well.  We  were  struck  eight  or  nine  times  by  round 
shot,  one  shot  passing  through  the  magazine  and  through  two  empty 
powder  tanks,  another  between  the  engine  and  machinery  and  through 
one  of  our  two  water  tanks. 

Had  the  enemy  fired  shell  instead  of  round  shot  we  must  have  been 
destroyed.  As  it  was,  I  have  no  serious  injury  of  the  vessel  to  report. 

Providence  was  on  our  side,  and  I  have  only  one  serious  accident  to 
mention.  Andrew  Horton,  private,  Company  D,  Fourth  Rhode  Island 
\  olunteers,  was  shotman  at  one  of  the  guns,  and  had  a  leg  broken  by 
a  splinter.  My  officers  and  men  behaved  well. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  etc.,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  W.  Flusser, 
Lieutenant,  Commanding.

Abstract  log  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Commodore  Perry. 

February  7, 1862. — Entrance  to  Croatan  Sound.  At  30  minutes  p.  m. 
fired  the  first  shot  at  the  enemy.  At  4  p.  m.  fired  the  last  loaded  shell",’ 
withdrew  and  loaded  the  last  remaining  hollow  shot,  and  returned  again 
in  range  of  the  enemy  and  opened  a  fresh  fire  on  the  battery.  Nine 
shot  pierced  our  vessel.  One  shot  went  through  our  shell  room,  but  did 
not  do  much  damage.  One  man  slightly  wounded.  At  6,  fired  our  last 
charge  of  powder  and  hauled  off. 

February  8.— At  4:40  p.  m.  the  stars  and  stripes  floated  from  the 
rebel  battery.  At  4:55  the  magazine  exploded  in  the  rebel  battery. 


Report  of  Lieutenant  Chaplin,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Valley  City. 

U.  S.  S.  Valley  City, 

Off  Elizabeth  City,  A.  C.,  February  10,  1862. 
Sir  :  I  respectfully  beg  to  submit  the  following  report  of  the  action 
taken  by  this  vessel  in  the  reduction  of  Roanoke  Island,  North  Carolina, 
on  the  7th  and  8th  days  of  February,  1862: 

February  7. — At  9  a.  nu,  agreeably  to  the  instructions  of  Commander 
H.  K.  Davenport,  commanding  the  third  column,  I  took  a  position 


566 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


astern  of  the  II.  8.  S.  Putnam ,  steaming  along  the  southern  shore  of 
Roanoke  Island. 

At  meridian,  in  obedience  to  general  signal  to  u  close  with  the  enemy,” 
I  ran  this  vessel  within  three-quarters  of  a  mile  of  the  shore,  and  engaged 
the  rebel  battery  in  company  with  U.  S.  steamers  Commodore  Perry , 
Morse ,  Whitehead ,  and  Brinker. 

On  the  second  exchange  of  the  enemy’s  fire  a  round  shot  struck  the 
foremast  of  this  vessel,  grazing  it  nearly  to  the  core,  rendering  the  mast, 
I  consider,  unable  to  bear  the  weight  of  the  foresail. 

At  2  p.  m.  the  enemy’s  fort  was  set  on  fire  by  the  shells  from  this  and 
the  other  vessels  with  whom  we  were  in  company. 

At  3  p.  m.  the  flames  within  the  enemy’s  fort  raging  fiercely,  and  their 
fire  having  considerably  slackened,  I  ran  this  vessel  a  quarter  of  a  mile 
nearer  shore,  keeping  up  a  brisk  fire  of  shell  and  round  shot  against 
the  fort.  Received  exchanges  of  the  fire  from  two  guns  on  the  eastern 
angle  of  the  enemy’s  battery. 

At4p.  m.,  the  enemy  keeping  up  only,  a  desultory  fire,  continued 
replying  to  it  until  I  had  expended  all  the  shells  I  had  on  board.  I  then 
resorted  to  round  shot  and  continued  the  fire  until  5 : 30,  when,  in  obe¬ 
dience  to  signal,  I  retired  out  of  range  and  came  to  anchor,  having 
expended  as  follows : 


184  6-pound  charges,  32-pounder. 

99  1-pound  charges,  12-pound  rifle  how¬ 
itzer. 

99  5- second  shells,  32-pounder. 


40  10-second  shells,  32-pounder. 
32  15-second  shells,  32-pounder. 
14  32-pound  solid  shots. 

105  12-pounder  rifle  shells. 


In  the  evening  I  received  from  schooner  Hartvood  the  following  sup¬ 
ply  of  ammunition : 


300  pounds  cannon  powder.

I  am  happy  to  report  no  casualties  during  the  day  on  board  this  ves¬ 
sel,  the  enemy’s  shot  generally  flying  too  high. 

I  take  pleasure  in  bringing  under  your  notice  the  very  able  assistance 
rendered  me  by  Master’s  Mates  Benjamin  Page  and  Charles  W.  Camp¬ 
bell,  and  the  unflinching  devotion  to  their  duty,  evinced  generally  by 
the  other  officers  and  the  crew  under  my  command  throughout  this  day. 

February  8. — At  10  a.  m.,  in  obedience  to  signal,  I  got  this  vessel 
underway,  stood  toward  the  shore,  and  again  opened  fire  on  the  rebel 
battery,  the  enemy  returning  gun  for  gun.  After  expending  18  6-pound 
charges,  32-pounder;  3  32-pound  solid  shots,  10  10-second  shells, 
32-pounder;  6  15-second  shells,  32-pounder,  and  3  Hotchkiss  percussion 
shells,  in  obedience  to  signal  from  flag-officer,  I  retired  out  of  range, 
steamed  alongside  the  flagship  and  received  orders  to  report  for  duty  to 
Captain  Jeffers,  of  the  steamer  Underwriter. 

Having  received  orders  to  follow  him  up  the  sound,  got  underway 
and  proceeded  up  the  sound.  Came  to  anchor  in  company  with  the 
other  vessels  of  the  flotilla. 

Upon  request  of  Captain  Jeffers  I  dispatched  two  boats  under  charge 
of  Master’s  Mates  Brooks  and  Page  with  our  pilot  to  unmask  the  chan¬ 
nel,  which  was  obstructed  by  a  row  of  piles,  reaching  from  shore  to  shore. 

The  channel  having  been  discovered,  got  underway  in  the  evening  in 
company  with  the  other  vessels,  stood  across  the  piles,  and  came  to 
anchor  off  the  western  point  of  Roanoke  Island.

Abstract  log  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Valley  City. 

February  ? ,  IS 6 2.-  At  9  a.  m.  got  underway  in  obedience  to  signal  and 
stood  up  the  sound  along  the  southern  shore  of  Roanoke  Island,  in  com¬ 
pany  with  the  rest  of  the  fleet.  At  II :  30  the  van  of  the  fleet  exchanged 
snots  with  rebel  batteries  on  shore;  several  rebel  steamers  in  sight  off 
the  western  point  of  the  island.  Called  the  crew  to  quarters  and 
manned  the  port  battery.  At  meridian,  flag-officer  having  made  the 
signal  Close  with  the  enemy,”  ran  within  three-fourths  of  a  mile  of 
the  shore  and  engaged  the  rebel  battery  in  company  with  the  gunboats 
Commodore  Ferry ,  Morse,  Whitehead,  and  sloop  Brinker.  At  1  •  30  p  m 
the  fort  m  flames  from  the  effect  of  our  shells.  A  round  shot  struck 
the  foremast,  grazing  it  nearly  to  the  core.  At  2  the  fire  within  the 
tort  raging  fiercely;  the  whole  fleet  pouring  an  incessant  fire  of  shot 
and  shell  into  the  fort.  At  2:30  the  efforts  of  those  within  the  fort 
apparently  devoted  to  quenching  the  flames.  At  3  gunboats  Commo¬ 
dore  Perry  and  Morse  retired  out  of  range,  having  expended  all  their 
ammunition;  the  flames  within  the  fort  nearly  extinguished.  At  3:15 
stood  in  a  quarter  of  a  mile  nearer  shore,  keeping  up  an  incessant  fire 
ot  shell  and  round  shot;  the  enemy  returning  brisk  exchanges.  The 
firing  from  the  fleet  gradually  subsiding.  At  4,  still  exchanging  shots 
with  the  battery,  crew  working  the  guns  with  unabated  vigor.  No 
casualties,  the  enemy’s  shot  generally  flying  too  high.  From  4  to  6 
the  fort  again  in  flames,  and  completely  enveloped  in  smoke.  At  4 : 45 
the  flames  within  the  fort  apparently  being  got  under,  and  the  fire  from 
the  battery  becoming  desultory,  ran  in  and  let  fly  several  broadsides  and 
stood  out  again.  At  5 : 30  the  enemy  still  exchanging  shots  with  us. 
Our  ammunition  nearly  expended,  hauled  off’ in  obedience  to  signal  and 
came  to  anchor.  From  8  to  midnight  at  anchor  off  the  enemy’s  batterv 
with  the  rest  of  the  fleet. 

February  8. — At  10 : 30  a.  m.,  in  obedience  to  signal,  stood  in  and 
engaged  the  rebel  battery,  exchanging  the  fire  of  the  enemy  until 
11:30,  when,  in  obedience  to  signal,  retired  out  of  range  and  passed 
within  hail  of  the  flagship.  Received  orders  to  report  to  Captain 
Jeffers,  of  steamer  Underwriter.  At  1  p.  m.  steamed  up  the  sound  in 
company  with  four  other  steamers.  At  3  sent  two  boats  to  discover 
the  channel.  At  4: 30,  observing  the  American  ensign  flying  over  the 
enemy’s  battery,  cheered  ship.  From  8  to  6  stood  up  the  sound  across 
a  row  of  piles  driven  by  the  enemy  to  obstruct  the  channel.  Came  to 
anchor  off  the  western  point  of  Roanoke  Island.

ting  in  deep  water  again,  I  took  position  for  15-second  fuzes,  an  i

Report  of  Acting  Lieutenant  Collioun,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Hunchback. 

U.  S.  S.  Hunchback, 

Croatan  Sound ,  North  Carolina ,  February  10,  1862. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  order  of  this  date,  I  respectfully  submit 
the  following  report  of  the  operations  of  this  vessel  in  the  engagement 
of  the  7th  instant  with  the  enemy’s  battery  and  gunboats: 

We  went  into  action  about  11  a.  in.,  directing  most  of  our  efforts 
against  their  gunboats.  They  having  in  a  short  time  withdrawn  from 
range  of  our  guns,  in  obedience  to  your  signal,  I  closed  in  with  the 
battery  on  Pork  Point,  going  as  far  in  as  my  draft  of  water  would  per¬ 
mit.  At  3 :  30  p.  m.  a  shot  struck  the  engine,  carrying  away  the  top  of 
one  of  the  cylinder  guide  rods  and  the  spring  bow,  and  disabled  it.  I 
then  anchored  and  sprung  on  the  battery,  with  which  I  was  engaged 
until  nearly  dark,  part  of  the  time  being  under  a  cross  fire  from  the 
enemy’s  gunboats.  The  Hunchback  was  struck  by  the  enemy’s  shot 
eight  times,  one  coming  through  the  hull  just  above  the  water  line. 
We  fired  201  shell  and  4  shrapnel  from  the  three  IX  inch  guns,  and  24 
solid  shot,  12  percussion,  and  64  paper-case  fuze  shells  from  the  100- 
pounder  rifle.  Though  we  were  in  the  thickest  of  the  engagement,  no 
one  was  hurt. 

Too  much  praise  can  not  be  given  to  the  officers  and  men  under  my 
command  for  the  manner  in  which  they  did  their  duty.  No  commander 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  569 


ill  battle  was  ever  better  supported,  and  they  all  deserve  well  of  their 
country.  . 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Edm.  E.  Colhoun, 

Acting  Lieutenant ,  Commanding. 

Flag-Officer  L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  off  Roanoke  Island,

February  7,1862. — Off  Eoanoke  Island,  North  Carolina.  At  9:55 
a.  m.  hove  up  anchor  and  proceeded  up  the  sound  in  company  with 
other  gunboats.  At  10 : 15  flagship  made  signal,  “  Our  country  expects 
every  man  to  do  his  duty.”  At  10:30  prepared  for  action,  steamed  in 
toward  the  battery,  as  signaled  by  flagship,  and  opened  fire  on  Pork 
Point  battery  and  also  the  rebel  fleet  ou  the  left  of  the  battery,  consist¬ 
ing  of  eight  gunboats,  using  15-second  shell  from  100-pounder  gun,  dis¬ 
tance  about  2  miles,  the  rebel  fleet  and  battery  answering  our  fire.  At 
12:45  p.  m.  the  flagship  signaled  to  engage  battery  at  mortar  range, 
ISO.  3370.  Steamed  in  close,  using  10-second  shell  from  IX-inch  guns. 
At  3: 30  received  a  32-pound  shot  from  the  battery,  striking  the  guide 
rod  of  the  engine,  breaking  it  off  15  inches  from  the  top  and  disabling 
the  engine.  Signaled  the  flagship  that  the  engine  was  disabled:

ceased  firing,  got  up  our  anchor  and  hauled  out  of  range  and  came  to

remaining  aboard’of  us,  the  remaining  seven  passing  through  the  upper

nel;  total,  208  IX-inch.  Eifle'ammunition :  24  solid  shot,  12  percussion, 
and  G4  paper  fuzes,  viz,  38  15-second,  1  20-second,  and  25  5-second; 
total,  100  shot  and  shell  for  100-pounder  rifle.

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Behm,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Southfield, 
transmitting  an  account  of  ammunition  expended. 

U.  S.  S.  Southfield, 
Croatan  Sound ,  February  10, 1862. 

Sir  :  In  obedience  to  your  order  of  this  day,  I  have  the  honor  to 
state  that  the  U.  S.  S.  Southfield ,  under  my  command,  and  hon¬ 
ored  by  your  presence  and  flag,  opened  fire  on  the  rebel  fleet  between 
Weir’s  Point  and  Pork  Point  and  on  the  fort  at  Pork  Point  at  11:30 
a.  m.  on  the  7th  instant.  We  continued  firing  until  sundown,  when 
you  gave  the  order  to  cease  firing,  and  we  came  to  an  anchor  in  11  feet. 
As  you  were  on  deck  during  the  whole  of  the  engagement,  it  will  be 
unnecessary  for  me  to  particularize.  Officers  and  creAV  behaved  coolly. 


570 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


Allow  mo  to  call  your  attention  to  the  valuable  services  rendered  by 
Acting  Master  Richard  VeverSj*  my  executive  officer,  who  had  charge 
of  the  forward  division  of  guns,  and  contributed  largely  to  the  efficiency 
of  the  100-pounder  Parrott  rifle  and  No.  2  IX-inch  shell  gun.  The 
captains  of  both  those  guns  showed  coolness  aud  skill,  and  made  some 
splendid  shooting.  Their  names  are  John  Johnson  and  Charles  Cole¬ 
man.  Acting  Master’s  Mate  W.  F.  Pratt,  who  had  charge  of  the  after 
division  and  directed  all  the  firing  there,  deserves  much  praise.  He 
had  as  gun’s  crew  17  men  of  the  Ninth  New  Jersey  Regiment,  who 
behaved  remarkably  well,  considering  that  they  were  not  used  to  the 
handling  of  large  guns.  Mr.  Pratt  made  excellent  shots  whenever  he 
could  get  the  range,  clear  of  other  vessels.  In  fact,  I  believe  we  never 
fired  a  shot  over  or  near  any  of  our  own  vessels,  and  the  Southfield  being 
very  long,  and  often  very  near  the  bottom,  made  her  difficult  to  manage. 
Mr.  Haynes  [Haynie^J,  acting  master  and  pilot,  rendered  me  very  valu 
able  assistance.  On  the  8th  we  commenced  firing  on  the  fort  again  at 
9:20  a.  m.  and  ceased  firing  at  10  a.  m.  by  your  orders.  Came  to  an 
anchor  immediately  after  in  10  feet  of  water  and  stopped  there  till  you 
left  us  at  6  p.  m.,  when  the  Philadelphia  came  alongside. 

We  met  with  no  casualties  and  had  only  one  shot  (a  32-pounder)  pass 
through  our  upper  works,  and  that  was  about  5  p.  m.  on  the  7th,  when 
we  were  in  range  of  the  Hunchback ,  who  was  at  anchor  with  a  spring 
on  her  cable.  We  have  received  no  injury,  and  have  been  ready  for 
service  all  the  time. 

The  slight  damage  done  to  the  upper  works  was  repaired  by  a  gang 
of  carpenters  kindly  sent  by  you  on  the  9th.  Annexed  please  find 
account  of  ammunition  received,  expended,  and  on  hand. 

Most  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Chs.  F.  W.  Behm, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Southfield. 

Commodore  L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Flag- Officer,  U.  S.  Flag-  Steamer  Philadelphia.

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Behm,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Southfield 

regarding  captured  material. 

U.  S.  S.  Southfield, 
Croatan  Sound ,  February  11 ,  1862 — 1  p.  rn. 
Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  yon  that  we  have  two  32-pounders 
with  carriages  complete  on  board  sloop  Granite,  and  that  before  night 
1  trust  to  have  another  one  and  the  32-pounder  on  the  Curlew 
We  have  a  large  quantity  of  grape,  solid  shot,  shell,  and  ali  sorts  of 
inmumtion,  two  lull  tanks  (marked  U.  S.  S.  Merrimack ),  and  many 
other  things  I  shall  try  to  save  all  I  can,  which  may  be  of  use  to  us, 
and  will  send  in  my  report  in  full  when  we  have  linished.  The  fort  was 
made  by  hauling  two  canal  boats  along  the  shore  and  then  filling  up 
with  sod,  or  rather  both  mud  and  sod,  interlined  with  and  braced  on 
the  outside  with  timber.  The  whole  battery  had  seven  32-pounders,  all 
stolen  trom  the  L  mted  States.  One  of  the  canal  boats  was  fired  and 
the  magazine  was  blown  up.  The  other  is  the  C.  A.  Nichols ,  of  Norfolk, 
Va.,  and  when  we  have  all  we  want  out  of  her  I  shall  have  her  set  on 
fire  also,  and  then  there  will  be  nothing  to  build  on  again.  I  sent  Act- 
ing  Masters  Mate  Hammond,  belonging  to  the  Delaware,  this  morning 
to  reconnoiter,  and  this  will  be  handed  to  you  by  him.  He  had  charge 
ol  a  div  ision  of  the  launches,  and  went  in  the  launch  Union  to  see  about 
the  state  ot  things  on  shore.  He  will  be  able  to  give  you  all  the  news 
he  lias  picked  up.  I  thought  it  best  to  send  him  to  you  so  that  .you 
might  examine  him  yourself.  We  shall  be  able  to  get  some  5  or  6 
anchors,  4  water  tanks  of  about  400  gallons  each  (one  marked  Colorado ) 

2  chains,  and  many  other  things.  The  fort  is  about  220  feet  long,  and’ 
as  I  said  before,  was  mounted  by  7  guns.  Mr.  Hammond  will  give  you 
all  the  news  about  the  inhabitants,  and  about  a  fort  some  3  miles  above 
this.  If  you  make  no  different  disposition  of  him,  I  should  be  glad  to 
have  him  on  boa- 1  here  until  the  Delate  are,  to  which  he  belongs,  returns. 

I  shall  try  to  keep  you  informed  of  my  proceedings,  and,  if  you  would 
allow  me  to  give  the  fishermen  permission  to  use  their  nets  I  might  be 
able  to  supply  you  with  fresh  shad.  Mr.  Hammond  will  speak  to  you 
about  this. 

I  am,  most  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Chs.  F.  W.  Behm, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant,  Commanding  U.  S.  S.  Southfield. 
Flag-Officer  L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Flag- Steamer  Philadelphia,  Croatan  Sound. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Hays,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Morse,  transmitting  account 

of  ammunition  expended. 

U.  S.  S.  Morse, 

Off  Roanoke  Island,  February  11,  1862. 

Sir  :  In  obedience  to  your  order  of  the  10th  instant,  I  have  the  honor 
to  submit  herewith  the  following  report  of  the  operations  of  this  vessel 
during  the  engagement  of  the  7th  instant: 

At  11 : 30  a.  m.  I  approached  the  shore  to  within  about  1,500  yards 
and  opened  fire  with  15-second  shell  upon  the  enemy’s  steamers,  dis¬ 
abling  the  steamer  Curlew'. 

About  the  same  time  I  commenced  firing  with  10-second  and  5-second 
shell  upon  the  battery  on  [Pork]  Point,  but  finding  that  the  latter 
exploded  short  of  the  battery  I  ran  in  near  enough  to  do  execution.  I 


572  NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

% 

then  continued  firing  until  my  shell  were  all  expended.  At  4:30  p.  m., 
signalized  to  the  flagship  uIn  want  of  shell,”  whereupon  Captain  Case 
ordered  me  to  withdraw  and  anchor  for  the  night.  I  have  to  report  the 
loss  of  one  man,  Eli  Holden  (seaman),  of  New  Bedford,  Mass.,  during 
the  engagement.  The  vessel,  although  struck  by  shot  and  shell,  sus¬ 
tained  no  material  injury.  It  affords  me  great  pleasure  to  call  your 
attention  to  the  brave  and  gallant  conduct  of  my  officers  and  crew  dur¬ 
ing  the  whole  engagement.  I  herewith  enclose  a  report  of  ammunition 
expended. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Peter  Hays, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding.

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  Roanoke  Island.

Abstract  log  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Morse. 

February  7,  1862—  At  8  a.  m.  the  flagship  signaled  to  get  underway. 
At  10:30  saw  the  rebel  fleet  and  batteries  in  northeast  direction.  At 
11  commenced  firing  at  the  enemy,  and  continued  the  engagement  until 
5 : 45  [p.  m.].  At  4  p.  m.  a  ball  from  the  enemy  passed  through  the  hull 
near  the  bluff  of  the  bow.  *  At  4: 30  a  seaman  was  killed  by  a  shot  from 
the  enemy.  At  5 :  45  signaled  the  flagship  that  shot  was  expended.  At 
6  went  alongside  the  Philadelphia  and  took  on  board  16  shell  and  2  kegs 
powder. 

February  8. — At  10 : 30  a.  m.  buried  E.  Holden,  of  New  Bedford,  Mass., 
on  shore  at  Roanoke  Island.  From  12  until  4  p.  m.  two  divisions  of  the 
fleet  succeeded  in  removing  the  piles  driven  in  the  channel  by  the  rebels. 
At  4:30  p.  m.  the  flagship  signaled,  “The  victory  is  ours.” 


Report  of  Acting  Master  French,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Whitehead. 

U.  S.  S.  Whitehead, 

Off  Roanoke  Island ,  North  Carolina ,  February  9 ,  1862. 

Sir:  I  engaged  the  battery  on  the  7th  instant  at  12  in.,  and  kept  up 
a  continual  fire  till  5:45  p.  m.  at  the  distance  of  1,300  to  1,500  yards, 
throwing  shell  effectively. 

I  expended  during  the  time  98  shell,  and  am  happy  to  say  no  casual¬ 
ties  occurred. 

My  officers  and  men  merit  my  warmest  thanks  for  their  promptness 
during  the  action,  particulary  T.  W.  Cook,  paymaster’s  clerk,  who  ren¬ 
dered  important  aid  in  attending  to  the  signals. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Charles  A.  French, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding  Steamer  Whitehead. 

Commander  S.  C.  Rowan, 

Commanding  Naval  Flotilla ,  Pamlico  and  Albemarle  Sounds. 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  573 

Abstract  log  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Whitehead. 

February  7,  1862. — At  11  a.  m.  entered  tlie  marshes  and  proceeded 
up  tor  the  fort.  At  12 : 30  engaged  the  rebel  battery  at  long  range,  fir¬ 
ing  an  occasional  shot  at  the  rebel  steamers,  which  had  taken  a  position 
to  windward.  The  action  soon  became  general,  and  was  kept  up  with¬ 
out  intermission  during  the  afternoon.  Shortened  our  range  to  1,200 
yards.  At  2  p.  m.  the  batteries  were  discovered  to  be  on  fire,  which, 
however,  the  rebels  soon  succeeded  in  extinguishing.  At  3  the  seces¬ 
sion  flag  was  shot  away,  but  was  soon  replaced.  At  4  the  Federal 
forces  were  being  landed  from  the  transports.  At  5,  having  expended 
all  our  shell,  we  retired  from  the  action,  having  received  no  injury  dur¬ 
ing  the  day.  The  number  of  shells  fired,  98. 

February  8.— From  8  to  meridian :  Owing  to  the  supply  of  ammunition 
and  ordnance  stores  in  the  schooner  Howard  being  nearly  exhausted, 
we  took  on  board  from  her  eight  empty  shell,  being  all  there  were  on 
the  schooner  suitable  for  our  gun.  Received  on  board  powder,  fuzes, 
and  one  package  of  overshirts  to  make  cartridge  cylinders.  Filled  eight 
shell  and  put  in  10-second  fuzes.  Started  for  the  barricade.  At  4  p.  m. 
started  to  pass  through  the  obstructions  placed  across  the  river.  At  5 
steamer  Lockwood  discovered  a  passage,  passed  through,  and  anchored. 
At  6  the  magazine  of  one  of  the  rebel  forts,  which  had  been  set  on  fire 
when  they  retreated,  blew  up  with  a  terrific  explosion. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Graves,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  John  L.  Lockwood. 

U.  S.  S.  Lockwood, 
Elisabeth  City,  JJ.  C.,  Febr  uary  12,  1862. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  forward  the  following  report  of  the  action 
at  Roanoke  Island  on  the  7th  instant: 

Commenced  the  engagement  at  12  m.  and  continued  it  until  6  p.  m., 
without  any  casualties. 

Total  expenditure  of  ammunition:  Eighty-six  rounds,  12-pounder; 
62  rounds,  80-pounder. 

Resumed  the  action  with  the  enemy’s  battery  at  9  a.  m.  on  the  8th  in¬ 
stant,  which  lasted  about  forty-five  minutes.  No  casualties.  Expended 
8  rounds  80-pounder  ammunition. 

I  can  not  speak  too  highly  of  the  conduct  of  the  officers  and  men 
under  my  command. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

G.  W.  Craves, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding  TJ.  8.  8.  Lockwood. 

Lieutenant  Commanding  Alex.  Murray, 

Commanding  Second  Column. 


Report.of  Acting  Master  Giddings,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Henry  Brinker. 

U.  S.  S.  Henry  Brinker, 

Off  Roanoke  Island ,  February  13,  1862. 

Sir  :  Agreeably  to  your  orders  of  the  10th  instant,  I  have  the  honor 
to  submit  the  following  report  of  my  engagement  with  the  enemy  on 
the  7th  instant: 

At  10:15  a.  m.  weighed  anchor  and  took  up  my  position  in  column, 
agreeable  to  signal. 


574 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


At  11  a.  m.  observed  tbe  following  signal  from  tbe  flagship:  “Our 
country  expects  every  man  to  do  his  duty,”  which  was  observed  by  my 
crew  with  cheers. 

At  32  m.  opened  fire  upon  the  enemy  from  my  position  in  column, 
and  shortly  after  obtained  permission  from  Lieutenant  Werden,  of  the 
/Stars  and  Stripes,  to  go  in  nearer  and  engage  the  battery.  .Ran  in  close 
and  continued  the  engagement  until  3 : 20  p.  m.,  when,  having  expended 
my  ammunition,  I  was  obliged  to  withdraw. 

I  immediately  proceeded  to  the  Stars  and  Stripes  for  a  supply,  and 
was  sent  to  the  Delaware;  from  her  went  to  the  Philadelphia,  thence  to 
the  Stars  and  Stripes;  from  her  to  the  flagship,  and  back  to  the  Phila¬ 
delphia,  but  could  get  none.  Night  coming  on,  I  came  to  an  anchor 
near  the  Stars  and  Stripes. 

The  vessel  was  not  injured  by  the  enemy’s  fire  and  no  casualties 
occurred  among  my  ship’s  company. 

I  take  pleasure  in  saying  that  throughout  the  action  my  officers  and 
crew  all  behaved  with  the  utmost  gallantry  and  coolness. 

I  am,  sir,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  E.  Giddings, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding  U.  S.  S.  Henry  Drinker. 

Flag-Officer  L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 


Abstract  log  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Henry  Brinker. 

February  7,  1862. — Weighed  anchor  and  proceeded  in  line  through 
the  marshes.  Action  commenced  by  Southfield.  Fired  first  gun  and 
ran  alongside  Stars  and  JStripes  and  asked  permission  to  go  nearer 
inshore,  which  was  granted.  At  12:20  the  action  became  general; 
battery  responding  slowly,  but  without  effect.  At  3:20  p.  m.  hauled 
off  and  made  signal,  “Ammunition,  in  want  of.”  Ean  to  Stars  and 
Stripes,  was  sent  to  Delaware,  returned  to  Stars  and  Stripes,  sent  to  flag¬ 
ship  Southfield ,  Captain  Case  sent  us  to  schooner  Howard  and  alongside 
Philadelphia;  found  none;  again  to  Philadelphia;  finding  none,  ran 
ahead  and  anchored  at  7  p.  m. 

February  8.— At  7 :30  a.  m.  captain  took  the  second  cutter  and  went 
aboard  the  Stars  and  Stripes  and  procured  1  keg  of  powder.  Cruised 
around  among  the  army  gunboats  and  procured  30  shell  and  20 
charges  of  powder.  Engaged  filling  shell  and  making  cartridges.  At 
12  m.  flagship  signalized  “Attack  batteries.”  At  12:20  ran  in  toward 
battery  and  was  signaled  from  Southfield,  “Pass  within  hail.”  Ean 
alongside  and  was  ordered  to  report  to  Lieutenant  Commanding  Jeffers 
and  was  ordered  to  follow  on  the  left  and  assist  in  passing  spiles.  At 
4:15  p.  m.  Federal  troops  took  possession  of  batteries;  4:30  rebels  set 
fire  lO  buildings  and  battery  on  Croatan  and  to  steamer  Curlew,  which 
was  abandoned  and  ashore.  Passed  spile  blockade  in  company  with 
Lockwood.  Ean  about  a  mile,  taking  possession  of  a  lighter  load  of 
shovels  and  was  signalized,  “Eeturn.”  At  6:50  came  to  anchor  above 
the  spiles  blockade  one-fourth  of  a  mile. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Wells,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Isaac  N.Seymour. 

IT.  S.  S.  1.  N.  Seymour, 
Croatan  Sound,  February  16.  1862. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  orders  of  the  10th  instant,  I  herein  have 
the  honor  to  report  the  amount  of  ammunition  expended,  together  with 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  575 

the  casualties  on  board  this  vessel  during  the  action  of  the  7th  and  8th 

1U.  StRillti* 

At  11  o’clock  and  40  minutes  a.  in.,  took  a  position  within  14  miles  of 
the  lower  battery  on  Roanoke  Island.  I  opened  fire  with  both  bow  and 
stern  guns,  using- percussion  shell  from  Parrott  gun  and  shot  and  shell 
alternately  m  rifled  howitzer,  directing  my  fire  wholly  at  the  three 
barbette  guns  on  the  southern  extremity  of  the  battery,  keeping  up  a 
continuous  fire  until  5:30  p.  in.,  when,  finding  our  ammunition  to  be 
reduced  to  23  rounds,  having  expended  91  rounds  from  30-pounder  Par- 
lott  and  112  from  rifled  howitzer,  I  hauled  off  to  procure  a  fresh  supply, 
being  detained  until  dark  in  obtaining  the  same,  by  which  time  the 
filing  on  both  sides  had  ceased.  My  boat,  in  company  with  others,  was 
ordered  on  picket  duty  near  the  barricade  extending  across  the  sound 
from  Koanoke  Island  to  the  mainland.  I  regret  to  add  that  Mr.  Stephen 
Melius,  head  engineer,  was  dangerously  wounded  in  the  hip,  and  Will¬ 
iam  Singleton,  powderman,  instantly  killed  by  the  enemy’s  shot  during 
the  afternoon.  No  damage  was  done  to  vessel,  if  I  except  the  joiner 
work  and  windows,  broken  by  the  concussion  of  our  own  guns,  and  a 
hawser  cut  twice  in  two  by  an  enemy’s  shot. 

Saturday,  the  8th  instant,  at  8:40  a.  in.,  got  underway  and  ran  down 
to  within  1,500  yards  of  the  battery,  returning  the  enemy’s  fire,  com¬ 
pletely  silencing  for  the  time  the  three  barbette  guns  before  mentioned. 
At  10:55  a.  m.  a  signal  from  the  flagship  to  cease  firing.  Hauled  off 
and  anchored. 

Very  respectfully,  your  most  obedient  servant, 

P.  S.  Wells, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding  U.  S.  S.  I.  A.  Seymour. 

Flag-Officer  L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  MacDiarmid,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Ceres. 

IT.  S.  S.  Geres, 

Off  Roanoke  Island ,  February  15 ,  1862. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  order  of  the  1 0th  instant,  I  have  the  honor 
to  submit  the  following  report  of  the  operations  of  this  vessel  on  the 
7th  and  8th  instant  at  the  attack  on  Koanoke  Island.  About  10:45 
a.  in.,  the  Ceres  in  advance  of  the  right  column,  I  received  permission 
from  Commander  S.  C.  Kowan  to  open  fire  with  my  rifled  Parrott

Report  of  Acting  Master  Hotehkiss,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  General  Putnam. 

IT.  S.  S.  General  Putnam, 

Croatan  Sound,  February  14,  1862. 

Sir  :  In  obedience  to  your  order  of  the  10th  instant,  I  have  the  honor 
to  submit  the  folio  wing  report  of  our  engagement  with  the  enemy  on 
the  7th  and  8th  instant: 

After  12  o’clock  m.  of  the  7th  I  steamed  up  on  the  right  of  the 
squadron  and  commenced  firing  upon  the  battery  with  my  20-pounder 
Parrott  gun,  using  shrapnel,  with  20-second  fuzes,  bursting  them 
directly  over  the  battery;  kept  approaching  the  battery  and  steadily 
firing,  changing  the  fuze  to  15-second,  then  to  10-second,  and  to  5-second, 
until  within  700  yards  of  the  battery.  Then,  with  broadside  to,  keep¬ 
ing  the  boat  in  motion,  I  commenced  firing  shot  and  shell  from  our 
32-pounder,  directing  my  fire  at  the  enemy’s  guns,  continuing  a  steady 
fire  from  both  guns  until  half  past  5  o’clock  p.  m.  The  shots  from  the 
enemy’s  battery  passed  to  the  right  and  left,  but  mostly  over  our  heads. 
For  about  one  hour  we  received  a  cross  fire  from  the  rebel  steamers  on 
our  left.  We  were  once  on  fire  near  the  machinery  on  the  hurricane 
deck,  but  it  was  soon  extinguished  and  but  little  damage  done. 

My  powder  being  expended,  I  reported  to  the  commander  in  chief, 
who  ordered  me  to  the  schooner  Howard  for  a  supply.  During  the 
night  we  made  100  cartridge  bags;  on  the  morning  of  the  8th  we  filled 


577 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

them  and  started  in  company  with  the  Under  tor  iter  and  several  other 
boats  to  pass  the  blockade  of  sunken  vessels.  The  battery  opened  fire 
upon  us,  which  we  replied  to  for  nearly  one  hour,  when  we  were  recalled. 
Through  the  whole  engagement,  I  am  thankful  to  say,  no  one  was  hurt 
on  board  this  vessel. 

T  take  great  pleasure  in  saying  that  the  officers  and  men  under  my 
command  pointed  the  guns  with  'weat  precision,  doing  much  credit  to 
themselves  and  honor  to  that  g  rious  flag  which  waves  so  proudly 
over  us.  1  J 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

.  .  Wm.  J.  Hotchkiss,

Report  of  Acting  Master  Woodward,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Shawsheen. 

TJ.  S.  S.  Shawsheen, 

Off  Roanoke  Island,  February  17,  1862. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  order,  I  have  the  honor  to  submit  to  you 
the  following  report  of  the  part  taken  by  this  steamer  in  the  bombard¬ 
ment  off  Eoanoke  Island  on  the  7th  and  8th  instant: 

On  the  7th  instant,  at  11.45  a.  m.,  our  first  shell  was  fired,  which  fell 
shoit  ot  the  battery.  Stood  in  until  within  g’ood  range,  when  we  took 
a  position  on  the  front  wing  and  engaged  the  battery,  firing  alternately 
from. both  rifled  guns.  This  position  was  maintained  until  sunset,  when 
the  signal  was  made  on  board  the  flagship  to  cease  firing,  having  received 
no  material  injury  throughout  the  action. 

I  have  only  to  add  that  I  was  ably  sustained  by  all  the  officers  and 
crew  under  my  command. 

After  dark  I  was  ordered  to  take  a  position  in  advance  of  the  fleet, 
to  watch  any  movements  of  the  enemy  which  might  take  place  through 
the  night.  Nothing  occurring  worthy  of  note,  at  8.30  a.  m.,  8th  instant,

Report  of  Midshipman  Porter,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  howitzer  battery  in  cooperation  with 

the  army. 


U.  S.  S.  Hunchback, 

Off  Roanoke  Island ,  February  10,  1S62. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  order  of  the  10th  instant,  I  now  submit 
to  you  a  detailed  account  of  the  operations  of  my  battery  during  the 
engagement  with  the  rebels  on  Eoauoke  Island,  February  S,  1862. 
The  officers  of  the  battery  were  as  follows,  viz: 

Acting  Master  Charles  Daniels,  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Hetzel ;  Lieutenants 
Tillotson  and  Hughes,  of  the  Union  Coast  Guard;  Flag-Officer’s  Clerk 
Edward  P.  Meeker,  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Philadelphia ;  Acting  Master’s  Mate 
J.  B.  Hammond,  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Delaware ;  Acting  Master’s  Mate  Wal¬ 
ter  Griffith,  of  the  IT.  S.  S.  Underwriter. 

At  4:30  p.  m.,  February  7,  the  signal  was  made  to  land  the  troops, 
and  Brigadier-General  Burnside  ordered  me  to  proceed  to  Ashby’s 
Cove  and  report  to  General  Beno. 

This  I  immediately  did  and  was  ordered  by  him  to  disembark  the 
pieces. 

As  soon  as  they  were  landed,  I  formed  them  in  column  of  pieces  and 
advanced  inland  to  the  fork  of  the  roads;  here  I  stationed  two  of  the 
pieces.  Two  of  the  remaining  pieces  I  stationed  about  one-half  a  mile 
in  advance  on  the  left  fork,  and  the  other  two  about  the  same  distance 
in  advance  on  the  right  fork. 

Here  we  remained  until  7  a.  m.,  February  8,  when  General  Foster 
came  up  with  his  brigade  to  make  the  advance  and  ordered  me  to  follow 
on  after  the  Twenty-fifth  Regiment  Massachusetts  Volunteers. 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  579 

We  immediately  manned  the  drag  ropes  and  advanced  about  2  miles 
when  I  received  an  order  from  General  Foster  to  bring  the  battery 
forward  as  fast  as  possible. 

I  now  ga\  e  the  order,  “  F orward,  double  quick,”  aud  we  soon  sighted 
the  lebel  battery ?  which,  was  situated  so  as  to  rake  a  road  which  crossed 
the  one  upon  which  we  were  advancing  at  right  angles,  and  was  flanked 
on  either  side  by  a  very  thick  swamp. 

As  soon  as  I  saw  the  enemy’s  fortification  I  halted  aud  formed  the 
pieces  into  battery,  with  three  pieces  in  the  road  upon  which  we  were 
advancing  and  three  on  the  right  of  it,  and  opened  fire  on  the  enemy 
with  grape  and  shell  from  the  rilled  guns,  and  canister,  shrapnel,  and 
shell  from  the  smoothbore,  doing  good  execution  among  their  reserve 
in  the  rear  of  their  battery. 

As  I  received  orders  to  keep  the  artillery  on  a  line  with  the  infantry, 
I  ad\  anced  tlic  pieces  after  eacli  fire  until  tliey  were  in  tlie  open  space 
directly  in  front  of  the  rebel  battery,  where  we  made  a  stand  under  a 
most  destructive  fire  from  the  rebel  infantry.  The  men,  however, 
worked  the  guns  with  great  coolness  and  determination,  until  all  but 
10  rounds  from  each  piece  had  been  fired,  when,  as  I  received  orders  to 
reserve  10  rounds  for  each  gun,  we  ceased  firing  for  a  short  time,  but 
commenced  again,  firing  about  once  every  two  minutes,  to  scatter  the 
enemy’s  reserve. 

We  had  been  firing  about  three  and  one-half  hours  when  the  fortifi¬ 
cation  was  stormed  and  the  rebels  retreated  toward  Weir’s  Point. 

As  soon  as  we  reached  the  rebel  battery  we  started  on  for  Weir’s 
Point.  After  marching  with  the  artillery  about  2  miles  we  met  General 
Foster,  who  told  us  that  the  enemy  had  surrendered  and  that  we  would 
not  be  required  any  more. 

I  therefore  started  on  again  for  the  point,  and  the  next  morning 
embarked  the  battery  and  returned  to  the  flotilla. 

All  praise  is  due  my  officers  and  men  for  their  bravery  and  the 
alacrity  and  coolness  with  which  they  executed  all  of  my  orders. 

I  particularly  recommend  to  your  notice  Acting  Master’s  Mate  J.  B. 
Hammond,  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Delaware  who,  by  his  coolness  and  intre¬ 
pidity,  elicited  my  warmest  praise. 

I  would  also  recommend  to  your  notice  Lieutenants  Tillotson  and 
Hughes,  Union  Coast  Guard,  who  served  their  pieces  in  the  most 
gallant  manner  throughout  the  action. 

I  now  most  respectfully  submit  the  above  report  to  your  considera¬ 
tion,  hoping  that  the  operations  may  meet  with  your  approval. 

I  am  very  sorry  to  report  the  following  casualties  in  my  battery: 

Killed. — John  McCoy,  private,  Union  Coast  Guard,  Company  B; 
John  Doyle,  private,  Union  Coast  Guard,  Company  B;  James  Herbert, 
private,  Ninth  Begiment  New  Jersey  Volunteers. 

Wounded  seriously. — William  Miller,  private,  Ninth  Begiment  New 
Jersey  Volunteers;  John  Saddler,  private,  Union  Coast  Guard,  Com¬ 
pany  B. 

Wounded  slightly. — Nathan  Stanford,  private,  Union  Coast  Guard, 
Company  B;  David  Lloyd,  private,  Union  Coast  Guard,  Company  B; 
Benj.  Clinton,  private,  Ninth  Begiment  New  Jersey  Volunteers. 

Bespectfully  submitted. 

Benj.  I L  Porter, 

Midshipman ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  Commanding  Launches. 

Flag-Officer  L.  M.  Goldsborougii, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Letter  from  Rear-Admiral  Goldsborough,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy,  in  com¬ 
mendation  of  Midshinnian  Porter’s  action  in  command  of  howitzer  battery,  February  7  and  8, 
1862. 

Washington  City,  October  11 ,  1862. 

Sir:  In  my  detailed  report  to  the  Department  ot  the  capture  of 
Roanoke  Island,  etc.,  dated  off  Roanoke  Island,  February  18,  1862,  I 
remarked  that,  in  the  course  of  the  afternoon  of  the  7th  of  that  month, 
sis  launches,  under  the  command  ot  Midshipman  Benj.  H.  I  orter, 
landed  their  howitzers  and  joined  the  army  for  the  purpose  of  com¬ 
manding  the  main  road  and  its  two  forks  during  the  night,  and  of 
assisting  in  more  active  operations,  the  following  morning,  and  also, 
that  I  was  promised  a  report  by  General  Burnside  with  regard  to  Mid¬ 
shipman  Porter’s  association  with  his  forces,  and  would  with  pleasure 
forward  it  to  the  Department  as  soon  as  it  was  received. 

Owing,  no  doubt,  td  nothing  but  incessant  and  pressing  demands 
upon  his  time,  the  general  has  not  yet  complied  with  his  promise,  and  as 
it  may  be  still  some  time  longer  before  he  can  command  time  enough  to 
carry  out  his  intentions  upon  the  subject,  1  deem  it  but  justice  to  this 
interesting  youth  to  say  that  both  Generals  Burnside  and  1  oster  assured 
me  in  conversation  immediately  after  the  battle,  which  came  off  on  the 
8th  of  February  and  resulted  so  advantageously  to  our  arms,  that  his 
gallantry  was  very  conspicuous  on  the  occasion.  The  battery  under 
his  command,  of  six  naval  howitzers,  was  placed  in  the  advance,  and  it 
was  there  handled  with  a  degree  of  skill  and  daring  which  not  only 
contributed  largely  to  the  success  of  the  day,  but  won  the  admiration 
of  all  wTho  witnessed  the  display.  No  other  ffeldpieces  were  employed 
by  our  army  in  the  engagement.  Mr.  Porter  was  but  about  17  years  of 
age,  and  in  my  belief  no  father  in  the  land  can,  with  truth,  boast  of  a 
nobler  youth  as  a  son.  I  sincerely  trust  that  he  may  be  regarded  by 
the  Department  as  highly  worthy  of  its  lasting  consideration,  and  that 
he  may  at  all  times  have  bestowed  upon  him  all  that  his  merits  deserve. 
Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Rear-Admiral ,  U.  8.  Navy. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington  City,  1 >.  C.

Rough  notes  of  the  naval  expedition  to  Roanoke  Island,  etc.,  by  Henry  Van  Brunt,  secretary  to 

flag-officer. 

(  Sunday ,  January  12.— Flag-officer  and  staff  left  Hampton  Roads  in  the 
Spaulding  at  5:30  p.  m.  Minnesota  hauled  down  flag-officer’s  broad 
pennant  as  we  passed. 

Monday,  Januaiy  lo.  Passed  Cape  Hatteras  at  8:30  a.  m.  Several 
transports  of  Burnside’s  fleet  in  our  company  during  night  and  morn¬ 
ing.  Spoke  the  Ceres  outside  Hatteras  Inlet."  Passed  over  the  bar  and 
anchored  in  the  inlet  at  10:30  a.  m.,  crowded  among  transports  and 
gunboats,  which  are  continually  arriving  during  the  day.  At  about 
meridian  General  Burnside  arrived  in  the  Picket,  and  soon  afterwards 
came  on  board  to  see  flag-officer.  Tide  ebbing  strong,  with  stiff  breeze 
from  N.  N.  E.  Lying  at  the  inlet  we  found  on  onr  arrival  the  following

Tuesday ,  January  14. — A  strong  N.  E.  gale  all  last  night  and  this 
morning  prevailed,  inflicting  considerable  damage  among  the  trans¬ 
ports  and  shipping,  crowded  together  in  the  narrow  roadstead.  The 
army  gunboat  Zouave  ran  afoul  of  her  anchor  during  the  night  and 
sunk. "  During  the  day  wreckers  were  set  to  work  to  save  from  her  as 
many  articles  as  possible.  General  Burnside  on  board  during  the  day. 
No  active  operations  could  be  carried  on  this  day  on  account  of  the 
gale.  Many  naval  officers  came  on  board. 

Wednesday ,  January  15. — Gale  subsided  during  the  night.  General 
Burnside  came  on  board  twice  during  the  day  with  Commander  Hazard 
and  officers  of  his  staff'.  The  command  of  the  Putnam  was  temporarily 
conferred  on  Lieutenant  McCook,  of  the  Stars  and  Stripes.  The  Granite , 
an  armed  sloop,  Avas  towed  in  from  the  outside  in  the  a.  in.  by  the 
Ceres.  At  10:30  a.  m.  the  Whitehead  Avent  over  the  swash  and  took  up 
a  position  in  the  sound.  She  was  followed  by  the  Valley  City,  which, 
after  grounding  once,  got  safely  over.  Then  in  succession  the  Seymour , 
Lockwood ,  and  Brinlcer  followed  successfully,  except  that  the  last  named 
got  tAvice  aground.  Ceres  was  meanwhile  employed,  under  direction  of

at  2:30  p.  m.  toAved  the  sloop  Granite  OArnr  into  the  sound.  At  3 : 45 
p.  m.  the  PLetzel  followed  successfully.  At  4  p.  m.  the  Underwriter  got 
underway  and  grounded.  With  the  assistance  of  the  Ceres  she  got  off 
in  tAVO  hours  and  anchored,  Avaiting  for  the  morning.  Immediately 
after  the  Underwriter  Avent  the  Louisiana ,  which  easily  passed  over 
into  the  sound.  The  Morse  at  about  the  same  time  got  off  from  the 
bar,  where  she  had  been  aground  since  the  morning,  but  immediately 
got  aground  again.  At  4:15  p.  m.  Commander  Rowan,  commanding- 
naval  division  of  gunboats,  went  over  in  the  Delaware.  General 
Burnside  on  board  at  4:15  p.  in.  He  informed  us  that  Colonel  Allen

drowned  on  the  outer  bar.  At  G:05  p.  m.  flag-officer  sent  to  request 
the  general  to  have  all  lights  about  the  vessels  lowered  and  extin¬ 
guished.  In  the  a.  in.  William  A.  Smith,  an  old  sound  pilot,  came  on 
board  to  advise  Avitli  the  flag-officer;  also  James  Parsons,  a  Union 
refugee  from  Portsmouth,  Va.,  who  had  made  his  escape  last  Friday. 
In  the  evening  Generals  Burnside,  Foster,  and  Reno  came  on  board 
with  maps  to  consult  concerning  the  attack  on  Roanoke  Island.  The 
line  of  battle  formed  by  our  gunboats  in  the  sound  is  nearly  as  follows, 
beginning  from  extreme  left:  Delaware ,  Granite ,  Seymour ,  Whitehead, 
Valley  City,  Lockwood,  Drinker,  Hetzel,  Louisiana.

and  Ceres  got  over  into  the  line  at  daybreak.  Ceres  and  Putnam 
occupied  all  day  towing,  etc.  Morse  got  afloat  at  9 :  30  a.  m.  At  9 : 40

swash  pilots  on  board.  At  11  a.  m.  army  transport  Eastern  Queen

Friday,  January  17. — At  9:30  a.  in.  the  Southfield  came  in  from  sea. 
Several  army  vessels  aground,  but  none  in  the  sound.  At  10  a,  m.  the

Saturday ,  January  18. — Cloudy,  with  light  west  wind.  Hunchback 
went  over  at  9  a.  m.  into  the  sound.  Southfield  partly  over  and  aground 
at  9 : 30  a.  m.  Stars  and  Stripes  still  making  slow  progress  over  swash. 
Whole  morning  occupied  in  examination  of  Chickamicomico  fishermen 
concerning  Roanoke  Island  and  the  soundings  and  landings  thereabout. 
Most  of  them  unwilling  to  take  the  responsibility  of  piloting.  Generals 
Burnside,  Foster,  and  Reno  present  at  examination.  Much  local  infor¬ 
mation  obtained  from  negro  Ben  and  his  brother,  escaped  slaves  from 
Roanoke  Island.  Late  in  p.  m.  Southfield  and  Stars  and  Stripes  still 
working  their  way  slowly  over. 

Sunday,  January  19. — Foggy.  The  army  transports  are  reported  to 
be  lightened  as  much  as  possible.  The  generals  were  on  board  early. 
Stars  and  Stripes  got  over  into  the  sound  and  took  her  place  in  the 
fleet  beyond  the  swash  at  10:45  a.m.  Lieutenant  McCook  relieved 
from  command  of  Putnam  and  restored  to  Stars  and  Stripes.  At  1:45 
p.  m.  the  army  steamer  Picket  towed  over  a  schooner,  followed  by  the 
Pilot  Boy  with  troops  to  transfer  to  schooner.  This  is  .the  first  move¬ 
ment  over  the  swash  by  the  army.  Two  natives  came  on  board  at  4: 20 
p.  m.,  and  reported  that  the  army  steamer  Pocahontas  had  gone  ashore 
20  miles  above  Cape  Hatteras,  and  19  only  of  her  cargo  of  103  horses 
were  saved ;  GO  men  on  board  all  saved.  At  5  p.  m.  Generals  Burnside, 
Reno,  and  Parke  came  on  board  reporting  that,  by  sounding,  they  had 
discovered  an  8-foot  passage  over  the  swash.  It  was  probably  a 
“pocket”  or  cul  de  sac. 

Monday,  January  20. — At  7  a.  m.  the  Vidette,  army  steamer,  which 
got  aground  on  her  way  over  yesterday,  succeeded  in  joining  the  fleet 
in  the  sound.  At  11:30  a.  in.  the  South  field  got  over  into  the  sound. 
As  usual,  the  Ceres  and  Putnam,  and  also  the  Lockwood,  were  engaged 
all  day  towing  and  tugging.  At  meridian  Picket  towed  over  a  schooner, 
followed  by  Pilot  Boy  with  troops  to  be  transferred  to  schooner.  Lock- 
wood  also  towed  over  schooner. 

At  3  p.  m.  the  commanding  officer  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Western  World 
came  on  board  to  report  the  arrival  of  his  vessel.  He  put  in  for  har¬ 
bor  on  his  way  to  Port  Royal. 

Tuesday,  January  21. — At  8  a.  m.  the  army  steamer  Pioneer,  a  schooner, 
and  the  army  steamer  Picket  were  all  aground  on  the  swash.  As  usual, 
the  Ceres,  Putnam ,  Lockwood,  and  Shawsheen  were  all  engaged  during  the 
day  tugging,  provisioning,  and  assisting  the  army.  At  11:15  a.  m. 
the  army  steamer  Cossack  attempted  to  get  over  the  bar.  At  12:20  the 
Pioneer  got  over  and  joined  the  fleet.  AT  11:30  an  army  schoouer  got 
over.  At  1 : 50  p.  m.  about  a  dozen  pilots  were  sent  over  to  Commander 
Rowan  for  his  use.  At  1:30  p.  in.  a  couple  of  rebel  steamers  appeared, 
apparently  reconnoitering  to  the  westward  of  us.  Chase  was  at  once 
given,  but  without  success.  Early  in  the  evening  the  army  steamer 
Cossack  got  over  and  joined  the  fleet.

Wednesday ,  January  22. — A  stiff  breeze  all  last  night  and  to-day 
from  the  northward,  making  C  or  8  inches  more  in  depth  of  water  on 
the  swash.  The  army  quartermaster’s  steamer  Spaulding  arrived  in  the 
night  from  Port  Royal.  The  army  steamer  Lancer  attempted  to  get 
over  and  succeeded  finally  in  joining  the  sound  fleet  at  10:10  a.  m. 
Army  steamer  Ranger  got  over  the  swash  at  12:35.  At  the  same  time 
the  army  steamer  Guide  started  and  finally  grounded,  when  nearly 
over,  at  1:30  p.  m.  The  Army  had  over  in  the  sound  at  this  time  t 
steamers  and  4  or  5  schooners,  and  the  Navy,  16  steamers  and  1  sloop. 

Thursday ,  January  23. — A  violent  N.  E.  gale  prevailed  all  last  night 
and  to-day,  rendering  impossible  any  active  movements  in  the  expedi¬ 
tion.  At  11:50  a.  m.  the  Guide  hoisted  a  signal  of  distress  as  she  laid 
aground.  She  had  three  steamers  near  her.  It  was  impossible,  how¬ 
ever,  to  render  assistance  at  that  time.  Signal  lowered  after  it  had 
been  flying  an  hour.  In  the  evening  the  gale  seemed  to  abate  some¬ 
what.  Water  very  high  and  Fort  Hatteras  apparently  surrounded  by 
water.  At  8:35  p.  m.  three  minute  guns  were  fired  from  the  fleet  in 
the  sound  as  signals  of  distress. 

Friday ,  January  24. — N.  E.  gale  continued  unabated.  At  10  a.  m.  the 
Picket  signalized  “  The  Guide  requires  the  assistance  of  a  tug.”  We 
replied,  “  After  the  gale.”  At  12:30  the  gale  at  last  abated,  after  a  very 
heavy  rain.  The  army  steamers  Few  York ,  Northerner ,  and  Peabody 
got  up  steam.  At  12:55  we  signalized  to  the  Delaware,  Commander 
Rowan’s  flagship,  “Render  immediate  assistance  to  the  Guide.”  At  1 
p.  m.  Generals  Burnside  and  Reno,  Commander  Hazard  and  staff  offi¬ 
cers  came  on  board.  No  disasters  of  any  importance  were  reported, 
and  many  vessels  before  aground  were  reported  to  be  afloat  again  in 
consequence  of.  the  increased  depth  of  water.  At  1 : 35  p.  m.,  the  Dela¬ 
ware  having  answered,  sent  the  Shawsheen  to  the  assistance  of  the 
Guide ,  with  which  she  remained  tugging  all  the  rest  of  the  day,  with 
the  army  steamers  Union  and  Patuxent.  At  2 : 20  p.  m.  the  flag-steamer 
Philadelphia  got  underway  and  ran  alongside  the  army  steamer  New 
Yorlc  to  offer  her  assistance  in  getting  her  over  the  swash.  As  the 
offer  was  declined,  for  the  present  at  least,  the  flag-steamer  proceeded 
over  the  swash  to  the  Guide ,  and  for  two  hours  aided  in  tugging  at  her 
without  success.  At  3:10  p.  m.  General  Burnside  came  on  board  to 
thank  the  flag-officer,  and  remained  to  dine  with  the  flag-officer.  The 
Peabody ,  which  attempted  to  follow  the  flagship,  grounded  on  the  swash, 
where  she  was  tugged  by  the  Seymour  without  effect.  At  4:20  p.m. 
the  Delaware  signalized  from  the  fleet  in  the  sound  asking,  “Have you 
a  pilot  on  board  “?”  We  replied,  and  at  4:30  p.  m.  stopped  tugging  at 
the  Guide ,  and  proceeded  to  an  anchorage  for  the  night  near  the  fleet 
beyond  the  swash.  At  5:30  p.  m.  an  army  schooner  was  towed  over 
full  of  soldiers.  At  6:10  p.  m.  the  army  steamers  Curlew  and  Eagle 
passed  over  into  the  sound.  During  the  p.  m.  there  was  but  little 
effective  movement  among  the  vessels  still  lying  in  the  inlet. 

Saturday,  January  25. — At  1:30  a.  m.  the  army  steamer  Peabody 
passed  over.  Between  8:30  and  9:30  the  flag-steamer  telegraphed  to 
Commander  Rowan,  commanding  naval  division,  “Vessels  in  want  of 
fuel,  will  get  coal  for  fourteen  days;”  also,  “Take  provisions  if  wanted 
for  sixty  days.”  At  2 : 15  the  flag-steamer  Philadelphia  joined  the  Ceres , 
Putnam,  and  army  steamer  Patuxent  in  tugging  at  the  army  steamer 
Guide,  which  was  still  aground  on  the  swash,  while  the  Picket  was  at 
work  on  the  army  steamer  Northerner,  also  aground,  but  no  success 
was  met  with  in  either  case.  At  3 : 15  p.  in.  the  army  steamer  Pilot  Boy 
took  over  a  schooner  load  of  troops.  At  5:30  p.  m.  the  flag-steamer

Monday,  January  27. — Flag-steamer  Philadelphia  down  at  the  inlet 
coaling  during  the  day.  At  8  a.  m.  the  army  steamer  Eastern  Queen

Tuesday,  January  2S. — The  army  steamer  Eastern  Queen  got  over 
into  the  sound  at  7:18  a.  m.  and  the  Commodore  Barney  at  7:40  a.  m. 
The  army  steamer  Spaulding  started  to  come  over  at  5:15  p.  m.,  and  a 
similar  movement  was  attempted  by  the  army  steamers  New  Brunswick 
and  New  York,  but  all  stopped  at  the  outer  entrance  of  the  swash 
for  the  night.  Several  schooners  were  towed  over  into  the  sound  in

Wednesday,  January  29. — Army  steamer  New  Brunswick  passed  over 
at  5  a.  m.,  but  got  aground  in  the  sound.  At  9:15  a.  m.  the  army 
steamer  Chasseur  passed  over.  At  10:45  a.  m.  the  four  generals  went 
on  board  flag-steamer.  At  12:45  Lieutenant  Commanding  Murray 
reported  to  flag-officer  that  at  12:30  a  schooner  made  its  appearance  in 
the  sound,  and  that  a  couple  of  our  steamers  were  in  pursuit.  No 
result  followed.  The  army  steamer  Spaulding  passed  safely  over  at 
5:15  p.  m.  Several  schooners  towed  over  during  the  day. 

Thursday,  January  30. — The  army  steamer  Sentinel  passed  over  at 
8:30  a.  in.  At  3:45  p.  m.  the  army  steamer  New  Brunswick  floated 
again.  Between  5:30  and  6  p.  m.  three  small  army  tug  propellers 
passed  over;  also  a  schooner  and  brig  loaded  with  troops. 

Friday,  January  31. — At  7  a.  m.  a  schooner  with  five  deserters  from 
the  rebel  militia  at  Middletown,  N.  C.,  ran  down  to  our  fleet.  At  S :  50 
a.  m.  the  army  steamer  Virginia  passed  over  the  swash.  At  9: 15  a.  m. 
the  five  deserters  were  brought  on  board  and  examined  by  flag  officer 
and  General  Burnside;  their  statements,  as  regarded  the  number  and 
position  of  the  enemy,  confused  and  doubtful.  They  concurred,  how¬ 
ever,  in  saying  that  the  militia  was  hastily  and  ill  provided  for,  and 
the  Union  feeling  was  growing  in  the  eastern  counties  of  North  Caro¬ 
lina.  At  10:11  a.  m.  army  steamer  New  York  passed  over  into  the 
sound.  At  10:30  a.  m.  the  mail  arrived  from  the  North.  General 
Burnside  on  board  again  in  the  p.  m.  He  thought  he  would  be  ready

to  move  on  Monday.  The  Patuxent  passed  over  in  the  a.  m.  loaded

Saturday ,  February  1. — Rain  all  night  and  in  the  morning.  Generals 
Burnside  and  Reno  came  on  board  flag-steamer.  At  4:30p.  m.  the 
army  steamer  Eastern  State  was  sent  to  Wilmington,  N.  C.,  in  haste, 
with  orders  from  the  flag-officer  to  the  IT.  S.  S.  Chippewa ,  blockading 
off  that  port,  to  proceed  at  once  off  Nag’s  Head,  opposite  the  northern 
end  of  Roanoke  Island,  to  dislodge  the  enemy’s  troops  said  to  be  there, 
and  to  prevent  retreat  northward  by  that  way  from  Roanoke  Island. 
Schooners  and  troops,  as  usual,  passed  over  the  swash  during  the  day. 

Sunday ,  February  2. — Hay  occupied  by  the  army  in  bringing  vessels 
over  the  swash,  in  coaling,  provisioning,  reorganizing,  etc.  No  move¬ 
ment  by  the  navy. 

Monday ,  February  3. — The  weather  was  unfavorable  for  any  general 
movement.  Nineteen  fugitive  slaves — men,  women,  and  children — were 
picked  up,  much  exhausted,  at  7  a.  m.  in  a  small  boat  by  the  Ceres  and 
brought  on  board  at  10  a.  m.  They  made  their  escape  from  Middle- 
town,  N.  C.,  the  previous  night.  They  reported  that  others  were  com¬ 
ing.  General  Burnside  came  on  board  at  10:30  a.m.  He  pronounced 
the  army  nearly  ready  to  move.  The  following  is  a  recapitulation  of 
the  army  steamers  now  in  the  sound :  Picket,  Pilot  Boy ,  Vidette,  Pioneer , 
Cossack,  Lancer,  Banger,  Curlew,  Eagle,  Peabody ,  Union ,  Guide,  Patuxent , 
Phoenix,  Eastern  Queen,  Chasseur,  New  Brunswick ,  Sentinel,  New  York , 
Virginia,  Spaulding ,  and  Hussar.  Besides  these,  there  are  between 
20  and  30  schooners,  sailing  troop  vessels,  and  other  craft,  including 
4  small  propeller  tugs.  The  naval  gunboats  now  in  the  sound  are 
as  follows :  Delaware,  Stars  and  Stripes,  Louisiana ,  Hetzel,  Valley  City , 
Underwriter,  Commodore  Perry,  Commodore  Barney,  Southfield,  Hunch¬ 
back,  Morse ,  Loclnvood,  Ceres,  Putnam,  Seymour ,  Whitehead,  Brinker, 
Shawsheen,  sailing  sloop  Granite,  and  Philadelphia,  the  latter  being 
the  flag-steamer  of  Flag-Officer  Goldsborougli.  The  naval  division  is 
under  Commander  Rowan,  whose  flag-steamer  is  the  Delaware.  It  is 
divided  into  three  columns,  under  the  command,  respectively,  of  Lieu¬ 
tenant  Commanding  Werclen,  of  the  Stars  and  Stripes ,  Lieutenant 
Commanding  Murray,  of  the  Louisiana,  and  Lieutenant  Commanding 
Davenport,  of  the  Hetzel.  At  12: 15  General  Williams  came  on  board, 
and  afterwards  Generals  Burnside,  Parke,  and  Colonel  Hawkins.  At 
4:30  p.  m.  our  mail  for  the  North  left  the  flag-steamer  to  go  in  the 
Suieanee,  steamer. 

Tuesday ,  February  4. — The  Philadelphia  was  at  the  inlet  coaling  dur¬ 
ing  the  greater  part  of  the  day.  The  Suwanee,  mail  steamer,  left  for 
the  North  at  1  p.  m.  The  arrangements  for  departure  were  completed 
by  the  army  to-day,  and  at  5:45  p.  m.  Generals  Burnside  and  Reno 
came  on  board  flag-steamer  to  report  the  fact. 

Wednesday,  February  5. — Clear  and  cool.  At  6 :  45  a.  m.  flag-steamer 
got  underway  and  proceeded  to  the  front  of  the  fleet.  At  7 : 15  a.  m. 
the  signal  was  made,  “The  fleet  will  prepare  to  get  underway.”  At 
7:30  a.  m.  the  signal  was  made,  “Get  underway.”  The  signal  was 
repeated  by  divisions  and  columns,  and  at  8  a.  m.  the  navy  columns 
were  formed  and  underway,  a  half  an  hour  afterwards  followed  by  the 
army  vessels  in  three  brigades.  At  9:30  a.  m.  signal  was  made  from 
the  Delaicare  to  the  three  columns,  “Form  line  abreast.”  Underwriter 
and  sloop  Granite  were  sent  ahead  to  Long  Shoal  Point  to  examine,  and 
place  buoy  if  necessary.  At  9 :  50  a.  m.  two  schooners  hove  in  sight  to 
the  westward.  At  11:50  a.  m.  the  army  steamer  Picket  overhauled  us

with  General  Burnside  on  board,  who  desired  the  flag-officer  to  heave

At  2:20  ii.  m.  we  came  up  to  the  Underwriter  and  Granite  lying  to,

aiul  laid  to  until  it  had  been  ascertained,  by  the  movements  of  the 
entire  fleet,  that  the^  signal  had  been  understood.  Boanoke  Island 
hove  in  sight  at  4:55  p.  in.  right  ahead.  At  5:20  p.  m.,  off  Stumpy 
Point,  10  miles  south  of  the  island,  the  flag-steamer  signalized  to  the 
naval  fleet,  “Anchor  in  three  columns.”  At  5:25  p.  m.  the  smoke  of 
two  or  three  steamers  was  seen  near  Boanoke  Marshes.  At  5 :  43  p.  in. 
the  flag-officer  spoke  the  general  on  board  the  army  steamer  Spaulding , 
advising  him  to  come  to  anchor  with  all  his  vessels  for  the  night.  Gen¬ 
erals  Burnside  and  Foster  came  on  board  flag-steamer  at6:30p.  m. 
and  supped  with  the  flag-officer.  The  Ceres  was  sent  to  the  mainland 
with  Lieutenant  Commanding  Jeffers  in  the  evening  to  bring  off  a 
Union  resident,  supposed  to  possess  knowledge  of  the  enemy’s  latest 
movements.  At  10:20  p  m.  Lieutenant  Jeffers  returned,  bringing  the 
man  with  him.  Little  information,  however,  from  him. 

Thursday ,  February  6. — Wind  FT.  E.,  cloudy,  with  rain.  At  4:30 
a.  m,  orders  were  given  to  have  all  the  boats  in  the  squadron  ready  for 
disembarking  troops.  General  Burnside  was  on  board  flag-steamer  at 
7  a.  m.  At  7  :25  a.  m.  flag-officer  shifted  his  flag  from  the  Philadelphia 
to  the  South  field,  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Behm  commanding. 
At  7 :35  flag-steamer  signalized,  “Prepare  to  get  underway.”  At  7:45 
a,  m.  signalized,  “Get  underway.”  At  8:30  a.  m.  the  whole  fleet,  army 
and  navy,  were  steaming  ahead  in  columns  and  brigades,  the  Ceres  and 
Putnam  running  ahead  to  reconnoiter.  At  9 :  53  a.  m.  signal  was  made 
from  the  Delaware  to  the  naval  division,  “Keep  in  closer  order  by  clos¬ 
ing  toward  the  center.”  Lieutenant  Commanding  Murray  led  the  left 
column,  Werden  the  right,  and  Davenport  the  center.  At  10:05  a.  m. 
the  Delaware  signalized,  “Prepare  for  action.”  At  10:10  a.  m.  the 
Southfield,  flag-steamer,  signalized,  “  Keep  in  closer  order  by  closing 
toward  the  leading  ship.”  At  1 0 : 15  a.  m.  the  Ceres  and  Putnam  entered 
the  channel  of  Boanoke  Marshes  and  passed  through  into  Croatan 
Sound,  without  meeting  with  any  obstruction.  At  10:25  a.  m.  heavy 
fog  with  rain  set  in.  At  10:35  a.  m.  the  Ceres  and  Putnam  returned 
and  reported  that  they  had  run  up  3  or  4  miles  above  the  marshes  into 
Croatan  Sound  and  had  seen  15  steamers  and  10  sailing  vessels  of  the 
enemy  at  anchor  in  a  line  extending  from  Weir’s  Point  about  a  mile 
southward  near  the  island.  At  10:40  a.  m.,  the  fog  and  rain  increasing, 
the  Southfield ,  flag-steamer,  signalized,  “Anchor  in  three  columns,”  and 
the  signal  was  repeated  to  the  army.  At  2:40  p.  m.  the  Delaware 
signalized,  “The  enemy  is  approaching,”  referring  to  the  gunboats  we 
could  see  moving  beyond  the  marshes  of  Boanoke.  Southfield  signal¬ 
ized,  “  Be  on  the  alert.”  During  the  p.  m.  five  army  vessels,  which  were 
armed,  discharged  their  troops  into  other  vessels,  and  steamed  forward 
into  line  with  the  navy  gunboats,  the  army  steamer  Picket,  with  Com¬ 
mander  Hazard  on  board,  leading.  Wind  shifted  to  southward  at  noon, 
with  frequent  rains  and  mist.

Friday,  February  7. — At  7  a.  m.  the  flag-steamer  Southfield  signalized, 
“Let  the  men  take  their  breakfast  j”  a  heavy  fog  bank  to  the  north¬ 
ward  driven  over  and  dispersed  by  9  a.  m. ;  troopships  steaming  for¬ 
ward  a  little  into  line  and  taking  their  tows.  At  9:  40  a.  m.  the  army 
steamer  Chasseur  joined  the  other  army  gunboats.  At  9:40  a.  m.  the 
flag-steamer  hoisted  signal,  “Prepare  to  get  underway;”  at  9:55  a.  m., 
“Get  underway.”  At  10: 10  a.  m.  the  Delaware  signalized  to  her  divi¬ 
sion,  “In  two  columns,  keep  in  close  order.”  At  10:15  a.  m.  the  flag- 
steamer  hoisted,  “Our  country  expects  every  man  to  do  his  duty.”  At 
10:30  a.  m.  the  enemy  discharged  a  heavy  gun.  At  10:25  the  flag- 
steamer  signalized,  “Steamers  with  9  inch  guns  close  up.”  At  10:50 
a.  m.  the  Putnam  and  Louisiana  both  got  aground  in  passing  through 
the  marshes  into  Croatan,  but  both  were  soon  got  off.  At  10: 55  a.  m. 
flag-steamer  signalized,  “Prepare  for  action.”  At  11 : 20  a.  m.  the  Dela- 
ware  hoisted,  “  Keep  the  lead  going.”  During  the  great  movement  into 
the  sound  the  Ceres  and  Underwriter  were  sent  ahead,  the  former  to  feel 
the  way  and  ascertain  if  there  were  obstructions  in  the  channel,  the 
latter  with  orders  to  discover  if  there  was  a  fortification  on  Sand  Point. 
At  11:25  a.  m.  the  Underwriter  fired  the  first  shot  into  the  point,  with¬ 
out  drawing  a  reply,  and  hoisted  accordingly,  “No  battery  on  Sand 
Point.”  At  11 :  50  a.  m.  all  the  gunboats  were  fairly  in  Croatan  Sound, 
the  transports  meanwhile  crowding  after,  and  the  signal  was  made, 
“Keep  in  close  order.”  As  we  approached  the  enemy’s  boats  appeared, 
eight  in  number,  behind  a  barrier  built  of  piles  and  sunken  vessels,  and 
extending  from  Redstone  Point  on  the  mainland  eastward  to  within 
half  a  mile  of  the  island.  The  action  became  general  about  meridian, 
our  gunboats  being  engaged  with  the  enemy’s  vessels,  with  a  battery 
of  9  guns  on  Pork  Point,  a  battery  of  4  guns  2  miles  above  this  point, 
and  a  battery  of  8  guns  on  Redstone  Point  on  the  mainland,  the  last 
two  batteries,  however,  firing  only  occasionally  and  with  little  effect. 
During  the  action  most  of  our  fire  was  directed  against  the  Pork 
Point  battery,  with  reference  to  which  the  signal  was  several  times 
made  from  the  flag-steamer,  “Close  in.”  Throughout  the  day  it  was 
the  effort  of  the  enemy’s  vessels  to  draw  our  fire  from  this  battery, 
and  by  retreating  when  pursued,  to  get  our  vessels  entangled  among 
the  piles  and  sunken  vessels  of  the  barrier,  where  they  would  be 
exposed  not  only  to  the  fire  of  the  three  batteries  above  named,  but 
especially  to  that  of  a  battery  on  Weir’s  Point  mounting  12  guns. 
At  1:30  p.  m.  the  barracks  and  storehouses  behind  the  Pork  Point 
battery  were  set  on  fire  by  our  shells.  At  2  p.  m.  General  Burnside 
ran  alongside  the  flag-steamer  to  communicate  concerning  the  land¬ 
ing  of  troops,  etc.  At  2 : 15  p.  m.  the  buildings  of  the  fort  seemed  to  be 
on  fire  in  many  places,  burning  furiously ;  the  signal  halyards  had  been 
shot  away  and  the  rebel  flag  floated  from  a  staff  temporarily  raised  on 
the  earthworks.  At  about  this  time  the  fire  was  hottest  from  the  fleet, 
and  the  fort  responded  steadily  but  with  considerable  deliberation.  At 
2: 30  p.  m.  the  Iletsel  signalized,  “I  am  struck  below  water.”  The  flag- 
steamer  replied,  “Haul  off  and  repair.”  At  3  p.  m.  the  army  steamers 
Patuxent  and  Union  filled  with  troops  left  the  transports  (which  were 
lying  at  anchor  in  a  body  about  2  miles  above  the  marshes)  and  ap¬ 
proached  Ashby’s  Harbor,  a  landing  place  2  miles  south  of  Pork  Point. 
At  3:25  p.  m.  the  army  steamer  Pilot  Boy  followed,  towing  a  large  num¬ 
ber  of  boats  and  a  pontoon  bridge,  all  loaded  with  troops.'  At  3 : 55  p.  m. 
the  Ceres  and  afterward  several  other  vessels  signalized,  “Ammunition 
nearly  expended.”  These  vessels  were  directed  to  obtain  a’  supply  of

the  articles  wanted  from  the  schooner  Howard  and  the  steamer  Phila¬

was  dispersed  by  our  shrapnel.  The  two  lower  batteries,  after  having 
been  silent  for  about  three-quarters  of  an  hour,  opened  again  at  about 
5  p.  m.  At  the  same  time  several  small  steamers  of  the  enemy  appeared 
to  be  landing  troops  at  Weir’s  Point  by  means  of  flatboats.  At  5: 10 
p.  m.  the  flag  steamer  signalized,  “Shots  are  falling  short,”  and  at 
about  the  same  time  the  enemy’s  gunboats  ran  down  toward  us,  but 
v  ere  driven  back  before  5:45  p.  m.,  and  at  G  p.  m.  signal  was  hoisted 
from  flag-steamer,  “Cease  firing.”  In  the  evening,  at  9:30,  General 
Burnside  went  on  board  flag-steamer  and  reported  that  0,000  men  had 
landed,  and  that  through  the  night  he  would  land  his  men  at  the  rate 
of  1,000  an  hour.  In  the  evening  six  naval  launches,  under  the  com¬ 
mand  of  Midshipman  Porter,  landed  their  howitzers  and  reported  to 
the  general  for  orders. 

Saturday,  February  S. — At  9  a.  m.  most  of  our  gunboats  got  under¬ 
way,  and  at  the  same  time  the  battery  at  Pork  Point  opened  fire  once 
more  on  them.  At  9:10  a.  m.  our  vessels  engaged  the  enemy  and 
threw  shell  with  great  precision  into  the  battery,  which  replied  lan¬ 
guidly  and  finally  not  at  all;  at  9:35  a.  m.  the  flag-steamer  signalized, 
“Cease  firing,”  it  being  feared  that  our  own  troops  were  in  the  rear  of 
the  fort,  as  throughout  the  morning  firing  had  been  heard  in  the 
interior  of  the  island.  Early  in  the  morning  a  rebel  tugboat  appeared 
at  the  northward,  towing  five  schooners,  followed  by  a  larger  steamer, 
towing  aflatboat,  all  apparently  filled  with  troops  and  coming  from  the 
direction  of  Elizabeth  City.  They  landed  at  Weir’s  Point  at  about 
9 : 15  a.  in.,  reenforcing  the  enemy  by  about  a  thousand  men.  At  9 : 45 
a.  m.  the  flag-steamer  hoisted  a  general  recall,  as  the  Commodore  Ferry, 
Valley  City,  and  several  other  gunboats  were  approaching  very  near 
the  Pork  Point  battery.  At  11  a.  m.  a  signal  of  general  attack  was 
made  on  board  flag-steamer,  but  immediately  revoked.  At  about 
meridian  the  Valley  City  and  Louisiana  fired  several  shots  at  the  fort, 
eliciting  no  response.  The  fort  was  silenced  and  abandoned.  At 
12:45  a  fog  came  up  and  all  firing  ceased  among  the  vessels.  The 
rebel  steamers  did  not  appear  to-day,  with  the  exception  of  one,  the 
Curlew,  which,  disabled  by  our  shot,  had  been  run  ashore  near  the 
Eedstone  Point  battery  the  previous  night.  At  1  p.  m.  the  Under¬ 
writer,  Valley  City,  Seymour,  Lockwood.  Whitehead,  Ceres ,  Putnam,  and 
Brinlcer,  having  been  placed  under  the  command  of  Lieutenant  Com¬ 
manding  Jeffers,  proceeded  toward  the  barrier  to  break  or  find  a  way 
through  it.  At  1:15  p.  m.  the  Delaware,  which  had  been  lying  near 
the  landing  at  Ashby’s  Harbor  to  protect  it,  got  underway  and 
approached  the  flag-steamer.  Occasional  firing  heard  inland. "  At  4 
p.  m.  we  could  see  the  Ceres  on  the  other  side  of  the  barrier.  At  4:45 
p.  m.  the  Pork  Point  battery  was  occupied  by  our  troops  and  the 
American  flag  hoisted  there.  The  flag-steamer  made  [signal]  “The 
fort  is  ours.”  At  5  p.  m.  the  fort  on  Eedstone  Point  was  abandoned 
by  the  enemy  and  its  buildings  set  on  fire  by  them;  at  the  same

Sunday ,  February  9. — At  about  9  a.  m.  a  schooner  appeared  running 
down  to  the  Ceres ,  which  was  lying  beyond  the  barrier.  At  10: 30  a.  m. 
the  schooner’s  captain  was  brought  on  board  the  flag-steamer  a  captive. 
His  vessel  was  a  coal  schooner  of  the  enemy,  which  mistook  our  gunboats 
for  those  of  the  rebels.  At  2: 50  p.  m.  the  flag  of  the  Redstone  Point 
battery  was  brought  on  board  flag-steamer  by  an  officer  of  the  Commo¬ 
dore  Perry.  In  the  morniug  a  deserter  from  the  rebel  steamer  Fanny 
was  brought  on  board.  He  made  his  escape  the  previous  night  in  a 
small  boat  from  Elizabeth  City  and  gave  valuable  information.  At  3 
p.  m.  Commander  Rowan  left  for  Elizabeth  City  with  tli  e  Delaware,  Under- 
writer ,  Valley  City ,  Louisiana ,  Hetzel,  Lockwood ,  Seymour,  Morse,  Shaw- 
sheen,  Brinlcer ,  Perry ,  Ceres ,  and  Whitehead ,  to  destroy  the  enemy’s 
gunboats  and  break  up  canal  communications  between  the  North  and 
Albemarle  Sound. 

Monday ,  February  10. — Between  9  and  10  a.  m.  firing  was  heard  in  the 
direction  of  Elizabeth  City.  At  1 :  45  p.  m.  General  Burnside  came  on 
board.  At  2:25  p.  m.  the  Southfield  made  signal,  aI  see  the  smoke 
of  a  steamer  N.  W.”  On  examination  smoke,  as  of  vessels  or  houses 
on  fire,  could  be  seen  in  the  direction  of  Elizabeth  City.  In  the  p.  m. 
an  army  expedition  was  dispatched  to  Nag’s  Head.  At  10:07  p.  m. 
our  private  night  signal  was  burned  in  the  northwest  direction,  indi¬ 
cating  the  return  of  one  of  our  vessels  from  Elizabeth  City.  At  10 :  40 
p.  m.  the  Ceres  came  alongside  flag-steamer  and  announced  the  complete 
success  of  the  expedition,  the  enemy’s  steamers  Sea  Bird ,  Fanny ,  Forrest , 
and  Accomac  being  either  sunk  by  collision  or  burned  by  the  enemy, 
the  times  of  the  engagement  and  burning  coinciding  with  our  obser¬ 
vations  of  the  morning.  The  enemy’s  steamer  Ellis  was  captured ; 
and  it  was  thought  that  the  enemy’s  steamers  Beaufort  and  Raleigh , 
both  having  received  shots,  had  made  their  escape  up  the  canal,  which 
had  been  obstructed  by  the  enemy  by  the  destruction  of  a  lock  about 
30  miles  above  Elizabeth  City.  Our  forces  took  possession  of  and 
destroyed  a  fort  mounting  4  guns  and  a  schooner  mounting  1  gun, 
which  had  been  used  in  the  effort  to  oppose  the  advance  on  the  enemy’s 
vessels.  We  lost  two  or  three  killed  and  about  a  dozen  wounded.  The 
enemy’s  loss  in  killed,  wounded,  and  prisoners  was  large.  The  news 
was  communicated  to  General  Burnside  at  once. 

Tuesday,  February  11. — General  Burnside  went  on  board  flag-steamer 
at  4:30  a.  m.  with  his  dispatches  to  General  McClellan,  and  again  at 
9  a.  m.  with  Mr.  L’Amy,  who  was  to  carry  his  dispatches.  At  11  a.  m. 
this  gentleman,  together  with  Mr.  Van  Brunt,  secretary  to  the  flag- 
officer  and  bearer  of  his  dispatches  to  the  Navy  Department,  went  on 
board  Stars  and  Stripes ,  which  at  11 : 30  a.  m  got  underway,  bound  for 
Old  Point  Comfort  via  Hatteras  Inlet. 

(Rough  notes  taken  in  the  absence  of  Mr.  Van  Brunt.)

arrived  from  Elizabeth  City  with  40  prisoners.  Southfield  went  over 
to  Fort  Forrest  on  Redstone  Point  and  completed  destruction  and
