I.  N.  Seymour,  of  the  loss  of  that  vessel ,  February  20,  1862. 

U.  S.  S.  Shawsheen, 
Croatan  Sound ,  February  24,  1862. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  orders  of  the  18th  instant  to  proceed  to 
Hatteras  Inlet  with  the  U.  S.  S.  I.  N.  Seymour,  for  the  purpose  of  assist¬ 
ing  the  U.  S.  S.  Stars  and  Stripes,  etc.,  I  regret  to  inform  you  that  while 
transporting  ammunition  from  the  IT.  S.  S.  Stars  and  Stripes  to  a 
schooner  lying  at  the  head  of  Swash  Channel  my  vessel  struck  on 
an  anchor  which  had  been  left  by  the  transport  steamer  Louisiana  in 
the  center  and  near  the  entrance  of  the  channel.  The  vessel  sunk 
before  it  was  possible  to  run  her  aground,  taking  the  bottom  in  7|-  feet 
of  water.  From  the  time  she  struck  till  she  filled  did  not  exceed  two 
minutes.  Lieutenant  Commanding  It.  Werden,  of  U.  S.  S.  Stars  and 
Stripes ,  came  promptly  to  my  assistance,  as  did  also  the  U.  S.  S. 
Shawsheen.  Lieutenant  Werden  decided  to  save  everything  possible.

Report  of  Chief  Engineer  Stimers ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the  trial  trip  of 

the  if.  S.  S.  Monitor. 

New  York,  February  20,  1862. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  that  the  ironclad  steamer 
Monitor  is  at  the  navy  yard. 

She  left  Green  Point  at  2  p.  m.  yesterday  under  steam,  but  in  conse¬ 
quence  of  the  engine  builders  having  set  the  cut-off  valves  for  backing, 
instead  of  her  going  ahead,  we  made  but  slow  progress,  40  revolutions 
per  minute  of  the  engines  and  3  J  knots  an  hour  of  the  vessel  being  the 
maximum  performance.  The  effect  of  this  mistake  in  the  cut-off  valves 
was  to  admit  steam  to  the  cylinder  after  the  piston  had  performed  one- 
half  its  stroke,  so  that  the  consumption  of  steam  was  equal  to  run¬ 
ning  full  stroke;  whereas  the  effect  was  only  one-half  what  was  due  to 
that  consumption,  without  expansion. 

There  was  another  difficulty:  One  of  the  blower  engines  had  a  valve 
come  off  its  stem,  so- that  during  nearly  the  whole  trip  only  one  was  in 
operation. 

We  came  to  anchor  off  the  navy  yard  at  7 : 30  p.  m.,  and  towed  her  in 
to  the  wharf  with  a  towboat  this  morning. 

In  the  operation  of  weighing  the  anchor  this  morning  I  found  that 
the  windlass  will  require  some  alterations  to  make  it  efficient.  This,  I 
think,  must  detain  us  several  days,  but  I  have  not  been  able  to  see 
Captain  Ericsson  yet  this  morning. 

From  what  I  have  seen  thus  far  I  think  your  estimate  of  her  speed 
being  6  knots  an  hour  will  prove  very  correct,  though  Captain  Ericsson 
feels  confident  of  8. 

Aside  from  the  foregoing  easily  adjusted  difficulties,  everything  was 
perfectly  satisfactory. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Alban  0.  Stimers, 

Superintendent. 

Commodore  Joseph  Smith,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Chief  Bureau  of  Yards  and  Bocks ,  Navy  Bept.,  Washington ,  B.  C.

Report  of  the  senior  officer  in  Hampton  Roads,  regarding  the  defenses  near 

Norfolk. 

IT.  S.  S.  Eoanoke, 
Hampton  Roads,  February  21, 1862. 

Sir:  In  compliance  with  your  wishes  to  have  the  Department 
advised  as  nearly  as  possible  what  are  the  defenses  at  Sewell’s  Point, 
Craney  Island,  Nansemond  Eiver,  etc.,  I  beg  leave  to  report  that  as 
near  as  can  be  ascertained  from  observation  and  from  contrabands  the 
battery  at  Sewell’s  Point,  on  the  water  side,  consists  of  at  least  20 
guns,  all  in  barbette,  and  in  a  well-constructed  fort.  In  the  rear  of  this 
battery  is  another,  intended  to  defend  the  land  side.  The  strength  of 
this  latter  is  not  ascertained,  but  it  mounts  several  heavy  guns.  The 
whole  of  Craney  Island  is  a  fortified  camp,  mounting  at  least  30  guns, 
perhaps  more,  bearing  directly  down  the  river.  Above  Craney  Island 
and  below  the  hospital  is  another  battery  mounting  7  guns,  which  rake 
the  whole  channel.  The  sloop  of  war  Germantown  is  also  anchored  off 
Craney  Island,  and  has  6  or  8  guns.  Between  Sewell’s  Point  and 
the  land  opposite  the  Eip  Eaps  are  several  guns  mounted,  of  a  large 
caliber,  but  which  are  hidden  from  view  by  the  trees.  At  Pig  Point  is 
a  well-constructed  battery  mounting  8  or  9  guns;  and  up  the  Nanse¬ 
mond  are  two  other  batteries,  apparently  small;  also  to  the  north  and 
east  of  Pig  Point  are  two  5-gun  batteries,  but  not  as  formidable  as  that 
on  the  point.  These  constitute  all  the  defenses  of  the  approach  to  Nor¬ 
folk  of  which  I  have  any  information. 

By  a  dispatch  which  I  received  late  last  evening  from  General  Wool, 
I  learn  that  the  Merrimack  will  positively  attack  Newport  News  within 
live  days,  acting  in  conjunction  with  the  Jamestown  and  Yorktown  from 
James  Eiver,  and  that  the  attack  will  be  at  night.  I  can  only  regret 
that  the  Roanoke  should  be  without  an  engine,  and  has  a  deficiency  of 
180  men  in  her  crew;  but  you  may  be  assured  we  shall  do  our  best. 
Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  Marston, 
Captain  and  Senior  Officer.

Report  of  the  senior  officer  in  Hampton  Roads,  regarding  the  defective 
condition  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Whitehall. 

U.  S.  S.  Roanoke, 
Hampton  Roads,  February  22,  1862. 

Sir:  I  have  had  the  steamer  Whitehall  surveyed,  and  both  her  ma¬ 
chinery  and  hull  are  very  defective,  particularly  the  latter;  and  it  is 
highly  probable,  when  her  engine  is  removed,  it  will  be  discovered  to  be 
still  more  so  than  it  is  now  supposed  to  be,  and  possibly  so  rotten  as 
not  to  [be]  worth  the  expense  of  repairing.  Under  these  circumstances 
I  would  recommend  that  she  should  be  sent  to  Philadelphia,  or  some 
other  navy  yard,  where  she  will  be  under  the  special  supervision  of  a 
naval  commandant,  who  can  decide  whether  she  is  worthy  of  repairs. 
If  she  goes  to  Baltimore  and  gets  into  the  hands  of  outside  mechanics 
I  fear  the  cost  will  be  very  great. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  Marston, 
Captain  and  Senior  Officer. 

Hou.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington ,  I).  C.

Report  of  the  senior  officer  in  Hampton  Roads,  referring  to  the  chartered 

schooner  L.  B.  Myers  and  the  expected  attach  of  the  C.  S.  S.  Virginia 

(Merrimack). 

IT.  S.  S.  Boanoke, 
Hampton  Roads ,  February  22 ,  1862. 

Sir:  The  schooner  L.  B.  Myers  is  now  loading  with  provisions  of  all 
kinds,  except  sugar,  of  which  there  is  none  here.  If,  however,  there 
had  been,  the  schooner  could  not  have  taken  it,  as  she  is  full  even  to 
the  cabin;  the  sugar,  however,  will  be  forwarded  by  the  first  opportu¬ 
nity.  I  enclose  invoice  and  bill  of  lading,  all  of  which  I  hope  will 
arrive  in  good  time.  I  have  directed  Captain  Somers  (a  grand-nephew 
of  Tripoli  Somers)  to  go  directly  up  the  sound  to  any  point  where  you 
may  be.  He  is  well  acquainted  in  those  waters,  having  been  an  old 
trader  there,  and  as  his  vessel  will  draw,  when  light,  only!  feet,  he  may 
be  able  to  render  you  some  service.  I  also  enclose  to  you  the  charter 
of  the  L.  B.  Myers ,  signed  by  Captain  Somers  and  myself.  Captain 
Somers  will  sail  as  soon  as  the  weather  is  favorable.  At  present  it  is 
not  so — thick  and  rainy. 

The  different  ships  of  your  squadron  hoisted  at  sunrise  this  morning 
the  American  flags  at  the  main  and  mizzen,  with  French  flag  at  the 
fore.  At  12  o’clock  all  the  ships  having  proper  armament  will  fire  a 
salute  of  thirty- four  guns.  I  have  deviated  from  the  general  order  rel¬ 
ative  to  salutes,  believing  in  this  period  of  the  history  of  our  country 
the  whole  Union  should  be  represented.  I  communicated  yesterday 
with  Commodore  le  Marquis  de  Montaignac  and  informed  him  of  the 
programme,  and  he,  with  much  courtesy,  replied  that  he  should  partici- 
pate  in  it,  and  at  sunrise  the  four  French  vessels  now  here  hoisted  the 
American  flag  at  the  fore  and  French  flags  at  the  main  and  mizzen,  and 
the  Pomone  will  fire  thirty-four  guns  at  12  o’clock. 

I  would  remark  that  much  kindness  of  feeling  exists  between  the 
marquis  and  myself.  A  few  days  since  I  received  a  note  from  him  writ¬ 
ten  on  red,  white,  and  blue  paper,  with  the  American  coat  of  arms  at  the 
corners,  surrounded  by  the  motto,  “  Union  and  the  Constitution.”  This 
may  be  a  small  affair,  and  it  may  be  a  significant  sign,  for  I  can  hardly 
think  the  marquis  would  have  done  such  a  thing  had  he  not  received  a 
hint  from  higher  authority. 

We  are  still  in  expectation  of  a  visit  from  the  Merrimack.  Bight 
before  last  General  Wool  sent  me  off  a  dispatch  he  had  received  from 
Norfolk,  informing  him  that  u the  Merrimack,  in  conjunction  with  the 
Yorlctown  and  Jamestown ,  would  attack  Newport  News  within  the  next 
five  days;  the  attack  will  be  at  night.”  When  I  think  of  this  ship’s  crip¬ 
pled  condition — no  engine  and  180  of  her  crew  deficient — it  makes  me 
sick  at  heart;  but  we  shall  do  the  best  we  can.  We  are  all  ready  to 
slip,  and  have  the  Young  America  and  Dragon  to  attend  us.  The  Cohas- 
set  and  Zouave  are  at  Newport  News,  and  the  Rescue  is  intended  to 
cripple,  if  possible,  the  rudder  of  the  Merrimack. 

You  will  observe  that  the  charter  of  the  L.  B.  Myers  allows  us  to  keep 
her  one  month,  or  thirty  days,  and  afterwards  $22.50  for  every  day’s 
detention;  but  if  you  should  discharge  her  within  the  specified  month, 
she  will  still  be  entitled  to  the  sum  of  $G00. 

Trusting  that  everything  will  reach  in  safety  and  in  good  time,  I 
remain,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  Marston, 

Captain. 

Flag-Officer  L.  M.  Goldsboroitgh, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  Hatter  as  Inlet.

Headquarters  Department  of  Virginia, 

Fort  Monroe,  Va.,  February  20,  1862. 

Sir:  I  hasten  to  send  the  copy  of  the  dispatch  just  received  from 
Norfolk.  In  five  days  the  Merrimack  (steamer),  in  conjunction  with  the 
Yorhtown  and  Jamestown,  will  attack  Newport  News,  supported  by  a 
land  force.  The  attack  will  be  made  in  the  night.  We  want  a  larger 
naval  force  than  we  have  at  present.  I  will  be  prepared  for  them  on 
the  land.  The  Secretary  of  the  Navy  ought  to  be  informed. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  E.  Wool, 

Major-General. 

Hon.  Edwin  M.  Stanton, 

Secretary  of  War. 

P.  S. — The  dispatch  alluded  to  I  sent  to  Gape  Charles  to  be  tele¬ 
graphed.  Major  Jones,  aid-de-camp,  who  went  there  with  the  dispatch, 
has  not  yet  returned.  It  being  half  past  4  p.  m.,  I  forward  my  dis¬ 
patches  by  a  special  messenger.  I  intended  to  have  done  so  yester¬ 
day,  but  was  prevented  by  the  early  departure  of  the  steamer. 

John  E.  Wool, 

Major-  General. 


Letter  from  the  senior  officer  in  Hampton  Roads  to  Flag-Officer  Golds- 
borough,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron, 
regarding  affairs  in  that  vicinity. 

U.  S.  S.  Roanoke, 
Hampton  Roads,  February  23,  1862. 
My  dear  Goldsborough  :  I  have  this  moment  heard  that  the 
steamer  Eastern  State  leaves  in  au  hour  for  Hatteras,  and  I  avail  myself 
of  the  opportunity  to  say  that  the  L.  B.  Myers,  with  your  provisions, 
stores,  etc.,  is  loaded,  and  will  sail  as  soon  as  the  weather  is  favorable 
for  her.  I  have  kept  for  her  all  my  letters,  papers,  etc.,  as  I  have 
ordered  her  to  go  directly  to  you,  no  matter  where  you  may  be.  If 
you  should  get  this  first,  you  can  send  orders  to  the  inlet  in  case  you 
would  not  wish  the  L.  B.  M[yers]  to  come  up  the  sound  to  you. 

Van  Brunt  has,  I  presume,  kept  you  fully  posted  in  everything  that 
is  going  on,  but  really  I  have  not  had  time  even  to  write  to  Mrs.  M. 
The  Department  keeps  me  employed  constantly.  To-day  a  double  mail 
came,  and  I  have  been  half  crazy. 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


663 


I  bear  that  General  Wool  and  staff  have  gone  by  invitation  to 
Norfolk.  I  am  inclined  to  think  it  is  Craney  Island  and  not  Norfolk. 
Bnt  what  he  can  be  invited  over  there  for  I  can  not  conceive,  unless 
they  are  inclined  to  give  up.  The  blow  you  gave  them  at  Roanoke, 
followed  by  the  victory  at  Donelson,  has  staggered  the  rebels  a  great 
deal,  and  I  should  not  be  surprised  to  hear  of  anything.  You  know 
General  McClellan  said  some  time  since  that  when  the  rebellion  began 
to  go  it  would  go  quickly. 

We  got  through  the  22d  very  well,  though  the  weather  was  wretched. 
The  French  commodore  participated  with  us,  which  I  acknowledged  in 
a  letter  this  morning. 

But  I  must  hurry,  or  I  shall  miss  the  opportunity.  [Win.]  Smith  is 
detached  from  the  C[ongr ess]  and  ordered  south;  no  substitute.  Liv¬ 
ingston  is  relieved  on  a  sick  ticket,  and  Commander  Radford  has  taken 
command  of  the  Cumberland. 

Remember  me  most  kindly  to  Case,  and  also  all  my  friends,  and 
believe  me,  in  much  haste,  truly  and  affectionately,  yours, 

John  Marston. 

Flag-Officer  Goldsborough. 


Letter  from  Captain  Van  Brunt ,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  8.  8.  Min¬ 
nesota,  to  Flag-Officer  Goldsborough,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  North 
Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  referring  to  the  expected  attack  of  the 
C.  8.  S.  Virginia  ( Merrimack ). 

IT.  S.  S.  Minnesota, 
Hampton  Roads,  February  23,  1862. 
My  Dear  Goldsborough:  I  have  this  moment  learned  that  the 
Eastern  State  is  to  leave  for  Hatteras  this  evening,  and  I  only  write 
this  to  tell  you  that  we  are  all  well  on  board  and  anxiously  expecting 
the  long-looked-for  Merrimack.  We  are  told  that  she  came  out  of  dock 
on  Monday  last  and  is  everything  they  expected  to  make  her;  in  other 
words,  a  complete  success.  We  are  all  ready,  and  the  sooner  she  gives 
us  the  opportunity  to  test  her  strength  the  better. 

I  send  you  your  trunk  containing  clean  clothes  for  you  and  Case. 
There  have  been  several  arrivals  of  troops  here  within  a  few  days 
(about  4,000),  all  of  which  have  been  immediately  sent  to  Newport 
News,  as  General  Wool  believes  a  combined  attack  will  be  made  upon 
that  point. 

I  send  you  all  the  late  papers  with  your  mail,  which  will  give  you  all 
the  glorious  news  from  the  West.  I  think  it  rather  unfortunate  that 
the  Western  victory  came  so  immediately  after  yours,  as  it  had  a  tend¬ 
ency  to  throw  yours  in  the  shade;  however,  you  will  give  them  some 
more  glorious  news  soon.  I  see  by  last  accounts  from  Hatteras  that 
you  are  again  preparing  to  be  off.  If  there  is  anything  I  can  do  for 
you  here,  it  will  give  me  pleasure  if  you  will  inform  me. 

I  hope  Henry  [Yan  Brunt]  executed  his  mission  to  Washington  to 
your  satisfaction. 

Please  remember  me  affectionately  to  Case  and  Rowan,  and  believe 
me,  my  dear  Goldsborough, 

Your  friend,  truly  and  affectionately, 

Yan  Brunt. 

Flag-Officer  L.  M.  Goldsborough.

Confidential  letter  from  the  Assistant  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Flag-Officer 
Goldsborough ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading 
Squadron ,  regarding  proposed  operations. 


Navy  Department,  February  24,  1862. 

My  Dear  Sir:  An  official  letter  goes  to-day  stating  that  the 
Department  would  like  to  see  you  in  two  weeks,  if  the  public  service 
will  admit. 

General  McClellan  is  cutting  out  some  big  work,  which  requires  your 
cooperation ;  but,  as  our  army  friends  change  their  minds  pretty  often, 
I  would  not  leave  anything  undone  which  you  may  have  in  hand,  as  we 
can  write  again  if  the  matter  gets  urgent.  The  general  tells  me  that 
he  has  written  to  Burnside  to  press  the  New  Berne  and  Beaufort  mat¬ 
ter  as  the  most  important.  I  think  that  plan  the  best,  as  it  gives  us  a 
fine  base  to  push  any  number  of  troops  into  the  interior,  so  that  with 
North  Carolina  and  Tennessee  in  our  possession,  or  nearly  so,  we  divide 
them. 

The  Powhatan  will  be  ready  in  about  three  months.  I  do  not  see  why 
Eowan  should  not  have  her  for  that  gallant  dash  past  their  forts. 

How  came  that  80-pounder  rifled  gun  to  burst"?  Maury’s  letter  has 
been  published.  The  rebels  are  getting  it  all  round,  but  it  is  not  yet 
finished. 

Yours,  truly, 


G.  V.  Fox. 

Flag-Officer  L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 


Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Flye,  U.  S.  Navy  late  command¬ 
ing  U.  S.  S.  R.  B.  Forbes,  regarding  the  loss  of  that  vessel,  February 
25,  1862. 

IJ.  S.  Steam  Frigate  Eoanoke, 
Hampton  Roads,  February  27,  1862. 
Sir:  I  regret  to  have  to  inform  the  Department  that  the  IJ.  S.  S. 
R.  B.  Forbes,  under  my  command,  was  wrecked  about  1  o’clock,  on  the 
morning  of  the  25th  instant,  about  4  miles  to  the  south  of  Currituck 
Inlet. 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


665 


.  I  sailed  from  New  York  in  company  with  the  U.  S.  gunboats  West- 
field,  Clifton,  and  J.  P.  Jackson,  having  received  orders  from  Com¬ 
mander  D.  D.  Porter  to  accompany  them  to  the  south  of  Cape  Hatteras. 

During  a  severe  gale  on  the  24th  instant,  the  gunboats  stood  in  to 
the  N.  and  W.,  the  if.  B.  Forbes  following  them.  I  was  on  deck  until 
midnight.  My  orders  to  the  officers  of  the  watch  were  to  follow  astern 
of  the  1  Vest-field .  About  twenty  minutes  of  1,  on  the  morning  of  the 
25th,  Acting  Master  J.  H.  Hammond,  who  was  officer  of  the  watch, 
informed  me  that  the  gunboats  were  standing  to  the  eastward.  I 
ordered  him  to  go  about  and  follow  them,  but  had  hardly  given  the 
order  before  the  Forbes  struck  the  ground.  The  engines  were  immedi¬ 
ately  reversed  to  endeavor  to  back  her  off,  but  it  was  without  any 
effect.  The  vessel  soon  settled  so  much  in  the  sand  that  one  of  the  pro¬ 
pellers  was  broken  and  the  others  would  not  work.  As  soon  as  it  was 
light  I  succeeded  in  landing  all  my  crew  and  most  of  their  effects.  Early 
yesterday  morning  the  gunboat  Young  America  came  to  our  assist¬ 
ance.  As  it  was  utterly  impossible  to  expect  that  the  R.  B.  Forbes 
could  ever  be  got  off,  1  deemed  it  my  duty  to  destroy  her,  so  that  she 
might  not  fall  into  the  hands  of  the  rebels. 

Therefore,  having  saved  as  much  of  the  Government  property  as  was 
possible,  I  set  her  on  fire,  and  then  embarked  all  of  my  officers  and  men 
on  board  the  Young  America.  We  reached  the  U.  S.  steam  frigate 
Roanoke  last  evening.  As  soon  as  possible  I  shall  forward  to  the 
Department  a  list  of  the  property  saved  from  the  wreck. 

I  respectfully  request  that  a  court  of  enquiry  may  be  ordered  in 
regard  to  the  circumstances  of  the  loss  of  my  vessel. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

William  Flte, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  TJ.  S.  Navy. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington ,  D.  C.

Navy  Department,  February  25, 1862.

[Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  Consulate, 
Liverpool ,  February  4 ,  1862. 

Sir:  In  my  last  two  dispatches  I  called  attention  to  the  iron  screw 
steam  gunboat  Oreto  or  Oretis ,  being  built  at  Liverpool  and  fitted  out 
by  Fawcett,  Preston  &  Co.  She  is  now  taking  in  her  coal,  and  appear¬ 
ances  indicate  that  she  will  leave  here  the  latter  part  of  this  week  with¬ 
out  her  armament.  The  probability  is  she  will  run  into  some  small 
port  and  take  it  and  ammunition  on  board.  This  of  itself  is  somewhat 
suspicious.  They  pretend  she  is  built  for  the  Italian  Government,  but 
the  Italian  consul  here  knows  nothing  about  it.  There  is  much  secrecy 
about  her,  and  I  have  been  unable  to  get  anything  definite  about  her, 
but  my  impressions  are  strong  that  she  is  intended  for  the  Southern 
Confederacy.  She  has  one  funnel,  three  masts,  bark-rigged,  eight  port¬ 
holes  for  guns  on  each  side,  and  is  to  carry  10  guns. 

The  brigantine  Fanny  Lewis ,  loaded  with  cotton  and  rosin,  under  the 
Confederate  flag,  from  Charleston,  arrived  here  last  night.  She  left 
Charleston  about  the  1st  of  January. 

#*##### 

Thos.'H.  Dudley.

Report  of  the  senior  officer  in  Hampton  Roads  regarding  the  condition 
and  movements  of  the  U.  S.  vessels  in  those  waters. 

U.  S.  S.  Roanoke, 
Hampton  Roads,  February  26,  1862. 

Sir:  I  am  in  receipt  this  day  of  your  letter  of  the  17th  instant,  and 
in  reply  beg  leave  to  say  that,  with  you,  I  am  fully  alive  to  the  neces¬ 
sity  of  keeping  a  rigid  and  strict  blockade.  Circumstances,  however, 
have  been  such  as  to  prevent  the  fulfillment  of  my  wishes  on  that  point 
being  carried  out  as  closely  as  I  could  wish.  The  steamers  Albatross 
and  Monticello  are  now  at  Baltimore,  having  been  condemned  for 
repairs  by  aboard  of  survey.  Both  these  vessels  will  now  soon,  I  hope, 
be  in  readiness  to  resume  their  stations. 

The  only  vessel  of  the  blockading  force  now  here  is  the  Gemsbok, 
having  come  for  repairs  and  provisions,  and  as  soon  as  she  can  get  her 
wood  she  will  again  go  south. 

■The  tug  11  hitehall  has  been  found  so  rotten  that  I  have  written  to 
the  honorable  Secretary  for  permission  to  send  her  to  Philadelphia, 
doubting  in  my  own  mind  whether  she  is  worth  repairing.  Mr.  Thomp¬ 
son,  carpenter  of  the  Minnesota,  says  he  does  not  know  what  prevents 
her  whole  bottom  falling  out,  so  perfectly  rotten  are  her  timbers  and 
keelson.  The  Cohasset  has  been  found  to  leak  so  badly  that,  after  hav¬ 
ing  had  a  survey  held  on  her,  I  have  ordered  her  to  Baltimore.  She 
could  not  be  repaired  here,  as  she  must  go  on  or  into  a  dock. 

This,  you  will  observe,  reduces  our  tug  force  very  much,  which,  at 
this  time,  when  we  are  expecting  the  Merrimack,  is  felt  most  sensibly. 

1  have  received  an  order  from  the  Department  to  send  the  Congress 
to  Philadelphia  as  soon  as  the  St.  Lawrence  arrives  at  this  place  I 
have  before  informed  you  that  Captain  Smith,  of  the  Congress ,  lias 
been  detached  and  is  ordered  south.  He  is  still  here. 

On  the  24th  we  had  the  heaviest  gale  from  the  northwest  that  has 
been  known  for  many,  many  years,  and  I  trust  it  did  not  injure  your 
tleet.  the  schooner  A.  B.  Myers,  with  provisions,  stores,  etc.,  for  you, 
sailed  a  short  time  previous  to  its  commencement,  but  as  she  is  a  stroim 
and  stanch  vessel  I  do  not  have  any  apprehensions  for  her  safety^ 
1  he  gale  has  caused  sad  havoc  to  the  steamers  of  the  bomb  fleet.  The 
Clifton  and  John  P.  Jackson  came  in  yesterdav  much  disabled,  and  I 
have  ordered  both  to  Baltimore  for  repairs.  The  R.  B.  Forbes  is  on 
shore  about  25  miles  south  of  Cape  Henry,  and  I  fear  she  will  be  lost 
1  sent  the  tug  Young  America  last  evening  to  her  assistance,  and  I  prav 
she  will  arrive  in  time  to  afford  it.  I  endeavored  to  get  the  Spaulding 
from  tlie  Quartermaster’s  Department  to  go  down,  but  was  unsuccess 
tub  This  morning  I  sent  the  Cambridge.  The  Spaulding,  which  came

in  yesterday  afternoon  and  reported  tlie  Forbes  on  sliore,  says  her  flag

Report  of  Chief  Engineer  Stimers,  U.  S.  Navy ,  of  the  expected  sailing  of 

the  U.  S.  S.  Monitor. 

New  York,  February  26,  1862. 

Sir:  The  Monitor  would  have  gone  to  sea  this  morning,  but  was 
detained  for  her  ammunition.  At  dusk  this  evening,  however,  the  last 
shell  was  snugly  stored,  and  we  sail  at  daylight  iu  the  morning,  unless 
the  weather  prove  unfavorable. 


670  NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

% 

The  draft  of  water,  taken  at  the  extremes  of  upper  vessel,  is:  For¬ 
ward,  9  feet  2  inches;  aft,  10  feet  5  inches;  mean  draft,  9  feet  9J  inches. 
She  has  SO  tons  of  coal  in  the  bunkers,  wliich  will  lighten  the  stern  as 
it  comes  out,  and  I  consider  it  advisable  that  she  shall  always  trim  by 
the  stern  at  sea,  as  when  a  sea  breaks  over  the  bow  it  has  to  sustain 
the  superincumbent  weight  of  the  wave  while  it  rolls  across,  which,  of 
course,  depresses  it,  and  if  we  trimmed  to  an  even  keel  in  smooth  water 
we  would  always  be  down  by  the  head  when  underway  in  rough  weather. 

I  have  not  yet  had  time  to  describe  her  completely  to  you,  and  per¬ 
haps  had  better  defer  it  now  until  called  upon  by  you  to  give  you  the 
“list  of  omissions”  contemplated  in  the  contract. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Alban  C.  Stimers, 

Superintendent. 

Commodore  Joseph  Smith,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Chief  of  Bureau  of  Yards  and  Docks,  Navy  Dept.,  Washington,  I).  C.

Camp  Butler,  Newport  News ,  February  24,  1862. 

Sir  :  From  reliable  information  I  am  able  to  inform  you  tliat  two 
gaff-topsail  schooners,  Thomas  Benjamin  and  Mary  Ellen ,  run  the 
blockade  at  the  mouth  of  York  Biver  about  once  a  fortnight,  with 
valuable  return  cargoes.  Where  they  obtain  their  cargoes,  whether 
at  Baltimore,  Philadelphia,  New  York,  etc.,  I  am  unable  to  say. 

I  think  it  would  be  well  to  trace  these  vessels  at  some  one  of  our 
large  ports.  They  probably  take  oysters  or  sweet  potatoes  as  far  as 
Maryland  and  get  in  return,  perhaps,  salt,  percussion  caps,  coffee, 
sugar,  etc. 

I  shall  write  to  you  again  in  a  few  days  and  give  you  an  account  of 
sundry  batteries  and  masked  batteries  from  Yorktown  to  the  mouth  of 
the  river. 

Very  sincerely  and  truly,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  K.  F.  Mansfield, 

Brigadier-  General ,  Commanding  at  Camp  Butler.

Letter  from  Captain  Van  Brunt ,  U.  8.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Min¬ 
nesota,  to  Flag-Officer  Qoldsborough ,  TJ.  8.  Navy ,  regarding  affairs  in 

Hampton  Boads. 

U.  S.  Ship  Minnesota, 
Hampton  Roads,  February  28,  1862. 

My  Dear  Goldsborough  :  I  send  by  the  Thomas  Jefferson  all  the 
letters  and  the  latest  papers.  The  boat  did  not  arrive  from  Baltimore 
this  morning’  until  10  o’clock.  I  am  told  she  was  detained  to  bring  the 
news  that  General  McClellan  had  made  a  forward  movement,  and  there 
is  a  rumor  that  General  Banks  had  been  repulsed  at  Winchester,  Va., 
and  another  that  he  had  been  taken  prisoner.  All  the  means  of  con¬ 
veyance  had  been  seized  to  convey  troops  from  Washington.  One 
thing  is  certain,  they  are  fighting  on  the  Potomac.  I  will  send  you  the 
result  by  the  earliest  conveyance.  You  know  how  little  reliance  can 
be  placed  upon  reports,  but  I  give  you  what  I  have  heard  within  the 
last  hour.  We  shall  undoubtedly  know  more  [by]  to-morrow’s  boat.  I 
sincerely  hope  the  report  respecting  Banks  is  not  true. 

We  have  nothing  new  here;  all  is  quiet.  The  Merrimack  is  still 
invisible  to  us,  but  report  says  she  is  ready  to  come  out.  I  sincerely 
wish  she  would;  I  am  quite  tired  of  hearing  of  her. 

What  are  you  doing?  The  last  we  heard  of  you  was  that  you  were 
preparing  for  another  expedition.  Go  ahead  and  prosper  is  the  earnest 
wish  of  all  your  friends.  For  myself,  I  am  heartily  sick  of  this  state  of 
inactivity.  They  are  sending  down  troops  here  slowly,  and  I  presume 
an  attack  upon  Norfolk  is  contemplated,  but  when !  That  is  the 
question. 

The  R.  B.  Forbes  went  on  shore  about  25  miles  south  of  Cape  Henry 
in  the  gale  on  Monday  last.  W e  sent  down  the  Young  America,  brought 
up  the  officers  and  crew,  and  such  articles  as  could  be  saved,  and  burned 
her.  The  Young  America  arrived  just  in  time  to  prevent  them  all  from 
becoming  prisoners,  as  a  rebel  force  was  then  in  sight. 

The  chaplain,  Mr.  Jones,  has  just  come  in  and  says: 

General  Banks  lias  crossed  tlie  Potomac  with  40.000  men,  and  that  General 
McClellan  has  gone  to  his  assistance  with  30,000.  I  send  you  these  reports  as  they 
were  given  to  mo.  One  thing  is  certain,  ‘‘  Something  is  up.” 

******* 


Van  Brunt. 


Flag-Officer  L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  Hatteras  Inlet.

Report  of  the  senior  officer  in  Hampton  Roads ,  referring  to  the  wreck  of 

the  U.  S.  S.  R.  B.  Forbes. 

U.  S.  S.  Roanoke, 
Hampton  Roads ,  February  28,  1862. 

Sir  :  Since  I  wrote  to  you  on  the  26tli  instaut,  my  fears  relative  to 
the  safety  of  the  R.  B.  Forbes  have  been  realized.  On  the  evening  of 
the  26th  the  tug  Young  America  returned  to  this  place,  with  all  the 
officers  and  men  of  the  Forbes ,  having  found  that  vessel  on  shore  and 
a  total  wreck,  about  4  miles  from  Currituck  Inlet.  Previous  to  leaving 
the  Forbes ,  all  her  small  arms,  chronometers,  spyglasses,  etc.,  were  put 
on  board  the  Young  America,  when  she  was  tired,  and,  as  reported  by 
Lieutenant  Commanding  Flye,  totally  destroyed.  We  have  on  board 
all  the  officers  (13)  and  men  (51)  of  the  Forbes. 

I  have  informed  the  Department  of  the  loss  of  the  Forbes,  and 
enclosed  the  reports  of  her  commander.  I  am  happy  to  say  that  I 
believe  the  Westfield  is  safe,  as  a  large  ferryboat  steamer  was  seen  on 
the  25th  instant,  20  miles  north  of  Cape  Hatteras,  standing  to  the 
southward. 

Since  my  last,  the  Chippeica  and  the  Amanda  have  come  in  for  stores, 
provisions,  and  repairs.  The  former  I  hope  to  make  short  work  of,  and 
get  her  away  again  in  two  or  three  days.  The  latter  has  been  handled 
rather  roughly  by  the  constant  bad  weather,  and  will  require  some 
repairs,  but  you  may  be  assured  she  will  not  be  detained  a  moment 
longer  than  is  necessary.  I  received  yesterday  from  Lieutenant  Com¬ 
manding  Arnold  the  report  of  the  survey  on  the  engine  of  the  Mystic. 
That  report  I  submitted  to  Chief  Engineer  Loring,  asking  his  opinion 
what  had  better  be  done,  and  that  officer  recommended  that  the  Mystic 
should  come  here,  as  she  could  be  of  no  service  off  the  Rappahannock, 
and  all  her  repairs  could  be  done  at  this  place.  I  have  accordingly 
ordered  Lieutenant  Arnold  to  come  here  with  the  Mystic  as  soon  as 
possible. 

I  need  not  say  to  you  how  anxious  I  feel  at  this  constant  decrease  of 
the  blockading  force,  but  under  the  circumstances  it  could  not  bo 
avoided,  and  I  hope  soon  to  have  everything  straight  again.  The 
Gemsbok  has  gone  to  sea. 

I  remain,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  Marston, 

Captain. 

Flag-Officer  L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Commander  Oils  son,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Mount 
Vernon,  of  assistance  rendered  by  that  vessel  to  the  IT.  8.  transport 
Mississippi,  February  28,  1862. 

IT.  S.  S.  Mount  Yernon, 

Off  Wilmington,  N.  C.,  March  1,  1862. 
Sir  :  I  have  to  report  to  you  that  yesterday  I  discovered  a  vessel  to 
the  southward  and  eastward.  At  11  a.  m.  I  got  underway  and  stood 
for  her  and  soon  discovered  her  to  be  a  vessel  on  shore  on  the  Frying 
Pan  Shoals.  On  a  nearer  approach  she  proved  to  be  a  large  steamer 
with  the  American  ensign  hoisted  [union]  down.  We  were  soon  boarded 
by  a  boat  containing  an  army  officer,  who  informed  me  that  the  vessel 
was  the  steam  transport  Mississippi  from  Boston  for  Ship  Island,  Miss., 
having  Major-General  Benjamin  F.  Butler  and  1,400  troops  on  board. 
I  approached  her  cautiously,  sending  a  boat  in  charge  of  Acting  Mas¬ 
ter  Henry  L.  Sturges  to  sound  between  us  and  the  Mississippi.  At 
half  past  3  p.  m.  we  were  enabled  (though  at  a  great  risk  to  this  vessel) 
to  anchor  sufficiently  near  to  send  a  hawser  to  the  steamer.  We 
steamed  ahead  and  succeeded  in  moving  her  about  half  her  length 
ahead,  and  in  hauling  her  head  around  about  two  points,  but  at  about 
5  o’clock  we  found  this  vessel’s  head  paying  off  broadside  onto  the  shoal 
and  were  compelled  to  let  go  the  hawser.  Her  head  still  paying  off, 
we  let  go  the  starboard  anchor  to  get  the  vessel’s  head  to  the  wind  and 
sea.  She  then  struck  heavily  on  the  shoal  three  times,  and  we  were 
obliged  to  slip  the  cable  and  steam  ahead  to  clear  the  shoal.  In  steam¬ 
ing  ahead  the  buoy  rope  of  the  slipped  cable  got  foul  of  the  propeller 
and  we  had  to  stop  the  engine  and  cut  it,  thereby  losing  the  starboard 
bow  anchor  and  15  fathoms  of  chain  cable,  but  saving  the  ship.  1  sent 
Acting  Master  Henry  L.  Sturges  on  board  the  Mississippi  to  assist  in  get¬ 
ting  her  off.  She  was  leaking  badly  in  the  forward  compartment,  that 
compartment  being  filled  with  water  up  to  the  berth  deck,  in  spite  of  the 
bailing  of  the  troops,  which  was  continued  through  tlie  night.  They 
kept  throwing  overboard  provisions  and  other  heavy  articles  to  lighten 
the  ship,  and  all  of  our  boats  were  kept  assisting  those  of  the  Missis¬ 
sippi  in  transporting  the  troops  to  this  vessel  to  lighten  her  further.  I 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


675 


received  Mrs.  General  Butler  and  lier  attendant  on  board  this  vessel. 
At  about  7  p.  m.,  when  we  had  received  about  300  troops  on  board,  we 
had  the  pleasure  of  seeing  the  Mississippi  come  off  the  shoal.  I  imme¬ 
diately  weighed  anchor  and  proceeded  very  cautiously  into  deeper  water, 
displaying  lights  to  guide  the  other  vessel.  At  midnight  both  vessels 
anchored  off  Bald  Head  light-house.  This  morning  we  transferred  the 
troops  to  the  Mississippi;  also  Mrs.  General  Butler  and  attendant.  I 
am  thankful  to  be  able  to  report  to  you  that  we  were  instrumental  in 
saving  this  noble  ship  with  her  large  number  of  passengers;  it  also 
affords  me  much  gratification  to  have  to  inform  you  that  every  officer 
and  man  under  my  command  exerted  himself  to  liis  utmost  abilities  in 
this  noble  cause.  The  damage  and  loss  sustained  by  this  vessel  is 
trivial  when  compared  with  the  saving  of  the  lives  of  1,400  persons  who 
were  on  board  the  Mississippi. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

O.  S.  Glisson, 
Commander ,  U.  8.  Navy. 

Flag-Officer,  L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 


Report  of  Commander  Glisson ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Mount 

Vernon ,  regarding  the  capture  by  that  vessel  of  the  schooner  British 

Queen. 

U.  S.  S.  Mount  Yernon, 

Off  Wilmington ,  March  1 , 1862. 

Sir  :  I  have  to  report  that  this  morning  about  10  o’clock  I  observed 
a  sail  to  the  southward  and  westward.  I  immediately  weighed  and 
proceeded  in  chase.  On  my  approaching  her  she  hoisted  an  English 
ensign,  union  down. 

On  boarding  her,  I  found  her  to  be  the  British  schooner  British 
Queen ,  of  and  from  Nassau,  New  Providence,  for  Baltimore,  with  a 
cargo  consisting  of  1,500  bushels  of  salt,-  23  bags  of  coffee,  and  some 
ship  stores.  The  master  of  her  is  a  North  Carolinian ;  his  manner  was 
suspicious  and  his  statements  were  contradictory.  I  therefore  sent  an 
officer  and  crew  on  board  of  her  and  towed  her  up  to  this  place.  A 
further  search  disclosed  an  American,  a  Spanish,  and  secession  flag  in 
addition  to  the  English  one  that  was  hoisted.  This  fact,  added  to  that 
of  her  cargo,  consisting  of  articles  much  needed  by  the  rebels,  con¬ 
vinced  me  that  it  was  her  intention  to  run  the  blockade,  or,  failing  in 
that,  to  run  his  vessel  on  shore.  I  therefore  detailed  Acting  Master 
John  D.  Barclay,  of  this  vessel,  to  take  her  to  the  port  of  Philadelphia 
for  adjudication,  with  the  following  crew,  viz:  John  Newitt,  gunner’s 
mate;  William  Boston,  seaman;  George  Han  ell  and  George  W.  Hill, 
ordinary  seamen.  I  also  send  in  her  the  master’s  mate,  one  passenger, 
and  two  of  the  seamen  of  the  schooner. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,  O.  S.  Glisson, 

Commander ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Flag-Officer  L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

on  board  the  Mount  Vernon:

[Enclosure.] 

Headquarters  Department  of  Virginia, 

Fort  Monroe ,  Va.,  February  28,  1862. 

Sir:  Owing  to  the  exchange  of  prisoners  and  other  duties,  I  am  not 
able  to  fulfill  my  promise  of  yesterday.  I,  however,  avail  myself  to  say 
that  I  want  one  or  two  gunboats,  with  two  guns  each.  The  Navy  has 
but  one  fit  for  use  in  this  harbor,  and  that  can  not  be  spared  for  the 
service  I  require.  1  have  a  steamer  that  plies  daily  between  this  post 
and  Newport  News,  which  transports,  back  and  forth,  large  amounts 
of  property  and  soldiers.  As  the  enemy  have  several  tugboats  that 
ply  about  Sewell’s  Point,  Craney  Island,  and  Pig  Point,  I  am  not  with¬ 
out  apprehensions  we  may  lose  the  steamer,  and  perhaps  a  large 
amount  of  stores,  including  ammunition,  arms,  etc.  As  the  Navy  can 
not  furnish  me  with  the  requisite  protection,  I  hope  you  will  be  able  to 
obtain  two  boats  to  be  at  my  disposal  for  the  protection  of  our  common 
steamers,  which  could  be  sunk  by  a  single  ball,  or  at  least  captured. 
We  have  but  recently  lost  a  schooner  for  the  want  of  this  protection. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  E.  Wool,  1 
Major-  General. 

Hon.  Edwin  M.  Stanton, 

Secretary  of  War.

Report  of  the  senior  officer  in  Hampton  Roads  regarding  the  injuries 
received  by  TJ.  S.  vessels  in  a  gale. 

U,  S.  Steam  Frigate  Roanoke, 
Hampton  Roads,  Virginia,  March  4,  1862. 

Sir:  I  regret  to  inform  you  that  during  the  heavy  gale  of  last  night 
the  U.  S.  steamers  Chippeica  and  Mystic  drifted  foul  of  each  other  and 
both  vessels  seriously  damaged.  The  U.  S.  bark  Amanda  also  received 
injury;  all  of  which  I  shall  endeavor  to  repair  as  soon  as  the  proper 
surveys  are  held  on  them.  The  Minnesota  and  this  ship  escaped  almost 
by  a  miracle. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  Marston, 
Captain  and  Senior  Officer.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Gillespie ,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  If.  S.  hark 
Braziliera ,  of  the  collision  of  that  vessel  with  the  TJ.  S.  hark  Amanda 
in  a  gale. 

IT.  S.  Bark  Braziliera, 

Hampton  Roads,  March  5,  1862. 

Sir  :  In  the  S.  S.  E.  gale  we  experienced  on  the  night  of  the  3d,  the 
U.  S.  bark  Amanda  dragged  her  anchor  and  fell  foul  of  us,  striking  us  on 
the  port  bow,  carrying  away  the  port  cathead,  martingale,  and  port  jib- 
boom  guys,  also  dialing  us  severely.  With  the  help  of  11  men  from  the 
Amanda,  gave  our  vessel  15  fathoms  more  chain.  The  bark’s  anchor 
having  hooked  our  moorings,  she  lay  in  this  position,  chafing  us  badly 
till  1  a.  m. ;  then  she  swung  round  on  our  starboard  bow,  carrying  away 
cathead  and  chafed  our  head-stay  considerably.  At  1 : 30  swung  clear, 
the  bark  lying  close  aboard  to  starboard  and  the  ship  Marcia  Greenleaf 
close  to  on  the  port  quarter.  At  11 : 20  a.  m.,  tide  making  flood,  the  bark 
fouled  us  again,  carrying  away  mainsail  in  the  way  of  Ho.  3  gun  on 
starboard  side,  starting  three  stanchions  and  damaging  our  rigging 
severely.  With  the  assistance  of  14  men  from  the  Amanda  hove  in 
spare  chain,  housed  topgallant  mast,  and  rigged  jibboom. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  T.  Gillespie, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding. 

Captain  John  Marston, 

TJ.  S.  Steam  Frigate  Roanoke,  Hampton  Roads,  Virginia.

Order  of  Flag- Officer  Goldsborough ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  North 

Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  to  the  navy  agent  at  Philadelphia  to 
forward  coal  to  RoanoTce  Island. 

U.  S.  Flag-Steamer  Philadelphia, 

Croatan  Sound,  March  5,  1862. 

Sir  :  I  will  tliank  you  to  dispatch  from  Philadelphia,  direct  for  this 
island  by  the  20th  instant,  another  thousand  tons  of  coal.  Any  vessel 
drawing  less  than  8  feet  (say  not  more  than  7  feet  9  inches)  can  now 
get  over  the  bulkhead  or  swash  at  Hatteras  Inlet  and  deliver  her  coal 
to  us  here.  Charter  the  vessel,  if  you  please,  to  come  here.  No  appre¬ 
hension  of  any  interference  by  the  enemy  need  be  entertained  for  a 
moment,  as  I  keep  a  force  constantly  this  side  of  the  inlet,  between  it 
and  the  mainland,  to  guard  our  intercourse. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

L.  M.  Goldsborough, 

Flag-  Officer. 

James  S.  Chambers,  Esq., 

Navy  Agent,  Philadelphia.

Report  of  the  senior  officer  in  Hampton  Roads,  regarding  the  supplying  of 
coal  to  the  U.  S.  revenue  steamer  Flora. 

U.  S.  S.  Roanoke, 
Hampton  Roads,  March  6,  1862. 

Sir  :  I  beg  leave  to  report  that  the  revenue  steamer  Flora  arrived 
this  morning  on  her  way  to  Port  Royal,  in  want  of  coal.  As  the  Flora 
was  ordered  to  report  to  the  military  authorities  at  Port  Royal,  I 
referred  Captain  Coffin,  the  commander  of  the  Flora,  to  General  Wool, 
but  that  officer  refused  to  supply  the  coal  and  referred  him  to  me! 
Under  these  circumstances,  for  the  public  good,  I  gave  Captain  Coffin 
20  tons.  As  this  is  the  second  instance  that  vessels  in  the  military 
service  have  failed  to  receive  assistance  from  General  Wool  in  the  way 
of  coal,  I  beg  leave  to  ask  whether  I  am  right  in  doing  so  under  any 
circumstances? 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  Marston, 
Captain  and  Senior  Officer. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  I).  G.

[Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  Consulate,  Liverpool,  February  12,  1862. 

Sir:  The  Bermuda  is  taking  on  board  her  cargo  as  fast  as  possible. 
She  has  already  taken  200  cases  of  shells  (supposed  to  contain  6  shells 
in  each  case),  7  rifled  cannon,  12  field  carriages  for  cannon,  and  00  bags 
saltpeter.  I  understand  she  is  to  sail  about  Tuesday  next,  and  go 
direct  to  Bermuda,  where  her  cargo  will  be  placed  on  the  two  steamers, 
the  Caroline  and  the  steamer  Herald,  hereinafter  referred  to,  and  run 


684 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


into  Savannah  or  Charleston.  All  that  has  been  put  on  board  thus  far 
has  come  from  Fawcett,  Preston  &  Co.  A  small  silk  Confederate  flag 
hangs  at  one  of  the  windows  in  the  officers’  cabin  on  the  deck,  which 
can  be  seen  from  the  pier.  The  Southern  agents  have  purchased  the 
steamer  Herald ,  one  of  the  liners  between  Dublin  and  Glasgow.  The 
purchase  was  effected  through  the  house  of  Cunard,  Wilson  &  Co., 
who  brought  her  to  this  port  last  week,  and  have  put  her  up  nominally 
for  Bermuda.  She  is  said  to  be  a  very  fast  boat.  In  order  to  secure 
her,  they  had  to  pay  a  large  price.  She  has  taken  in  her  coal  and  is 
receiving  her  cargo,  which  will  consist  of  arms  and  munitions  of  war. 
She  is  to  sail  on  Friday  next,  and  will  make  direct  for  Charleston  or 
Savannah.  Her  clearances  will  be  for  Bermuda,  but  she  will  not  visit 
this  port  until  after  she  has  landed  her  cargo  at  Savannah  or  Charleston. 
Captain  Coxetter,  formerly  of  the  U.  S.  Navy  [?],  and  more  recently 
the  commander  of  the  Jeff.  Davis ,  is  to  command  her.  This  gentleman 
was  on  the  Trent  at  the  time  Mason  and  Slidell  were  taken  off.  He 
passes  himself  here  as  Captain  Mitchell,  and  most  probably  will  assume 
this  name  when  on  the  Herald.  A  man  by  the  name  of  Atroll  will  be 
the  nominal  commander  until  after  they  clear  and  leave  the  port.  After 
she  lands  her  cargo,  she  is  intended  to  run  between  the  Southern  States 
and  Bermuda,  and  has  been  purchased  especially  for  this  purpose.  I 
understand  that  the  Bermuda  and  other  vessels  now  loading  will  land 
their  cargoes  at  Bermuda,  and  that  the  Herald  and  Caroline  will  run 
regularly  and  carry  all  of  these  cargoes  into  the  Southern  ports.  They 
have  also  purchased  two  other  steamers,  one  called  the  Bahama ,  the 
other  the  Victoria ,  so  I  am  informed,  the  latter  now  at  Queenstown. 
The  purchase  of  the  two  last-mentioned  vessels  requires  confirmation. 
I  will  ascertain  the  truth  and  report  to  the  Department.  I  have  com¬ 
municated  the  facts  about  the  Bermuda  and  Herald  to  Mr.  Adams,  our 
minister  at  London.  Enclosed  find  a  full  description  of  the  steamer 
Herald ,  marked  No.  1. 

Everything  I  see  and  hear  confirms  me  in  the  belief  that  the  gunboat 
Oreto ,  referred  to  in  previous  dispatch,  and  which  is  being  built  and 
fitted  out  at  this  place,  is  intended  for  the  Southern  Confederacy.  Mr. 
Miller,  the  man  who  built  the  hull,  says  she  is  owned  by  Fawcett,  Pres¬ 
ton  &  Co.,  or  at  least  they  gave  him  the  contract  and  have  paid  him  for 
his  labor.  She  is  a  very  complete  and  perfect  vessel,  no  pains  or 
expense  having  been  spared  in  her  construction,  and  will,  when  fully 
armed  and  equipped,  in  the  opinion  of  those  competent  to  judge,  be  a 
formidable  and  dangerous  craft.  I  enclose  you  a  more  full  and  accurate 
description  of  her,  marked  No.  2. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thomas  H.  Dudley, 

TJ.  S.  Consul. 

Hon.  Wm.  H.  Seward, 

Secretary  of  State.

Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  the  senior  officer  in  Hampton 

Boads,  transmitting  information  regarding  suspected  blockade  runners 

Robert  Bruce ,  Gambia,  and  Windward. 

Navy  Department,  March  7, 1862. 

Sir:  I  herewith  enclose  a  copy  of  a  communication  that  has  been 
referred  to  the  Department  from  Ed.  Brennan,  dated  at  Bristol,  Feb¬ 
ruary  14,  1862,  in  relation  to  the  Robert  Bruce ,  the  Gambia,  and  the 
Windward,  vessels  that  are  suspected  of  a  design  to  attempt  to  run 
the  blockade. 

The  U.  S.  consul  at  Halifax  [Nova  Scotia]  telegraphs  under  date  of 
the  1st  that  the  British  brig  Stanley  and  British  schooner  Oasis,  with 
general  cargo,  have  been  chartered  for  Matanzas,  but  their  actual  des¬ 
tination  is  believed  to  be  some  Southern  blockaded  port.  The  Depart¬ 
ment  desires  to  know  if  the  information  it  sends  to  you  from  time  to 
time  in  relation  to  suspicious  vessels  is  communicated  to  the  vessels  of 

the  blockading  squadron. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Gideon  Welles. 

Captain  John  Marston, 

Senior  Officer,  Hampton  Roads,  Virginia. 


[Enclosure.] 

Bristol,  j February  14, 1862. 

Sir:  The  Robert  Bruce  (a  brig  of  about  350  tons,  black  hull,  with 
white  topsides,  white  galley  abaft  foremast,  a  bust  of  a  man  for  figure¬ 
head),  Captain  Muir,  which  lias  before  succeeded  in  running  the  block¬ 
ade,  left  here  yesterday  in  ballast  for  Cardiff  to  load  coals  there,  thence 

for  Havana.  ,  „ 

The  Gambia,  loaded  with  gunpowder  (as  heretofore  reported),  is  also 
a  brig  of  about  300  tons,  black  hull  with  yellow  streak,  fiddle  figure¬ 
head  and  a  smart  craft.  She  is  said  to  be  bound  to  the  west  coast  of 
Africa,  but  I  have  ascertained  that  she  is  about  to  attempt  running  the 
blockade. 

The  Windward  left  at  4  a.  m.  this  day. 

There  is  a  smart-looking  screw  boat  of  about  500  tons,  pierced  for 
eight  guns,  fitting  out  here,  but  great  secrecy  is  observed  as  to  her 
destination.  I  will  keep  my  eyes  upon  her,  as  I  have  good  reasons  for 
believing  that  she  is  intended  for  the  Southerners. 

I  am,  sir,  yours,  etc., 


J.  POLLAKY,  Esq. 


Ed.  Brennan.

Report  of  the  senior  officer  in  Hampton  Roads  of  the  departure  of  the 
U.  S.  S.  Chippewa  to  Baltimore  for  repairs. 

U.  S.  S.  Roanoke, 
Hampton  Roads,  March  7,  1862. 

Sir:  The  Chippewa  has  been  found  to  be  so  much  injured  by  her  col¬ 
lision  with  the  Mystic  that  I  have  deemed  it  best  to  send  her  to  Balti¬ 
more  to  be  repaired.  This  work  could  have  been  done  here,  but  the 
Amanda,  Mystic,  and  Mount  Vernon  fully  employ  all  the  carpenters  wo 
can  raise  from  the  several  ships.  The  Chippewa  sailed  this  afternoon. 
A  large  ship  is  anchored  below,  which  I  presume  is  the  St.  Laivrence. 
As  soon  as  she  comes  in,  I  shall  send  the  Conyress  to  Philadelphia.  I 
have  received  your  second  telegraphic  dispatch  about  the  Monitor ,  and 
shall  send  her  to  Washington  immediately  on  her  arrival. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  Marston, 
Captain  and  Senior  Officer. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington ,  D.  C.

Abstracts  of  logbooks  of  United  States  vessels*  which  served  in  the  Atlantic 
and  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadrons  during  the  period  from  July 
16 ,  1861,  to  March  7,  1862. 

Abstract  log  of  tbe  IJ.  S.  S.  Albatross,  June  25,  1861,  to  March  7,  1862. 


June  25,  1861. — Ship  put  in  commission. 

July  11. — At  11 : 30  a.  m.,  2^  miles  distant  from  Oregon  Inlet,  lati¬ 
tude  35°  48'  N.,  longitude  75°  297  W.,  opened  fire  from  a  rifle  gun  on  an 
earthwork  battery  of  6  guns  and  an  encampment  of  16  tents  and  a 
large  number  of  men.  As  we  approached  the  shore  the  men  were 
mustering  in  flue  style,  but  before  they  could  man  their  guns  the  balls 
from  our  rifle  gun  were  flying  through  the  embrasures  of  their  battery, 
dismounting  one  of  their  guns  and  rendering  the  pi  ace  quite  untenable; 
after  throwing  in  6  shots  from  rifle  gun,  7  balls  and  5  (6-inch)  shells 
from  long  32s,  some  of  which  were  seen  to  explode  directly  in  their 
camps  and  fort,  the  soldiers  were  distinctly  seen  putting  off  from  shore, 
some  wading  and  swimming,  in  their  hurry  to  get  away.  Two  small 
rebel  steamers  picked  them  up  and  started  up  the  Roanoke  Sound. 

July  18. — At  3  p.  m.  spoke  and  boarded  the  schooner  Velasco ,  of 
Galveston,  Tex.,  from  Matanzas,  with  sugar  for  New  York.  Her 
papers  being  incorrect,  and  being  under  the  Texan  flag,  she  was  seized 
as  a  prize. 

July  21. — At  11  a.  m.  beat  to  quarters  and  cast  loose  the  guns,  fired 
9  shots  from  long  32s  and  10  shots  from  rifle  gun  on  spar  deck  at  a 
steamer  lying  inside  of  Bodie’s  Island.  Our  fire  was  returned  by  the 
enemy  with  some  9  or  10  shot  and  shell,  some  going  over  us,  others 
falling  short,  none  taking  effect.  At  11:30  the  enemy  hauled  off' out 
of  reach  of  our  guns  and  stood  away  for  the  mainland. 

July  22. — At  9  a.  m.  sighted  a  steamer  S.  |  B.;  ran  in  toward  her. 
Steamer  stood  out  for  us  till  within  about  6  miles,  when  she  put  about 
and  ran  in  for  Hatteras  Inlet.  We  ran  within  34  miles  of  the  har¬ 
bor,  and  discovered  inside  the  inlet  9  schooners  and  2  steamers  at 
anchor  under  cover  of  an  earthwork  battery.  Also  2  ships’  hulls 
under  water,  with  masts  standing,  on  the  beach  to  the  northeast  of  tho 
inlet.  Put  to  sea  again.  Gave  chase  and  came  up  with  a  schooner  at 
1:45.  Hailed  schooner,  when  a  negro  jumped  overboard,  exclaiming, 
“Save  me,  captain,  she’s  bound  to  Charleston.”  Turned  our  guns  on 
her  and  ordered  her  to  heave  to,  and  sent  a  boat  aboard  with  Lieuten¬ 
ant  Neville,  picking  up  [the]  negro  on  the  way.  Boat  returned  at  2, 
with  schooner’s  crew  of  5  men.  Name  of  schooner,  Enchantress,  of 
Newburyport,  taken  by  the  pirate  Jeff.  Davis  on  6th  of  July,  in  charge

August  1. — At  6:45  a.  m.  boarded  schooner  Elizabeth  Ann ,  of  Acco- 
mac,  Ya.  from  Penn’s  Grove  [1ST.  J.],  bound  to  Ohincoteague.  Her 
papers  being  incorrect,  seized  her  as  a  prize  and  took  her  in  tow. 

September  14. — Cruising  along  the  Maryland  shore,  near  mouth  of 
the  Potomac.  At  5  p.  m.  boarded  schooner  Alabama ,  of  New  York, 
bound  to  Washington.  Her  papers  incorrect;  took  charge  and  sent 
Master’s  Mate  J.  H.  Harris  with  one  seaman  on  board.  Took  prize  in 
tow  and  proceeded  down  the  Chesapeake. 

September  17. — At  5  p.  m.,  Fort  Macon  [N.  C.]  distant  5  miles,  observed 
a  number  of  troops  on  top  and  a  rebel  flag  flying  from  the  same. 

October  1. — At  5  p.  m.  came  up  Avith  and  spoke  French  war  steamer 
Gatina t,  on  a  cruise.  At  6  she  came  to  anchor  off  Beaufort  [N.  C.]. 
At  7  sent  a  boat  aboard  the  Gatinat ,  but  they  refused  to  allow  anyone 
on  board  by  order  of  their  admiral. 

October  2. — At  3:30  p.  m.  the  French  war  steamer  Gatinat  got  under¬ 
way  and  stood  out  to  sea. 

October  7. — At  11  p.  m.,  off  Bogue  Inlet  [N.  C.],  Lieutenant  Neville, 
with  gig  and  12  men,  and  Master’s  Mate  Harris,  in  first  cutter  and  12 
men,  in  company  with  three  boats  from  the  Cambridge ,  left  on  an  expe¬ 
dition  to  fetch  some  schooners  out  of  the  inlet.  Ships  laid  outside. 

October •  8. — At  2  a.  m.  Lieutenant  Gwin,  in  the  Cambridge  cutter,  came 
alongside  and  informed  us  our  boats  had  capsized  in  the  surf,  and  that 
he  had  picked  up  one  of  our  men,  H.  E.  Hopkinson,  outside  the  breakers 
on  an  oar.  Manned  the  second  cutter  and  sent  her  in  search  of  the 
men,  in  charge  of  R.  O.  Patterson,  master.  At  4  a.  in.  saAV  our  two  boats’ 
crews  and  officer  on  the  beach  at  Bogue  Inlet.  The  second  cutter  and 
two  boats  from  the  Cambridge  went  in  to  their  rescue  and  succeeded  in 
bringing  them  off',  with  the  exception  of  James  R.  Hobby,  ordinary 
seaman,  and  Samuel  Nichols,  seaman,  who  were  lost  out  of  the  gig  when 
she  capsized,  and  supposed  to  be  drowned.  Captain’s  gig  Avas  stove 
in  and  a  quantity  of  arms  and  a  compass  were  lost  in  the  expedition. 

November  6. — At  2  p.  m.  sighted  a  steamer  wrecked  on  the  beach  to 
the  east  of  Bogue  Inlet.  Observed  people  on  shore  signaling  for  us  to 
communicate.  They  displayed  a  flag  of  truce.  LoAvered  the  first  cut¬ 
ter  with  Master’s  Mate  Harris  to  speak  with  them.  At  5:50  boat 
returned,  the  surf  being  too  high  to  land. 

November  7. — Called  away  the  first  cutter,  and  Master’s  Mate  Harris 
went  ashore  with  a  flag  of  truce  to  get  information  respecting  the  wreck 
and  fate  of  the  crew,  etc.,  of  wrecked  steamer.  At  12  boat  returned, 
having  learned  from  the  so-called  Confederate  officers  that  the  Avreck 
was  the  U.  S.  steam  transport  Star  of  the  Union ,  Captain  John  J.  Gar¬ 
vin,  laden  with  hay,  horses,  provisions,  etc.,  bound  south.  Was  run 
ashore  on  the  night  of  Friday,  1st  instant,  during  a  S.  E.  gale,  all  on 
board  being  taken  prisoners,  with  exception  of  one  man ;  he  Avas  drowned. 
They  also  report  tAvo  steamers  ashore  off  Charleston  and  twooff  Hatteras. 

December  14. — At  daybreak  a  suspicious-looking  schooner  was  in 
sight  off  Lookout  Breakers.  Signaled  U.  S.  S.  State  of  Georgia  to  give 
chase.  Got  underway  and  stood  out  W.  by  S.  At  10:45  the  Georgia 
came  in  Avith  the  schooner  [Jane  Campbell]  in  tow. 

December  15. — At  12  m.  master  went  aboard  prize  schooner.  Observed 
the  rebel  flag  on  Fort  Macon  at  half-mast  all  day.

December  16. — At  12:30  p.  in.  made  signals  and  fired  two  guns  at  a 
strange  steamer;  she  still  kept  on  her  course;  supposed  to  be  the  U .  S. 
transport  S.  R.  Spaulding. 

December  17.— At  8  p.  m.  Master  T.  [B.]  Du  Bois  went  aboard  prize 
schooner  Jane  Campbell  with  her  sailing  orders  for  New  York.  Returned 
at  9;  brought  eight  Enfield  rifles  from  the  schooner. 

December  18.— At  4  p.  m.  stood  down  the  coast;  signaled  State  of 
Georgia  to  follow.  Saw  a  large  fire  inshore;  beat  to  quarters  and  ran 
close  in.  Proved  to  be  the  wreck  of  the  steamer  bnion  on  fire.  Mr. 
li.  O.  Patterson  went  in  the  dingey,  in  company  with  a  boat  from  the 
State  of  Georgia ,  to  reconnoiter. 

December  19.— At  9 : 15  State  of  Georgia  fired  8  guns  at  wreck  of  the 
steamer  Union ;  we  ran  within  500  yards  and  tried  our  port  battery  at 
the  wreck,  and  2  shots  from  rifled  gun.  At  4  p.  m.  fired  a  shot  from 
rifled  gun  at  a  squad  of  men  on  beach  near  light  house. 

January  16. — At  7  a.  m.  lookout  reported  a  ship  ashore  to  the  east  of 
Bogue  Inlet.  Steamed  in  to  the  wreck ;  made  her  out  to  be  the  British 
ship  York ,  of  Dublin.  U.  S.  bark  Gemsbok  came  up  and  was  ordered 
to  anchor  abreast  the  wreck.  At  3  p.  in.,  our  guns  being  trained  to 
cover  our  boats,  two  boats  from  us  and  three  from  the  Gemsbok  pulled 
in  for  the  ship  York,  Acting  Master  Du  Bois  boarded  the  wreck; 
found  the  cargo  had  been  discharged  and  set  fire  to  her. 


Abstract  log  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Cambridge,  August  29,  1861,  to  March  7,  1862. 

August  29,  1861— Went  into  commission,  navy  yard,  Boston,  Mass. 

September  7.— At  10:30  a.  m  came  to  anchor  off  Fortress  Monroe. 

September  9.— At  G  a.  m.  got  underway  and  steamed  through  the 
roads.  At  8:30  passed  Cape  Henry.  At  11  boarded  the  schooner 
Louisa  Agnes ,  of  Lunenburg,  Nova  Scotia.  Finding  her  papers  unsat¬ 
isfactory,  and  from  letters  found  on  board  showing  her  intention  to  run 
the  blockade,  considered  her  a  legitimate  prize.  Placed  a  prize  crew 
in  charge  of  her  and  sent  her  to  New  York. 

September  10.— At  3:30  p.  m.  boarded  English  schooner  Revere,  of 
Yarmouth,  Nova  Scotia,  with  a  cargo  of  salt  and  fish,  bound  for  Beau¬ 
fort,  N.  O.  Put  her  in  charge  of  a  prize  crew.  At  10  p.  m.  anchored 
off  Beaufort. 

September  23—  At  5  a.  m.  weighed  anchor  and  went  in  chase  of  a 
schooner.  At  9 : 20  came  in  hail  of'  English  schooner  Julia ,  of  St.  John, 
New  Brunswick.  Considering  her  a  lawful  prize,  put  on  her  a  prize  crew 
and  sent  her  to  Boston,  Mass. 

September  24. — At  7  a.  m.  saw  an  English  ship  of  war  standing  to  the 

w.  s.  w. 

September  25. — At  4:30  p.  m.  made  a  steamer  bound  in.  Proved  to 
be  the  British  steam  sloop  Rinaldo. 

September  26. — At  9:30  a.  m.  the  Rinaldo  started  for  New  York. 

October  1. — At  10  a.  m.  spoke  the  schooner  Edwin,  of  Barbados, 
bound  to  Baltimore.  Sent  her  into  Hampton  Roads  in  charge  of  a 
quartermaster  and  two  men. 

November  6. — At  10:30  a.  m.  came  to  anchor  off  Corrotoman  River, 
Virginia.  At  12:15  p.  m.  sent  an  expedition  under  command  of  Lieu¬ 
tenant  Gwin,  composed  of  4  officers  and  30  men,  in  the  steamer  Rescue 
and  one  of  our  boats,  to  cut  a  schooner  out  of  the  Corrotoman  River. 
At  4 : 45  the  Rescue  returned,  having  been  engaged  by  the  enemy  on

both  sides  of  the  river  with  rifled  camion  on  one  side  and  rifled  muskets 
on  the  other.  The  schooner  being-  fast  aground,  stripped  her  of  sails 
and  rigging  and  burned  her  with  her  cargo  of  wood.  Also  burned 
some  75  cords  of  wood  on  shore.  The  only  damage  on  our  side  was  the 
destruction  of  a  canoe  and  a  boat’s  spar.  The  firing  was  returned  vig¬ 
orously  from  the  Rescue ,  one  of  our  shells  exploding  in  and  nearly 
destroying  a  house,  from  which  muskets  were  being  fired  upon  us. 

November  8. — At  8  a.  m.  stood  down  the  river.  At  11 : 04  a.  in.,  abreast 
of  Grey’s  Point,  opened  fire  on  said  point  with  broadside  and  pivot 
guns  with  shell,  in  company  with  the  tug  Rescue.  Fired  from  pivot 
guns  and  broadside  battery  in  all  10  shells.  At  11:17  ceased  firing, 
stood  up  river  again,  and  at  1  p.  m.  opened  fire  upon  a  house  in  ITrbana, 
said  by  the  negroes  to  be  a  storehouse  of  ammunition,  and  upon  a  camp 
of  soldiers  in  the  rear  of  the  town.  At  2 : 30  ceased  firing  and  anchored 
in  front  of  the  town.  Lieutenant  Gwin  went  on  board  the  Resctie  and 
went  closer  inshore,  and  fired  round  shot  and  shell  at  the  house  and 
camp.  At  3  the  Rescue  ceased  firing,  came  out  and  weighed  anchor, 
and  stood  down  the  river.  Expended  22  8-inch  shells  and  cartridges, 
27  Parrott  shells  and  cartridges,  and  18  Schenkle  shells  and  cartridges. 

November  12. — At  6  a.  m.  proceeded  up  river.  At  8  threw  3  shell 
from  Parrott  gun  at  the  magazine  at  Urbana,  turned  down  the  river, 
and  anchored. 


Abstract  log  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Commodore  Perry,  February  19  and  20,  1862. 

February  19,  1862. — Albemarle  Sound.  At  4:15  p.  m.  found  the 
rebels  encamped  abreast  of  the  town  of  Winton,  FT.  C.  They  fired  a 
volley  of  musketry  at  the  U.  S.  gunboat  Delaware ,  we  returning  their 
fire  with  8  shrapnel.  Finding  it  too  dark  to  engage,  stood  down  the 
river  and  anchored. 

February  20. — Winton,  Chowan  River  [FT.  C.].  Got  underway  and 
took  the  lead  of  all  the  gunboats.  At  9:30  a.  m.  commenced  shelling 
the  shore  close  to  the  town.  Landed  Colonel  Hawkins’s  zouaves  and 
naval  forces  and  set  fire  to  the  town.  At  1 : 30  took  zouaves  on  board 
and  took  a  raft  in  tow  and  stood  down  the  river,  and  anchored  abreast 
of  Edenton  Bay. 


Abstract  log  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Daylight,  July  17,  1861,  to  March  7,  1862. 

July  17,  1861. — At  2  p.  m.  saw  a  steamer  inshore,  making  her  way 
for  Fort  Caswell,  FT.  C.;  tried  to  cut  her  off,  but  she  had  the  heels  of 
us  and  escaped  past  the  fort.  Fired  a  rifled  howitzer  at  her,  but  could 
not  see  the  result.  Hauled  off  again,  being  in  range  of  the  guns  of 
Fort  Caswell,  and  came  to  anchor.  At  4:30  weighed  anchor,  seeing 
a  steamer  within  the  mouth  of  the  river,  but,  as  she  did  not  come  out¬ 
side,  we  ran  outside  a  little  farther  and  anchored. 

July  18. — At  5:45  p.  m.  saw  a  sail  skimming  along  the  land,  making 
for  Cape  Fear  River.  Stood  in  to  head  her  off,  but  having  the 
wind  and  tide  in  her  favor,  she  far  reached  us  and  dodged  into  the 
river.  We  could  not  pursue  her  farther  than  the  bar,  owing  to  our 
draft  of  water.  We  fired  10  shot  at  her,  but  the  steamer  rolled  so 
heavily  could  not  sight  the  guns.  Every  ball,  however,  struck  very 
near  her.

July  21. — At  10  a.  m.  Lieutenant  Lynch  and  Master’s  Mate  Kelly 
went  on  shore  in  the  whaleboat  with  a  flag  of  truce,  carrying  informa¬ 
tion  of  the  blockade.  They  were  not  allowed  to  proceed  to  the  fort, 
but  were  obliged  to  land  in  the  surf.  Were  received  by  a  person  call¬ 
ing  himself  Colonel  Allen;  delivered  the  documents  and  returned  on 
board. 

July  21. — From  12  to  4  p.  m.  very  heavy  firing  at  Fort  Caswell. 

August  3. — At  1:30  p.  m.  proceeded  up  James  Kiver  [Virginia], 
reconuoitering.  Fired  4  shot  at  the  shore,  but  could  see  no  effect. 


Abstract  log  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Delaware,  December  7,  1861,  to  March  7,  1862. 

December  7,  1861. — At  2  p.  m.  vessel  went  into  commission,  navy 
yard,  Philadelphia. 

December  13. — At  1  p.  m.  came  to  anchor  off  Fortress  Monroe.  At  7 
batteries  ready  for  action. 

December  29. — At  7  a.  m.  was  hailed  by  a  boat  from  the  flagship,  who 
reported  an  enemy  off  Newport  News,  and  with  the  command  to  take 
her.  Hastened  toward  Newport  News,  hearing  continuous  firing  from 
the  enemy,  who  had  made  prize  of  a  schooner,  taking  her  from  the 
steamer  Express.  Gave  up  the  chase  when  off  Newport  News,  as  the 
enemy  were  inside  of  Craney  Island.  Fired  at  the  batteries  on  Sewell’s 
Point.  Rifle  gun  expended  2  grapesliot,  4  rifle  shell;  32-pounders,  3 
5-second  shell  and  2  15-second.  At  5  p.  m.  got  underway  and  pro¬ 
ceeded  to  Newport  News. 

February  5. — At  12  m.  running  slowly  up  Pamlico  Sound,  the  squad¬ 
ron  all  keeping  along.  At  5  p.  in.  came  to  anchor. 

February  19. — At  11 : 30  a.  m.  steamed  at  a  moderate  rate  up  Chowan 
River,  followed  by  the  steamers  Louisiana ,  Morse,  Hunchback,  White- 
head,  Barney,  Perry ,  and  Lockwood.  When  off  the  town  of  Winton, 
and  within  50  yards  of  the  shore,  was  assailed  by  the  enemy  with  a 
discharge  of  musketry.  Called  all  hands  to  quarters,  and  running 
above  the  bank  from  which  the  firing  proceeded,  gave  them  back  shell 
and  shrapnel  from  the  IX-inch  gun  and  the  32-pounder.  Returned 
back  by  the  embankment,  and  with  the  Perry  and  balance  of  the  fleet 
came  to  anchor  7  miles  below.  Found  185  bullet  holes  in  and  around 
the  ship,  damage  sustained  from  the  enemy. 

February  20. — At  8  a.  in.,  in  company  with  squadron,  proceeded  on 
up  the  Chowan  River.  When  off  the  town  of  Winton  part  of  fleet 
opened  fire  and  landed  D’Fpineuil  Zouaves,  who  advanced  toward  the 
town.  After  destroying  buildings,  etc.,  returned  and  were  reembarked 
on  board  their  respective  vessels.  Cavalry  of  the  enemy  reported  in 
sight  by  the  lookout  at  the  masthead.  We  fired  from  32-pounder  and 
IX-inch  gun.  Steamed  down  the  river  with  flotilla  and  anchored  at  the 
mouth  at  G :  30  p.  m. 

March  5.— At  10:30  a.  m.  passed  Brant  Island  Shoal,  off  Swan 
Quarter  Island  [Pamlico  Sound] ;  captured  a  schooner  with  10  men  on 
board.  Sent  crew  on  board  in  charge  of  Master’s  Mate  Kerens;  took 
her  in  tow  and  proceeded  back  toward  Hatteras. 

March  6. — At  G:  30  a.  m.  fired  a  howitzer  to  bring  to  a  sail  discovered 
off  Jones  Bay.  Took  prize  the  schooner  Zenith,  laden  with  corn,  and 
took  prisoners  her  captain  and  crew,  3  in  number.  At  the  same  time 
a  small  open  boat,  schooner-rigged,  having  on  board  a  few  barrels  of 
corn,  was  made  prize  of  and  her  captain  and  crew  (3)  taken  prisoners. 
Master’s  Mate  J.  H.  Raymond,  with  a  crew  of  4  men,  was  placed  in 
charge  of  the  Zenith,  taking  her  in  tow  toward  the  Ceres ,  who  Avas

Abstract  log  of  the  U.  S.  bark  Gemsbok,  August  30,  1861,  to  March  7,  1862. 

August  30 , 1861. — Went  into  commission  at  the  Charlestown  [Boston] 
navy  yard. 

September  11. — At  2:15  p.  m.  came  to  anchor  between  the  Rip  Raps 
and  Fortress  Monroe. 

September  19. — At  4:30  a.  m.  made  a  sail  standing  to  the  westward; 
made  sail  for  pursuit.  Threw  a  32-pound  shot  across  her  bow;  hove 
her  to;  Mr.  Lunt,  executive  officer,  boarded  and  took  possession.  Her 
captain  stated  he  was  bound  to  Key  West,  but  her  log  and  private 
papers  found  in  her  cabin  proved  that  she  was  bound  to  evade  the 
blockade  for  a  market.  The  schooner  captured  was  of  about  30  tons 
burden,  Captain  James  M.  Davis,  called  the  Harmony ,  of  Yarmouth, 
Nova  Scotia,  loaded  with  fish  and  other  cargo.  The  captain  subse¬ 
quently  confessed  that  he  was  bound  for  Ocracoke,  and  signed  a  state¬ 
ment  to  that  effect.  Latitude  34°  47',  longitude  75°  41'. 

September  22. — At  6 :  30  a.  m.  fired  2  32-pound  shot  and  3  8-iuch  shell 
at  a  sail  on  weather  bow.  All  fell  short.  Continued  the  chase  to 
windward.  At  9  schooner  came  to  anchor  close  inshore  and  her  crew 
deserted  her,  landing  in  boats  on  the  beach.  Federal  Point  bears 
S.  W.  by  W.  J  W.,  distant  12  miles.  Sent  port  cutter,  in  charge  of 
Mr.  Lunt,  to  take  possession.  At  10  she  was  boarded;  at  10:30  she 
was  alongside.  She  proved  to  be  the  Mary  E.  Pindar ,  of  Edenton, 
N.  C.,  with  about  50  casks  of  lime  on  board.  At  12:40  she  was 
placed  in  command  of  Mr.  Burke,  master’s  mate,  and  4  men  and 
ordered  to  report  at  Hampton  Roads.  At  4  p.  m.  passed  Camp  Weir, 
5  miles  south  from  New  Inlet  [Cape  Fear  River];  hoisted  jack  fora 
pilot,  keeping  men  out  of  sight  and  officer  of  deck  in  plain  clothes. 
Two  men  came  off  in  a  boat  and  were  made  prisoners  of  war.  They 
stated  they  were  Union  men  at  heart  and  glad  of  the  protection  of  the 
stars  and  stripes  once  more,  and  of  their  own  accord  took  the  oath  ot 
allegiance  and  joined  the  ship.  They  stated  that  there  were  2  rified 
guns  and  1,000  men  in  Camp  Weir.  At  6  Bald  Head  light  house  bore 
S.  W.  by  W.  and  Federal  Point  light  house  W.  by  S. 

November  12. — As  we  approached  Bogne  Inlet,  saw  the  wreck  of  a 
steamer  and  a  great  crowd  of  people  on  the  beach;  also  discovered  a 
great  many  barrels  and  boxes,  horses,  etc.  When  abreast  of  them, 
kept  oft’  and  threw  some  shell  amongst  them,  at  which  they  scattered. 
We  must  have  killed  and  wounded  a  great  many,  as  our  shells  exploded 
in  their  midst.  Expended  10  68-pound  shell  [and]  1  32-pound  shell. 
We  then  beat  up  toward  Beaufort  Harbor.

December  1. — At  4:30  p.  in.  got  underway  and  proceeded  to  our 
night  station,  Newport  News  bearing  S.  E. 

December  2. — At  G:20  a.  m.  a  rebel  steamer  ran  out  from  under  the 
lee  of  the  eastern  shore  [James  Biver,  Virginia]  and  fired  a  shot,  which 
passed  over  us.  Called  all  hands  to  quarters  and  cleared  ship  for 
action.  At  6 : 25  slipped  cable  and  opened  fire  with  our  after  gun.  At 
0:30  the  action  became  general;  firing  was  kept  up  by  the  II.  S.  steam¬ 
ers  Hetzel ,  Shawslieen ,  Seymour ,  and  Whitehead,  against  the  so-called 
Confederate  steamer  Yorlctown  [ Patriclc  IIenry\.  Alter  an  action  of 
one  hour  and  forty  minutes  the  Yorlctown  stood  up  river.  During  the 
engagement  this  vessel  expended  28  solid  shot  and  3  15-second  shell. 
At  8: 15  stood  for  Newport  News  and  anchored. 

December  11. — At  7 : 30  a.  m.  the  Congress  made  signal  “Come  within

December  28.— At  8  a.  in.  made  Cape  Hatteras  light,  bearing  N.  N.  E.,

January  13,  1862. — Twenty-four  steamers  of  Genenal  Burnside’s 
expedition  arrived  and  several  gunboats  under  command  of  Flag-Officer 
Goldsborough. 

January  14.— Fresh  gale  from  N.  W.  At  7 : 30  a.  m.  a  steamer  out¬ 
side  the  bulkhead  raised  ensign,  union  down.  At  8  one  of  the  steam¬ 
ers  of  General  Burnside’s  expedition  ran  ashore  on  the  bar.  At  8:45 
steamer  on  bar  cut  away  her  foremast  and  at  11  her  smokestack  went

January  15. — At  3 : 30  p.  m.  proceeded  over  the  bulkhead  and  came

January  21. — At  1:30  p.  m.  saw  two  of  the  enemy’s  steamers.  Got

Abstract  log  of  the  U,  S.  S.  Monticello,  July  16,  1861,  to  March  7,  1862. 

July  16,  1861.— Discovered  a  new  camp  of  40  tents,  as  near  as  we 
could  tell,  across  the  river  [James  Biver,  Virginia]  from  Jones’s  house. 

July  17. — Proceeded  up  river  to  Godwin’s  Point;  went  close  inshore 
and  fired  one  10-inch  shell,  15-second,  and  three  32-pounder,  15-second 
shells,  but  could  not  reach  the  encampment.  Beconnoitered  the  shore 
carefully,  but  could  see  nothing  new. 

August  26. — At  2 : 25  p.  m.  got  underway  and  followed  the  frigate 
Minnesota  and  other  vessels  as  one  of  the  expedition  bound  to  Hatteras 
Inlet  to  attack  the  fort  there.

October  19. — Off  Savannah  [Ga.]. 

October  30. — At  10 : 15  a.  m.  discovered  a  sail  ashore  at  the  mouth  of 
Wassaw  Inlet.  Saw  two  other  schooners  in  the  inlet  and  a  steamer. 
At  3  p.  m.  took  two  launches  from  the  Savannah  in  tow  and  proceeded 
down  the  coast.  At  5  p.  m.,  close  in  to  Wassaw  Inlet,  sent  the  launches, 
accompanied  by  second  cutter;  opened  tire  with  our  rifle  gun  on  a 
schooner  near  shore.  All  the  shell  fell  short.  At  7 : 30  boats  returned 
to  the  ship,  after  making  an  unsuccessful  attack  upon  the  schooner. 
Several  shots  were  exchanged  on  both  sides,  but  no  one  was  hurt. 
The  rebels  seemed  to  be  in  great  force  and  ready  to  resist  an  attack. 
Boats  were  commanded  by  Lieutenants  A.  W.  Johnson  and  W.  P. 
Buckner. 

November  5. — Came  to  anchor  off  Portress  Monroe. 

November  11. — Bound  down  the  coast. 

November  12. — Prom  8  to  meridian  stood  in  toward  Beaufort  [1ST.  C.] 
and  reconnoitered.  At  1:45  stood  in  toward  the  land.  At  2  discov¬ 
ered  a  number  of  men  on  the  beach  at  work  on  the  wreck  of  the  IT.  S. 
transport  Union.  Opened  fire  upon  them.  At  3  stood  off. 

November  15.— Stood  in  toward  Federal  Point  light-house,  reconnoit- 
ering.  Pound  a  large  fort  near  Federal  Point  light  house  commanding 
the  inlet,  as  near  as  we  could  ascertain,  mounting  8  guns,  and  one 
small  fort  of  3  guns  and  an  earthen  casemate  mounting  3  guns.  Could 
see  men  at  work  on  the  same.  On  Zeek’s  Island  could  see  still  another 
fort,  but  not  see  the  number  of  guns.  Both  forts  flying  a  red  flag  with 
a  white  star.  At  11  a.  m.  came  to  anchor. 

November  18.— While  reconnoitering  close  inshore  5  miles  northeast 
of  Federal  Point  saw  a  new  house  with  a  battery  of  2  guns  close  to  it. 
While  in  the  act  of  turning  round  a  gun  was  fired  to  the  northward, 
when  the  battery  near  the  house  opened  on  us  and  tired  3  shots. 
Hoisted  our  colors  and  fired  the  rifle  gun  three  times,  reaching  them 
once.  All  their  shot  fell  short.  Discovered  another  battery  near  by, 
making  in  all  three. 

November  26. — At  9  a.  m.  off  the  east  end  of  Smith’s  Island,  it  bear¬ 
ing  W.  S.  W.,  distant  4  miles;  ran  along  shore  to  the  northward  and 
eastward  reconnoitering.  After  passing  the  fort  on  Federal  Point,  saw 
red  flags  every  half  mile  for  the  distance  of  8  miles.
