Abstract  log  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Mystic,  November  30,  1861,  to  March  7,  1862. 

November  30, 1861. — At  2  p.  m.  put  the  ship  in  commission. 

December  15. — Anchored  iu  the  Eappahannock  Eiver. 

December  19. — At  5:  30  p.  m.  sent  second  cutter  with  armed  crew,  in 
charge  of  W.  E.  Morton,  master’s  mate,  to  cooperate  with  the  Dawn  in 
an  expedition. 

December  21. — At  7  p.  m.  observed  boat  inshore  of  us;  armed  boats 
and  pursued  her,  but  she  escaped  up  the  river. 

December  27. — Got  underway  iu  company  with  the  Dawn  and  ran  up 
to  the  mouth  of  Indian  Greek  for  a  reconnoissance.  Saw  nothing  of  the 
enemy,  and  at  noon  returned  and  proceeded  up  the  Eappahannock. 
Steamed  up  the  river  as  far  as  Carter’s  Creek ;  saw  nothing,  and  returned 
and  anchored  at  the  mouth  of  the  river. 

January  6,  1862. — At  9:30  a.  m.  got  underway  and  went  up  to  Mos¬ 
quito  Point  for  oysters.  Sent  in  two  boats.  At  1  p.  m.  the  boats  were 
fired  on  from  the  woods  on  shore;  as  no  person  could  be  observed, 
did  not  return  the  fire.  Proceeded  on  board  and  dropped  a  shell  into 
the  woods  where  the  shot  came  from.  Eeturned  to  our  previous  anchor¬ 
age  off  Windmill  Point. 

January  15. — At  11:30  a.  m.  discovered  a  vessel  bearing  W.  S.  W.; 
got  underway  and  ran  for  her.  At  12: 15  first  and  second  cutters  left 
the  ship  in  chase.  As  they  pulled  in,  we  opened  fire  on  the  shore  to 
cover  their  attack.  At  12 : 45  the  enemy  opened  fire  on  the  boats  with 
a  small  fieldpiece  and  rifies,  when  the  boats  were  recalled.  At  1  we 
were  joined  by  the  Dawn,  when  the  enemy  opened  on  both  vessels,  which 
was  returned  promptly  by  both,  and  a  brisk  interchange  of  shots  was 
kept  up  for  thirty  minutes,  when  we  deemed  it  prudent  to  haul  off,  the 
enemy’s  guns  being  concealed  by  the  trees  and  their  range  superior  to 
our  own.  Expended  in  the  action  9  shell  and  8  shot. 

January  25.— At  8:15  p.  in.  sent  Acting  Master  Meader  with  first 
cutter  to  reconnoiter.  At  11 :  45  first  cutter  returned. 

January  2d.— At  2: 15  a,  m.  sent  first  cutter  with  Acting  Master  Blak- 
iston  to  reconnoiter.  At  5  a.  m.  the  first  cutter  returned. 

February  12.— Ean  up  as  far  as  Grey’s  Point  to  reconnoiter.  At  6 
p.  m.  steamed  down  the  river. 

February  28.— At  8  a.  m.  left  for  Fortress  Monroe.  At  3:30  p.  in. 
arrived  at  Fortress  Monroe. 

March  2. — Boilers  undergoing  repairs.

Abstract  log  of  the  TJ.  S.  S.  Stars  and  Stripes,  September  19,  1861,  to  March  7,  1862. 

September  19,  1861. — At  1  p.  ru.  ship  was  put  in  commission  [New 
York  navy  yard]. 

October  29.— [Hatteras  Inlet.]  At  11:30  a.  m.  a  steamer  in  sight  to 
northward  and  westward;  called  to  general  quarters  and  exchanged 
shots;  fired  4  shots  from  pivot  gun,  when  the  enemy  retreated. 

November  18. — A  rebel  steamer  came  insight,  coming  to  within  about 
4  miles,  when  she  rounded  to  and  stood  away  to  the  northward. 

November  20. — A  steamer  in  sight;  called  all  hands  to  quarters,  the 
enemy  firing  2  shots  at  us.  At  12:30  p.  m.  the  enemy  left;  secured  the 
guns. 

December  i. — At  4: 45  p.  m.  mustered  the  crew  at  quarters,  armed  the 
watch,  and  got  the  battery  ready  for  action;  saw  the  masts  of  a  large 
schooner,  supposed  to  be  inside  Ocracoke. 

December  5. — At  6:30  a.  m.  discovered  two  steamers  in  the  N.N.  W., 
coming  into  the  Swash  Channel;  fired  5  shots  from  the  pivot  gun  with 
shrapnel  (plugged),  one  15-second  shell  from  broadside  gun,  and  1 
shot  from  howitzer.  The  rebels  returned  the  fire  sharply  for  some 
thirty  minutes,  when  they  ceased  firing,  and  at  8  o’clock  rounded  to 
and  stood  off  to  the  N.  N.  W.  The  nearest  shot  from  the  enemy  fell 
short  about  200  yards.  At  1  p.  m.  a  steamer  in  sight.  At  1 : 30  made 
our  number,  which  was  not  answered.  At  1 : 45  made  signal  for  the 
Ceres  to  get  underway  and  overhaul  her.  After  getting  underway,  in 
turning  around,  she  got  aground  and  could  not  get  off.  At  2:20  the 
steamer  in  sight  passed  the  inlet. 

January  21,  1862. — At  1  p.  m.  two  rebel  steamers  in  sight;  flagship 
Delaware ,  with  six  of  the  fleet,  gave  chase. 

February  6. — From  8  a.  m.  to  meridian  [Pamlico  Sound] :  Two  rebel 
steamers  in  sight  ahead.  From  4  to  6  p.  m. :  Called  to  quarters  and  got 
the  battery  ready  for  action.

Order  of  Captain  Barron,  Virginia  Navy,  Chief  of  Office  of  Detail  and 
Equipment,  to  Lieutenant  Jones,  Virginia  Navy,  regarding  construction 
of  batteries  in  BurwelVs  Bay. 


Office  of  Naval  Detail  and  Equipment, 

Bichmond ,  Va.,  April  29,  1861. 

Sir:  Proceed  to  Burwell’s  Bay  in  company  with  Colonel  Talcott,  and 
after  obtaining  from  him  such  information  as  you  may  require  in  the 
construction  of  the  battery  there,  you  will  proceed  to  execute  the 
work.  Guns  and  munitions  will  be  sent  to  you,  and  there  will  be  a 
volunteer  force  to  aid  you  in  the  protection  of  the  battery. 

Captain  H.  H.  Cocke  is  in  command,  and  you  will  report  to  him  by

and  Equipment,  to  Captain  Cocke ,  Virginia  Navy,  regarding  a  force  for 
the  protection  of  batteries  under  construction. 

Office  of  Naval  Detail  and  Equipment, 

Richmond,  Va.,  May  5,  1861. 

Sir  :  Please  say  to  Captain  Allen  that  Major-General  Lee  wishes  him 
to  assume  command  of  his  company  and  station  them  for  the  support 
of  your  work.  Should  this  not  be  a  sufficient  force  for  the  protection 
of  the  works,  you  are  authorized  to  call  on  Major  Ewell  at  Williams¬ 
burg  for  such  contingent  as  you  may  deem  necessary. 

When  application  is  made  by  Captain  Allen,  the  major-general  will 
have  his  company  mustered  into  service. 

We  have  received  information  that  the  vessels  of  the  blockading 
squadron  are  extending  their  visits  high  up  the  river.  You  are  directed 
to  prevent  their  ascent  above  your  fort,  observing  the  usual  practice  in 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


699 


such  cases,  first,  a  shot  across  the  bow;  if  not  attended  to,  one  imme¬ 
diately  over  the  vessel.  Should  these  signals  be  disregarded,  you  must 
fire  into  them.  It  is,  however,  the  major-general’s  desire  to  keep  off 
hostile  collision,  if  it  be  properly  avoidable.  It  is  thought  advisable 
that  no  opportunity  of  gaining  information  by  the  enemy  of  what  we 
are  doing  should  be  afforded.  To  this  end  you  are  authorized  to  pre¬ 
vent  any  vessel  from  passing  down  the  river.

Respectfully,  etc.,  S.  Barron,

Report  of  Lieutenan  t  Jones ,  Virginia  Navy ,  of  the  selection  of  Jamestown 
Island  as  a  suitable  position  for  a  battery. 

Jamestown  Island,  May  5, 1861. 

Sir  :  In  obedience  to  your  order  of  the  29tli  ultimo,  I  proceeded  the 
next  morning,  in  company  with  Lieutenant  Randolph,  to  Norfolk,  for 
the  purpose  of  hastening  the  prejparation  of  a  battery  for  Burwell’s 
Bay.  Finding  that  I  could  not,  without  much  delay,  obtain  more 
than  six  guns  (one  IS-inch  and  five  32-pounders),  I  made  the  necessary 
arrangements  for  that  number  and  left  Lieutenant  Kandolph  to  bring 
them  on  when  ready,  whilst  I  accompanied  Colonel  Talcott  on  a  recon- 
noissance  for  a  suitable  position  for  a  battery.  After  some  days’  exam¬ 
ination,  Colonel  Talcott  selected  this  island  as  the  lowest  place  on  the 
river  for  a  battery,  and  therefore  a  very  important  position.  Mr.  Wil¬ 
liam  Allen  (the  proprietor  of  the  island)  had,  himself,  commenced  con¬ 
structing  a  battery  here,  for  which  he  informs  me  eight  32-pounders 
are  preparing  at  Norfolk,  but  these,  it  is  to  be  apprehended,  will  not 
be  sent  here  now  without  an  order  from  you,  as  it  may  be  thought  that 
the  battery  for  Burwell’s  Bay  will  answer;  but  supposing  them  to  be 
sent,  there  will  yet  remain  two  guns  to  complete  the  battery  as  laid 
out,  which  Colonel  Talcott  recommends  shall  be  taken  from  the  twelve 
IX-incli  guns  now  mounted  at  Fort  Norfolk.  Lieutenant  Randolph 
writes  that  some  of  the  guns  and  articles  selected  for  this  place  have 
been  appropriated  for  batteries  above.  This  will  cause  delay  where  it 
is  most  injurious,  as  from  our  position  we  are  most  exposed.  The  Glen- 
cove  was  fired  into  yesterday  only  a  few  miles  below  this.  I  requested 
Major  Ewell,  of  Williamsburg,  to  order  a  force  to  protect  our  opera¬ 
tions.  He  last  night  sent  a  detachment  of  the  Junior  Guard,  consist¬ 
ing  of  17,  but  without  artillery.  They  may  serve  to  reassure  the  work¬ 
men,  who  have  been  most  alarmed,  and  thus  hasten  the  work. 

I  have  assumed  command  and  commenced  constructing  the  battery. 
The  work  will,  owing  to  the  course  of  the  channel  which  it  is  to  com¬ 
mand,  be  aD  extensive  one,  with  five  faces  and  sixteen  guns.  We  have 
over  a  hundred  negroes,  but  are  delayed  for  want  of  barrows,  tools, 
and  provisions.  We  shall,  however,  be  ready  to-morrow,  if  the  guns 
arrive,  to  mount  a  portion  of  them  temporarily.  Mr.  Allen  and  other 
gentlemen  have  thus  far  supplied  the  negroes,  but  they  are  short  of 
meat,  and  we  require  1,000  pounds  of  meat,  besides  subsistence  for  the 
volunteers.  Please  have  it  furnished,  or  direct  me  how  to  obtain  it.  I 
have  been  embarrassed  in  this  and  other  cases  where  expenditures 
were  necessary,  and  respectfully  request  instructions.

Report  of  Lieutenant  Jones ,  Virginia  Navy ,  commanding  Jamestown 
battery ,  regarding  the  lack  of  suitable  force  for  its  protection. 

Jamestown  Island,  May  6, 1861. 

Sir:  Yesterday  evening  Commander  Maury,  by  your  order,  delivered 
four  32  pounders  for  this  battery,  but  without  purchases,  tackles,  or 
any  other  means  of  handling  them,  and  we  have  consequently  been 
forced  to  suspend  operations  on  the  work  and  employ  all  hands  to  land 
and  place  the  guns  where  they  can  be  fired,  which  I  do  not  expect  to 
accomplish  this  forenoon.  No  train  or  side  tackles  have  been  sent, 
Commander  Maury  informing  me  that  Captain  Cocke  said  they  were 
all  needed  at  Fort  Powhatan ;  nor  has  there  been  any  force  sent  to  work 
the  guns  or  to  protect  them. 

The  17  men  from  Williamsburg  were  ordered  to  return  there  last 
evening,  leaving  the  guns  entirely  unprotected.  Commander  Maury, 
at  my  request,  represented  our  condition  at  the  fort  above,  Avhere  I 
understand  there  were  some  200  men,  and  returned  last  night  with  20 
men,  a  detachment  of  the  Greenville  Guards,  which  is  now  the  only 
guard  we  have. 

Y"our  letter  to  Captain  Cocke  of  the  5th  instant  has  been  placed  in 
my  hands.  I  shall  act  as  if  it  were  addressed  to  me.  I  have  called 
upon  Captain  Allen  this  morning  for  his  company.  He  informs  me 
that  they  are  without  arms  or  uniform.  I  respectfully  request,  as 
they  are  fine  marksmen,  that  rifled  guns  be  sent  them  at  this  place.  I 
shall  also  call  upon  Major  Ewell  for  two  companies,  though  I  do  not 
expect  to  obtain  them,  as  his  command  are  somewhere  on  York  Eiver. 

Yesterday  I  received  a  message  from  Captain  Cocke,  saying  that  he 
would  send  some  provisions  down  to  day.  I  would  respectfully  request 
that  immediate  steps  be  taken  to  provision  the  forces  shortly  expected 
here. 

The  above  message  is  the  only  communication  of  any  kind  that  I 
have  had  from  Captain  Cocke.  It  would  appear  that  the  fort  above  is 
considered  of  much  greater  importance  than  this.  Of  course  I  am  not 
the  judge  of  that,  but  I  consider  it  my  duty  to  represent  tlie  facts,  so 
that  you  can  determine  whether  it  is  proper  that  we  should  be  left  with 
guns  without  men  or  means  of  working  them,  and  without  a  force  to 
protect  them.  It  would  appear  that  they  consider  themselves  at 
liberty  above  to  supply  themselves  without  reference  to  our  wants, 
though  we  are  more  exposed  to  attack  and  more  remote  from  the  source 
of  supply. 

I  will  conclude  by  stating  that  imperfect  as  are  the  means  of  defense, 
1  shall  endeavor  to  use  them  to  the  best  advantage,  and  in  accordance 
with  the  instructions  in  your  letter  to  Captain  Cocke. 

Very  respectfully,  Catesby  ap  E.  Jones, 

Virginia  Navy,  Commanding  Battery. 

Captain  S.  Barron,  Virginia  Navy, 

Richmond.

Report  of  Lieutenant  Jones,  Virginia  Navy,  regarding  the  mounting  of 

guns  in  the  J amestown  battery. 

Jamestown  Battery,  May  10,  1861. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  order  conveyed  by  Lieutenant  Randolph, 
I  have  ordered  the  remaining  tug  to  return  to  Richmond.  She  will 
have  the  lighter  that  brought  the  guns  in  tow.  I  have  previously  stated 
the  importance  of  having  a  steamer  here.  I  will  add  that  I  have  no 
reason  to  change  opinion. 

We  have  now  8  guns  mounted,  two  IX-incli,  and  six  32-pounders  ot  57 
hundredweight,  and  had  succeeded,  after  great  labor,  in  having  tempo¬ 
rary  platforms  constructed  where  they  could  be  worked,  but  it  proved 
to  be  labor  thrown  away,  for  Captain  Cocke  yesterday  visited  the  bat¬ 
tery  and  ordered  the  side  and  train  tackles  for  three  of  the  guns  to  be 
sent  to  his  battery  at  Fort  Powhatan.  I  considered  it  my  duty  to  say 
to  him  that  this  battery  must  first  be  attacked,  and  that  the  guns  above 
(32-pounders  of  52  hundredweight)  were  lighter  than  ours,  and  could, 
with  less  difficulty,  be  worked  without  tackles  than  ours,  and  that  they 
had  more  men  than  we  had.  He  replied  that  it  was  necessary  to  com¬ 
plete  the  battery  above,  and  he  had  ordered  other  tackle  for  this  bat¬ 
tery.  The  IX-inch  sent  from  Richmond  has  no  sights  or  sight  boxes, 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


703 


and  is  without  an  elevating-  screw  or  roller  handspike.  Captain  Cocke 
brought  some  cartridges  for  the  Enfield  rifles,  but  the  balls  were  too 
large  to  enter.  I  suppose  they  must  have  been  made  for  the  new  rifled 
musket  which  was  purposely  made  a  few  thousandths  of  an  inch  larger 
than  the  Enfield. 

We  are  working  a  large  force;  about  250  are  now  employed.  Our 
supply  of  provisions  is  running  low,  a  company  from  Charles  City,  num¬ 
bering  50,  having  just  arrived. 

This  morning  we  fired  a  32-pounder  with  0  pounds  of  powder  and 
round  shot  to  see  if  the  breeching  could  not  be  dispensed  with.  The 
recoil  was  but  little  more  than  necessary  to  the  load.  The  inclination 
of  the  platform  is  1  inch  to  the  foot.  As  anticipated,  the  breeching  is 
entirely  unnecessary. 

Mr.  Myers,  the  engineer  of  the  work,  is,  I  regret  to  say,  quite  unwell; 
if  possible  he  will  see  you  in  person  and  give  you  any  information  you 
may  require  in  reference  to  the  work. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Catesby  ap  E.  Jones. 

Captain  Barron, 

Richmond ,  Ya. 


Personal  letter  from  Captain  Barron ,  Virginia  Navy,  to  Lieutenant  Jones, 
Virginia  Navy,  regarding  the  issuance  of  a  general  order. 


May  11,  1801. 


My  Dear  Jones:  I  have  succeeded  in  getting  a  general  order  issued, 
which,  I  think,  will  relieve  you  of  all  embarrassment  hereaiter.  I  have 
sympathized  with  you  fully  in  your  annoyance,  and  hope  that  you  have 
found  comfort  in  the  full  appreciation  of  your  very  successful  efforts  in 
preparing  for  the  defense  of  our  “  good  old  mother.’7  The  navy  batteries 
are  designed  for  the  defense  of  the  rivers,  and  the  military  force  for  the 
protection  of  the  batteries.  They  all  are  expected  to  play  into  each 
other’s  hands.  We  have  nothing  particularly  new.  President  Davis  is 
looked  for  here  in  a  few  days,  and  the  next  Congress  will  probably  meet 
here. 

Bert  has  resigned  and  wants  to  know  where  you  are. 

Very  sincerely,  yours, 


S.  Barron. 


Lieutenant  Catesby  ap  E.  Jones,  C.  S.  Navy. 


Letter  from  Captain  Barron,  Virginia  Navy,  to  Lieutenant  Jones,  Virginia 
Navy,  expressing  appreciation  of  his  zealous  prosecution  of  the  work  on 
the  battery. 

ElCIIMOND,  May  12,  1861. 

My  Dear  Sir  :  Your  two  letters  were  duly  received  yesterday.  Pro¬ 
visions  will  be  sent  you  to-morrow,  also  some  tackles  for  your  battery. 
I  wish  it  were  in  my  power  to  settle  things  in  such  a  mauner  as  to  give 
you  less  trouble  and  more  entire  control.  As  it  is,  we  must  work  away 
with  all  our  might  and  main.  Be  assured  that  both  the  major-general 
and  I  fully  appreciate  your  promptness,  energy,  and  zeal  in  the  efficient 
prosecution  of  the  work  confided  to  your  well-known  and  appreciated

intelligence  and  patriotism.  You  have  overcome  immense  difficulties, 
and  your  success  lias  given  great  comfort  to  the  good  people  of  this

safe-keeping  and  proper  expenditure  of  the  provisions  that  may  be  sent . 
The  guns  at  York  River,  Gloucester  Point,  and  West  Point  are  at  last

Letter  from  Captain  Barron ,  Virginia  Vary,  Chief  of  Office  of  Detail 
and  Equipment ,  to  Lieutenant  Jones ,  Virginia  Navy ,  regarding  the  erec¬ 
tion  of  an  additional  battery. 

Richmond,  May  23, 1861. 

My  Dear  Jones:  Colonel  Magruder  is  to  assume  command  of  the 
forces  between  your  station  and  York  River.  You  are  to  hold  inter¬ 
course  with  him.  I  shall  send  you  an  officer  or  two  midshipmen;  sorry 
I  can’t  do  better  for  you.  Your  battery  is  to  be  increased  five  more 
heavy  guns;  that  is,  another  battery  is  to  be  erected  on  your  island. 
This  is  to  be  the  future  capital.  Davis  will  probably  be  here  in  a  few 
days.  Excuse  great  haste. 

Yery  truly,  yours, 

S.  Barron. 


Lieutenant  Catesby  ap  R.  Jones,  C.  S.  Navy.

Port  Pocahontas  [Jamestown  Island?],

Sir  :  There  are  2  IX-inch  and  6  32-pounders  in  this  battery.  One  of 
the  IX-incli  is  marked  W.  P.,  and  numbered  110;  the  other  I.  F., 
No.  276. 

The  32-pounders  are  all  marked  I.  F.,  and  numbered,  respectively, 
392,  394,  401,  406,  403,  and  408.  Weight,  57  hundredweight. 

For  the  IX-inch  we  have  70  cartridges  (10  pounds),  700  pounds,  35 
rounds;  70  shell,  35  rounds;  8  stand  of  grape,  4  rounds. 

For  the  32-pounders  we  have  396  cartridges  (8  pounds),  3,168  pounds, 
66  rounds;  498  shot,  83  rounds;  75  shell,  12  rounds;  20  stand  of  grape, 
3  rounds;  four  barrels  of  powder  (400  pounds). 

The  following  ammunition  is  required:  130  10-pound  cartridges  for 
IX-inch,  65  rounds;  130  shell,  filled  and  fuzed,  for  IX-inch,  65  rounds; 
22  stand  of  grape  for  IX-inch,  11  rounds;  12  canister  for  IX-inch,  6 
rounds;  204  9-pound  cartridges  for  32-pounder,  34  rounds;  102  shot  for 
32-pounder,  17  rounds;  45  shell,  filled  and  fuzed,  32-pounder,  7  rounds; 
70  stand  of  grape,  32-pounder,  12  rounds;  36  canister,  32-pounder,  6 
rounds ;  200  spare  fuzes,  500  primers,  2  fuze  wrenches. 

There  are  also  required:  Spare  lock  strings  (ours  are  all  too  short),  2 
vent  drills,  2  spare  beds  and  quoins,  2  spare  trucks,  spare  double 
blocks  and  spare  rope  for  falls  (our  falls  are  too  short),  spun  yarn,  1 
ladle  for  IX-inch  gun,  1  worm,  12  lanterns,  black  lead,  red  lead,  india- 
rubber  shoes  (2  pair)  for  magazine,  1  set  of  weights  and  scales,  1  set  of 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


705 


measures  (copper),  1  funnel  for  filling  shell,  copper  tools  for  opening 
powder  barrels,  water  buckets  (2),  copper  bound,  dustpan  (copper). 

It  is  very  important  that  a  sufficient  number  of  men  should  be  sta¬ 
tioned  at  this  battery  to  man  all  the  guns  and  to  be  solely  and  exclu¬ 
sively  engaged  in  the  duties  appertaining  to  it.  The  efficiency  of  the 
battery  would  be  very  much  increased  by  the  addition  of  a  competent 
gunner  and  a  few  seamen  accustomed  to  the  handling  of  heavy  guns. 

I  have  just  been  informed  that  five  8-inch  army  guns  have  been  dis¬ 
patched  to  this  place.  This  will  readily  suggest  the  necessity  of  an 
experienced  gunner,  to  avoid,  as  much  as  possible,  the  necessary  com¬ 
plications  arising  from  the  supply  of  guns  of  three  different  calibers  in 
the  same  battery. 

P.  S. — For  8-inch  army  guns,  500  cylinders,  2  gunner’s  quadrants, 
cartridge-formers  for  32-pounder  8-inch  and  9-inch  guns,  and  cartridge 
material. 

[Catesby  ap  E.  Jones  (?), 

Lieutenant ,  C.  S.  Navy.] 


Letter  from  Captain  Barron ,  Virginia  Navy ,  Chief  of  Office  of  Detail 
and  Equipment ,  to  Lieutenant  Jones ,  Virginia  Navy ,  regarding  the 
command  of  the  battery  on  Jamestown  Lsland. 


Eichmond,  May  27,  1861. 

My  Dear  Jones:  The  Army  have  been  within  the  last  few  days 
landing  troops  and  supplies  at  the  Grove’s  [wharf],  or  some  point  sev¬ 
eral  miles  below  your  station,  which  is  considered  to  be  rather  hazard¬ 
ous.  Let  me  know,  for  the  information  of  the  general,  your  opinion  on 
this  point,  and  whether  the  same  sort  of  troops  and  supplies  may  not 
be  landed  under  the  protection  of  your  battery  at  or  near  Jamestown 
Island.  I  am  very  sorry  about  the  thoughtlessness  in  sending  your 
guns  down  in  a  vessel  drawing  so  much  water.  We  are  getting  to  be 
anxious  about  your  island,  and  the  general  and  Colonel  Talcott  deter¬ 
mined  on  the  additional  guns  which  have  been  sent  you.  The  spot  on 
which  the  battery  or  redoubt  is  to  be  erected  was,  or  is  to  be,  selected 
by  Colonel  Talcott,  the  batteries  to  be  under  your  command;  and  when 
the  requisition  for  men  to  work  the  guns  is  filled,  you  are  to  have  the 
entire  control  of  them,  exercising,  stationing,  etc.  There  has  been 
some  sad  mistake  on  this  point  on  your  river  and  at  Norfolk,  which  I 
trust  I  have  succeeded  in  correcting.  If  Captain  Cocke  be  not  on  the 
spot,  when  you  have  opportunities  to  write  me,  or  when  you  have 
requisitions  or  reports  to  make  to  this  office,  don’t  hesitate  to  do  so 
direct.  This  is  no  time  for  circumlocution.  I  am  trying  to  get  a  gun¬ 
ner’s  mate  for  you.  Had  you  not  better  write  to  Page,  at  Norfolk,  and 
ask  him  to  beat  up  a  volunteer  or  so  for  you?  You  can  offer  the  gun¬ 
ner’s  mate’s  pay,  etc.,  to  four  men.  Be  assured  that  you  have  my 
sympathies  in  all  your  trials,  and  shall  have  my  hearty  cooperation  in 
all  that  you  may  desire  to  have  done,  nor  shall  you  be  superseded  by 
any  person.  Pegram  has  been  ordered  to  Pig  Point,  and  now  it  is  pre¬ 
sumed  that  Cocke  will  devote  himself  still  more  exclusively  to  his  first 
love — Powhatan. 

President  Davis  is  expected  here  early  this  week.  Page  will  give 


you  all  the  news. 

Yery  sincerely,  yours, 


S.  Barron. 


[Lieutenant  Catesby  ap  E.  Jones.]

General  instructions  from  Captain  Barron ,  Virginia  Navy,  Chief  of  Office 
of  Detail  and  Equipment,  to  Lieutenant  Jones,  Virginia  Navy. 


Richmond,  May  29,  1861. 

My  Dear  Jones:  The  Teaser  is  ordered  to  be  stationed  near  to  your 
battery.  Her  principal  service  is  to  transport  or  aid  in  transporting 
men,  arms,  munitions,  etc.,  from  the  island  to  the  mainland,  it  being 
deemed  inadvisible  to  send  troops  or  anything  else  to  landings  lower 
down  the  river.  There  is  now  a  large  force  at  Hampton  and  the  neigh¬ 
borhood,  which  may  be  designed  for  this  city,  passing  up  the  peninsula. 
Therefore,  keep  a  bright  lookout  and,  if  necessary,  spike  your  guns 
and  retire  to  the  stream.  There  may  be  attempted  an  ascent  of  the 
river  on  its  right  bank;  if  so,  your  steamer,  with  the  scows  or  lighters 
placed  under  your  orders,  will  be  used  for  transporting  the  army  to 
that  bank  of  the  river.  The  major-general  commanding  directs  that 
no  enterprise  be  undertaken  without  special  orders.  We  must  still  act 
on  the  defensive. 

President  Davis  arrived  here  this  morning;  have  not  yet  seen  him. 
Cabinet  will  all  be  here  in  a  day  or  two.  Events  are  crowding  in 
upon  us.  Your  battery  is  looked  to  with  deep  anxiety.  It  is  consid¬ 
ered  in  Richmond  the  battery  for  the  defense  of  the  city. 

Yours,  very  sincerely, 

S.  Barron. 


[Lieutenant  Catesby  ap  R.  Jones.] 


Have  any  men  been  transferred  to  you  yet  for  your  battery?

Letter  from  Captain  Lee ,  Virginia  Navy,  Chief  of  Office  of  Ordnance  and 

Hydrography,  to  Lieutenant  Jones,  Virginia  Navy,  commanding  James- 

town  battery,  regarding  supplies. 

Office  of  Ordnance  and  Hydrography, 

Richmond,  May  29,  1861. 

Sir:  Your  letter  of  tlie  28tli  [24th?]  instant  is  received,  and  in  reply 
I  have  to  state  that  your  request  in  regard  to  the  future  transportation 
of  guns  shall  be  strictly  attended  to.  I  did  not  send  your  cartridges 
because  we  had  but  one  man  in  Richmond  who  could  till  them,  and  he 
was  absent  at  the  time.  We  sent  the  powder  cylinders. 

As  previously  advised,  we  have  no  tilled  or  live  shells  of  any.  size  here. 

We  have  no  scales,  weights,  or  measures,  but  as  soon  as  they  are 
received  from  Norfolk  they  shall  be  forwarded  to  you.  Also  the  other 
articles  you  require  for  elevating  the  guns. 

That  portion  of  your  letter  referring  to  the  want  of  a  gunner  and 
crew  for  the  more  effectual  working  of  your  batteries  has  been  referred 
to  Captain  Barron  for  his  action. 

The  sending  to  you  the  army  guns  was  a  sudden  determination  from 
headquarters.  They  were  ordered  to  be  sent  without  delay,  and  we 
had  no  time  to  advise  you  of  their  coming. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  S.  Lee, 
Captain,  in  Charge. 

Lieutenant  Catesby  ap  R.  Jones, 

Commanding  Battery  at  Jamestown  Island.

General  order  from  Captam  Lee ,  Virginia  Navy,  Chief  of  Office  of 
Ordnance  and  Hydrography ,  urging  care  in  the  expenditure  of  ammu¬ 
nition. 

Office  of  Ordnance  and  Hydrography, 

Richmond,  May  31,  1861. 

Sir  :  This  office  feels  called  upon  to  remind  the  officers  in  charge  of 
the  several  batteries  along  the  rivers  that  unnecessary  expenditure  of 
ammunition,  shells,  and  other  projectiles  must  be  avoided. 


708 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCK ADING  SQUADRON. 


You  will  please,  therefore,  impress  upon  the  minds  of  the  officers  in 
charge  of  said  batteries  the  great  necessity  of  not  throwing  away  their 
ammunition,  shells,  etc.,  uselessly,  as  our  means  of  supplying  ammuni¬ 
tion  and  projectiles  is  very  limited.  Of  live  shells  we  have  none  and 
no  person  upon  whom  we  can  lay  our  hands  to  till  a  shell,  consequently 
are  dependent  upon  the  small  supply  that  has  been  already  furnished 
to  the  batteries.  Hence,  you  will  perceive  the  stern  necessity  of  care¬ 
fully  holding  on  to  those  we  may  now  have. 

You  will  please  furnish  each  officer  commanding  a  battery  with  a 
copy  of  this  order. 

I  am,  very  respectfully, 

S.  S.  Lee, 
Captain ,  in  Charge. 

Captain  H.  H.  Cocke, 

Commanding  District ,  James  River ,  City  Point. 


Letter  from  Captain  Barron ,  Virginia  Navy ,  Chief  of  Office  of  Detail 
and  Equipment ,  to  Lieutenant  Jones ,  Virginia  Navy ,  commanding 
Jamestown  battery ,  regarding  guns  and  shells. 

June  1, 1861. 


My  Dear  Jones:  I  have  made  out  an  appointment  as  acting  car¬ 
penter  for  Mr.  Ditchings,  and  as  soon  as  he  appears  I  will  send  him  to 
you.  I  have  also  caused  Mr.  Myers’s  case  to  be  laid  before  the  Gover¬ 
nor  and  council,  and  hope  to  get  his  commission  properly  dated.  I  am 
endeavoring  to  get  slides,  beds,  etc.,  made  for  some  of  our  casemates. 
If  I  succeed,  I  will  send  you  some  of  the  light  guns  for  your  redoubt. 
We  have  no  filled  or  fuzed  shells.  We  are  trying  to  manufacture  fuzes 
at  the  Norfolk  yard.  When  we  get  some  you  shall  be  supplied.  I  have 
heard  of  a  gunner,  who,  if  I  get,  shall  be  sent  to  you.  If  any  more 
officers  present  themselves  I  will  not  forget  you,  be  assured.  The 
council  think  of  making  you  a  visit  on  Tuesday  next. 

President  Davis  is  here.  Toombs  also.  Mallory  and  Walker  are  to  be 
here  to-day.  To-morrow  or  next  day  we  shall  all  be  placed  under 
President  Davis,  I  think. 

Yours,  very  truly, 


S.  Barron. 


[Lieutenant  Catesby  ap  K.  Jones.] 


The  officers  of  our  Navy  will  be  incorporated  in  the  Confederate 
States  Navy  without  any  application  other  than  such  as  will  be 
attended  to  by  the  Government  here.  I  have  been  before  the  coun¬ 
cil  on  this  subject.  Walker  must  be  rated  by  you — i.  e.,  his  date  of 
entrance  on  duty  with  you,  and  the  rate  of  pay  received  by  ship’s  car¬ 
penters  will  be  allowed  him  as  if  he  had  been  at  work  in  the  Norfolk 
navy  yard. 

S.  Barron.

Order  of  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  of  the  Confederate  States  to  Captain 
Barron ,  C.  S.  Navy ,  Chief  of  Office  of  Orders  and  Detail ,  to  proceed 
to  the  command'  of  naval  defenses  of  Virginia  and  North  Carolina. 

C.  S.  Navy  Department, 

Richmond ,  July  20,  1861. 

Sir  :  You  are  hereby  detached  from  the  office  of  Orders  and  Detail 
and  will  take  charge  of  the  naval  defenses  of  the  States  of  Virginia 
and  North  Carolina  afloat,  and  adopt  every  means  in  your  power  to 
make  them  efficient  against  the  enemy. 

You  will  make  an  examination  of  the  coast  and  waters  of  North 
Carolina,  and  make  such  suggestions  as  your  judgment  may  dictate 
for  the  protection  of  the  honor  and  interests  of  the  country. 

The  Department  is  unwilling  to  circumscribe  your  action  by  detailed 
instructions,  relying  as  it  does  upon  your  judgment. 

The  following  vessels,  to  which  others  will  be  added,  are  placed  under 
your  command,  viz :  The  Patrick  Henry ,  Jamestown,  St.  Nicholas ,  George 
Page,  Raleigh,  Edwards,  and  Ellis. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  E.  Mallory, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  Flag-Officer  Barron,  C.  8.  Navy,  commanding  naval  defenses  of 
Virginia  and  North  Carolina,  regarding  vessels  available  for  purchase 
by  the  Confederate  Government. 

Navy  Yard,  Gosport  [Norfolk],  July  25, 1861. 
Sir:  I  hope  to  get  the  Edwards  off  for  Hatteras  to-morrow  and  the 
Ellis  on  Monday.  There  is  an  iron  propeller  here — the  Kahuha  [Eaha- 
Tceef] — which  can  be  purchased  for  $ 15,000  or  $20,000,  95  feet  length, 
17-foot  beam,  100  tons;  speed  about  9  or  10  miles;  boiler  six  years  old. 
She  is  now  in  the  service  of  the  Army,  and  can  carry  one  VTII-incli 
gun.  In  North  Carolina  there  is  a  side-wheel  steamer,  the  Curlew ; 
length,  about  150  feet,  260  tons;  draft,  44  feet;  speed,  12  or  13  miles; 
carries  from  eight  to  ten  days’  fuel;  can  probably  be  bought  for  $35,000. 

Shall  I  purchase  either  of  these  vessels?  If  yea,  I  should  like  to 
have  Commander  Arthur  Sinclair  detailed  with  me  in  the  waters  of 
North  Carolina.  He  is  anxious  for  this  service. 

There  is  a  strongly  built  boat  here,  without  anything  in  her,  which 
can  be  bought  for — say  $4,000.  She  can  carry  three  guns,  to  wit,  one 
Xl-inch,  one  X-incli,  and  one  solid-shot  VUI-inch,  together  with  a  fur¬ 
nace  for  heating  shot.  She  can  be  towed  down  to  attack  the  Minnesota. 
If  I  can  thus  fit  her,  shall  I  make  the  purchase? 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  Barron, 

Gomdg.  Navy  Defenses  in  waters  of  North  Carolina  and  Virginia.

Letter*  from  Major  Thompson ,  G.  8.  Army ,  chief  engineer  Department 

Coast  Defense ,  to  Colonel  Winslow ,  regarding  measures  of  defense  in 

Hatteras  Inlet. 

Fort  Hatteras,  July  25, 1861. 

Colonel  :  The  day  before  yesterday  we  hoisted  our  glorious  flag 
over  Fort  Clark,  a  strong  battery  I  have  nearly  finished,  of  live  heavy 
32-pounders,  about  half  a  mile  from  Fort  Hatteras,  which  secures  to  us 
a  cross  fire  upon  the  bar  and  the  entrance  to  this  inlet.  I  now  consider 
this  inlet  secure  against  any  attempt  of  the  enemy  to  enter  it.  Our 
force  of  men  I  think  rather  weak  to  resist  a  land  attack  in  case  the 
enemy  should  effect  a  landing  in  the  bight  of  Hatteras.  If  we  had 
three  or  four  additional  companies  here,  1  should  feel  quite  safe,  even 
in  that  event. 

As  I  have  before  remarked,  this  inlet  is  the  key  to  Albemarle  Sound, 
and  it  can  not  be  too  strictly  guarded.  We  certainly  are  under  the 
espionage  of  the  United  States  steamers,  as  they  are  seen  every  day 
or  two  in  the  offing,  although  they  keep  without  the  range  of  our  guns. 

If  I  had  received  the  10-inch  columbiad,  we  could  have  damaged  them 
some  on  their  last  visit  three  days  since. 

We  now  have  two  privateers  in  this  harbor,  besides  the  war  steamer 
Winslow.  The  Cordon,  of  Charleston,  Captain  Lockwood,  armed  with 
three  guns,  is  a  fine,  large  steamer.  She  returned  this  morning  with  a 
prize  brig  laden  with  360  hogsheads  of  molasses. 

We  have  also  a  saucy-lookiug  little  pilot  schooner,  the  Florida, 
mounting  one  6-pounder  rifled  cannon.  She  captured  a  prize  two 
days  since,  took  her  crew  out,  and  sent  her  in  with  her  own  men.  A 
U.  S.  Government  steamer  gave  chase  to  the  prize,  and  they  were 
obliged  to  beach  her  near  Nag’s  Head.  She,  of  course,  is  a  total  loss. 

W.  Beyershaw  Thompson, 

Major,  Chief  Engineer  Department  Coast  Defense. 

Colonel  Warren  Winslow, 

Military  Secretary. 


Instructions*  from  Major  Thompson,  C.  8.  Army,  chief  engineer  Depart¬ 
ment  Coast  Defense,  to  Thomas  II.  Allen,  esq.,  assistant  engineer,  regard¬ 
ing  execution  of  work  at  Fort  Clark ,  JST.  C. 

Headquarters  Engineers’  Department, 

Fort  Hatteras,  July  26,  1861. 

Dear  Sir:  The  following  are  your  instructions  for  the  execution  of 
the  work  at  Fort  Clark,  which  you  are  hereby  directed  to  carry  out 
literally.  The  work  is  to  be  constructed  in  all  respects  as  indicated 
upon  the  plan  and  explained  to  you  from  time  to  time.  The  broken 
line  enclosing  the  gorge  of  the  work,  it  is  important  to  bestow  care 
upon,  in  order  that  the  parapet  may  not  exceed  5  feet  between  the 
internal  and  external  crests,  the  superior  slope  of  the  gorge  being  6 
feet  horizontal  to  1  foot  vertical.  The  entrance  to  the  fort  will  be 
through  the  gorge,  as  pointed  out  this  morning.  It  will  be  7  feet  wide, 
properly  riveted  with  sod  at  as  abrupt  a  slope  as  you  can  make  the 
material  stand,  by  using  the  sod  as  in  the  revetment  of  the  interior 
slope.  The  opening  will  be  protected  by  a  traverse,  allowing  a  passage 


*  From  Richmond  Dispatch,  September  6,  1861. 


7l4  NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

*. 

between  it  and  the  interior  slope  of  7  feet.  The  top  of  the  traverse 
will  slope  outward  in  the  same  manner  as  the  superior  slope  of  the 
parapet  at  the  gorge,  and  be  provided  with  a  similar  banquette  on  its 
interior  face. 

First,  erect  the  magazine  and  bombproof,  and  then  the  traverses,  as 
shown  upon  the  drawing,  binding  the  material  throughout  at  every  toot  of 
elevation  by  brush  of  proper  dimensions,  in  order  that  they  may  stand 
as  nearly  vertical  as  possible.  These  will  be  15  feet  wide  on  the  bottom 
and  battered  so  as  to  have  a  width  at  top  of  7£  to  8  feet,  and  7  to  8 
feet  high,  the  sod  well  secured  by  stakes.  The  banquette  will  rise  to 
within  44  feet  of  the  interior  crest.  It  should  be  2  feet  wide  on  top 
and  sodded. 

Should  a  steamer  arrive  from  Norfolk  with  guns  and  barbette  car¬ 
riages,  take  out  eleven  guns — three  8-inch  shell  guns  and  eight  heavy 
32-pounders.  Should  the  X-inch  columbiad  arrive  from  Fort  Macon, 
have  it  landed  and  taken  into  Fort  Hatteras;  it  will  occupy  the  pan¬ 
coupe  facing  the  encampment  and  the  sea  front,  the  8-iueh  shell  gun 
taking  the  place  of  one  of  the  heavy  32s. 

Yours,  respectfully, 

W.  Be verse aw  Thompson, 

Major ,  Chief  Engineer  Department  Coast  Defense. 

Thomas  H.  Allen,  Esq., 

Assistant  Engineer.

Sir  :  I  can  probably  purchase  a  North  Carolina  steamer  of  115  or 
120  feet  length,  23£  feet  beam,  7  or  7£  feet  hold,  2  years  old,  well  built,

Letter  from  Flag-Officer  Barron,  C.  S.  Navy,  commanding  naval  defenses 
of  Virginia  and  North  Carolina,  to  Lieutenant  Jones ,  C.  S.  Navy,  com¬ 
manding  Jamestown  battery,  regarding  the  fitting  of  the  C.  S.  S.  Ger¬ 
mantown  as  a  floating  battery. 

New  Berne,  N.  C.,  August  23,  1861. 
My  Dear  Jones:  On  the  eve  of  my  leaving  Norfolk  your  letter 
reached  me.  To  day  1  forward  an  application  to  have  you  ordered  to 
command  the  Germantown,  now  being  fitted  up  as  a  floating  battery.  I 
confess,  the  more  I  reason  upon  the  propriety  and  expediency  of  getting 
this  ship  thus  prepared  afloat,  the  more  my  anxiety  is  increased  and  my 
confidence  in  the  project  confirmed.  She  is  to  have  her  bulwarks  cut 
down  to  her  spirketing  all  around,  from  her  spar  deck  down  to  her 
berth  deck,  which  is  some  18  inches  below  the  water  line.  She  will  have 
a  bulkhead  running  around  the  ship  about  7  feet  from  the  sides  of  the 
ship,  which  locker  will  be  filled  with  sand,  thus  placing  14  feet  of  sand 
in  addition  to  the  sides  of  the  vessel  herself  between  the  enemy  and  the 
steamer  which  will  have  us  in  tow.  This  arrangement,  I  think,  will 
render  our  motive  power  secure  against  the  shot  from  an  adversary. 
No  masts,  no  machinery,  or  anything  else  in  the  vessel,  but  provisions 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


717 


and  other  necessaries  for,  say,  one  month.  Her  battery  will  consist  of 
1  rille  gun,  pivot,  forward;  1  VIII  inch  solid-shot  gun  aft;  1  Xl-inch 
gun  amidship,  and  4  IX-inch  guns  for  either  side,  giving  us  7  broadside 
guns.  With  this  ship  well  manned  and  officered,  assisted  by  the  Pat¬ 
rick  Henry  and  perhaps  the  four  gunboats,  carrying  each  1  32-pounder, 
could  we  not  render  very  important  aid  to  General  Magruder  when  he 
attacks  Newport  News'?  Indeed,  would  it  be  very  unreasonable  in  us 
to  attack  the  Savannah  and  her  two  steamers,  which  are  not  much,  any¬ 
how,  even  though  they  bo  under  the  guns  of  Newport  News?  And, 
lastly,  must  we  do  nothing  with  these  means?  I  really  do  not  think 
we  would  be  thought  overrash  to  attempt  to  worry  the  Wabash,  if  she 
dared  to  come  out  from  under  Fortress  Monroe.  Why  not?  We  have 
land  batteries  to  take  refuge  under  if  she  worsts  us,  and  we  get 
fatigued.  Think  of  all  this.  The  Navy  must  do  something ! 

I  shall  remain  here  until  I  get  this  service  organized.  The  vandals 
have  their  eyes  upon  us  here.  A  report  lias  just  come  in  that  a  large 
vessel  of  the  Confederate  States  has  arrived  at  Beaufort  from  Europe. 
If  true,  it  will  make  our  Northern  friends  even  more  wrathy.  If  you 
be  ordered,  I  shall  apply  for  Bobert  Carter  to  go  with  you,  unless  you 
prefer  another. 

Very  truly,  your  friend,

Bluff,  at  or  near  the  point  where  the  others  were  sunk,  but  which  failed 
to  accomplish  the  obstruction  of  the  channel  as  intended.  You  will 
select  the  exact  spot.  The  general  also  desires  that  you  will  retain  at 
Jamestown  Island  the  other  canal  boats  now  on  their  way  down  the 
river  from  Richmond  until  their  final  disposition  is  determined  upon, 
which  will  be  communicated  to  you.  You  will  please  report  progress. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,

Letter  from  H.  K.  Burgwyn,  esq.,  to  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  of  the  Con¬ 
federate  Shies,  regarding  the  condition  of  Fort  Macon ,  N.  C. 

Goldsboro,  September  4, 1861. 

Fort  Macon  has  not  one  practical  gunner;  has  only  forty  reliable 
faxes,  no  rifled  cannon,  no  ordnance  officer,  and  only  raw  troops, 
without  proper  supplies.  It  must  fall.  It  should  be  supplied  at  once 
with  a  competent  naval  ordnance  officer.  May  I  suggest  Lieutenant 
G.  T.  Sinclair,  with  gunners,  with  two  rifled  cannon,  fuzes,  etc.?  I  beg 
to  refer  to  Mr.  President  Davis  for  my  position. 

H.  K.  Burgwyn. 

Hon.  S.  R.  Mallory, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Instructions  from  the  commandant  navy  yard,  Norfolk,  to  Commander 
Hunter,  C.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the  defenses  at  Roanoke  Island. 

Navy  Yard,  Gosport  [Norfolk],  September  4,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  received  your  dispatch  by  Lieutenant  Spotswood  and 
one  by  Lieutenant  Butler,  and  am  glad  to  find  that  you  are  so  actively 
engaged  in  preparing  the  defenses  of  the  island  of  Roanoke.  I  will 
forward  to  you  the  steamer  and  the  barge  Superior ,  with  all  the  mate¬ 
rial  you  mention,  having  already  anticipated  many  of  your  require¬ 
ments.  f  wish  we  could  furnish  the  gunboats,  but  it  is  not  practicable. 

N  W  R — VOL  (j - 40 


722  NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

* 

The  Superior,  with  her  battery,  will  be  of  infinite  importance  to  you, 
and  I  am  glad  you  sent  her  to  me.  I  do  not  understand  why  you  desire 
a  hot-shot  furnace,  since  you  have  only  to  contend  with  boats  of  small 
dimensions  and  draft  of  water.  Grape  and  canister  are  the  best  lor 
such  purposes.  I  have  ordered  Lieutenant  Parker  to  command  the 
Beaufort.  I  believe  she  is  at  New  Berne,  subject  to  the  approval  ot 
the  Department.  You  can  keep  Midshipmen  Gardner  and  Gregory 
under  your  command.  I  have  no  chart  that  I  can  rely  upon  to  ascer¬ 
tain  your  exact  position  in  regard  to  defenses  necessary  for  the  different 
points  in  the  immediate  vicinity  of  Eoanoke  Island.  You  will  there¬ 
fore  exercise  your  best  judgment  in  protecting  them,  and  should  you 
require  additional  guns  and  ammunition  to  that  already  furnished,  as 
well  as  the  amount  about  being  sent,  you  will  take  the  earliest  occasion 
to  communicate  with  me  on  the  subject.  I  believe,  from  what  I  can 
learn  from  Lieutenant  Butler,  that  you  could,  with  the  Harmony  alone, 
drive  everything  from  the  sound  in  the  neighborhood  of  Hatteras.  I 
send  projectiles  to  enable  you  to  make  the  attack,  while  at  the  same 
time  a  sufficient  force  can  be  left  to  go  on  with  the  defenses  at  the 
island  of  Eoanoke.  In  the  matter  you  must  of  course  use  a  wise  dis¬ 
cretion.  It  will  be  remembered  that,  although  a  force  of  but  4,500  men 
are  left  by  the  enemy,  the  vessels  badly  crippled,  and  no  guns  on  the 
boats  they  left  inside  the  bar,  they  could  be  easily  whipped.  If  the 
steamer  Curlew  can  be  had  to  mount  the  rifled  gun,  she  should  accom¬ 
pany  you,  and  two  small  guns  mounted  in  the  stern,  to  be  used  in  case 
of  a  retreat. 

Eespectfully, 

F.  Forrest. 

[Commander  T.  T.  Hunter,  C.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  Expedition  to  Inlets  of  North  Carolina.] 

p.  S— The  spiked  guns  should  be  sent  to  Norfolk  by  the  very  first 
conveyance.  You  ask  if  the  approaches  to  Norfolk  by  the  canal  are 
being  fortified.  The  work  is  going  on  rapidly.  The  KakaJiee  I  will

Letter  from  Lieutenant  Minor,  C.  S.  Navy,  to  Lieutenant  Jones,  C.  S, 
Navy,  commanding  Jamestown  battery,  regarding  requisitions. 

Bureau  Ordnance  and  Hydrography, 

Richmond,  September  4,  1861. 

My  Dear.  Sir:  Mr.  Castolor  [Oastelar?],  from  Tredegar,  will  report 
to  you  to-morrow,  and  I  hope  he  may  be  able  to  attend  to  the  vents  of 
the  IX-inch  gun  to  your  satisfaction. 

There  is  some  difficulty  in  procuring  the  steel  taps  for  the  locks,  as 
the  threads  are  not  known  to  be  of  the  same  size  as  those  on  hand  at 
Tredegar.  If  you  will  permit  Castolor  [Castelar?]  to  take  the  measure 
of  the  threads,  or,  which  is  better,  to  bring  up  a  lock  with  him,  it  can 
be  attended  to  very  soon. 

Your  requisition  for  paints,  oils,  etc.,  a  drum  and  fife,  canvas,  and 
other  articles  has  been  ordered,  and  they  will  reach  you  by  the  North¬ 
ampton  on  Friday.  Instead  of  sending  you  fuzes,  we  send  100  VIII- 
inch  shells.  I  have  been  unable  to  see  Mr.  Anderson  yet  about  the 
expense  incurred  for  your  boxes,  etc.,  but  Mr.  Tanner  tells  me  that 
some  charges  were  entered  against  Mr.  Anderson’s  account  for  the

freight  on  them.  He  (Anderson)  has  been  made  a  brigadier-general

mation  received  from  below,  there  may  be  an  expedition  up  the  ii\er

Letter  from  Brigadier- General  Magruder,  C.  S.  Army,  to  Lieutenant 
Jones,  C.  S.Navy,  commanding  at  Jamestown,  regarding  the  obstruction 
of  the  mouth  of  the  Wancick  River. 

Headquarters,  Williamsburg,  September  7,  1861. 
Sir  :  General  Magruder  desires  me  to  state  that  he  is  very  much 
pleased  to  learn  that  the  canal  boats  have  been  sunk  in  the  swash 
channel,  and  desires  you  to  have  the  remainder  of  them  and  such  others 
as  may  come  down  sunk  across  the  mouth  of  the  Warwick  River  with 
the  least  possible  delay.  It  would  be  well  to  have  the  mouth  of  the 
river  sounded  before  sinking  them.  General  Magruder  says  that  Lieu¬ 
tenant  Young,  Virginia  volunteers,  who  resides  at  the  mouth  of  War¬ 
wick  River,  will  be  able  to  show  the  officer  in  charge  of  the  boats  the 
best  locality  for  sinking  them.  The  general  understood  to-day  that  you 
had  taken  charge  of  the  steamer  Towns  for  this  purpose,  and  he  hopes 
that,  with  her  light  draft  of  water  and  experienced  pilot,  there  will  be 
no  difficulty  in  towing  the  boats  into  Warwick  River. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

G.  A.  Magruder, 

Aid-de-Qamp , 


Captain  Jones.

Letter  f  rom  the  governor  of  North  Carolina  to  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy 
of  the  Confederate  States ,  regarding  an  intended  attach  by  the  Federals 
upon  Fori  Macon. 

Raleigh,  September  7, 1861. 

The  British  ship  Alliance ,  at  Beaufort,  communicated  with  a  British 
war  steamer  off  the  port  yesterday,  which  informed  them  that  the  block¬ 
ading  fleet  would  attack  Fort  Macon  to-morrow.  I  hope  the  fort  is 
ready,  but  they  have  no  gunners  who  can  manage  the  guns,  and  the 
same  complaint  is  made  at  Fort  Caswell.  Can  it  be  supplied  with  offi¬ 
cers  who  understand  the  use  of  guns? 

Henry  T.  Clark. 

S.  R.  Mallory, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

North  Carolina ,  to  Brigadier -  General  Huger ,  C.  S.  Army ,  commanding 
at  Norfolk,  regarding  the  holding  of  Roanoke  Island. 

C.  S.  S.  Raleigh, 

Off  Roanoke  Island ,  September  10,  1861. 

General:  As  you  have  doubtless  been  informed  by  the  engineer  of 
the  progress  of  our  works  here,  I  will  confine  myself  to  one  remark. 
It  is  this:  From  all  I  have  seen  and  heard  since  taking  possession  of 
this  island,  I  am  free  to  declare  that  I  regard  the  maintenance  of  this 
position  possible  only  so  long  as  it  is  defended  by  troops  from  another 
State,  or  from  a  more  loyal  part  of  North  Carolina.

Letter  from  Brigadier- General  Magruder,  C.  S.  Army,  to  the  Secretary  of 
the  Navy  of  the  Confederate  States,  regarding  the  Yorktown  battery. 

Department  Headquarters, 
Williamsburg ,  Ya.,  September  11,  1861. 
Sir:  Captain  Henderson  was  detached  from  the  naval  battery  at 
Yorktown  three  or  four  weeks  ago.  I  have  detained  him,  nevertheless, 
until  a  naval  officer  could  be  sent  to  relieve  him.  W  hen  in  Richmond 
ten  days  ago,  I  was  informed  that  Lieutenant  Fauntleroy,  of  tlie  C.  S. 
Navy,  had  been  ordered  to  report  to  me  at  Yorktown  to  All  Captain 
Henderson’s  place.  He  has  not  yet  arrived,  and  I  am  much  in  need  of 
his  services.  About  the  same  time  I  ordered  Major  Randolph  to  report 
to  the  Navy  Department  the  utter  worthlessness  of  the  carriages  in 
this  battery.  He  informed  me  that  the  Navy  Department  had  imme¬ 
diately  ordered  every  barbette  carriage  for  these  guns  (8-inch  colurn- 
biads,  sis  in  number),  and  that  they  would  be  furnished,  probably  one 
a  week.  I  have  not  heard  of  the  arrival  of  any  as  yet.  Pleaso  do  me 
the  favor  to  let  me  know  when  to  expect  them.  They  are  of  the  first 
importance,  indeed,  and  absolutely  essential  to  the  successful  defense 
of  the  mouth  of  York  River.  Please  address  me  at  Yorktown. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  B.  Magruder, 
Brigadier- General,  Commanding. 

Hon.  S.  R.  Mallory, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  C.  S.

General  report  of  Flag-Officer  Lynch ,  G.  S.  Navy.  commanding  naval 
defenses  of  Virginia  and  North  Carolina. 

New  Berne,  N.  C.,  September  12 ,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  Colonel  Bridgers  having  requested 
me  to  be  present  with  the  officers  under  my  command,  I  repaired  to  the 
fort  with  two  of  them,  having  first  come  to  this  place  to  consult  with 
General  Gatlin,  and  returned  with  him,  his  staff,  and  800  men  to  sup¬ 
port  the  regiment  stationed  on  the  coast  about  G  miles  south  of  the 
fort. 

In  consequence  of  traveling  by  night,  I  made  an  error  in  the  compu¬ 
tation  of  time  and  dated  my  last  but  one  preceding  letter  the  11th 
instead  of  the  10th. 

On  Sunday  morning  there  was  only  one  large  steamer  in  sight,  and  I 
directed  Commander  Sinclair  to  proceed  to  Norfolk  for  a  rifled  gun, 
reconnoitering  as  he  passdfl  Hatteras  Inlet  and  touching  at  Roanoke 
Island,  with  conditional  instructions  to  remain  there  if  his  services  were 
required,  and  Commander  Muse  was  directed  to  proceed  with  the 
steamer  Ellis  to  the  mouth  of  the  Pamlico  River  and  keep  a  vigilant 
watch  for  the  enemy. 

On  Sunday  night  the  ship  off  the  port  again  interchanged  signals  with 
others  further  in  the  offing,  but  the  next  morning  the  ship  at  anchor 
was  alone  visible.  This  satisfied  me  that  a  strict  blockade  was  being 
kept,  either  to  prevent  the  escape  of  the  British  ship  Alliance ,  loading 
with  naval  stores,  or  to  intercept  the  expected  steamer  with  a  cargo  of 
ordnance  stores. 

On  Monday  night  no  signals  were  seen,  and  on  Tuesday  night  the 
large  steamer  moved  off  and  was  replaced  by  a  smaller  one,  resembling 
the  Daylight. 

Being  now  persuaded  that  no  attack  was  in  contemplation,  and  as  an 
ordnance  officer  had  arrived  at  the  fort,  I  took  my  departure  with  the 
officers.  Last  night  I  sent  Lieutenant  Commanding  Parker  with  the 
Beaufort  to  the  mouth  of  the  Neuse  River,  with  similar  instructions  to 
those  given  to  Commander  Muse. 

On  the  bar  about  5  miles  below  this  town  a  line  of  vessels  is  sunk 
across  the  river,  leaving  only  a  narrow  passage,  which  can  be  speedily 
blocked  up. 

In  similar  manner  on  the  Pamlico,  below  the  town  of  Washington, 
strong  piles  are  driven  across,  leaving  also  a  narrow  and  easily  closed 
passage. 

Abreast  of  and  immediately  above  these  barricades  on  each  river  are 
two  efficient  batteries;  on  this  river,  one  of  eight  heavy  32s  and  [one] 
of  six  of  the  same  caliber,  but  lighter  metal.  On  the  Pamlico  are  two  of 
four  32s  each,  which  General  Gatlin  considers  sufficient. 

The  commanders  of  the  Ellis  and  the  Beaufort  are  directed,  on  the 
first  approach  of  the  enemy  in  force,  to  come  up  the  rivers,  giving 
information  to  the  military  commandant  and  taking  position  at  the  bar¬ 
riers  to  aid  in  the  defense. 

Pinding  among  Commodore  Barron’s  papers  a  telegram  from  you 
directing  him  to  take  charge  of  the  steamer  Uncle  Ben ,  and  it  being 
represented  to  me  that  the  citizens  of  Wilmington  are  complaining  bit¬ 
terly  because  of  her  not  being  fitted  out,  and  General  Gatlin  expressing 
an  earnest  desire  to  turn  her  over  to  the  Confederate  service  for  the 
purpose  of  aiding  in  the  defense  of  the  Gape  Fear,  I  have  determined  to 
take  preparatory  measures  until  your  pleasure  can  be  known. 

Under  your  authority  to  purchase  the  cargo  of  coal  at  Beaufort,  I 
send  Lieutenant  Commanding  Murphy  to  Charleston  for  that  purpose, 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


727 


with  instructions  as  soon  as  the  purchase  is  effected  to  proceed  to  Wil¬ 
mington  and  with  Carpenter  Ed.  Williams,  who  has  been  ordered  to 
report  to  him,  together  with  a  competent  engineer,  to  survey  the  Uncle 
Ben  and  the  Arctic  and  report  to  me  their  condition. 

I  have  included  the  latter  vessel  in  the  survey,  as  from  all  I  can 
learn  she  is  admirably  fitted  for  a  floating  battery  if  her  machinery  be 
not  worthy  of  transportation.  The  latter  lies  at  Norfolk. 

But  for  the  anticipated  attack  upon  and  the  inexperience  of  the  gar¬ 
rison  of  Fort  Macon,  I  would  long  since  have  been  at  Roanoke  Island, 
which  is  the  back  door  to  Norfolk;  but  I  knew  that  men  and  guns  bad 
been  taken  there  and  that  it  was  not  remote  from  the  control  of  high 
military  capacity;  while  here,  with  so  much  at  stake,  the  capacity  for 
defense  was  questionable. 

I  felt,  too,  that  the  disaster  would  be  overwhelming  and  the  disgrace 
irretrievable  if  it  fell  into  the  hands  of  the  enemy. 

Now  it  mounts  upward  of  40  guns  (one  rifled),  and  is  impregnable. 

Paymaster  De  Bree  arrived  last  night.  I  leave  this  morning  for  Nor¬ 
folk  and  Roanoke  Island. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  etc.,  W.  F.  Lynch, 

Flag-  Officer. 

Hon.  S.  R.  Mallory, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Letter  from  Lieutenant  Minor,  C.  S.  Wavy,  to  Lieutenant  Jones,  C.  S. 

Navy,  commanding  Jamestown  battery,  on  general  matters  relating  to 

the  C.  S.  Navy. 

Bureau  Ordnance  and  Hydrography, 

September  14,  1861. 

My  Dear  Sir:  I  wrote  rather  hurriedly  yesterday,  and  did  not  have 
time  to  “say  my  say.” 

I  saw  Gorgas  about  the  saddles.  Someone  had  drawn  a  pen  across 
that  item  in  your  requisition,  but  on  explaining  to  him  your  wants  he 
directed  them  to  be  supplied,  and  I  hope  you  will  receive  them  by  the 
next  trip  of  the  Northampton.  No  martingales  are  allowed. 

De  Bree  is  at  present  on  a  visit  to  North  Carolina,  but  will  return  in 
a  few  days.  If  you  will  address  a  letter  to  him  he  will  no  doubt  attend 
to  your  pecuniary  affairs  with  promptness,  for  he  is  one  of  the  most 
accommodating  paymasters  I  have  ever  been  associated  with.  No 
detail  yet  for  the  Merrimack.  I  hope  to  be  one  of  her  lieutenants,  and 
I  need  not  say  how  pleased  I  would  be  to  serve  with  you.  Brooke,  too, 
will  join  her,  I  suppose.  He  is  an  indefatigable  fellow,  and  works  with 
heart  and  head  for  our  glorious  cause. 

Your  letter,  or  that  part  of  it  at  least  referring  to  the  Curtis  Peck  and 
Schultz,  has  worked  its  way  all  right  with  the  officials  here.  I  read  it 
to  Ingraham,  and  this  morning  to  the  Secretary,  who  expressed  a  wish 
that  Walker,  Secretary  of  War,  should  know  its  contents,  and  when  I 
read  it  to  him  arid  Mr.  Benjamin  at  the  same  time  he  thanked  me  for 
the  information,  and  will  no  doubt  act  upon  it  by  arming  the  two  boats, 
as  I  suggested.  Captain  Wood,  of  the  Quartermaster’s  Department, 
will  refer  it  also  to  headquarters,  and  the  result  will  be  that  the  North¬ 
ampton  will  be  armed  also.  General  Lee  will  soon  have  a  fight  in 
western  Virginia,  as  a  general  order  of  his  just  issued  says  the  march 
of  his  army  “must  be  onward.”  The  telegram  about  Floyd’s  defeat  is 
not  credited  here,  as  it  comes  from  Northern  sources,  and  reads  like 
a  lie. 

Farrand  has  the  Evansport  battery,  and  in  ten  days,  if  the  roads 
remain  passable,  the  Potomac  will  be  closed  to  the  enemy.  He  is  to 
have  15  guns,  and  the  battery  is  to  be  supported  by  a  large  force  of 
infantry.  Ingraham  is  absent  for  a  few  days.  Please  have  the  hun¬ 
dred  VIILinch  solid  shot  (landed  by  mistake  at  Jamestown  Island)  sent 
to  the  Grove’s  Landing  for  batteries  at  Williamsburg  immediately,  if 
you  have  not  already  done  so,  as  transportation  was  provided  for  them 
to  that  point,  and  Hicks  or  his  mate  blundered  in  landing  them  for  you 
when  they  were  intended  for  General  Magruder.

Letter  from  the  Inspector  of  Ordnance ,  navy  yard ,  Norfolk,  to  Brigadier- 
General  Eager,  C.  S.  Army,  commanding  at  Norfolk,  regarding  the 
removal  of  guns. 

Ordnance  Department,  Gosport  Navy  Yard, 

Norfolk,  Va.,  September  16,  1861. 

General:  1  am  directed  by  the  commandant  to  apprise  you  that 
already  15  of  the  guns  laid  aside  for  the  defenses  of  Norfolk  and  its 
vicinity,  on  the  requisition  of  the  engineer,  approved  by  yourself,  have 
been  otherwise  disposed  of  by  the  Bureau  of  Ordnance  and  Hydrog¬ 
raphy,  and  to  suggest  the  propriety  of  the  speedy  removal  of  the 
remainder  to  the  custody  of  your  own  ordnance  officers.  The  comman¬ 
dant  also  recommends  the  garrisoning  of  the  outworks  for  the  defense 
of  this  yard  between  Paradise  and  Scotch  creeks  previous  to  and  pre¬ 
paratory  to  laying  the  platforms  and  mounting  the  guns,  which  would 
not  be  safe  without  a  guard.  There  is  as  yet  but  one  magazine  among 
them  all.  Some  definite  understanding  between  the  engineer  and 
myself  as  to  the  kind  of  carriages  to  be  used  there  is  desirable.  Your 
12  last  2I-pounder  shells  from  Eichmond  will  be  ready  to-day  with 
navy  fuzes. 

Bespectfully,  etc., 

A.  B.  Fairfax, 
Inspector  of  Ordnance. 

Brigadier-General  Huger. 


Letter  from  Flag-Officer  Lynch,  C.  S.  Navy,  commanding  naval  defenses 
of  North  Carolina  and  Virginia,  to  Brigadier-General  Huger,  C.  S. 
Army,  commanding  at  Norfolk,  making  suggestions  regarding  army 
cooperation  in  the  defense  of  Roanoke  Island. 

Flagship  Manassas, 

Off  Roanoke  Island,  September  17, 1861. 

General:  So  great  is  the  breadth  of  Croatau  Sound,  with  a  channel 
of  G  feet  near  the  mainland,  3  miles  distant,  that  I  am  reluctantly 
forced  to  the  conclusion  that  but  little  dependence  can  be  placed  upon 
land  batteries  for  its  defense.  After  a  careful  reconnoissance,  I  am  per¬ 
suaded  that  the  defense  of  this  sound  must  be  made  at  the  marshes,  7 
miles  below,  with  floating  batteries  and  gunboats,  there  being  no  soil 
wherewith  to  construct  redoubts.  But,  general,  if  my  information  be 
correct,  there  is  another  point  demanding  immediate  and  serious 

consideration.  . ,  , ,  „ 

The  fortification  at  Oregon  Inlet,  being  on  the  south  side  thereof, 
was  of  course  untenable  with  Forts  Hatteras  and  Clark  in  the  posses¬ 
sion  of  the  enemy ;  but  if,  as  pilots  represent  to  me,  a  fleet  outside  can 
sail  within  a  mile  of  the  beach,  thus  covering  an  advancing  force 
toward  Norfolk,  it  seems  to  me  important  that  the  northern  side  of  the 
inlet  be  fortified,  with  a  strong  sustaining  force  at  hand,  and  the  troops 


730 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


upon  this  island  be  held  in  constant  readiness  to  be  conveyed  across 
Roanoke  Sound,  to  reenforce  the  former. 

I  respectfully  suggest,  if  the  information  I  have  received  be  con¬ 
firmed  by  experienced  pilots,  that  you  send  an  officer,  in  whose  judg¬ 
ment  you  confide,  to  accompany  me  to  the  inlet. 

Before  this,  I  would  have  made  a  recon noissance  of  that  locality,  but 
that  I  had  not  a  vessel  of  sufficiently  light  draft  at  my  command. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  etc., 

W.  P.  Lynch, 

Flag-Officer,  Comdg.  Naval  Defenses  N.  C.  and  Va.

Letter  from  Brigadier-General  Huger,  C.  S.  Army,  commanding  at  Nor¬ 
folk,  Va.,  to  Flag-Officer  Lynch ,  C.  S.  Navy,  commanding  naval  defenses 
of  North  Carolina  and  Virginia,  acknowledging  suggestions  regarding 
the  defense  of  Roanoke  Island. 


Headquarters  of  the  Forces, 

Norfolk,  September  18,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  received  your  letter  of  the  17th  instant,  and  am  obliged  for 
the  suggestions.  As  Colonel  Custis  Lee,  aid-de-camp  to  the  President, 
has  been  to  Roanoke  Island  especially  to  examine  it  and  the  defenses, 
and  I  hope  to  see  him  to-morrow,  I  will  defer  immediate  action  until  I 
consult  with  him.  It  does  not  appear  to  me  possible  for  any  large  body 
of  men  to  advance  on  Norfolk  by  the  sand  spit  along  the  coast. 

I  remain,  very  respectfully, 

Benj.  Huger,

Letter  from  Brigadier -General  Magruder,  G.  S.  Army,  to  the  Chief  of 
Bureau  of  Ordnance  and  Hydrography,  urging  the  placing  of  additional 
guns  in  the  battery  at  Yorktown. 

Department  Headquarters, 
Williamsburg,  Va.,  September  19,  1861. 
Sir:  Several  weeks  ago  Captain  Henderson  was  detached  from  the 
Yorktown  naval  battery,  but  no  officer  ordered  in  his  place.  I  applied 
to  the  Navy  Department  for  an  officer,  and  was  informed  that  Com¬ 
mander  Fauntleroy  had  been  ordered  to  repair  to  Yorktown  in  his 
place.  He  has  not  arrived.  I  have  since  written  once  or  twice  on  the 
subject,  but  have  received  no  answer.  As  Yorktown  is  perhaps  the 
most  important  point  on  the  coast  at  which  there  is  a  naval  battery,  I 
beg  that  this  may  be  attended  to  as  soon  as  possible. 

The  heaviest  ships  can  be  brought  against  naval  batteries  at  the 
mouth  of  York  River,  and  in  great  numbers.  It  is  obvious,  therefore, 
that  the  heaviest  guns  should  be  placed  there.  This  subject  has  been 
again  brought  to  my  notice  by  Colonel  G.  W.  Randolph,  Chief  of 
Ordnance,  an  officer  in  whose  judgment  I  place  great  confidence.  He 
says  in  a  letter  just  received: 

If  the  expedition  fitting  out  at  Washington  should  come  here  and  bring  with  it  a 
large  number  of  10  and  11  inch  Dahlgren  guns  the  odds  against  us  would  he  very 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


731 


great.  Should  our  batteries  he  silenced,  the  fleet  may  pass  up  and  land  troops  at 
defenseless  points,  and  either  take  the  James  River  batteries  and  the  fortified  lines 
of  the  peninsula  in  reverse  or  march  on  Richmond,  passing  by  them.  Guns  of  equal 
caliber  are  necessary  to  put  us  on  an  equal  footing  with  the  enemy. 

I  concur  fully  in  this  opinion,  aud  would  respectfully  recommend 
that  six  of  the  long  32-pounder  rilled  guns,  said  to  be  now  in  Rich¬ 
mond,  be  placed  in  battery  at  this  point,  or  that  six  of  the  10  and  11 
inch  Dahlgren  guns  be  sent  if  possible.  I  would  also  report  that  I 
fired  two  shots  from  the  8-inch  columbiad  at  Spratley’s  farm,  opposite 
Hog  Island,  on  James  River,  with  15-second  fuzes  and  charges  of  8 
pounds,  giving  the  gun  the  highest  elevation  which  its  casemate  car¬ 
riage  would  admit.  The  river  is  about  If  miles  wide,  and  the  shells 
fell  short  of  the  other  side  and  exploded  in  the  water,  showing  that 
the  charges  were  too  small.  The  carriage,  however,  was  a  good  deal 
injured  even  by  these  small  charges,  and  if  the  charges  were  increased 
to  10  pounds  it  would  be  shattered  after  a  few  rounds.  This  carriage 
is — like  that  on  which  similar  guns  are  mounted  in  the  naval  battery 
at  Yorktown — almost  entirely  worthless.  The  columbiads  at  James¬ 
town  are  mounted  on  equally  unreliable  carriages.  I  indulge  a  hope, 
however,  from  the  last  letter  received  from  the  Navy  Department,  that 
the  columbiads  at  Yorktown  will  soon  be  mounted  on  army  barbette 
carriages,  after  which  I  recommend  that  those  on  James  River  be  so 
mounted  with  the  least  possible  delay.  I  beg  leave  to  ask  the  atten¬ 
tion  of  the  Navy  Department  to  the  immediate  necessity  of  placing  in 
battery  at  Yorktown  the  32-pounder  rilled  guns  mentioned  in  the 
above. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  Bankhead  Magruder, 
Brigadier-  General ,  Commanding. 

Captain  Lynch, 

Chief  of  Bureau  of  Ordnance. 


Letter  from  Lieutenant  Minor,  C.  S.  Navy,  to  Lieutenant  Jones, C.  8.  Navy, 
commanding  Jamestown  battery,  referring  to  the  C.  8.  S.Virginia  (Mer¬ 
rimack)  and  the  arrival  from  England  of  munitions  of  war. 

Bureau  Ordnance  and  Hydrography, 

September  20,  1861. 

My  Dear  Sir  :  Brooke  and  I  have  read  your  letter  with  suggestions 
for  the  armament  of  the  Merrimack,  and  as  you  say  heavy  guns  are  to  be 
mounted,  but  not  one  of  X-inch  but  rather  of  IX-inch,  the  heaviest  to 
be  cast  of  this  caliber,  say  14,000  pounds.  Buchanan  will  probably  be 
her  captain,  and  I  hope  you  will  be  her  first  lieutenant.  I  am  over¬ 
whelmed  with  duty,  some  of  it,  too,  not  mine,  and  as  rilled  guns  and 
projectiles  are  all  the  go,  I  am  kept  hard  at  work  preparing  them  for 
service.  A  steamer  from  England  has  come  into  Savannah  with  pow¬ 
der  (thank  God!),  blankets,  and  munitions  of  war.  North,  who  is  in 
England,  had  a  hand  in  it,  I  believe.  I  hope  this  supply  will  not  make 
the  people  in  power  here  relax  their  efforts  to  make  a  supply  for  our¬ 
selves.  I  am  glad  to  say  that  our  prospects  for  a  plenty  of  this  muni¬ 
tion  are  improving,  and  on  yesterday  I  had  the  pleasure  of  obtaining  a 
quantity  of  saltpeter  and  sulphur  for  a  mill  at  Raleigh.  Good  news,  is 
it  not?  and  I  confess  that  my  breath  comes  easier  now  than  it  did 
when  our  prospects  were  so  blue.  Officers  are  being  sent  off  to  New 
Orleans  for  defenses  there,  and  it  seems  to  be  the  opinion  now  that 
Fernandina  will  soon  be  attacked.

Letter  from  the  commandant  navy  yard,  Norfolk,  to  Flag-Officer  Lynch, 
C.  S.  Navy,  commanding  naval  defenses  of  North  Carolina  and,  Virginia, 
regarding  the  preparation  of  the  C.  S.  S.  Curlew,  and  other  matters. 

Navy  Yard,  Gosport  [Norfolk],  September  23,  1861. 
Sir  :  I  wrote  you  by  the  captain  of  the  Currituck  a  very  hasty  note, 
and  sent  you  some  provisions  and  other  articles  you  mentioned  as  being 
necessary  for  your  squadron.  I  am  sorry  I  was  unable  to  send  you 
bread,  but  by  this  conveyance  have  directed  3  barrels  to  be  sent. 

I  have  received  your  letter  to-day  from  Edenton.  I  am  glad  to  hear 
that  the  Curlew  is  nearly  ready  for  service.  Most  of  your  boats,  I 
believe,  burn  wood,  but  at  your  desire  I  send  you  6  tons  anthracite 
coal.  This  will,  no  doubt,  be  sufficient  until  you  receive  that  which

733 


was  purchased  by  Lieutenant  Murphy  for  your  use.  I  am  now  busily 
engaged  fitting  out  the  large  barge  you  sent  here.  You  have  four 
rilled  guns,  one  of  which  you  will  have  to  put  on  the  Curlew ,  as  the 
demand  for  rifled  guns  is  so  great  that  we  can  not  supply  them  fast 
enough.  We  have  just  sent  those  that  were  ready  to  New  Orleans. 
Y"our  requisition  for  two  32-pounders  of  61  hundredweight,  with  car¬ 
riages,  etc.,  with  the  other  articles  mentioned,  will  be  sent  to  you.  I 
am  very  glad  to  find  that  you  have  made  a  discovery,  the  information 
of  which  the  pilots  could  not  afford  you  in  relation  to  the  depth  of  the 
water  east  of  the  channel.  I  suppose  you  will  have  it  all  shipped  out 
to  enable  you  to  take  advantage  of  it. 

You  mention  having  sent  a  requisition  for  stationery.  It  has  not 
reached  me.  I  will,  however,  send  some  to  you.  I  am  clearly  of  the 
opinion  that  the  lieutenants  of  the  Navy  should  be  detached  from  some 
of  the  batteries  and  placed  upon  their  appropriate  duty.  You  certaiuly 
ought  to  have  the  benefit  of  their  services,  while  commanders  should 
also  be  designated  for  such  positions  as  their  rank  entitles  them  to. 
These  matters  are  being  entirely  overlooked  or  neglected  at  Richmond.

did  not  design  to  part  with  her  longer  than  a  day  or  two  at  furthest 
when  she  left  here. 

I  am,  truly,  yours, 

F.  Forrest,

Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  of  the  Confederate  States  to  the 
Secretary  of  War  of  the  'Confederate  States,  transmitting  suggestions 
regarding  the  river  batteries  in  Virginia. 

0.  S.  Navy  Department, 
Richmond,  Va.,  September  26,  1861. 

Dear  Sir:  The  enclosed  letter  was  this  day  handed  to  me  by 
the  officer  in  charge  of  orders  and  detail  of  this  Department,  Captain 


734  NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

\L 

Buchanan.  I  find  a  decided  impression  prevailing  in  circles  informed 
upon  the  condition  of  the  river  batteries  in  Virginia  that  they  are  less 
efficient  than  they  might  be  made  by  certain  changes,  and  Captain 
Buchanan’s  suggestions  are  therefore  worthy  of  consideration.  Per¬ 
haps  an  assignment  of  the  James  River  batteries,  especially  to  naval 
officers,  who  are  all  more  or  less  tamiliar  with  this  particular  river,  in 
the  manner  he  speaks  of  might  result  advantageously,  and  I  desire  to 
say  that  I  will  be  very  glad  to  adopt  this  or  any  similar  measure  which 
may  conduce  to  the  greater  security  of  the  river. 

I  am  informed  that  there  are  no  naval  officers  at  the  extensive  and 
important  works  on  Craney  Island. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  R.  Mallory, 
Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

Hon.  Secretary  of  War. 

[Enclosure.] 

Office  of  Orders  and  Detail, 

Navy  Department,  C.  S.,  Richmond ,  Va.,  September  26,  1861. 

Sir:  Under  the  present  arrangement  the  batteries  in  the  neighbor¬ 
hood  of  Norfolk  and  on  the  various  rivers  in  which  are  mounted  naval 
guns,  and  many  of  which  are  commanded  by  naval  officers,  are  not  as 
efficient  as  they  ought  to  be.  Several  of  these  batteries  are  under  the 
orders  and  control  of  the  Army  and  no  naval  officers  attached  to  them, 
and  others  are  commanded  by  naval  officers,  but  the  men  are  not 
placed  under  the  control  of  those  officers,  consequently  the  efficiency  of 
the  batteries  is  impaired.  Soldiers  should  be  detailed  for  duty  in  those 
batteries  and  placed  under  the  exclusive  orders  of  the  naval  officers, 
and  their  removal  subject  only  to  the  orders  of  the  commanding  general 
of  the  division  in  which  they  are  placed.  The  company  officers  should 
be  present  at  the  exercises  of  the  guns,  so  as  to  enable  them  to  succeed 
the  naval  officer  in  the  event  of  death,  and  they  should  drill  their  men 
daily  at  the  small  arms  and  assist  the  naval  officers  in  the  general 
police  duties  of  the  batteries.  Under  this  system  discipline,  efficiency, 
and  harmony  will  be  obtained,  and  the  batteries  rendered  much  more 
serviceable  to  the  country  than  they  now  are. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Pranklin  Buchanan, 

Captain ,  in  Charge. 

Hon.  S.  R.  Mallory, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Richmond,  Va.

route  to  Mexico  believed  impracticable  from  delay.  Steamer  Gordon 
now  chartered  by  Government  at  two  hundred  a  day  for  harbor  serv¬ 
ices;  light  draft;  strengthening  for  carrying  cannon  and  been  in  use 
as  a  privateer ;  a  good  seaboat;  tonnage  upward  of  500  tons;  can  go 
at  any  time  and  by  any  route  to  Nassau  or  Havana.  Offered  at  $62,000 
or  chartered  to  either  port  at  $10,000  for  the  trip;  owners  to  pay  all 
expenses;  Government  to  pay  value  if  captured.  Will  be  very  useful 
for  coast  defense.  We  will  go  at  once  in  her  if  authorized,  and  think 
the  charter  price  may  be  reduced  one-half.  'One  or  more  naval  officers 
to  go  in  her,  as  may  be  ordered. 

John  Slidell. 

J.  M.  Mason. 

Hon.  E.  M.  T.  Hunter,

October  4,  1861. 

Colonel:  I  have  just  received  yours  of  this  date,  conveying  Gen¬ 
eral  Magruder’s  order  to  send  a  naval  officer  to  Williamsburg  to  teach

intervals  of  my  duties  here,  give  the  necessary  instruction.

[Telegram.] 

Charleston,  October  12, 186[1]. 

Our  friends  left  here  last  night  at  1  o’clock.  A  fast  steamer,  good, 
officers,  and  very  dark  night,  with  heavy  rain.  The  guard  boat  reported 
that  they  crossed  the  bar  about  2  o’clock,  and  that  they  could  neither 
have  been  seen  nor  heard  by  the  fleet.  A  strong  northwest  wind  helped 
them,  and  the  fleet  this  morning  seems  not  to  have  changed  position 
at  all.  As  soon  as  we  hear  further  I  will  telegraph.  The  steamer 
ought  to  be  back  in  about  a  week,  and  nothing  said  until  her  return. 
Communicate  to  Mrs.  Mason. 

Wm.  Henry  Trescott. 

Hon.  E.  M.  T.  Hunter.
