tlie  pile  driver  and  schooner  with  it  and  placed  them  in  position,  then 
resumed  our  position  in  line.  At  8  p.  m.  steamer  Roanoke  arrived. 

January  9. — At  9  a.  m.  steamer  Raleigh  got  underway  and  stood  up 
the  sound;  soon  returned,  in  company  with  the  Powhatan.  At  10 
a.  m.  Commodore  Lynch  came  on  board  and  inspected  the  vessel;  had 
the  cotton  removed  from  the  boiler  so  as  to  heat  the  berth  deck. 
Received  six  charges  of  powder.  The  Raleigh  employed  in  towing 
vessel  to  be  sunk  in  the  channel  up  to  the  battery  to  be  filled  with 
sand.  At  5: 10  p.  m.  she  returned  to  her  position. 

January  10. — At  10  a.  m.  the  Cora  arrived  from  New  Berne  and  went 
alongside  the  flagship.  At  3  p.  m.  the  Powhatan  came  alongside  and 
gave  us  some  cable  for  ballast,  by  order  of  Commodore  Lynch.  At 
3:30  p.  m.  went  down  and  anchored  a  little  above  the  lower  battery 
E.  by  S.  from  the  Raleigh.  Fleet  in  position  at  that  place.  Sent  four 
men  ashore  to-day  to  assist  in  loading  a  schooner  with  piles.  At  5 
p.  m.  the  Cora  left  for  Elizabeth  City,  carrying  the  mail  with  her. 

January  11.  — At  9  a.  m.  C.  S.  S.  Raleigh  went  up  to  Weir’s  Point 
battery  to  tow  schooner  in  the  channel.  At  1:20  p.  m.  the  flagship 
left  her  anchorage  and  went  down  the  sound.  At  4  p.  m.  sent  a  boat 
on  board  the  schooner  Hawley  for  the  mail  from  Elizabeth  City.  At  8 
p.  m.  the  flagship  returned  to  her  anchorage. 

January  12. — At  10  a.  in.  the  Powhatan  left  for  Elizabeth  City.  At 
1  p.  m.  the  Curlew  went  down  the  sound;  the  Cora  returned  from  Eliz¬ 
abeth  City.  At  7  p.  m.  the  Curleio  returned  to  her  position. 

January  13. — At  8  a.  m.  the  Raleigh  went  up  the  sound  with  schooner 
in  tow.  Sea  Bird  employed  in  sinking  vessels.  Got  underway  and 
went  alongside  the  Manassas ;  took  her  in  tow  and  went  alongside  the 
barge.  Took  the  works  of  the  Leonora  and  put  them  on  the  barge. 
Blowing  very  hard  from  the  northward  and  eastward.  At  4  p.  m. 
returned  to  our  position. 

January  14. — At  3  p.  m.  schooner  Hawley  came  in  from  Elizabeth  City 
and  anchored. 

January  15. — At  8  a.  m.  Sea  Bird  and  Curlew  got  underway  and  went 
alongside  the  wood  schooner.  At  8: 20  went  alongside  and  took  the 
Manassas  in  tow  and  went  over  to  the  floating  battery.  At  2  p.  m.  the 
Raleigh  returned  from  Currituck.  At  4  p.  m.  returned  to  our  position, 
not  being  able  to  discover  the  gun. 

January  16. — At  9  a.  m.  got  underway  with  the  Raleigh  and  went 
down  to  Spencer’s  Creek  to  reconnoiter;  not  discovering  any  traces  of 
the  enemy,  returned  and  anchored  in  position  at  5 : 40  p.  m.  At  6  p.  in. 
steamer  Wilson  arrived  from  Norfolk. 

January  17. — At  8  a.  m.  got  underway;  employed  in  sinking  schoon¬ 
ers  at  the  barricade. 

January  18. — At  9  a.  m.  got  underway  and  went  up  to  Little  Alliga¬ 
tor  River  to  tow  the  Manassas  down.  At  3: 50  p.  m.  returned  and  took 
the  Curlew  up  to  her  position ;  then  anchored.  The  C.  S.  steamers  Fanny 
and  Beaufort  arrived  from  Beaufort. 

January  19. — At  3  p.  m.  went  alongside  the  Cora  and  placed  Nathan 
Walker,  seaman,  on  board  to  send  him  home.  Then  went  to  the  upper 
battery;  took  schooner  A.  C.  Williams  down  and  sank  her  at  the  barri¬ 
cade.  At  8  p.  m.  returned  to  our  position.  George  S.  Allen,  captain’s 
clerk,  resigned  and  left  the  ship. 

January  20. — At  10  a.  m.  Sea  Bird  and  Raleigh  went  down  the  sound. 
At  2  p.  m.  got  underway  and  went  up  to  the  upper  battery  with  two 
schooners  in  tow ;  then  took  one  down  to  the  barricade  and  sank  her — 
the  Josephine ;  then  returned  to  our  anchorage.

January  21. — At  8  a.  m.  took  a  schooner  up  to  the  upper  battery; 
then  went  down  to  the  barricade  and  chained  several  vessels  together. 
At  2  p.  m.  returned  and  took  the  schooner  Carter  down  and  sank  her.  At 
6:50p.  m.  returned  to  our  position.  Flagship  Sea  Bird  and  Raleigh 
returned  from  the  sound. 

January  22. — At  8  a.  m.  left  for  Elizabeth  City;  arrived  there  at  6 
p.  in. ;  filled  our  tanks  with  water.  At  8  p.  m.  left  for  Roanoke,  but 
came  into  Pasquotank  River. 

January  23.— At  8  a.  m.  left  for  Roanoke;  arrived  at  10 : 50  a.  m.  and 
came  to  anchor. 

January  25.— At  1 : 50  p.  m.  the  Hawley  arrived  from  Elizabeth  City. 
The  C.  S.  S.  Curlew  left  for  Elizabeth  City  at  4  p.  in. 

January  26—  At  8  a.  m.  went  to  the  barricade  and  sunk  the  schooner 
Spuell  and  Moss.  The  Cora  arrived  from  Norfolk.  At  10  a.  m.  the  Cur¬ 
lew  arrived  with  three  schooners  in  tow.  At  12  noon  took  a  schooner 
up  to  Weir’s  Point  battery  to  be  filled  with  sand.  At  4  p.  in.  carried 
some  troops  over  to  the  floating  battery;  then  returned  and  took  a 
schooner  in  to  the  battery  and  anchored  her;  then  took  a  schooner 
down  to  the  barricade  and  anchored  her  ready  to  scuttle.  At  8  p.  m. 
returned  to  our  position  and  anchored.  Captain’s  clerk,  George  Bag- 
ley,  reported  for  duty.  Received  on  board  three  supernumeraries  from 
the  Eighth  North  Carolina  Regiment. 

January  27. — At  8  a.  m.  got  underway  and  went  over  to  the  barricade 
and  sunk  the  schooner  Zenith ;  then  returned  and  went  up  to  the 
Manassas  for  wood;  returned  and  anchored  in  position.  At  4:30  p.  m. 
the  Curlew  left  for  Elizabeth  City.  The  Cora  went  down  to  the  marshes. 

January  28. — At  8  a.  m.  the  Cora  came  up  from  the  marshes;  no 
signs  of  the  enemy.  At  9  the  Curlew  arrived  from  Elizabeth  City  with 
two  schooners  in  tow.  At  10  a.  m.  went  over  to  the  barricade  and 
hauled  the  Rio  in  position ;  then  went  alongside  a  schooner  and  took 
her  alongside  the  Rio  and  put  some  ballast  in  her  to  sink  her;  then 
towed  the  same  schooner  to  Weir’s  Point  battery  to  be  filled  with  sand. 
At  3 : 40  p.  m.  the  Roanohe  arrived.  About  4  p.  m.  went  down  to  the 
barricade  and  towed  the  pile  driver  from  her  former  position  to  one 
about  the  center  of  the  sunken  vessels.  At  6  p.  m.  returned  to  our 
position  and  anchored. 

January  29. — At  8  p.  m.  the  Curlew  arrived  from  Elizabeth  City  with 
three  schooners  in  tow.  At  9  a.  m.  exercised  the  men  at  the  gun.  At 
10  a.  m.  went  up  to  the  Weir’s  Point  battery  and  took  the  schooner 
Tripleet  in  tow  and  sunk  her  at  the  barricade.  At  2  p.  m.  received  a 
howitzer  and  8  boxes  of  ammunition  from  Lieutenant  Simms.  At  3  p. 
m.  went  up  to  the  battery  and  anchored.  At  4:30  p.  m.  went  down  to 
the  fleet;  went  alongside  the  flagship  and  took  anew  schooner  and 
anchored  her;  then  returned  to  our  position. 

January  30. — At  8  a.  m.  the  Raleigh  employed  in  towing  schooners. 
At  8:20  a.  m.  the  Cora  came  up  from  the  marshes;  schooner  Hawley 
arrived  from  Elizabeth  City.  The  Cora  on  the  other  side  engaged  in 
making  soundings.  At  5  p.  m.  the  Cornet  went  up  to  Elizabeth  City. 
At  3  p.  m.  the  Raleigh  anchored  in  position.  At  7  p.  m.  the  Appomattox 
arrived. 

January  31. — At  8  a.  m.  got  underway  and  went  up  to  WeiPs  Point 
battery ;  took  the  schooner  Southern  Star  in  tow  and  carried  her  down 
and  put  ballast  in  her  from  the  new  schooner.  The  Raleigh  employed 
in  sinking  schooners  at  the  barricade.  At  11  a.  m.  the  Beaufort  came 
alongside  and  filled  her  tanks  with  water.  At  1  p.  in.  the  flagship  and

Appomattox  went  down  tlie  sound;  the  other  vessels  returned  to  their

February  1. — At  9  a.  m.  the  Appomattox  left  for  Elizabeth  City.  At

anchored  her  ahead  of  the  Manassas.  Men  of  the  Curlew  employed  in

February  2. — At  8  a.  m.  the  Appomattox  returned  from  Elizabeth  City

p.  m.  the  Appomattox  went  up  the  sound;  the  Curlew  returned  to  her 
position. 

February  3. — At  8  a.  m.  the  Appomattox  returned  with  a  schooner  in

position. 

February  4. — At  8  a.  m.  the  Raleigh  went  alongside  the  wood  schooner. 
At  9  a.  m.  the  Curlew  arrived  from  Edenton  with  a  schooner  in  tow. 
At  10  a.  m.  the  Rebel  arrived  from  Norfolk.  At  2 : 30  p.  m.  the  Sea  Bird 
went  alongside  the  wood  schooner. 

February  5. — At  8  a.  m.  the  Cora  left  for  Edenton.  At  8  a.  m.  the 
Rebel  left  for  Norfolk.  At  9  a.  m.  went  alongside  the  wood  schooner 
and  wooded  up;  the  Curlew  also  came  and  wooded  up.  At  11  a.  m. 
went  alongside  the  Fanny  and  gave  her  about  300  gallons  of  water; 
then  returned  and  anchored  in  position.  At  3:20  p.  m.  got  underway 
and  took  the  schooner  Manassas  alongside  the  large  schooner;  then 
went  up  and  took  the  new  schooner  from  the  Appomattox  and  towed 
her  up  to  Weir’s  Point  wharf  and  anchored  her.  At  6  p.  m.  returned 
and  anchored  in  position. 

February  6. — At  8  a.  m.  got  underway  and  weut  up  to  Weir’s  Point 
battery  to  raise  a  sunken  schooner.  At  11  a.  m.  six  steamers  of  the 
enemy  appeared  in  sight;  cleared  the  ship  for  action  and  waited  for 
them.  At  1:20  p.  m.  went  up  to  Weir’s  Point  battery  and  brought  a 
schooner  and  sunk  her  at  the  barricade.  The  Appom a t tox  went  down 
to  the  marshes  to  reconnoiter;  reported  51  vessels  of  the  enemy  below,, 
of  which  23  are  steamers.  We  then  went  to  Weir’s  Point  and  towed 
down  to  the  barricade  the  white  schooner  and  sunk  her.  At  7  a.  m. 
returned  and  anchored  in  position.  No  movement  so  far  upon  the  part 
of  the  enemy.  At  9  p.  m.  discovered  lights  among  the  enemy’s  vessels. 
At  12  p.  m.  [midnight]  Purser  Moore  came  alongside  to  try  to  get 
recruits  for  floating  battery. 

February  7. — At  12 : 30  a.  m.  weather  thickened  up  again,  wind  blow¬ 
ing  fresh  from  southwest.  At  1 : 30  a.  m.  wind  calmed  down  again,  but 
weather  remained  cloudy  during  the  balance  of  the  night.

Abstract  log  of  the  North  Carolina  naval  steamer  Beaufort,  Lieutenant 
R.  C.  Duvall,  commanding,  from  July  9  to  August  24,  1861. 

July  9,  1861. — Finished  all  preparations  for  sea,  hoisted  the  ensign, 
and  put  the  North  Carolina  naval  propeller  Beaufort  in  commission  [at 
Norfolk,  Va.].  During  the  day  occupied  in  getting  the  crew  on  board, 
the  sailors’  peculiarity  on  leaving  shore  for  a  cruise,  giving  us  much 
annoyance.  At  0  got  underway  and  went  down  to  the  magazine  for 
powder;  took  on  board  300  pounds  and  some  other  equipments.  The 
fort  gave  us  three  cheers  on  leaving,  which  we  answered.  The  engineer 
failing  to  get  his  crew  off,  anchored  near  the  navy  yard  and  sent  senior 
engineer  on  shore  to  find  his  absent  crew. 

July  go.— At  10 : 40  the  engineer  came  off,  bringing  his  crew  on  board. 
Hoisted,  up  boats,  weighed  anchor,  and  stood  up  for  our  destination. 
On  passing  the  frigate  United  States  she  dipped  her  flag  in  honor  of 
our  departure;  answered  by  dipping  ours.  At  12 :  20  entered  the  Albe¬ 
marle  and  Chesapeake  Canal.  Gave  an  order  on  Marshall  Parks,  navy 
agent,  for  tollage,  $26.50.  Discovered  fire  in  forward  bulkhead. 
Knocked  out  forward  bulkhead  door  and  extinguished  it.  At  6 : 30  p.  m. 
got  aground  off  and  to  southward  of  Currituck  Court-House.  At  8 
got  off  and  stood  for  the  entrance  of  the  North  Carolina  Canal.  Dis¬ 
covered  the  coal  on  fire  again;  came  to  anchor  and  extinguished  it. 

July  11. — At  9  [a.  m.]  passed  schooner  with  guns  for  Oregon  [Inlet], 
lying  at  anchor.  TLie  captain  certainly  is  not  in  a  hurry.  At  11:  20 
passed  schooner  Mary  Eliza,  Captain  Thompson,  standing  down  for 
Oregon  [Inlet],  with  guns  and  gun  carriages  and  lighter  in  tow  for 
Oregon  [Inlet].  Captain  Thompson  has  evidently  taken  advantage  of 
light  winds,  and  has  manifested  proper  anxiety  in  getting  his  vessel  to 
Oregon  [Inlet]..  At  12:40  [p.  m.]  passed  Nag’s  Head.  At  2:  30  [p.  m,] 
off  Croatan  light  house.  Heard  from  Captain  Hoft,  of  the  steamer 
Roanoke,  that  the  enemy  had  fired  about  40  shells  at  Oregon  Inlet  bat¬ 
tery.  Discovered  the  steamer  Currituck  standing  out  from  Oregon  Inlet 
toward  us.  Anchored  for  further  news. 

July  12. — At  6:30  a.  m.  C.  B.  Barney,  engineer  in  charge  of  Oregon 
Inlet,  and  Colonel  B.  J.  Sproel  [Spruill?],  commissary,  came  on  board 
and  reported  that  at  9  a.  m.  yesterday  three  steamers  appeared  off  the 
entrance  of  Oregon  Inlet,  two  of  which  commenced  shelling  the  works 
and  the  other  one  stood  to  the  southward  and  threw  shell  promiscuously 
over  the  island.  They  also  say  that  the  conduct  of  the  officers  was  such 
as  to  completely  demoralize  their  men,  and  a  general  stampede  took 
place.  The  engineer  had  some  130  negroes  (48  of  whom  were  slaves), 
who  broke  for  the  marshes,  and  have  not  as  yet  been  heard  from.  They 
also  suppose  that  forces  were  landed  at  New  Inlet,  and  fear  that  some 
of  the  negroes  were  captured.  Mr.  Barney  and  Colonel  Sproel’ s 
[Spruill'?]  party  left  the  island  in  a  scow,  and  succeeded  in  reaching 
Eoanoke  Island.  Boats  were  seen  to  land  afterwards,  and  it  is  sup¬ 
posed  that  the  works  are  certainly  destroyed,  and  Mr.  Barney  and 
Colonel  Sproel  [Spruill1?]  fear  that  a  number  of  muskets,  etc.,  which 
were  stowed  in  the  light  house  are  taken.  At  10  the  steamer  Roanoke, 
with  Mr.  Barney,  Captain  Johnson,  and  Captain  Thompson,  left  for 
Oregon  Inlet  to  ascertain  the  facts  and  to  return  and  report  the  facts 
to  me.  A  schooner  with  six  guns,  two  carriages,  and  a  quantity  of 
shot  arrived  here  and  anchored.  At  4:25  [p.  m.]  stood  for  Oregon 
Inlet.  Took  the  responsibility  of  sending  five  kegs  of  powder  on  board 
Captain  Thompson’s  schooner  to  have  it  in  readiness  to  serve  the  guns 
when  mounted.

July  13. — Sent  the  pilot  to  sound  out  the  channel.  At  10:45  a.  m. 
Mr.  Midget  came  alongside  and  left  with  me  his  black  boy  Sam  to 
assist  in  piloting  the  ship  over  the  bulkhead.  At  11 : 30  pilot  returned 
on  board,  bringing  Captain  Taylor  to  also  assist  in  piloting  the  ship.  At 
12:  35  stood  back  for  the  marshes  to  tow  Captain  Thompson’s  schooner, 
loaded  with  guns,  etc.,  up  to  the  bulkhead.  At  2  took  schooner  and 
lighter  in  tow  and  stood  back  for  the  bulkhead  off  Oregon  Inlet.  At 
4 : 35  anchored  off  the  bulkhead. 

July  11. — Another  schooner  arrived  with  guns,  etc.,  for  Oregon  Inlet. 
Captain  Dickerson  sent  an  order  to  Captain  Thompson  to  remove  his 
schooner  back  to  the  marshes,  but  I  advised  him  to  hold  on  until  General 
Gwynn  arrived.  At  6:30  p.  m.  a  steamer  appeared  to  the  southward 
which  was  believed  to  be  the  Post  Boy ,  with  General  Gwynn  and  suite. 
At  7  the  Post  Boy  came  in  and  anchored  near  us.  Boarded  her  and 
found  General  Gwynn  and  suite,  last  from  Hatteras,  with  gun  carriages, 
etc.,  for  this  place.  The  news  of  the  engagement  at  Hatteras  was  con¬ 
firmed,  and  it  was  ascertained  that  the  steamer  making  the  attack  was 
struck  three  times  with  shot,  when  she  drew  off,  dipping  her  flag  as 
a  parting  salute.  From  8  to  midnight  saw  signals  again  to  the 
southward. 

July  15. — At  8:20  [a.  m.]  Captain  Dickerson  came  off  and  informed 
me  that  it  would  require  ten  days  before  he  would  be  ready  to  mount 
any  guns,  the  previous  works  being  worthless;  moreover,  he  had  now 
with  him  ouly  about  fifteen  men.  He  expected  General  Gwynn  here 
to-day  with  more  men.  Sent  a  gang  of  men  under  boatswain’s  mate  to 
hoist  out  gun  carriages,  shot,  and  shot  heater  from  schooner  Mary  Eliza , 
and  place  them  on  a  camel,  in  readiness  to  tow  them  on  shore.  Captain 
Dickerson  signalized  me,  as  the  commanding  officer,  not  to  go  in  over 
the  bulkhead  nor  to  attempt  to  land  any  guns  now,  as  it  would  attract 
the  attention  of  the  enemy.  My  ideas  differ  from  his  in  this  respect, 
and  I  would  have  had  two  guns  mounted  and  in  readiness  for  use,  but, 
not  wishing  to  interfere  with  the  army,  I  shall  remain  where  I  am  and 
guard  the  channel  from  ingress  into  the  sound.  During  the  watch  from 
8  to  midnight  signal  lights  were  made  outside,  probably  to  some  accom¬ 
plices  on  shore.  I  hear  that  there  are  several  Northern  men  among 
our  forces  on  shore. 

July  16. — At  6:30  [a.  m.]  the  Post  Boy  got  underway  and  stood  up 
for  the  bulkhead;  shortly  after  the  Currituck  followed,  having  in  tow  a 
schooner  with  guns,  etc.  At  7  the  Post  Boy  got  aground  on  the  bulk¬ 
head  and  the  Currituck  grounded  the  schooner  on  this  side.  The  Cur¬ 
rituck  cast  off  and  went  alongside  the  Post  Boy ,  and  thence  to  the  shore. 
In  the  evening  the  Post  Boy  followed  and  returned  outside  at  5  and 
went  alongside  of  a  schooner  for  wood.  The  schooner  Mary  Eliza  got 
underway  and  stood  for  the  anchorage  off  the  fortifications.  A  boat 
came  alongside  and  reported  a  large  steamer  lying  off  and  on,  off  the 
inlet  outside;  supposed  to  be  the  same  engaged  in  the  bombardment 
of  the  works.  At  6:30  General  Gwynn  and  suite  came  on  board  to  visit 
the  ship.  General  Gwynn  informed  me  that  he  had  placed  Colonel  Mor¬ 
ris  in  command  on  shore,  and  requested  that  I  would  render  him  assist¬ 
ance  any  way  I  could,  and  concurred  in  the  great  importance  of  guard¬ 
ing  the  entrance  into  the  sound.  Colonel  Sproel  [Spruill?]  and  Captain 
Dickerson  also  came  on  board.  Let  them  have  the  use  of  my  boat  to 
get  on  board  the  steamer  Roanoke ,  they  being  bound  to  Edenton  for 
hands  to  work  the  fortifications.  At  8  the  steamer  got  underway  for 
Edenton.

July  18.— No  signals  seen  on  shore  and  no  steamer  in  sight  along  the 
coast.  That  the  enemy  have  some  spies  on  shore  there  can  be  no  doubt. 
When  any  of  the  blockading  vessels  are  lying  off  and  on  at  night,  sig¬ 
nals  have  always  been  seen  on  shore.  At  5  [a.  m.  j  stood  up  for  the  bulk¬ 
head.  At  5:30  anchored  about  1  mile  from  the  fortifications.  The 
schooner  Lynnhaven ,  with  coal,  etc.,  for  us,  came  up  and  anchored  near 
our  old  anchorage. 

July  19. — At  3  [a.  m.  j  determined  to  go  over  the  bulkhead  to  the  inlet 
and  insist  upon  the  guns  being  mounted  immediately.  After  getting 
aground  several  times  and  backing  off,  lowered  a  boat  and  sounded 
until  we  found  the  narrow  channel,  some  40  feet  wide,  and  passed  over 
bulkhead.  I  had  always  been  informed  that  after  passing  over  bulk¬ 
head  we  dropped  into  18  feet  of  water  and  no  further  difficulty  would 
offer  in  going  up  the  inlet.  This  information  proved,  as  most  informa¬ 
tion  has  here,  to  be  false.  We  had  great  trouble,  much  hard  work,  and 
placed  in  a  dangerous  position,  until  we  finally  brought  up  in  some  3 
feet  water.  The  shore  pilot  came  off;  we  finally  anchored  near  the 
marsh,  the  tide  running  out  and  very  strong;  this  placed  the  vessel  in 
such  a  position  as  to  prevent  the  use  of  the  gun  to  seaward.  Got  under¬ 
way  again,  dropped  near  the  shore,  ran  a  hawser  on  shore  to  a  stake, 
and  sprung  the  vessel  around  to  the  westward.  Made  preparations  for 
a  night  attack.  Received  the  following  note  from  Colonel  Morris,  com¬ 
manding  officer:  “A  schooner  passed  north  yesterday  at  7  p.  m.,  with 
fore-topsails  and  brailed  foresail,  evidently  a  man-of-war  of  the  revenue 
class.  At  9  a.  m.  this  day  a  three-masted  steamer  was  visible  in  the 
northeast  quarter,  watching  us.  She  is  now  out  of  sight.” 

July  20. — Got  up  steam  and  assisted  in  backing  up  against  the  wind 
and  tide.  The  tide  runs  here  stronger  than  I  have  ever  witnessed  in 
any  part  of  the  world,  rushing  through  the  inlet  seaward  6  or  8  miles 
per  hour.  No  ordinary  anchor  would  prevent  a  vessel  from  drifting- 
out  to  sea,  and  it  was  fortunate  that  we  got  alongside  the  marsh ;  other¬ 
wise  we  must  have  drifted  out.  The  steamer  Currituck  stood  up  for 
Nag’s  Head.  The  Post  Boy  came  in  and  anchored  in  the  sound  outside 
the  bulkhead.  I  examined  the  works  thrown  up,  and  find  them  a  com¬ 
plete  abortion  for  the  purpose  designed.  They  had  just  placed  a  gun 
in  position  without  any  rigging,  and  had  another  ready.  Colonel  Mor¬ 
ris  said  that  was  the  first  work  (to  day)  performed  by  the  volunteers. 
They  had  previously  refused  to  do  any  work.  Whilst  at  the  fort,  Captain 
Lee,  C.  S.  Army,  son  of  General  Lee,  landed  from  the  Post  Boy's  boats 
and  visited  the  works;  also  an  engineer.  They  are  on  a  tour  of  inspec¬ 
tion.  Captain  Lee  spoke  of  alterations  for  protecting  the  men  from 
seaward  and  south  and  eastward  immediately.  I  established  a  set  of 
signals  and  sent  a  man  at  daylight  to  the  light  house  to  look  out  for 
vessels,  to  be  relieved  every  four  hours  until  dark.  No  vessels  in  sight 
to-day.  More  preparations  for  a  night  attack. 

July  21. — [Fully  covered  by  report  on  page  21. — Compilers.] 

July  22. — At  11  a.  m.  a  signal  was  waved  from  the  light  house.  Sent 
a  boat  on  shore.  Received  a  note  from  Colonel  Morris  saying  that  a 
large  ship  was  coming  down  from  the  northward,  supposed  to  be  a  man- 
of-war,  but  if  a  merchantman  a  red  flag  would  be  shown.  At  11:15 
the  Currituck  came  out  and  anchored  near  us,  to  be  out  of  danger 
should  the  ship  prove  to  be  a  man-of-war.  Colonel  Morris  sent  off  a 
note  saying  he  had  12  rounds  of  ammunition  ready,  but  no  wads,  and 
asked  for  12.  I  sent  him  24. 

July  24. — Got  off  the  bank  south  side  of  the  channel,  and  in  the 
morning  would  have  got  over  the  bulkhead,  but  the  wind  having  blown 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


793 


the  water  out  of  the  sound,  struck  ou  a  flat;  ran  out  anchors  and  made 
all  efforts  to  get  off.  The  constant  firing  of  the  engine,  thumping  and 
jerking,  did  great  injury  to  the  bearing  and  gearing  of  the  machinery. 
Continued  at  intervals  during  the  day  [trying]  to  get  off,  but  failed  to 
do  so.  The  Post  Boy  came  in,  and  by  her  heard  of  the  great  and 
glorious  battle  at  Manassas.  The  enemy’s  loss  reported  at  16,000,  our 
loss  at  4,000.  This  victory  was  hailed  with  joyous  delight  and  gave 
new  vigor  to  our  crew. 

July  25. — At  2  [a.  m.  ]  we  had  the  satisfaction  of  getting  over  afloat, 
and  I  hope  never  to  be  compelled  to  try  to  enter  this  most  tortuous  and 
treacherous  inlet.  At  9:30  passed  the  marshes;  saw  Colonel  Sproel 
[Spruill!]  on  board  of  a  schooner  with  a  number  of  negroes,  bound  for 
Oregon  Inlet.  At  4,  made  fast  to  the  wharf  at  Elizabeth  City  [N.  C.j 
for  the  purpose  of  taking  on  board  water  casks.  After  making  efforts 
of  many  citizens  (who  appeared  indifferent  about  making  any  exertions 
to  supply  us)  we  finally  got  information  that  the  State  had  a  number  of 
40-gallon  casks  in  the  arsenal  in  charge  of  Captain  Vaughn;  made  out 
a  requisition  for  the  use  of  this  vessel  ten  40-gallon  casks  and  some 
sperm  oil  which  belonged  to  the  light-house. 

July  26. — Elizabeth  City,  N.  C.  Getting  engine  in  order,  making 
repairs,  etc. 

July  27. — Saluted  the  city  with  one  gun  and  steamed  away  for  Oregon 
Inlet;  hove  to  off'  Roanoke  Marshes.  At  7:20  [p.  m.]  came  to  anchor 
off  Oregon  Inlet. 

July  28. — There  was  to-day  considerable  interchange  of  news  between 
the  three  steamers  and  the  large  sailing  frigate  which  is  backing  and 
filling  to  the  southward  of  the  fort.  I  am  surprised  no  attack  was 
made  by  such  a  big  force.  Colonel  Morris  wrote  me  a  note,  saying 
that  they  were  tolerably  strong,  but  would  like  to  have  the  use  of  my 
long  32. 1  We  nearly  ruined  the  steamer  and  engine  in  getting  over  the 
bulkhead  and  coming  out  when  last  there,  and  without  it  is  of  vital 
importance  I  do  not  desire  to  try  it  again.  I,  however,  offered  myself 
and  the  volunteers  from  my  vessel  to  assist  in  working  the  guns  at  the 
fort  in  case  an  attack  was  made.  If  the  water  was  deep  enough,  I 
would  not  hesitate  to  go  up  and  select  my  position;  but  to  do  so  with 
the  certainty  of  getting  aground  in  range  of  the  enemy’s  heavy  guns  is 
reckless  foolishness,  and,  moreover,  1  do  not  think  that  250  men  with  4 
heavy  guns  mounted  and  ready  for  use  should  ask  ot  me  to  put  my 
vessel  and  one  gun  under  the  battery  of  four  40-gun  frigates.  One  of 
the  steamers  was  doubtless  the  Roanolce ,  with  the  new  flag-officer,  Pen- 
dergrast,  on  her  way  to  the  Gulf,  as  she  received  a  salute  from  one  of 
the  steamers  and  proceeded  southward.  One  of  the  other  steamers 
proceeded  down  the  coast  about  15  [miles]  to  Chickamicomico  and 
opened  a  heavy  shelling,  which  we  could  plainly  see  from  our  mast¬ 
head,  on  a  wrecked  brig,  run  on  shore  by  a  prize  crew,  chased  by  a 
steamer.  The  pilot  boat  Yorlc  had  captured  it  with  a  cargo  of  staves 
and  a  sugar  mill.  The  enemy  fired  some  30  or  40  shells  and  finally 
succeeded  in  setting  fire  to  a  part  of  the  cargo  which  had  been  landed. 
The  inhabitants  of  the  island  fled  in  dismay,  leaving  everything  to  the 
enemy  should  he  land.  Some  five  or  six  boats  passed  here  on  their 
way  to  Roanoke  Island,  filled  with  women  and  a  surprisingly  great 
number  of  small  children  for  such  a  small  population.  They  were  badly 
frightened.  At  sunset  only  one  of  the  enemy’s  ships  in  sight,  and  that 
the  same  sailing  frigate  that  was  off  last  evening,  keeping  her  position 
some  G  or  8  miles  to  the  southward.  They  don’t  allow  any  prizes  to  be 
caught  at  this  station.  I  am  nevertheless  ready  to  meet  any  number

% 

V 

of  launches  they  may  please  to  send  to  the  sound,  and,  as  they  hang 
around  New  Inlet,  it  may  he  that  they  intend  to  try  that  inlet  and  take 
me  in  the  rear. 

July  29. — At  9 :  40  [a.  m.]  got  under  way  for  Ocracoke.  At  7 :  30  [p.  m.] 
came  to  anchor  off  Old  Swash. 

July  30. — At  6  [a.  m.]  the  swash  pilot  came  on  board  and  took  charge, 
piloting  us  in  Wallace’s  Channel  and  opposite  Portsmouth  [N.  C.) ;  came 
to  anchor  at  8.  At  6:30  the  Post  Boy  arrived  from  New  Berne,  N.  C. 
One  of  her  officers  came  alongside,  bringing  a  document  to  Captain 
Duvall  from  the  honorable  Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

July  31. — At  7 : 30  [a.  m.]  the  pilot  came  on  board  and  took  us  outside 
the  bar;  discovered  a  large  steamer  outside;  returned,  and  came  to 
anchor  opposite  the  fort  and  distant  probably  2  miles.  At  2  p.  m.  sent 
two  of  the  crew  to  the  light-house  on  Ocracoke  Island  to  signalize  the 
approach  of  vessels. 

August  1. — The  lookout  at  the  light-house  signalized  a  man-of-war 
steamer  to  the  southward.  At  12  m.  cleared  ship  for  action  and  got  the 
ship  ready  for  slipping  cable.  Enemy  stood  down  for  the  entrance  and 
laid  to  for  some  time,  then  stood  back  close  inshore,  reconnoitering  the 
harbor,  and  finally  steamed  away  to  the  northward.  At  3 : 25  called  all 
hands  to  quarters  and  prepared  the  ship  for  action,  bringing  our  gun 
to  bear  on  the  steamer  standing  in  for  the  entrance  and  which  after¬ 
wards  was  ascertained  to  be  the  Mariner.  At  4: 25  the  Mariner  came 
to  anchor  in  the  Old  Swash.  At  5  p.  m.  steamer  JEdicards  signalized, 
bearing  to  the  southward.  At  5 :  30  the  Bdwards  came  to  anchor  in 
Wallace’s  Channel. 

August  2. — At  7:30  [a.  m.]  the  Mariner  put  to  sea,  returning  and 
anchoring  in  W allace’s  Channel.  At  10 : 15  the  Post  Boy  came  to  anchor 
off  Beating  [Beacon “?[  Island.  At  12:40  steamer  signalized  from  the 
light-house,  which  was  soon  discovered  to  be  the  privateer  Gordon , 
bound  to  the  northward. 

August  3. — At  5 : 10  [a.  m.]  a  fore -and- after  reported  off  the  bar.  Got 
up  steam  immediately  and  at  5:30  stood  out  in  chase  of  schooner,  the 
privateer  Teaser  also  getting  up  steam.  At  6: 15  crossed  the  bar,  the 
steamer  Teaser  standing  out  after  us.  Stood  up  N.  E.  by  E.  for  the  chase, 
and  when  near  enough  to  see  her,  a  squall  of  rain  being  between  us 
and  the  schooner,  saw  a  steamer  near  her,  which  we  took  to  be  the 
Gordon ,  and  being  satisfied  that  we  had  lost  the  prize  stood  back  again 
for  our  anchorage.  The  Teaser  stood  on  for  the  schooner.  The  Gordon 
finally  left  the  schooner  and  stood  in  for  Hatteras.  The  Teaser  went 
alongside  of  the  schooner  and  afterwards  left  her  and  stood  out  to  sea. 
The  schooner  must  have  been  one  of  our  own  vessels  or  under  British 
colors  and  clearance.  Took  up  our  usual  anchorage.  Sent  a  boat  with 
pilot  and  second  master  to  erect  a  proper  mast  for  signals.  At  10:45 
a  sail  reported  in  sight  to  the  southward.  At  11 : 20  the  steamer  Colonel 
Hill  hove  in  sight.  At  12 :  30  got  underway  and  stood  out  for  a  three- 
masted  schooner,  and,  on  nearing  her,  discovered  the  Gordon  near  by 
and  that  the  schooner  was  sailing  under  British  colors  and  bound  to  one 
of  our  ports — New  Berne,  I  think;  returned  to  our  anchorage. 

August  4. — At  daylight  signal  made  from  the  lookout  at  Ocracoke 
light-house,  “Man-of-war  to  the  northward.”  The  Mariner  and  Gordon 
went  to  sea.  The  Gordon  stood  to  the  northward  and  eastward,  the 
Mariner  to  the  southward  and  eastward.  Signals  made  from  the  light¬ 
house,  “Several  sail  in  sight.”  Waiting  the  appearance  of  the  man-of- 
war  signalized.  At  11,  not  seeing  any  man-of  war,  concluded  to  go  out 
to  sea,  and  got  underway,  crossed  the  bar,  and  stood  out  to  sea  S.  E.  by

795 


E.  and  ran  out  about  10  miles.  Saw  tlie  smoke  of  a  steamer  to  the  north¬ 
ward  and  eastward.  A  thick,  black  squall  of  rain  setting  in  ahead  of 
us  and  shutting  oft'  our  view  to  seaward,  and  not  considering  it  proper 
to  go  out  farther,  a  signal  made  from  the  light  house  which  we  read  to 
be  “A  man-of-war  to  the  northward,”  stood  iu  for  the  bar  and  steamed 
up  to  our  anchorage.  Sent  to  the  light-house;  signal  was  wrong,  and 
that  no  man-of-war  was  in  sight.  Also  learned  that  the  Winslow  had 
towed  one  brig  into  Hatteras  and  the  Gordon  two  schooners.  The  man 
at  the  lookout  said  had  we  stood  on  (which  we  should  have  done  if  the 
signal  had  been  made  right)  twenty  minutes  longer  we  would  have 
come  up  with  a  schooner,  the  thick  rain  squall  preventing  us  from  see¬ 
ing  her.  At  4: 30  the  Ellis  came  in  and  anchored  near  Portsmouth, 
Captain  Muse  commanding.  At  5:20  the  Junaluska  came  in  and 
anchored  near  Portsmouth,  having  on  board  Commodore  Barron  and 
suite,  on  a  tour  of  inspection  to  the  different  stations.  Captain  Cooke, 
of  the  Edwards ,  reported  his  ship  as  being  entirely  worthless,  the 
boilers  worn  out  and  the  timbers  of  his  vessel  rotten. 

August  5. — At  9:15  [a.  m.]  sent  a  boat  to  the  light-house  to  give 
instruction  relative  to  signals  and  to  attach  halyards  for  the  purpose 
of  more  distinctly  displaying  the  signals  to  us.  Signal  made  from  the 
light  house  on  Ocracoke  “A  small  sail  to  the  northward  and  eastward,” 
which  proved  to  be  the  privateer  York ,  which  stood  off  to  the  south¬ 
ward  and  eastward.  At  7  the  Gordon  came  in  and  anchored  inshore  of 
us.  No  chance  for  the  Beaufort  as  long  as  these  fast  steamers  are  here. 

August  6. — At  2  p.  m.  the  steamer  Post  Boy  came  m  and  anchored 
inshore,  near  Portsmouth.  At  5 : 40  a  fore-and-aft  schooner  went  to 
sea;  stood  for  the  east. 

August  7. — At  7:30  [a.  m.]  the  steamer  Curlew  came  to  anchor  in 
Wallace’s  Channel.  At  3: 15  [p.  m.]  lookout  for  light-house  signalized 
“Man-of-war  to  the  northward,”  which,  on  nearing  the  land,  discovered 
to  be  an  English  steamship.  She  displayed  her  colors,  which  we 
answered  by  hoisting  the  English  ensign  at  the  fore.  She  steamed 
along  close  inshore,  slowly,  and  disappeared  to  the  southward  down 
the  coast. 

August  8.— At  5:55  [p.  m.]  the  steamer  Albemarle  came  in  and 
anchored  near  Portsmouth  [N.  C.]. 

August  9—  At  10  [a.  m.]  the  schooner  Isabella  Bllis ,  having  finished 
discharging  gun  carriages  at  the  fort,  made  sail  and  took  her  departure 
for  Oregon  Inlet.  At  11 : 30  the  Post  Boy  came  in  and  anchored  off  the 
fort. 

August  10. — At  9:55  [a.  in.]  the  schooner  Crinoline  came  m  from 
Hatteras  and  anchored  off  the  fort. 

August  11. — At  9:10  [a.  m.]  a  boat  from  the  fort  came  alongside  hav¬ 
ing  on  board  Captain  Hanks,  from  whom  we  learned  that  a  few  days 
since  the  privateer  York ,  of  Norfolk,  Ya.,  was  chased  by  the  Federal 
steamer  Monticello  [Union]  and  so  closely  pressed  as  to  cause  the  crew 
of  the  York  to  beach,  set  fire  to,  and  abandon  her  near  New  Inlet.  At 
11 : 30  the  steamer  Colonel  Hill  took  departure.  At  12 : 10  the  schooner 
Crinoline  also  left  Hatteras. 

August  13. — At  4:35  a.  m.  pilot  boat  [arrived]  and  delivered  a  letter 
to  the  captain.  At  1:30  p.  m.  the  steamer  Gordon  came  in  and 
anchored  off  Portsmouth  [N.  C.].  At  2:20  the  schooner  Isabella  took 
her  departure. 

August  14. — At  7:35  a.  m.  stood  out  through  the  Old  Swash  tor  New 
Berne.  At  5: 15  p.  in.  came  to  anchor  at  New  Berne  and  saluted  with 
one  gun. 


796  NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

August  15. — Lying  at  anchor  in  New  Berne  Harbor. 

August  20. — At  8:30  a.  m.  steamer  Winslow  hove  in  sight,  having  in 
tow  prize  tug  Itasca.  At  10 : 30  left  the  harbor  and  started  for  Ocra- 
coke  Inlet.  At  5 : 20  p.  m.  came  to  anchor  in  the  mouth  of  Broad  Creek. 

August  21. — At  6:30  a.  m.  ran  out  into  the  sound,  but  finding  .that 
we  could  make  no  headway,  on  account  of  the  strong  head  wind  and 
heavy  sea,  came  back  to  the  mouth  of  Broad  Greek. 

August  22. — At  4:30  a.  m.  weighed  anchor.  Left  schooners  Isabella 
Ellis  and  Lady  Antrim  in  harbor.  At  7 : 30  passed  the  steamer  Colonel 
Hill,  bound  to  Washington.  At  9  passed  the  steamer  Ellis ;  at  9:05 
passed  light-boat;  at  9:30  came  alongside  the  schooner  Alexina ,  at 
anchor  in  Wale’s  [Wallace’s!]  Channel,  to  take  in  coal.  At  9:  40  Colonel 
Bradford  went  ashore  to  Portsmouth.  Steamer  Edwards  at  anchor 
in  Wale’s  [Wallace’s!]  Channel.  At  7:40  p.  m.  steamer  Ellis  came  in 
and  anchored  in  Wallace’s  Channel. 

August  24. — Steamers  Edwards  and  Ellis  at  anchor  in  Wallace’s 
Channel.  At  3:20  p.  m.  steamer  Colonel  Hill  came  to  anchor  off  and 
near  Portsmouth.  Crew  variously  employed  on  board  ship.
